species.name: Bistorta vivipara
species.tip: Upland grassland; slender spike of white or pale pink flowers, the lower part replaced by small purplish bulbils; narrow leaves.

species.name: Blackstonia perfoliata
species.tip: Blue-grey plant of chalk and limestone grassland with paired leaves fused around the stem and bright yellow flowers having eight petals that close in dull weather.

species.name: Blechnum cordatum
species.tip: Evergreen fern with a large tuft of leathery once-divided fronds with long untoothed leaflets, with new fronds often coppery red. Garden plant, occasionally escaping in mild areas.

species.name: Blechnum penna-marina
species.tip: Small creeping fern with narrow, once-divided, glossy dark fronds with fine untoothed leaflets, the fertile ones taller. Local on damp upland slopes in the north and west.

species.name: Blechnum spicant
species.tip: Fern of acid woods and heaths with two types of frond: sterile ones are glossy, once-cut and in a flat rosette, while fertile ones are upright and narrow.

species.name: Blitum bonus-henricus
species.tip: Farmyards and roadsides; mealy, broad triangular arrow-shaped leaves and tall leafless spikes of tiny greenish flowers.

species.name: Blysmus compressus
species.tip: A single flattened spike of two neat ranks of chestnut-brown florets on a creeping plant of damp, base-rich turf and flushes; the spike is larger and paler than Saltmarsh Flat-sedge.

species.name: Blysmus rufus
species.tip: A small, dark reddish-brown two-ranked spike on short stems in upper saltmarsh turf, mostly Scotland and northern coasts; much smaller and darker than Flat-sedge, with a short lowest bract.

species.name: Bolboschoenus laticarpus
species.tip: A tall, triangular-stemmed club-rush of brackish ditches and estuaries, bearing clustered brown spikelets with leafy bracts; very close to Sea Club-rush and needing a specialist to separate it by its fruit shape.

species.name: Bolboschoenus maritimus
species.tip: Tall triangular-stemmed plant of brackish marshes and estuaries with a tight clump of chestnut-brown spikelets and long leafy bracts overtopping the head; leaves flat, keeled and rough-edged.

species.name: Borago officinalis
species.tip: Bristly plant with bright blue starry flowers having a dark central cone. Garden escape on tips and waste ground; unlike other blue borages by its star shape.

species.name: Borago pygmaea
species.tip: Annual with bristly oval leaves and pale blue star-shaped flowers hanging on slender stalks. Rare casual or garden escape of waste ground; smaller than common borage.

species.name: Botrychium lunaria
species.tip: Small fern with a single half-moon shaped pinnae on a fleshy frond and a separate spore spike; short turf, dunes and grassland, often hard to spot.

species.name: Brachypodium pinnatum
species.tip: Tough tufted grass with stiff yellowish-green leaves and a spike of short-stalked spikelets in two rows; dominates chalk and limestone turf in the south, with rolled leaf tips.

species.name: Brachypodium sylvaticum
species.tip: Shade-loving, yellowish-green, drooping spike of short-stalked awned spikelets in woods and hedges; leaves broad, softly hairy and flopping.

species.name: Brassica napus
species.tip: Blue-grey hairless leaves whose upper ones clasp the stem; open flowers sit level with or just above the buds in crop fields and verges.

species.name: Brassica nigra
species.tip: Tall, bristly plant of riverbanks and coasts with small yellow flowers and short pods pressed tight against the stem; lower leaves lobed and rough.

species.name: Brassica oleracea
species.tip: Robust waxy blue-green perennial on sea cliffs, with fleshy wavy leaves and tall spikes of pale yellow flowers. Cliff plant of south and west coasts.

species.name: Brassica rapa
species.tip: Upper leaves clasp the stem with rounded basal lobes, grey-green and slightly waxy, and open flowers overtop the buds; found by rivers and on waste ground.

species.name: Briza maxima
species.tip: Annual quaking-grass with large, drooping, inflated spikelets over 1 cm long, bigger than those of Lesser Quaking-grass; garden escape and casual in the south.

species.name: Briza media
species.tip: Chalk grassland grass with heart-shaped, trembling, purplish spikelets hanging on hair-fine stalks in a loose open panicle; no awns.

species.name: Briza minor
species.tip: Delicate annual with tiny heart-shaped, trembling spikelets in a spreading panicle; much smaller spikelets than Greater, found on arable and waste ground in the south.

species.name: Bromopsis benekenii
species.tip: Brome of calcareous woodland with a nodding panicle and hairy leaf sheaths; the stem nodes are hairy, helping tell it from Hairy-brome. Local in the south and east.

species.name: Bromopsis erecta
species.tip: Chalk grassland brome with erect panicle and stiff erect branches, awned spikelets, and rolled leaves with hairs on the margins and sheaths.

species.name: Bromopsis inermis
species.tip: Rhizomatous perennial brome with an erect panicle and awnless or very short-awned spikelets; the creeping habit separates it from other bromes. Naturalised on roadsides.

species.name: Bromopsis ramosa
species.tip: Woodland brome with a drooping panicle of few long-awned spikelets and broad, hairy leaves; the sheaths bristle with spreading hairs.

species.name: Bromus hordeaceus
species.tip: Common brome with a short, dense, erect, softly downy panicle; leaves and sheaths soft with hairs, and spikelets bear short straight awns.

species.name: Bromus interruptus
species.tip: Brome with dense short-stalked clusters of velvety spikelets down a stout panicle; extinct as a wild plant, known from Cambridgeshire, now only in cultivation.

species.name: Bromus lepidus
species.tip: Annual brome with a compact panicle of small hairless-to-silky spikelets with short awns; scarce in grassland and waste ground. Told from Soft-brome by narrower, flatter spikelets.

species.name: Bromus pseudosecalinus
species.tip: Rare brome with a hairy sheath and a loose panicle bearing awned spikelets; a specialist should confirm it among the annual bromes, which are hard to separate.

species.name: Bromus racemosus
species.tip: Brome of damp meadows with an erect panicle of smooth spikelets, shorter awns than Rye Brome and sheaths often hairy; spikelets not downy.

species.name: Bromus secalinus
species.tip: Annual weed of cornfields with nodding spikelets that have short, outcurved awns; spikelets are swollen and plump, becoming weakly twisted.

species.name: Brunnera macrophylla
species.tip: Clump-forming plant with large heart-shaped, rough leaves and sprays of small bright blue forget-me-not flowers with white centres. Common garden plant, escaping onto shady verges.

species.name: Bryonia dioica
species.tip: Climbing hedge plant with tendrils, palmately lobed rough leaves and greenish-white flowers, followed by red berries; the only British climber with tendrils in this family.

species.name: Buddleja davidii
species.tip: Shrub of walls, railways and waste ground with long, arching cones of fragrant lilac-purple flowers, narrow pointed leaves white-felted beneath, loved by butterflies.

species.name: Buglossoides arvensis
species.tip: Hairy annual of arable fields with narrow leaves and small white funnel flowers. Scarce, in chalky and limy cornfields in southern England; flowers smaller than corn gromwell.

species.name: Bunias orientalis
species.tip: Tall rough bristly plant with bright yellow flowers and lumpy, warty seed pods. Lower leaves are deeply lobed. Increasingly found on road verges and waste ground.

species.name: Bunium bulbocastanum
species.tip: Slender umbellifer of chalk fields with finely divided, thread-like leaves and white umbels, growing from a dark rounded tuber; very rare, mainly in the Chilterns.

species.name: Buphthalmum salicifolium
species.tip: Garden escape with large yellow daisy heads on stems with narrow willow-like toothed leaves; occasional on grassy banks.

species.name: Buphthalmum speciosum
species.tip: Tall garden perennial with big yellow daisies with narrow rays and large heart-shaped toothed leaves; naturalised on streamsides and damp woods.

species.name: Bupleurum baldense
species.tip: Tiny, wiry annual with grass-like leaves and tiny clusters of yellow flowers wrapped in small pointed bracts; very rare, on sunny coastal rocks and short turf in southern Britain.

species.name: Bupleurum falcatum
species.tip: Tall, slender perennial with sickle-shaped upper leaves and small yellow-green umbels, lacking the encircling bracts of Thorow-wax; rare, in the south-east.

species.name: Bupleurum fruticosum
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with blue-green, leathery, oval leaves and yellow umbels in late summer; planted and sometimes self-sown on coastal slopes, as the only woody hare's-ear.

species.name: Bupleurum rotundifolium
species.tip: Hairless, blue-green annual with oval leaves that fully clasp the stem, and yellow-green umbels; a rare arable weed or casual, now mostly a bird-seed alien.

species.name: Bupleurum tenuissimum
species.tip: Thin, wiry, branched annual with narrow leaves and tiny, almost stalkless greenish-yellow umbels in the leaf forks; rare, on dry brackish ground, in the south-east.

species.name: Butomus umbellatus
species.tip: Tall plant of water margins with narrow triangular leaves and umbels of pink flowers on a tall stem; not a rush, summer.

species.name: Buxus sempervirens
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with small opposite glossy oval leaves; tiny greenish-yellow flowers in clusters in spring; native on chalk slopes, widely planted in hedges.

species.name: Cabomba caroliniana
species.tip: Aquatic plant with finely fan-divided underwater leaves and a few small floating oval leaves; white, yellow-centred flowers sit at the surface. Aquarium escape in canals and ponds.

species.name: Cakile maritima
species.tip: Fleshy, lobed-leaved plant of sandy and shingle beaches with pale lilac to white flowers and short, swollen, two-segmented pods.

species.name: Calamagrostis canescens
species.tip: Tall reed of fens and wet woods with a drooping, purplish panicle and short awns well inside the glumes; creeping and rare, mainly in eastern England.

species.name: Calamagrostis epigejos
species.tip: Tall, creeping, tough grass with a dense, purplish-brown plume and a hairy-based bristle on each floret; leaves rough and stiff, on scrub and rough ground.

species.name: Calamagrostis purpurea
species.tip: Rare small-reed of a few Scottish and northern damp sites, with a lax panicle and awn attached midway; a specialist should confirm it against Purple Small-reed.

species.name: Calamagrostis scotica
species.tip: Very rare small-reed of Caithness damp ground, with a narrow panicle and hairs shorter than the glume; only a specialist can separate it from related small-reeds.

species.name: Calamagrostis stricta
species.tip: Slender creeping small-reed of wet northern meadows, with a narrow, erect panicle and a short awn; much slimmer than Wood Small-reed, local in Scotland, northern England and Ireland.

species.name: Calceolaria chelidonioides
species.tip: Small annual with pinnately lobed, hairy leaves resembling greater celandine and tiny yellow pouched flowers. Rare casual of waste ground, from gardens, mostly in southern England.

species.name: Calendula arvensis
species.tip: Rare casual with small yellow-orange daisy heads and narrow smooth to slightly toothed leaves; sticky-hairy, with curved seeds, distinct from garden pot marigold.

species.name: Calendula officinalis
species.tip: Garden escape with bright orange or yellow large daisy heads, rather fleshy aromatic sticky leaves and curved ridged seeds. Found on tips, waste ground and field edges.

species.name: Calla palustris
species.tip: Creeping, marsh plant with shiny heart-shaped leaves, and a white open spathe around a short spike; red berries in autumn; in wet places, including one or two naturalised sites.

species.name: Callitriche brutia
species.tip: Tiny aquatic or mud-dwelling plant with starry leaf rosettes; fruits sit on distinct stalks, unlike other water-starworts whose fruits are stalkless. Often on seasonally drying pools and ditches.

species.name: Callitriche hermaphroditica
species.tip: Submerged aquatic with narrow, notched leaves in whorls without a floating rosette, and tiny flowers; a hard-to-see plant of clear still water.

species.name: Callitriche obtusangula
species.tip: Aquatic starwort making floating rosettes of broad leaves with slender submerged ones; tiny green flowers. Ripe fruit is needed to separate it from other water-starworts; check with a specialist.

species.name: Callitriche palustris
species.tip: Very rare starwort with small rosettes and notched submerged leaves; fruit small and narrowly keeled. Easily confused with other water-starworts, so confirmation by a specialist is needed.

species.name: Callitriche platycarpa
species.tip: Water-starwort with floating rosettes of rounded leaves; fruits are stalkless and winged at the top, with spreading styles. Common in ponds and ditches, often with Common Water-starwort.

species.name: Callitriche stagnalis
species.tip: Most frequent water-starwort; floating rosettes of broad rounded leaves and stalkless fruits that are broadly winged, with a clearly keeled edge. Ponds, ditches and wet mud.

species.name: Callitriche truncata
species.tip: Wholly submerged starwort with narrow, deeply notched leaves and no floating rosette; rare, mainly in southern England. Fruit is needed to be sure of the identification.

species.name: Calluna vulgaris
species.tip: Tiny scale-like leaves pressed along the stem and small pale pink-purple bells with a prominent calyx; common on moors and heaths, later than the other heaths.

species.name: Caltha palustris
species.tip: Large glossy kidney-shaped leaves; big golden cup flowers with no green sepals beneath; marshes and wet woods.

species.name: Calystegia pulchra
species.tip: Climber with large pink flowers, often with white stripes, and hairy stems; bracts under the flower do not overlap the sepals, and stems often hairy, unlike Hedge Bindweed.

species.name: Calystegia sepium
species.tip: Twining climber of hedges and wasteland with large white trumpets, arrow-shaped leaves, and bracteoles that are small and do not hide the sepals; hairless stems.

species.name: Calystegia silvatica
species.tip: Vigorous garden escape with large white or pink-flushed trumpets whose big bracts overlap and swell around the base of the flower; leaves broadly arrow-shaped.

species.name: Calystegia soldanella
species.tip: Trailing bindweed with fleshy kidney-shaped leaves and large pink funnel flowers striped white. Grows on sandy beaches and dunes.

species.name: Camelina sativa
species.tip: Slender yellow-flowered annual with clasping arrow-shaped stem leaves and pear-shaped pods. Occasional casual on arable land and waste ground.

species.name: Campanula alliariifolia
species.tip: Tall garden bellflower with creamy white nodding bells and heart-shaped, long-stalked basal leaves; rough-hairy. Occasional escape on banks and verges, unlike the blue native bellflowers.

species.name: Campanula cochleariifolia
species.tip: Small tufted bellflower with round toothed basal leaves and slender stalks of nodding, pale blue bells; spreads on walls and rocky ground. Smaller and more delicate than harebell.

species.name: Campanula fragilis
species.tip: Sprawling garden bellflower with rounded, scalloped, glossy leaves and flat, starry, pale violet-blue flowers on trailing stems. Rare wall and rock garden escape.

species.name: Campanula garganica
species.tip: Low, mat-forming rock-garden bellflower with hairy heart-shaped toothed leaves and flat, five-pointed, violet-blue stars. Escapes onto walls and pavements, mainly near gardens.

species.name: Campanula glomerata
species.tip: Stiff upright bellflower with tight terminal clusters of violet funnel-shaped flowers and unstalked upper leaves clasping the stem. Native on chalk and limestone grassland; also in gardens.

species.name: Campanula lactiflora
species.tip: Tall garden bellflower with big branched heads of pale milky blue or lilac bells and many leafy stalkless stem leaves. Occasional garden escape on banks and rough ground.

species.name: Campanula latifolia
species.tip: Tall leafy plant with large blue-purple bells in a leafy spike; stem rounded and hairy, leaves coarse and pointed; shady woods, north England and Scotland.

species.name: Campanula medium
species.tip: Tall biennial with large inflated bells in blue, pink or white and rough, hairy, toothed leaves. Garden plant occasionally found on waste ground and verges.

species.name: Campanula patula
species.tip: Slender branched bellflower with widely open lilac funnels on thin spreading stalks and narrow, rough-edged leaves. Rare native of hedgebanks and verges in southern and western England and Wales.

species.name: Campanula persicifolia
species.tip: Wide open bowl-shaped blue flowers on a slender stem with narrow, shiny, finely toothed leaves; a garden escape on banks and verges.

species.name: Campanula portenschlagiana
species.tip: Mat-forming wall plant with dense violet star-shaped bells, deeply five-lobed, and small rounded toothed leaves; garden escape on walls and pavements.

species.name: Campanula poscharskyana
species.tip: Sprawling plant with pale lilac starry flowers cut nearly to the base and heart-shaped toothed leaves; naturalised on walls and banks.

species.name: Campanula pyramidalis
species.tip: Very tall garden bellflower with long pyramid-shaped spikes of many blue stars and glossy heart-shaped lower leaves. Rare escape from cultivation, often on walls.

species.name: Campanula rapunculoides
species.tip: Spreading, invasive patches of tall stems with one-sided spikes of nodding purple bells; heart-shaped lower leaves. Spreads by underground runners, a persistent garden and roadside weed.

species.name: Campanula rapunculus
species.tip: Biennial with a fleshy white root, wavy-edged basal leaves and a narrow spike-like panicle of pale blue small bells. Rare, now mostly casual on banks and waste ground.

species.name: Campanula rhomboidalis
species.tip: Upright perennial with broad oval toothed stem leaves and nodding blue bells in a one-sided cluster. Garden plant occasionally recorded as a rare escape on grassy banks.

species.name: Campanula rotundifolia
species.tip: Slender nodding pale blue bells on wiry stems; basal leaves rounded, stem leaves very narrow; grassland and dunes, late summer.

species.name: Campanula trachelium
species.tip: Tall, roughly hairy, angular stem with nettle-like coarse toothed leaves and large blue-purple bells; woods and hedgerows, mainly lowland England and Wales.

species.name: Cannabis sativa
species.tip: Tall annual with palmate leaves of five to seven narrow toothed leaflets and a strong smell; flowers are tiny green clusters. Occasional casual on waste ground and from bird seed.

species.name: Capsella bursa-pastoris
species.tip: Common weed with tiny white flowers and flat heart-shaped or triangular pods like little purses; basal rosette of variably lobed leaves.

species.name: Cardamine amara
species.tip: Damp-ground bitter-cress with white flowers and distinctive purple anthers; stem is solid and leafy, with large flowers for the group.

species.name: Cardamine bulbifera
species.tip: Woodland plant with pink-lilac flowers and small dark bulbils at the leaf bases. Leaves are pinnate. Local in southern woodland, especially the Chilterns and the Weald.

species.name: Cardamine corymbosa
species.tip: Small white-flowered cress with simple oval leaves at the base and creeping stems. A garden weed and nursery escape common around towns.

species.name: Cardamine flexuosa
species.tip: Zigzag hairy stem with leaves on it; usually six stamens and a rosette of leaves; shady, damp ground and gardens, often taller than Hairy Bitter-cress.

species.name: Cardamine heptaphylla
species.tip: Woodland cress with white flowers and leaves that have several pairs of toothed leaflets. Flowers are large. Rare naturalised plant of shady places.

species.name: Cardamine hirsuta
species.tip: Small annual weed of bare ground with a rosette of pinnate leaves and few stem leaves; usually four stamens; pods shoot out when ripe.

species.name: Cardamine impatiens
species.tip: Tall biennial of shady limestone and woodland, with tiny white flowers, pinnate leaves with narrow leaflets and ear-like clasping bases. Pods open explosively.

species.name: Cardamine pratensis
species.tip: Pale lilac or pink flowers in damp meadows in spring; pinnate leaves with rounded leaflets on lower stem, narrow ones above; also called Lady's Smock.

species.name: Cardamine quinquefolia
species.tip: Rare garden escape with whorled leaves of five leaflets and pink-lilac flowers in spring. Easily confused with other woodland Cardamine; needs expert confirmation.

species.name: Cardamine raphanifolia
species.tip: Large, robust relative of Cuckooflower with pale lilac-pink flowers, bigger leaflets and thicker stem. Naturalised on stream banks and damp woodland.

species.name: Cardamine trifolia
species.tip: Evergreen woodland-edge plant with glossy three-part leaves and clusters of white flowers that are sometimes tinged pink. A garden escape in damp shady spots.

species.name: Carduus crispus
species.tip: Slender thistle whose stems are winged right up to the heads with wavy spiny wings, and small clustered purple heads. Verges and rough grass in summer.

species.name: Carduus nutans
species.tip: Big nodding purple heads with broad spreading spiny bracts, and spiny-winged stems below. Grows on chalk and limestone grassland and disturbed ground, summer.

species.name: Carduus pycnocephalus
species.tip: Spiny thistle with spiny-winged, cottony stems and small purple heads in clusters; very localised near Plymouth and other south-western coast sites.

species.name: Carduus tenuiflorus
species.tip: Spiny-winged thistle with small, narrow pink-purple heads in tight clusters; stems cottony, mainly coastal, and heads are smaller than welted thistle.

species.name: Carex acuta
species.tip: A creeping, stoloniferous sedge of wet meadows and river margins with sharply three-angled rough stems and flat leaves; unlike Tufted-sedge it does not form big tussocks and has narrower, pointed glumes.

species.name: Carex acutiformis
species.tip: Blue-green broad leaves with a ligule that is long and pointed; two or three thick male spikes above, stout upright females below with pointed utricles; wet ground and ditches.

species.name: Carex appropinquata
species.tip: A tussocky sedge of calcareous fens with tangled fibrous old leaf bases and short, pale brown spikes; separate from Greater Tussock-sedge by its shorter, compact spikes and the fibrous tufts rather than tall tussocks.

species.name: Carex aquatilis
species.tip: A tall, creeping sedge of wet peaty margins and fens with long grey-green leaves and dark spikes; the spikes are dark with blunt black-tipped glumes, and it forms extensive patches unlike tussocky relatives.

species.name: Carex arenaria
species.tip: Found on coastal dunes, with long creeping runners that send up stems in a straight line; spikes in a loose brownish cluster, each with male flowers on top and female below.

species.name: Carex atrata
species.tip: A mountain sedge of Scottish rocky ledges with a few dark, almost black, nodding spikes with the top spike mostly male; look for broad, bluish leaves and egg-shaped blackish spikes on drooping stalks.

species.name: Carex atrofusca
species.tip: A very rare, tiny, sooty-black sedge of high, wet, base-rich mountain flushes in Scotland, with one drooping dark spike on a slender stem and short, dark female glumes.

species.name: Carex bigelowii
species.tip: A creeping sedge of mountain tops and exposed heaths with stiff, upright stems and a bluish-green look; has one male spike and one to three short, dark, oval female spikes held upright.

species.name: Carex binervis
species.tip: Moorland and heath sedge with a single male spike above and spaced, stalked, upright to slightly nodding female spikes; leaves greyish-green and utricles with two clear green ribs.

species.name: Carex buchananii
species.tip: A coppery, bronze, tufted garden sedge from New Zealand that occasionally escapes; the very narrow curly leaves are the key feature, with slim brown spikes on thin stems.

species.name: Carex buxbaumii
species.tip: A rare, creeping sedge of coastal marshes with a club-shaped terminal spike that is male at the top and female below, plus blackish short spikes; blue-green leaves are an aid, and it occurs in a few eastern and Irish sites.

species.name: Carex canescens
species.tip: Small grey-green tufts in wet acid places, with several rounded, pale spikes spaced along the stem, each with female flowers above male; utricles pale and small.

species.name: Carex capillaris
species.tip: A small mountain sedge of base-rich flushes with extremely slender stems carrying one tiny male spike and a few small female spikes hanging on hair-fine stalks, the fruit having a long beak.

species.name: Carex caryophyllea
species.tip: Low early-flowering sedge of dry grassland and limestone with one male spike and short downy-fruited female spikes; base of stems has reddish-purple sheaths; leaves short and soft.

species.name: Carex cespitosa
species.tip: A very rare tufted sedge of damp grassland, resembling Tufted-sedge but with a larger dense tuft and blunt dark glumes; a specialist should confirm any record as this species is extremely scarce or lost in Britain.

species.name: Carex chordorrhiza
species.tip: A very rare creeping sedge of wet peat bogs in the Scottish Highlands, with long string-like underground runners and short, compact heads of small brown spikes.

species.name: Carex comans
species.tip: A pale olive to bronze tufted garden sedge from New Zealand that sometimes escapes, with fine arching leaves and drooping slender female spikes; looks like a thin mop-headed tuft of hair.

species.name: Carex depauperata
species.tip: A very rare woodland sedge confined to a few sites in the south of England, with a few widely spaced, fat spikes on slender stalks and large, plump, beaked fruits.

species.name: Carex diandra
species.tip: A tufted sedge of fens and wet meadows with compact heads of small brown spikes and shiny, rounded fruits; stems are rough, and it is lesser and neater than Greater Tussock-sedge.

species.name: Carex digitata
species.tip: A woodland sedge of limestone with spikes spread like fingers, the lowest sheaths purplish red and a pale, short male spike above a few female ones; leaves are short and narrow.

species.name: Carex dioica
species.tip: Tiny single-spiked sedge of base-rich flushes and fens, with male and female spikes on separate plants; stems slender, leaves narrow, spreading by short runners.

species.name: Carex distans
species.tip: Coastal and brackish sedge with bluish-green leaves and a short ligule; female spikes widely spaced, small, held close to the stem, with a long-beaked yellowish-green utricle.

species.name: Carex disticha
species.tip: Wet meadow and fen sedge with long creeping runners; the spike is a dense brown cylinder of stacked small spikelets, male flowers in the middle and female at both ends.

species.name: Carex divisa
species.tip: A creeping sedge of brackish grassland and dune slacks with a dense, compact head of many small spikes that look like a bunch; found mostly in the south and east near the coast.

species.name: Carex divulsa
species.tip: Greyish-green sedge of hedgebanks, with a long interrupted head of small spikes, lower ones well spaced, each with male above female; utricles brownish-green with a long beak.

species.name: Carex echinata
species.tip: Small yellowish-green sedge of wet acid ground whose few spikes cluster together and fruits spread out starlike when ripe; spikes show male above female within each.

species.name: Carex elata
species.tip: A big tussock-forming sedge of fens and lake edges with stiff yellowish-green leaves and dark spikes; the tussocks are the clue, as the similar Slender Tufted-sedge forms creeping patches.

species.name: Carex elongata
species.tip: A tufted sedge of wet woods and fen margins with a narrow, slender row of many small greenish spikes, a bit like an elongated bottle brush and quite distinct from other brown-headed ones.

species.name: Carex ericetorum
species.tip: A very rare, low creeping sedge of calcareous grassland in East Anglia and Scotland, flowering early with hairy fruits and small spikes tucked among the leaves.

species.name: Carex extensa
species.tip: A tufted sedge of saltmarsh and coastal rocks with stiff greyish-green, curled leaves and one or two stalkless female spikes with very long, leaf-like bracts that stick out.

species.name: Carex flacca
species.tip: Leaves distinctly blue-grey beneath, and stiff on chalk and limestone; blackish-purple male spikes with a short nodding female spike lower down; runs by rhizomes.

species.name: Carex flava
species.tip: A yellowish-green sedge of marshes and fens with a cluster of pale female spikes near the male spike, their long, down-curved beaks giving a spiky look; much larger than Common Yellow-sedge.

species.name: Carex hirta
species.tip: Leaves, sheaths and fruits all bear obvious hairs; creeping plant of rough grassland and ditches with widely spaced female spikes below two or three male spikes.

species.name: Carex hostiana
species.tip: Yellowish-tawny sedge of fens and flushes; compact female spikes are clustered near the male spike, each fruit with a bent-back short beak; leaves flat and rather pale.

species.name: Carex humilis
species.tip: A very rare tiny sedge of southern chalk grassland in Dorset, Wiltshire and Hampshire, flowering early with short spikes hidden among curly, grass-like leaves.

species.name: Carex lachenalii
species.tip: A mountain sedge of late snow patches in Scotland with a tight cluster of two to four small, brown, egg-shaped spikes that look like a hare's foot.

species.name: Carex laevigata
species.tip: Broad, shiny, bright green leaves with smooth edges in damp woods; slender female spikes slightly nodding, widely spaced, on smooth stems, with a pale winged utricle.

species.name: Carex lasiocarpa
species.tip: A creeping sedge of wet fens and bog pools with very narrow, rolled grey-green leaves and large, hairy fruits on thick female spikes that stand erect.

species.name: Carex leporina
species.tip: A tight oval cluster of pale straw-coloured spikes at stem top, each with male flowers above female; damp grassland and rushy pastures; the fruit is flat and winged.

species.name: Carex limosa
species.tip: A creeping sedge of wet peat bog pools with greyish, narrow leaves and short, plump, oval female spikes hanging on thread-like stalks.

species.name: Carex magellanica
species.tip: A rare northern sedge of acid bog and wet moorland with a few pale, drooping female spikes on slender stalks, and a male spike above; shorter stalks and paler greenish leaves tell it from Bog-sedge.

species.name: Carex maritima
species.tip: A tiny Scottish dune and sandy shore sedge with one little, rounded, rust-brown head sitting on curved stems and short, curved leaves, so it looks a bit like a bent shoot.

species.name: Carex microglochin
species.tip: A very rare tiny Scottish mountain sedge of base-rich flushes, with a single slender spike bearing a bristle-like extension of the fruit stalk beyond the sacs.

species.name: Carex montana
species.tip: A small sedge of dry, grassy limestone and heath with soft hairy fruits, early-flowering short spikes and leaves that look limp and soft; creeps slowly to form loose patches.

species.name: Carex muricata
species.tip: Green spikes on short compact stalks, with spreading fruit giving a prickly look; lowest spikes spaced, flowers male above female; includes similar close relatives, so check details.

species.name: Carex nigra
species.tip: Smooth blue-green leaves; one or two slender male spikes, and black-scaled narrow female spikes with short stalks in boggy and grassy places; fruit small and rounded.

species.name: Carex norvegica
species.tip: A rare Scottish mountain sedge with a tight head of two to four dark spikes crowded together, stalks drooping a bit; the dense head and blackish glumes are the clues.

species.name: Carex ornithopoda
species.tip: A rare, small, tufted sedge of limestone pastures in northern England with a group of spikes spreading like a bird foot and short, fine hairs on the fruits.

species.name: Carex otrubae
species.tip: Dense, green, clustered head of spikes, often over 5 cm, with a long pointed ligule and a lower sheath that stays pale; damp grassland, ditches, often brackish.

species.name: Carex pallescens
species.tip: Pale green sedge with hairy leaves and sheaths; short egg-shaped female spikes hang on thin stalks below a single male spike; woods and grassland.

species.name: Carex panicea
species.tip: Waxy blue-green leaves like carnation foliage; one male spike and widely spaced female spikes with plump, rounded fruits bearing a short beak; damp meadows and fens.

species.name: Carex paniculata
species.tip: Forms large tussocks in fens and carr; branched, plume-like head of many small spikes, male and female mingled; stem sharply triangular and rough; leaves stiff.

species.name: Carex pauciflora
species.tip: A creeping sedge of wet acid bogs with a single slim spike holding only two or three pale yellowish-green fruits that bend downward, giving a sparse look.

species.name: Carex pendula
species.tip: Big tufted sedge with long, thick, drooping female spikes up to 16 cm hanging on slender stalks; leaves broad and shiny; woods and damp shady banks.

species.name: Carex pilulifera
species.tip: Small tufted heath sedge with round, hairy-fruited female spikes clustered tight at the base of the male spike, like little pills; leaves are soft and slender.

species.name: Carex pseudocyperus
species.tip: Yellow-green leaves and long hanging female spikes with fruits bearing long, spreading awns; edge of ponds and slow water; looks like Pendulous Sedge but spikes thinner.

species.name: Carex pulicaris
species.tip: Small wiry tufted sedge of damp base-rich ground with one small spike, male flowers above and shiny dark brown fruits below that curve down like fleas.

species.name: Carex punctata
species.tip: A coastal sedge of rocky cliffs and damp seepage in south-west England, Wales and Ireland, with dotted, yellowish-green fruits, a male spike above and short stalked females beneath.

species.name: Carex rariflora
species.tip: A scarce creeping sedge of wet Scottish mountain bogs with greyish, narrow leaves and a few drooping dark, pale-glumed female spikes on thread-like stalks.

species.name: Carex recta
species.tip: A rare creeping sedge of upper saltmarsh and estuary banks in Scotland, with tall stems, stiff grey-green leaves and a few narrow dark spikes; a specialist should check hybrids with Water Sedge.

species.name: Carex remota
species.tip: Soft, thin, pale green leaves in shady damp woods and ditches; small green spikes well separated up the stem, with long leafy bracts below them; fruit tiny.

species.name: Carex riparia
species.tip: Big grey-green creeping sedge of pond edges with three to five thick male spikes and long upright females; leaves broad, rough-edged; the ligule is blunt.

species.name: Carex rostrata
species.tip: Bluish-green sedge of bogs and lake margins; yellowish female spikes with spreading bottle-shaped fruits having a long beak; leaves narrow and rolled.

species.name: Carex rupestris
species.tip: A small mountain sedge of calcareous rocky ledges, with a single small spike at the top of a curved, wiry stem and narrow, curly leaves; local in the Scottish Highlands.

species.name: Carex salina
species.tip: A rare saltmarsh and coastal sedge of northern coasts needing a specialist to identify; it is a smaller relative of Lyngbye's and Estuarine Sedge, with dark spikes and creeping runners.

species.name: Carex saxatilis
species.tip: A creeping sedge of wet peaty mountain flushes in Scotland with one male spike and a single stout, dark purplish-brown female spike that droops or stands up on short stalks.

species.name: Carex simpliciuscula
species.tip: A small, tufted mountain plant of limestone ground in northern England and Scotland with a single narrow spike and bristle-like leaves, looks like a small rush; stems are wiry.

species.name: Carex spicata
species.tip: Dense compact cluster of male and female spikes at the top of a sharply triangular stem; grassy verges and rough ground; fruits small, pointed and ribbed.

species.name: Carex strigosa
species.tip: A woodland sedge of damp clay with wide, bright green leaves and thin, long, spaced, drooping female spikes with few fruits, all on arching stalks; the shape is fine and sparse.

species.name: Carex sylvatica
species.tip: Bright green leaves and thin, long-stalked, drooping female spikes spaced up the stem; woodland sedge with fruit that is slender and beaked.

species.name: Carex vaginata
species.tip: A rare Scottish mountain sedge, creeping, with a single male spike and one nodding female spike on a thin stalk, and conspicuous pale sheaths on the stem.

species.name: Carex vesicaria
species.tip: Swollen, inflated yellowish-green fruits spreading from stout female spikes; wet places, pond margins; leaves yellow-green with blunt ligule; paler than Bottle Sedge.

species.name: Carex vulpina
species.tip: A tufted sedge of wet grassland and ditches with dense fox-brown spike heads that are bright green or brown and a sharply winged, rough three-angled stem; inner leaf sheaths are green not red.

species.name: Carex vulpinoidea
species.tip: A tufted sedge, introduced and naturalised in a few wet places, resembling True Fox-sedge but with finer, greener spike heads and narrow, long bracts reaching beyond the head.

species.name: Carlina vulgaris
species.tip: Stiff, spiny, small thistle with straw-coloured, shiny bracts spreading like rays around a brown centre; dead heads persist through winter. Dry chalk and limestone grassland.

species.name: Carpinus betulus
species.tip: Tree with fluted grey trunk and oval leaves with parallel pleated veins, double-toothed; fruit has three-lobed bracts.

species.name: Carpobrotus acinaciformis
species.tip: Mat-forming succulent with three-angled curved leaves and large magenta-pink flowers; often grown on sea cliffs, and hybridises with Hottentot-fig, so check intermediates.

species.name: Carpobrotus edulis
species.tip: Sprawling succulent carpeting coastal cliffs in the south-west, with thick three-sided leaves and big flowers that are yellow in the centre and pale pink toward the edge.

species.name: Carpobrotus glaucescens
species.tip: Coastal succulent close to Hottentot-fig with fleshy three-angled leaves and pink or purplish flowers; separating the two is hard, so confirmation by a specialist is wise.

species.name: Carum carvi
species.tip: Biennial with feathery leaves, a grooved stem and white umbels that lack bracts; leaves have small leaflet-like lobes at the stalk base; a casual on waste ground and field margins.

species.name: Castanea sativa
species.tip: Large tree with long toothed glossy leaves, long yellowish catkins and spiny husked nuts; deeply spiralled bark in older trees.

species.name: Catabrosa aquatica
species.tip: Soft, creeping grass of streams and ditches with a pyramidal panicle in whorls and blunt, notched tips to the glumes; the broad pale leaves float or sprawl in shallow water.

species.name: Catapodium marinum
species.tip: Stiff, short, one-sided spike of spikelets, close to the ground on rocks and sea walls; spikelets sit straight on the stem and are unawned.

species.name: Catapodium rigidum
species.tip: Small, rigid grass of dry walls and dry ground, with a triangular stiff panicle with very short branches carrying unawned spikelets.

species.name: Centaurea aspera
species.tip: Rare casual with purple heads whose bracts bear a stout spine and smaller spines at base; rough branched stems; formerly in dunes of south-west England.

species.name: Centaurea calcitrapa
species.tip: Spreading spiny plant with pink-purple heads, each bract bearing a long yellowish spine; found on waste ground and roadsides, mostly southern England.

species.name: Centaurea cyanus
species.tip: Slender grey-green plant with bright blue heads whose outer florets are large and spreading. Arable field edges, wasteland and sown wildflower strips, summer.

species.name: Centaurea debeauxii
species.tip: Slender knapweed with deeply cut stem leaves and rather small purple heads with narrow, pale-fringed bracts. Chalk grassland in southern England; hard to separate from Common Knapweed.

species.name: Centaurea jacea
species.tip: Knapweed with dry papery brown bracts and pink-purple heads, often with enlarged rays; leaves narrow; casual in Britain, scattered on grassland.

species.name: Centaurea montana
species.tip: Garden escape with large blue heads whose outer florets are spreading, and bracts edged with black fringes. Leaves are broad and unlobed; found on verges and waste ground.

species.name: Centaurea nigra
species.tip: Purple thistle-like heads with dark brown, comb-fringed bracts forming a rounded knob, over unlobed or slightly lobed leaves. Abundant in grassland; no spines.

species.name: Centaurea scabiosa
species.tip: Larger knapweed with deeply cut leaves and heads with black-tipped bracts that are not a dark mop; outer florets are enlarged. Dry calcareous grassland.

species.name: Centaurium erythraea
species.tip: Pink flowers with five petals and a yellow centre, in flat-topped clusters; stem leaves are oval, with a basal rosette; dry grassland, dunes and woodland rides.

species.name: Centaurium littorale
species.tip: Short centaury with narrow leaves, flowers in a compact head, and a yellow-green tone. Grows in dune slacks, mostly in north-west England, Wales and Scotland.

species.name: Centaurium portense
species.tip: Small pink-flowered centaury relative with narrow oval leaves. Specialist check needed. Rare, mainly as a casual or near coasts.

species.name: Centaurium pulchellum
species.tip: Branched, slender centaury with many small pink flowers on diverging branches and stalkless blooms. Scarce in southern England on grassy ground and dunes.

species.name: Centaurium tenuiflorum
species.tip: Slim branched centaury of coastal grassland, with small pink flowers on distinct short stalks and narrow leaves. Mostly south and east England.

species.name: Centranthus calcitrapae
species.tip: Small annual with pink flowers in lax clusters and a short spur, pinnately lobed lower leaves. Rare casual or naturalised in southern England and the Channel Islands.

species.name: Centranthus ruber
species.tip: Pink-red, occasionally white, flowers in dense clusters, each with a short spur; grey-green fleshy leaves; naturalised on old walls, cliffs and railway lines.

species.name: Cephalanthera damasonium
species.tip: Woodland orchid with creamy-white flowers that remain mostly closed, and broad ribbed leaves; mainly in southern beechwoods on chalk.

species.name: Cephalanthera longifolia
species.tip: Woodland orchid with open white flowers and long narrow leaves held in two ranks; local in woods mostly in the south.

species.name: Cephalanthera rubra
species.tip: Very rare orchid with showy rose-pink flowers, and narrow pointed leaves; found only in a few beechwoods in the Chilterns and Gloucestershire.

species.name: Cerastium alpinum
species.tip: Mountain mouse-ear with white flowers, grey-hairy woolly leaves and sepals that are densely woolly. Rare, in high rocky ground in the Scottish Highlands, Wales and northern England.

species.name: Cerastium arvense
species.tip: Sprawling mat-forming mouse-ear with large white flowers with deeply notched petals, longer than the sepals, and narrow, hairy leaves. Common on grassy banks and dry roadsides.

species.name: Cerastium brachypetalum
species.tip: Small, grey-green annual with flowers in tight dense clusters, tiny white flowers, and fruit stalks bent down. Very rare, on calcareous soils in East Anglia.

species.name: Cerastium cerastoides
species.tip: Mountain mouse-ear with creeping mats and white flowers with deeply notched petals, longer than the sepals, and tough hairless leaves. Rare, high ground in Scotland.

species.name: Cerastium diffusum
species.tip: Small coastal annual with tiny flowers, bracts leafy and bracts without membranous margins in tufts. Bears five stamens and four petals; found on sand and dunes.

species.name: Cerastium fontanum
species.tip: Perennial with hairy oval leaves, flowers with white notched petals about as long as sepals and sparse inflorescence. Common in grassland and lawns; a perennial, unlike the annual species.

species.name: Cerastium glomeratum
species.tip: Annual, sticky and hairy, with compact flower clusters of five-petalled white flowers with petals about equal to sepals. Waste ground, paths and arable fields.

species.name: Cerastium nigrescens
species.tip: Tiny tufted mouse-ear, endemic to Shetland, with grey-green leaves, white flowers, and strongly hairy leaves. Grows only on serpentine on the island of Unst.

species.name: Cerastium pumilum
species.tip: Small annual mouse-ear with tiny white flowers, blunt sepals with a papery margin, and sticky, glandular upper parts. Rare, on dry calcareous banks and short grass.

species.name: Cerastium semidecandrum
species.tip: Tiny, early-flowering annual of dry sandy places with sepals having broad papery margins and petals that are small. Flowers disappear by early summer.

species.name: Cerastium tomentosum
species.tip: Garden escape forming silvery-white woolly mats with narrow leaves and masses of larger white flowers. Walls, banks and waste ground.

species.name: Ceratocapnos claviculata
species.tip: Delicate climber of acid woods and heaths using tendril-tipped leaves and clusters of tiny cream flowers; the leaves are divided into small oval leaflets.

species.name: Ceratochloa carinata
species.tip: Large annual or perennial brome with a flattened, compressed spikelets and short awns; a casual of waste ground, told from Rescue Brome by shorter awns.

species.name: Ceratochloa cathartica
species.tip: Big brome with a drooping panicle of flattened, keeled spikelets and short awns; common casual on waste ground. Leaf sheaths are downy, unlike hairless Prairie Brome.

species.name: Ceratochloa marginata
species.tip: North American brome with big flattened spikelets and hairs at the stem nodes; occasional casual. A specialist should check it against similar Ceratochloa species.

species.name: Ceratophyllum demersum
species.tip: Submerged rootless plant with stiff dark green whorled forked leaves with tiny teeth; flowers seldom seen, in still and slow water.

species.name: Ceratophyllum submersum
species.tip: Submerged plant with soft, thrice-forked leaves in whorls, less stiff and spiny than rigid hornwort. Rare in ponds and ditches of southern and eastern England.

species.name: Chaenorhinum minus
species.tip: Small, sticky-hairy annual of arable fields and railway ballast; tiny pale purple flowers with a short spur, much smaller than Common Toadflax and with no yellow.

species.name: Chaenorhinum origanifolium
species.tip: Small tufted sticky-hairy wall plant with violet and whitish snapdragon flowers on long thin stalks. Naturalised on old walls, notably in Kent; much smaller than Ivy-leaved Toadflax.

species.name: Chaerophyllum aureum
species.tip: Stout, hairy chervil with feathery leaves that are yellowish when young and umbels of white flowers; rare, established in northern Britain, and best confirmed by specialist.

species.name: Chaerophyllum hirsutum
species.tip: Roughly hairy chervil with deeply divided leaves and white or pinkish umbels; a rare garden plant not established widely, best confirmed by a specialist.

species.name: Chaerophyllum temulum
species.tip: Hairy hedgerow plant with purple-spotted, bristly swollen-jointed stems; flowers later than Cow Parsley and is much coarser to the touch with rough leaves.

species.name: Chamaemelum nobile
species.tip: Low, sweet-scented, mat-forming daisy with feathery leaves and white-rayed heads, found on sandy commons, grazed lawns and heaths; apple-like smell when crushed.

species.name: Chamaenerion angustifolium
species.tip: Tall stands of magenta flower spikes on waste ground, clearings and railways; long narrow leaves arranged spirally; seeds with white fluff in late summer.

species.name: Chasmanthe bicolor
species.tip: Tall sword-shaped leaves and a one-sided spike of tubular orange-red flowers in spring. Naturalised on mild coasts, mainly in south-west England and the Isles of Scilly.

species.name: Chelidonium majus
species.tip: Plant of hedge banks and walls, with brittle stems that bleed orange latex, blue-green deeply cut leaves and clusters of small four-petalled yellow flowers.

species.name: Chenopodiastrum hybridum
species.tip: Hairless goosefoot with shiny, maple-like, lobed and coarsely toothed leaves and open branched clusters of green flowers; common arable and waste ground weed.

species.name: Chenopodiastrum murale
species.tip: Goosefoot with shiny, sharply toothed, nettle-like leaves, not mealy and a coarser look; common on farmyards and waste ground, with branched, leafy flower spikes.

species.name: Chenopodium album
species.tip: Common weed with mealy white-dusted leaves, diamond-shaped to toothed, and dense green flower clusters; arable and waste ground.

species.name: Chenopodium ficifolium
species.tip: Leaves with three lobes, central lobe long, parallel-sided, near-hairless; arable and disturbed ground, unlike Fat-hen.

species.name: Chenopodium opulifolium
species.tip: Mealy grey-green low goosefoot with small, three-lobed leaves and rounded dense flower clusters; scattered on arable fields and waste ground, mainly in southern England.

species.name: Chenopodium suecicum
species.tip: Variable annual with mealy-free, pale green oval or lobed leaves and flower clusters in open spikes; hard to tell from similar goosefoots, so specialist confirmation is needed.

species.name: Chenopodium vulvaria
species.tip: Grey mealy, spreading annual smelling strongly of rotten fish when rubbed; small diamond-shaped untoothed leaves; rare and declining, mainly southern coastal and sandy ground.

species.name: Cherleria sedoides
species.tip: Dense cushion-forming plant of mountain rocks, with narrow leaves, and tiny green-yellow flowers lacking petals. Local in Scottish Highlands, northern England and Ireland.

species.name: Chiastophyllum oppositifolium
species.tip: Fleshy toothed leaves in opposite pairs and arching spikes of small yellow flowers. A garden plant sometimes persisting on walls and rocky banks.

species.name: Chimonobambusa quadrangularis
species.tip: Bamboo with distinctly four-angled stems and tiny spines at the nodes, spreading by rhizomes in gardens; flowers almost never seen in Britain.

species.name: Choisya ternata
species.tip: Glossy evergreen shrub with leaves of three leaflets, and scented white flowers. Widely planted, rarely self-sown near gardens.

species.name: Chrysosplenium alternifolium
species.tip: Small damp-woodland plant with leaves alternate on the stem, kidney-shaped and hairy, with yellow-green bracts around tiny flowers; rarer than the opposite-leaved species.

species.name: Chrysosplenium oppositifolium
species.tip: Mat-forming plant of streamsides and wet woods with paired, rounded, fleshy leaves and flat clusters of tiny golden-green flowers amid yellowish leaf-like bracts.

species.name: Cicendia filiformis
species.tip: Tiny, thread-like annual with small yellow four-petalled flowers. Found on damp sandy heathy ground in the south-west, Wales and Ireland.

species.name: Cicer arietinum
species.tip: Hairy annual pea with small toothed pinnate leaflets and white to bluish solitary flowers; inflated short pods. A rare crop relic or casual on waste ground.

species.name: Cicerbita alpina
species.tip: Mountain plant of Scottish Highlands with tall leafy stems, pale blue-violet heads, and glandular-hairy bristles; shaded cliff ledges, unusual in a thistle-like plant.

species.name: Cicerbita bourgaei
species.tip: Tall garden escape with blue-violet heads and large lobed leaves with a big end lobe; rarely naturalised, hairy stem.

species.name: Cicerbita macrophylla
species.tip: Tall hairy plant with pale blue-violet dandelion-like heads and large leaves with a big triangular end lobe. Escaped from gardens to damp shady verges and woodland edges.

species.name: Cicerbita plumieri
species.tip: Tall naturalised plant of shady banks, with blue-lilac heads in loose clusters and large lobed leaves; stems lack glandular hairs, unlike common blue-sow-thistle.

species.name: Cichorium intybus
species.tip: Tall, stiff, branching plant with bright sky-blue dandelion-like heads that open in the morning, stalkless along the stems. Dry grassland, verges and field edges.

species.name: Cicuta virosa
species.tip: Very poisonous water plant with hollow, chambered rootstock and a stout hairless stem; leaves are twice-pinnate with long narrow toothed leaflets; rare, in ditches, fens and lake margins.

species.name: Circaea alpina
species.tip: Smaller, weaker than Enchanter's-nightshade, with heart-shaped leaves with shiny blades and tiny white flowers; grows in damp shady rocky places in the uplands of the north.

species.name: Circaea lutetiana
species.tip: Shade-loving woodland and garden weed with paired opposite oval leaves and slender spikes of tiny white flowers with only two notched petals; fruits are bristly burs.

species.name: Cirsium acaule
species.tip: Stemless thistle with a flat rosette of spiny leaves and one or more big purple heads sitting at ground level. Short chalk and limestone turf.

species.name: Cirsium arvense
species.tip: Common spreading thistle with lilac, scented heads in clusters, stems not winged and leaves spiny but only slightly cottony. Forms patches in fields and verges.

species.name: Cirsium dissectum
species.tip: Slender thistle of damp meadows with unlobed, hardly spiny leaves white-felted beneath, and a single dull purple head; no winged stems.

species.name: Cirsium eriophorum
species.tip: Large thistle of chalk grassland with a big globe head covered with cobweb-like white wool, and fiercely spiny deeply cut leaves.

species.name: Cirsium heterophyllum
species.tip: Spineless thistle with unlobed, lance-shaped leaves white and felted beneath, clasping the stem, and a single large drooping purple head. Upland meadows and verges.

species.name: Cirsium oleraceum
species.tip: Unusual thistle with pale creamy yellow heads surrounded by big leaf-like bracts and only soft bristly leaves; rare casual of damp places.

species.name: Cirsium palustre
species.tip: Tall, narrow thistle with spiny-winged stems and dense clusters of small purple heads at the top. Damp meadows, rushy pasture and heaths.

species.name: Cirsium tuberosum
species.tip: Rare thistle with a single large purple head on a nearly leafless stem and deeply cut leaves; only on Wiltshire chalk grassland.

species.name: Cirsium vulgare
species.tip: Large heads on a spiny-winged stem, with fierce spear-shaped spiny leaves that are bristly above. Common on grassland and waste ground, late summer.

species.name: Cladium mariscus
species.tip: A tall, robust fen plant forming dense stands, with sharply saw-edged, keeled leaves that cut, topped by branched clusters of small brown spikelets; the cutting leaf is the giveaway.

species.name: Claytonia perfoliata
species.tip: Annual with a round stem leaf cupping the tiny white flowers like a collar; spring weed of sandy cultivated ground and gardens, unlike the pink-flowered Pink Purslane.

species.name: Claytonia sibirica
species.tip: Succulent annual or biennial with a pair of separate stem leaves below pink, white-veined flowers; damp shady places, woods and gardens, not the single collar of Springbeauty.

species.name: Clematis flammula
species.tip: Slender climber with sweetly scented small white four-sepalled flowers in loose clusters and compound leaves; fruits are feathery heads. Rare escape from gardens, hedges and walls, mostly in the south.

species.name: Clematis vitalba
species.tip: Woody climber over hedges and scrub on chalk and limestone; creamy flowers with 4 sepals; feathery 'old man's beard' seed heads.

species.name: Clinopodium acinos
species.tip: Small annual with violet flowers marked white on the lower lip, in whorls on slender branched stems. Bare chalky arable ground and disturbed turf, mostly in southern England.

species.name: Clinopodium ascendens
species.tip: Hairy mint-scented perennial with loose branched clusters of lilac flowers in the leaf axils, on roadsides and dry banks. Told from Lesser Calamint by larger leaves and flowers.

species.name: Clinopodium menthifolium
species.tip: Tall, mint-scented hairy perennial with dense, many-flowered axillary clusters of pale pink flowers, with large leaves. Very rare, confined to the Isle of Wight woodland edges.

species.name: Clinopodium nepeta
species.tip: Smaller than Common Calamint, with small leaves and many tiny lilac flowers in stalked clusters. Dry chalk and limestone grassland, mainly in East Anglia and the south.

species.name: Clinopodium vulgare
species.tip: Flower whorls wrapped in long, bristly hairs, so they look woolly; only faintly aromatic.

species.name: Cochlearia anglica
species.tip: Fleshy scurvygrass of estuarine mud, with white flowers and clasping stem leaves. Seed pods are large and inflated, unlike other coastal scurvygrasses.

species.name: Cochlearia danica
species.tip: Small coastal and inland-roadside annual with ivy-shaped stalked basal leaves and clusters of small white to lilac flowers in early spring.

species.name: Cochlearia megalosperma
species.tip: Scurvygrass of the Cochlearia officinalis group with larger seeds, white flowers and fleshy leaves. Occurs near coasts. Specialist needed to confirm the identification.

species.name: Cochlearia micacea
species.tip: Small tufted scurvygrass of Scottish mountain springs and flushes, with long leaf stalks, white flowers and rounded pods. Grows only in uplands.

species.name: Cochlearia officinalis
species.tip: Fleshy, shiny, rounded to heart-shaped leaves in salt marshes and sea cliffs, with white flowers in dense clusters and rounded pods.

species.name: Cochlearia pyrenaica
species.tip: Upland scurvygrass of metal-rich streamsides in northern Britain, with kidney-shaped basal leaves, white flowers and small round pods. Not coastal.

species.name: Coeloglossum viride
species.tip: Small orchid with greenish-brown flowers with hooded top and a narrow, notched lip; grows in short grassland and dunes.

species.name: Coincya monensis
species.tip: Bright yellow, crucifer with lobed bristly leaves and large veined flowers. Coastal on cliffs and shingle in Wales, Lancashire and Isle of Man, and scattered inland.

species.name: Coincya wrightii
species.tip: Endemic to Lundy, in the Bristol Channel, with yellow veined flowers on bristly stalks and large lobed leaves. Very rare, only on Lundy cliffs.

species.name: Colchicum autumnale
species.tip: Crocus-like pink-lilac flowers appearing in autumn without leaves; large glossy leaves appear in spring. Told from autumn crocuses by six stamens.

species.name: Colutea arborescens
species.tip: Shrub with pinnate leaves, yellow pea flowers with red-marked standard, and puffed-up papery pods. Planted and naturalised on railway banks and waste ground.

species.name: Comarum palustre
species.tip: Wetland plant with dark purplish-red star-like flowers, sepals longer than petals; leaves with five or seven toothed leaflets; bogs, fens and wet margins.

species.name: Conium maculatum
species.tip: Tall, hairless, poisonous umbellifer with smooth stems blotched with purple and a mousy smell when crushed; much more finely cut and spotted than Cow Parsley or Angelica.

species.name: Conopodium majus
species.tip: Slender plant of old grassland and woodland edges whose feathery leaves are thread-like; stem leaves appear early, and a round edible tuber lies underground.

species.name: Consolida ajacis
species.tip: Garden escape; spikes of blue, pink or white flowers with one long spur; very finely divided leaves.

species.name: Convallaria majalis
species.tip: Low woodland carpeter with two broad, ribbed oval leaves per shoot and a one-sided spray of nodding, sweet-scented white bells; fruits red berries.

species.name: Convolvulus arvensis
species.tip: Trailing or climbing weed of fields and verges with small, scented pink or white funnels often striped, and small arrow-shaped leaves; bracts are tiny and far below the flower.

species.name: Corallorhiza trifida
species.tip: Leafless orchid with a coral-like underground root and a few pale yellow-green flowers on a thin stem; grows in damp woods and dune slacks in Scotland.

species.name: Coreopsis grandiflora
species.tip: Garden escape with big golden daisy heads with notched rays, and narrow or lobed leaves; hairless, found on banks and waste ground.

species.name: Coriandrum sativum
species.tip: Annual with two kinds of leaf: lobed lower leaves and feathery thread-like upper leaves, pungent smell and white to pinkish umbels; an occasional casual on tips and waste ground.

species.name: Cornus alba
species.tip: Shrub with bright red winter stems, creamy flowers in flat heads, and white or bluish-white berries. Widely planted and sometimes naturalised in hedges.

species.name: Cornus canadensis
species.tip: Low creeping plant with whorled oval leaves and flowerheads ringed by four white bracts. Naturalised in a few northern Scottish moorlands.

species.name: Cornus sanguinea
species.tip: Shrub with opposite oval leaves with curved veins, dark red autumn colour and winter twigs; white flower clusters in summer and black berries; hedges on chalk and clay.

species.name: Cornus sericea
species.tip: Suckering shrub with bright red winter stems, grown for colour and naturalised in damp ground; fruits white, unlike black berries of native Dogwood.

species.name: Cornus suecica
species.tip: Small upland plant with whorls of oval leaves and tiny dark purple flowers ringed by white bracts. Found on northern moors and mountains.

species.name: Coronilla valentina
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with grey-green pinnate leaves and rounded heads of scented yellow pea flowers. Garden shrub, rarely casual.

species.name: Correa backhouseana
species.tip: Evergreen, with oval leaves white-felted underneath and drooping greenish-yellow tubular bells. Very rare garden plant in mild areas, not often naturalised.

species.name: Corrigiola litoralis
species.tip: Prostrate annual with narrow, blue-green leaves and tiny white flowers in tight clusters. Very rare, found on shingle beaches near Slapton, Devon.

species.name: Cortaderia richardii
species.tip: Big tussock with feathery silver plumes and razor-edged leaves; flowers earlier than Pampas-grass, with plumes held well above the foliage. Escape on cliffs and waste ground.

species.name: Cortaderia selloana
species.tip: Huge garden escape forming giant clumps with silvery-white plumes up to a metre long; leaves have razor-sharp edges, ligule is a fringe of hairs.

species.name: Corydalis cava
species.tip: Early spring woodland plant with a hollow rounded tuber, finely divided blue-green leaves and a spike of dull purple or white flowers. Tuber is hollow, unlike Bird-in-a-bush.

species.name: Corydalis solida
species.tip: Spring woodland plant with a solid tuber, lobed pale blue-green leaves and a spike of pinkish-purple spurred flowers; bracts are fingered, unlike Hollowroot.

species.name: Corylus avellana
species.tip: Shrub with rounded, softly hairy toothed leaves; dangling yellow male catkins appear in late winter, tiny red female flowers.

species.name: Corylus maxima
species.tip: Large shrub like hazel but with nut husks fully enclosing the nuts, longer than the nut. Planted in hedges and gardens; yellow catkins appear in late winter.

species.name: Corynephorus canescens
species.tip: Small bluish-grey tufts of bristle-fine leaves, with a narrow panicle of club-shaped awned spikelets; confined to dry sandy heaths and coastal dunes, mainly in East Anglia.

species.name: Cota tinctoria
species.tip: Escape with golden yellow daisy heads and finely cut, whitish hairy leaves; unlike chamomiles with white rays, it is wholly yellow.

species.name: Cotoneaster apiculatus
species.tip: Spreading deciduous shrub with rounded leaves ending in a small point, solitary pinkish flowers and large bright red berries; often branches in a herringbone pattern.

species.name: Cotoneaster bullatus
species.tip: Large deciduous shrub with big puckered leaves with sunken veins, pink flowers in clusters and large red berries; common escape in scrub.

species.name: Cotoneaster cambricus
species.tip: Rare, small, evergreen shrub confined to limestone cliffs on the Great Orme in Wales; leaves are small, dark and rounded, with white-pink flowers and red fruit. Specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Cotoneaster dielsianus
species.tip: Arching deciduous shrub with small oval leaves, woolly beneath, pink flowers in small clusters and orange-red berries; escape in scrub. Distinguishing Cotoneaster species needs a specialist.

species.name: Cotoneaster divaricatus
species.tip: Deciduous shrub with stiffly spreading branches, glossy small leaves and pink flowers in pairs or threes, then red egg-shaped berries; leaves turn red in autumn.

species.name: Cotoneaster franchetii
species.tip: Evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub with grey-green leaves, white downy beneath, pinkish-white flowers and orange-red berries; frequent garden escape on waste ground and scrub.

species.name: Cotoneaster frigidus
species.tip: Large semi-evergreen shrub or small tree with big oval leaves and flat clusters of white flowers followed by many red berries; Cotoneaster species are tricky, so confirm with a specialist.

species.name: Cotoneaster horizontalis
species.tip: Low shrub with fishbone-pattern branches, tiny glossy rounded leaves and pinkish-white flowers; red berries persist; escapes onto walls, rocks and dunes. Flat habit separates it from other cotoneasters.

species.name: Cotoneaster induratus
species.tip: Evergreen, arching shrub with leathery dark leaves, felty white beneath, white flowers and red fruit. A rare escape; a specialist is needed to identify it.

species.name: Cotoneaster integrifolius
species.tip: Small evergreen shrub with leaves white-felted beneath, pink-tinged flowers and red fruits; spreads on limestone cliffs and rocks. Leaves smaller than Himalayan Cotoneaster.

species.name: Cotoneaster lacteus
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with leathery leaves that are densely felted beneath, dense heads of creamy white flowers and long-lasting red berries; frequent in hedges and scrub.

species.name: Cotoneaster microphyllus
species.tip: Evergreen low spreading shrub with tiny, dark, glossy leaves, solitary white flowers and crimson fruits; very common escape from gardens on walls and rough ground.

species.name: Cotoneaster nitens
species.tip: Deciduous shrub with small glossy leaves, pink flowers and dark purple-black berries; black fruit separates it from most escapes. A specialist should confirm.

species.name: Cotoneaster obtusus
species.tip: Low, deciduous or semi-evergreen shrub with blunt, rounded leaves, small pink flowers and red fruit; rare escape and tricky from other Cotoneaster species, so confirm with a specialist.

species.name: Cotoneaster salicifolius
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with long, narrow, wrinkled leaves like willow, creamy flowers in flat clusters and bright red berries; widespread escape.

species.name: Cotoneaster simonsii
species.tip: Upright semi-evergreen shrub with orange-red fruits and flowers pink outside; leaves hairy beneath. Common bird-sown escape on hedges and waste ground; taller than Wall Cotoneaster.

species.name: Cotoneaster zabelii
species.tip: Deciduous arching shrub with oval leaves, woolly beneath, pink flowers in drooping clusters and red pear-shaped berries; rare escape. Specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Cotula alpina
species.tip: Tiny creeping rock-garden plant with small yellowish button heads and finely divided hairy leaves; casual in a few spots only.

species.name: Cotula australis
species.tip: Small branched annual weed of bare ground with feathery leaves and tiny yellowish button heads lacking rays; scarce casual.

species.name: Cotula coronopifolia
species.tip: Fleshy hairless plant of brackish mud and saltmarsh, with narrow leaves and yellow button heads without rays; naturalised in places.

species.name: Cotula squalida
species.tip: Creeping mat-forming lawn weed from New Zealand with feathery, finely divided leaves and tiny yellowish-brown button heads; spreading in lawns, mostly Scotland and Ireland.

species.name: Crambe maritima
species.tip: Big waxy blue-green plant of shingle beaches, with wavy, crinkled leaves and domed masses of white honey-scented flowers. Hard to mistake for other seaside crucifers.

species.name: Crassula aquatica
species.tip: Tiny aquatic or mud plant with opposite narrow leaves and minute white flowers in the leaf axils. Very rare and easily overlooked.

species.name: Crassula decumbens
species.tip: Tiny succulent annual with small, fleshy opposite leaves and minute white flowers. Naturalised on bare ground and paths in the Isles of Scilly.

species.name: Crassula helmsii
species.tip: Invasive pond plant forming dense mats of paired, narrow, fleshy leaves; tiny four-petalled white flowers appear singly on leaf axils, often in water or on mud.

species.name: Crassula pubescens
species.tip: Tiny, slightly hairy succulent forming small mats, with minute white or pinkish flowers. A rare introduction on damp ground.

species.name: Crassula tillaea
species.tip: Minute reddish moss-like annual on sandy or gravelly ground, with tiny white flowers crowded among overlapping fleshy leaves.

species.name: Crataegus laevigata
species.tip: Hawthorn with shallow three-lobed leaves and flowers with two or three styles and fruits with two stones; ancient woodland and old hedges, mainly lowland England.

species.name: Crataegus monogyna
species.tip: Common hedge thorn with deeply cut lobed leaves and one style per flower, one stone per haw; flowers May, white; compare shallow-lobed Midland Hawthorn.

species.name: Crataegus orientalis
species.tip: Thorny small tree with grey, deeply lobed woolly leaves, white flowers and large orange-red fruits; rare planting differing from our native hawthorns in its grey, felted leaves.

species.name: Crepis biennis
species.tip: Tall hairy biennial with large golden heads and toothed, lobed leaves; outer bracts are bristly and the buds nod. Meadows and verges, early summer.

species.name: Crepis capillaris
species.tip: Small yellow dandelion-like heads in loose clusters, orange-red beneath, over mostly smooth leaves with arrow-shaped stem leaf bases. Lawns, walls, verges; flowers until late autumn.

species.name: Crepis foetida
species.tip: Annual hawk's-beard smelling unpleasantly, with nodding flower buds, pale yellow heads and downy lobed leaves; extremely rare, formerly Kent coast.

species.name: Crepis mollis
species.tip: Tall hawk's-beard of upland meadows and streamsides, with soft hairy, toothed clasping leaves and yellow heads; northern England and Scotland.

species.name: Crepis paludosa
species.tip: Leafy plant of damp places with unlobed or little-lobed clasping stem leaves and orange-yellow heads, black-hairy bracts. Wet meadows and streamsides, northern and western Britain.

species.name: Crepis praemorsa
species.tip: Hawk's-beard with a basal rosette and almost leafless stem bearing pale yellow heads; in Britain recorded long ago in the north, perhaps extinct.

species.name: Crepis vesicaria
species.tip: Hairy plant with deeply cut leaves and yellow heads, outer florets orange-streaked beneath; fruits have a beak. Roadsides, walls and waste ground, mainly southern England.

species.name: Crithmum maritimum
species.tip: Fleshy, aromatic plant with thick, narrow, grey-green leaflets, in tufts on sea cliffs and shingle; small greenish-yellow umbels are distinct from other cliff umbellifers.

species.name: Crocosmia masoniorum
species.tip: Tall plant with pleated sword leaves and large orange flowers held facing outwards in a zigzag spike. Larger flowers than common montbretia; garden escape.

species.name: Crocosmia paniculata
species.tip: Stiff, pleated, sword-like leaves and dense orange-red flowers on branched spikes. Taller and more upright than common montbretia; occasional garden escape.

species.name: Crocosmia pottsii
species.tip: Pleated sword-shaped leaves and a branched spike of orange-yellow flowers. Parent of common montbretia; naturalised in damp ground, mostly in western areas.

species.name: Crocus ancyrensis
species.tip: Small, bright yellow crocus with a narrow white stripe down the leaf, flowering very early. Occasionally naturalised in grass near gardens.

species.name: Crocus biflorus
species.tip: Small crocus with white or lilac flowers, often feathered purple outside and yellow throat. Naturalised in grassland and churchyards; the name reflects old garden use.

species.name: Crocus chrysanthus
species.tip: Small early crocus with honey-scented golden-yellow flowers, often marked bronze outside. Naturalised in lawns and grassy banks near gardens.

species.name: Crocus kotschyanus
species.tip: Autumn-flowering crocus with lilac flowers and a yellow throat, appearing with or before narrow leaves. Occasional garden escape in grass.

species.name: Crocus neapolitanus
species.tip: Spring crocus with large white to purple flowers and a single white stripe on the leaf. Naturalised in meadows and parkland, often confused with other spring crocuses.

species.name: Crocus nudiflorus
species.tip: Large purple crocus appearing in autumn without leaves, which come later. Not to be confused with the colchicum. Local in a few English grasslands.

species.name: Crocus speciosus
species.tip: Autumn crocus with blue-violet flowers that have darker veins, appearing before the leaves. Naturalised locally in lawns and grass near gardens.

species.name: Crocus tommasinianus
species.tip: Garden crocus naturalised on lawns and verges, with slender silvery-lilac flowers with pointed petals and grass-like leaves with a white stripe; flowers very early.

species.name: Crocus vernus
species.tip: Crocus naturalised in grass with large, goblet-shaped purple or white flowers with a throat that is often hairy; leaves narrow with a pale central stripe, flowering in early spring.

species.name: Cruciata laevipes
species.tip: Hairy bedstraw of grassland and hedge banks with whorls of four oval, three-veined leaves and tiny yellow honey-scented flower clusters in leaf axils.

species.name: Cryptogramma crispa
species.tip: Bright green, crinkled fronds like parsley, with separate narrow fertile fronds. In screes and rocky mountain places and walls, mostly north and west.

species.name: Cuminum cyminum
species.tip: Slender annual with very fine thread-like leaflets and small white or pinkish umbels; a rare casual from spice or bird-seed, best confirmed by a specialist.

species.name: Cupressus lawsoniana
species.tip: Planted conifer with flattened sprays of tiny scale leaves that smell of parsley when crushed, a drooping leading shoot and small round cones.

species.name: Cuscuta epithymum
species.tip: Leafless red thread-like parasite twining over gorse and heather, with small clusters of pink flowers. Slender stems and compact heads separate it from greater dodder.

species.name: Cuscuta europaea
species.tip: Thicker, reddish-yellow parasitic threads on nettles and hops with pinkish flowers in clusters. Rare, mainly in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Cyclamen coum
species.tip: Small rounded leaves, silver-patterned or plain, and compact flowers with a dark mark at base. Naturalised in gardens and woods; flowers in late winter, not autumn.

species.name: Cyclamen graecum
species.tip: Larger, leathery leaves patterned silver, appearing after the autumn flowers. Rarely found outside gardens; scented pink flowers in autumn.

species.name: Cyclamen hederifolium
species.tip: Pink swept-back petals appearing before marbled, angular ivy-like leaves; naturalised in woods and churchyards in autumn.

species.name: Cyclamen repandum
species.tip: Glossy, dark, ivy-like toothed leaves, with deeply lobed edges, and sweet-scented carmine flowers in spring. Occasional garden escape in southern shady places.

species.name: Cymbalaria hepaticifolia
species.tip: Tiny creeping wall plant with shallowly lobed, rounded leaves and minute pale lilac snapdragon flowers. Much smaller and more delicate than Ivy-leaved Toadflax; a rare garden escape.

species.name: Cymbalaria muralis
species.tip: Trailing plant hanging from walls with fleshy ivy-shaped leaves; small lilac flowers with a yellow patch and a short spur. Common on old walls and pavements.

species.name: Cymbalaria pallida
species.tip: Trailing wall plant like Ivy-leaved Toadflax but with softly hairy, thicker leaves and pale lilac flowers with a yellow patch in the throat. Occasional garden escape.

species.name: Cynodon dactylon
species.tip: Creeping mat-former with three to five finger-like spikes radiating from the stem top; rare on southern sandy coasts and the Channel Islands, with a fringe of hairs as ligule.

species.name: Cynoglossum germanicum
species.tip: Hairy plant with leaves shiny green above and tongue-shaped, and dull reddish-purple small flowers; nutlets have barbs. Rare in dry woods; leaves greener and less grey than hounds-tongue.

species.name: Cynoglossum officinale
species.tip: Grey-green softly hairy plant with tongue-shaped leaves and dull maroon funnel flowers, smelling of mice. Fruits are flat nutlets covered in sticky barbs. Dry grassland and dunes.

species.name: Cynosurus cristatus
species.tip: Narrow stiff one-sided spike like a comb, shiny and green; a small awn on each spikelet and wiry flower stems; common in pasture.

species.name: Cynosurus echinatus
species.tip: Annual with one-sided lobed clusters of spikelets bearing long awns, unlike Crested Dog's-tail; scarce on dry open ground and waste, mainly in southern England.

species.name: Cyperus eragrostis
species.tip: A yellowish-green tufted plant of damp waste ground with flat, umbrella-like heads of pale flat spikelets from a leafy whorl, introduced from South America and spreading in the south.

species.name: Cyperus fuscus
species.tip: A small, very rare annual of bare, damp pond mud, with small clusters of dark red-brown flattened spikelets on short stems; looks like a tiny version of other galingales.

species.name: Cyperus longus
species.tip: Rare tall plant of wet places with a spreading umbel of reddish-brown flat spikelets and long leafy bracts; stem triangular; unlike a sedge, no sac-like fruits.

species.name: Cypripedium calceolus
species.tip: Spectacular orchid with a large yellow slipper-shaped lip and twisted maroon petals; extremely rare, in one site in northern England.

species.name: Cyrtomium falcatum
