species.tip: Glossy, leathery, undivided pinnae with pointed tips, like holly leaves. Occasional escape on shaded walls and in urban cracks, especially in the south and west.

species.name: Cyrtomium fortunei
species.tip: Duller than House Holly-fern, with pinnae distinctly toothed towards the tip and less glossy. Rare garden escape on walls and in shaded urban places.

species.name: Cystopteris diaphana
species.tip: Delicate bladder-fern with thin, pale green, twice-divided fronds and tiny toothed lobes, growing on shaded rocks. Not clearly native in Britain; specialist confirmation required.

species.name: Cystopteris dickieana
species.tip: Delicate fern with pale, twice-divided short fronds with blunt toothed lobes, growing in shady damp coastal rock crevices and caves, mostly in north-east Scotland. Needs specialist checking.

species.name: Cystopteris fragilis
species.tip: Small delicate fern of walls, rock crevices and mountains with thin twice-cut fronds and round spore patches under a hood; fronds die back in winter.

species.name: Cystopteris montana
species.tip: Delicate fern with broad, triangular, finely divided fronds, found on damp rocky ledges in high Scottish mountains. Larger and more finely cut than brittle bladder-fern.

species.name: Cytisus nigricans
species.tip: Upright broom-like shrub with three-parted leaves and spikes of small yellow flowers in summer. Garden shrub, rare casual.

species.name: Cytisus scoparius
species.tip: Green, angular-stemmed shrub with bright yellow pea flowers and small trifoliate leaves; lacks spines unlike gorse.

species.name: Cytisus striatus
species.tip: Tall broom with silky, hairy pods and green angled twigs, yellow flowers in May. Local in the south and west, on waste ground and heaths.

species.name: Daboecia cantabrica
species.tip: Low heath shrub with long spikes of large purple bells, and white-felted leaf undersides. Native only in western Ireland.

species.name: Dactylis glomerata
species.tip: Coarse tufted grass with dense one-sided clusters of spikelets at the ends of branches; flattened folded shoots and long ligule.

species.name: Dactylis polygama
species.tip: Slender woodland form of cock's-foot with slimmer clumps and fewer tufts; a specialist should confirm it against ordinary Cock's-foot, which has stout dense heads.

species.name: Dactylorhiza fuchsii
species.tip: Commonest British orchid of grassland and verges; pale pink to white flowers with looped, dashed lines on a three-lobed lip and spotted leaves; spike is cone-shaped.

species.name: Dactylorhiza incarnata
species.tip: Orchid of damp fens and meadows with narrow, upright, unspotted leaves hooded at the tip and flowers whose lip edges fold back; flowers vary in colour from flesh to purple.

species.name: Dactylorhiza kerryensis
species.tip: Marsh-orchid with pink-purple flowers and narrow, unspotted or lightly marked leaves; western Ireland, but requires a specialist to separate from relatives.

species.name: Dactylorhiza maculata
species.tip: Small, slender spotted-orchid of acid heath and bog with pale pink flowers, a rounded shallow-lobed lip with the middle lobe tiny, and short spotted leaves.

species.name: Dactylorhiza praetermissa
species.tip: Stout marsh-orchid of damp lowland meadows, dunes and fens with unspotted or lightly spotted broad leaves and a dense head of deep magenta flowers with a broad lip.

species.name: Dactylorhiza purpurella
species.tip: Marsh-orchid of northern wet meadows, deep purple flowers with a diamond-shaped lip and dark flower stalks and bracts; leaves are unspotted or ringed with spots, shorter than Southern.

species.name: Dactylorhiza traunsteinerioides
species.tip: Slender marsh-orchid of wet places with narrow unspotted leaves and few small purple flowers with a slim lip; a specialist should confirm.

species.name: Damasonium alisma
species.tip: Very rare plant of drying pond mud in the south-east, small white flowers followed by spreading, star-shaped fruits of six spiky arms; leaves oval.

species.name: Danthonia decumbens
species.tip: Short grass of heaths with few large spikelets in a sparse panicle, no awns, and a ligule of hairs; leaves have long hairs at the base.

species.name: Daphne laureola
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with glossy, leathery oval leaves in tufts at the shoot tips, small green flowers, and black berries; shaded woods on calcareous soils, winter flowering.

species.name: Daphne mezereum
species.tip: Deciduous shrub flowering on bare twigs in late winter with clusters of scented pink-purple flowers; leaves appear after, with red poisonous berries. Rare in southern limestone woods.

species.name: Darmera peltata
species.tip: Large garden plant with big round peltate leaves on long stalks, and pink flowers in a rounded head borne on bare stems before the leaves appear in spring.

species.name: Dasiphora fruticosa
species.tip: Small shrub with silky grey-green five-parted leaves and bright yellow flowers; wild only on a few rocky river banks in Upper Teesdale, Cumbria and western Ireland, but often planted.

species.name: Datura stramonium
species.tip: Rank, foul-smelling annual of waste ground with large trumpet-shaped white or purplish flowers and spiny, egg-shaped seed capsules; poisonous, with coarsely toothed leaves.

species.name: Daucus carota
species.tip: Umbels with divided, three-pronged bracts below and often a single dark red central floret; bird's-nest shape in fruit; found on chalk and coastal grassland.

species.name: Delairea odorata
species.tip: Climber with glossy, fleshy, ivy-like lobed leaves and clusters of small yellow button heads; rare, in sheltered gardens and walls in the south-west.

species.name: Deschampsia cespitosa
species.tip: Big tussocks with very sharp-ridged leaves rough to the touch, and a large airy silvery-purple panicle of small spikelets with a short awn.

species.name: Descurainia sophia
species.tip: Slender grey-green annual with very finely divided leaves and tiny pale yellow flowers. Seed pods are long, narrow and held angled upward on spreading stalks.

species.name: Dianthus armeria
species.tip: Upright pink with bright pink flowers in tight clusters, with white spots, with narrow leaves and sepals with long points. Rare, on dry open grass, southern England.

species.name: Dianthus barbatus
species.tip: Biennial with dense flat-topped clusters of flowers in pink, red or white with toothed petals, and broad flat leaves. Garden plant, escapes onto verges and waste ground.

species.name: Dianthus caryophyllus
species.tip: Grey-green perennial with large clove-scented flowers in pink, with toothed petals, and long narrow leaves. Naturalised on old walls and castle ruins.

species.name: Dianthus deltoides
species.tip: Low, mat-forming pink with small, pink flowers with a ring of darker spots, with toothed petals. Local on dry, sandy, grassy ground, in Britain.

species.name: Dianthus gallicus
species.tip: Pink with deeply cut, fringed flowers in pink, and blue-green leaves, growing in tufts. Native on sandy dunes on Jersey, and naturalised in Cornwall.

species.name: Dianthus gratianopolitanus
species.tip: Small blue-green tufted plant with solitary pink flowers with toothed petals and a clove scent. Very rare, restricted to limestone cliffs in Cheddar Gorge.

species.name: Dianthus plumarius
species.tip: Garden pink with deeply fringed, fragrant pink or white flowers and grey narrow leaves growing in a loose clump. Escapes onto old walls and rockeries.

species.name: Diapensia lapponica
species.tip: Extremely rare cushion plant with cream-white five-petalled flowers over tight evergreen leaves. Known only in the Highlands, near Lochaber.

species.name: Dicentra eximia
species.tip: Garden perennial with finely cut greyish leaves and arching heart-shaped pink flowers; a rare escape, not usually long-established.

species.name: Dicentra formosa
species.tip: Garden plant with finely cut blue-green leaves and hanging pink heart-shaped flowers; locally naturalised, mainly in northern and western Britain.

species.name: Dicksonia antarctica
species.tip: Tree fern with a thick fibrous trunk and a crown of large arching fronds. Planted in mild gardens, occasionally self-sown in western areas.

species.name: Digitalis lutea
species.tip: Tall foxglove with slender spikes of small, narrow pale yellow bells and shiny narrow leaves. Smaller flowers than Common Foxglove and wrong colour; a rare garden escape.

species.name: Digitalis purpurea
species.tip: Tall spike of nodding, tubular purple-pink flowers spotted inside, above a rosette of large downy leaves. Woodland clearings, heaths and banks; the only large tubular purple spire in this family.

species.name: Digitaria ischaemum
species.tip: Small annual with two to six finger-like spikes joined at the top and hairless spikelets; rare casual, separated from Hairy Finger-grass by the lack of hairs.

species.name: Digitaria sanguinalis
species.tip: Sprawling annual with finger-like spikes and bristly hairy leaf sheaths, purplish when ripe; occasional casual on arable and waste land in the south.

species.name: Diphasiastrum alpinum
species.tip: Greyish-green clubmoss with flattened, branching shoots and tiny scale-like leaves pressed along the stems; grows on mountain heaths and grassland in northern and western uplands.

species.name: Diplotaxis muralis
species.tip: Yellow flowers with dark veins on walls and railway tracks; leaves lobed and mainly in a basal rosette, with a leafless-looking stem and strong smell.

species.name: Diplotaxis tenuifolia
species.tip: Yellow crucifer of walls and waste ground, with strong smell when crushed and deeply cut leaves. Taller and bushier than Annual Wall-rocket.

species.name: Dipsacus fullonum
species.tip: Very tall prickly biennial with egg-shaped spiny heads and long curved bracts, flowering as a purple ring; basal leaves form water-holding cups; rough grassland and verges.

species.name: Dipsacus laciniatus
species.tip: Tall teasel with deeply cut, divided stem leaves and spiny stems, white to pale pink heads. Rare casual or escape, differing from common teasel in its deeply lobed leaves.

species.name: Dipsacus pilosus
species.tip: Branched teasel with small rounded heads of pale lilac or white flowers, stalked leaves and recurved spines. Local in damp woods and hedgerows in southern England.

species.name: Dipsacus sativus
species.tip: Spiny teasel with prickly seed heads bearing stiff hooked bracts, once used for raising cloth. Lilac flowers; rare outside cultivation, found on verges and waste ground.

species.name: Dipsacus strigosus
species.tip: Tall teasel with pale yellow-white flowers in oval heads, bristly stems and long prickly leaves. Rare casual or escape, most likely misidentified as wild teasel.

species.name: Disphyma crassifolium
species.tip: Low creeping succulent with thick, bluish-green fleshy leaves and pale pink flowers; naturalised mainly on southern and south-western coasts, easily confused with other iceplants.

species.name: Dittrichia graveolens
species.tip: Sticky, strong-smelling plant with narrow leaves and small yellow heads with short rays, flowering late; casual on salted roadsides and waste ground.

species.name: Dittrichia viscosa
species.tip: Tall sticky, aromatic fleabane with leafy stems and many yellow daisy heads in autumn; rare casual from the Mediterranean, mostly roadsides in southern England.

species.name: Doronicum columnae
species.tip: Garden escape with large yellow daisies on stems with heart-shaped basal leaves and smaller clasping stem leaves; naturalised on shady banks.

species.name: Doronicum pardalianches
species.tip: Early-flowering plant with large yellow daisies and big heart-shaped basal leaves, clasping stem leaves. Naturalised in woods and shady verges, spring and early summer.

species.name: Doronicum plantagineum
species.tip: Garden escape with yellow daisy heads on stems with broad plantain-like basal leaves, finely hairy; occasionally naturalised in woods and verges.

species.name: Draba aizoides
species.tip: Tiny mountain cushion plant with bright yellow flowers and stiff fringed narrow leaves in a rosette. Rare, on rock in Wales, plus Gower coast.

species.name: Draba incana
species.tip: Whitlow-grass with small white flowers, a leafy stem and star-shaped hairs that make the plant look grey. Local on mountain rocks and dunes.

species.name: Draba norvegica
species.tip: Very small tufted mountain whitlow-grass with white flowers and hairy toothed leaves, usually without stem leaves. Very rare, on high Scottish rock ledges.

species.name: Drabella muralis
species.tip: Slender annual with white flowers, oval clasping leaves on the stem and a rosette. Rare, found on limestone walls and rocks, mainly Wales and west England.

species.name: Dracunculus vulgaris
species.tip: Large garden arum with deeply cut, fan-like leaves, a mottled stem and a huge dark purple spathe that smells foul; rarely naturalised in the south.

species.name: Drosanthemum floribundum
species.tip: Straggling shrubby succulent with narrow sausage-like leaves covered in glistening bumps and many small pink-purple daisy-like flowers; a coastal garden escape in the south-west.

species.name: Drosera anglica
species.tip: Sticky-leaved carnivorous bog plant with long narrow leaves held erect and small white flowers. Told from round-leaved sundew by its elongated leaves.

species.name: Drosera intermedia
species.tip: Carnivorous plant with oblong leaves that curve upwards in a fan and flower stalks that arise from below the rosette. Grows in wet peat and bog.

species.name: Drosera rotundifolia
species.tip: Insect-eating plant of bogs with a rosette of round red sticky-haired leaves; small white flowers on a slender spike, summer, in acid wet moors.

species.name: Dryas octopetala
species.tip: Mat-forming mountain plant with small oak-like glossy leaves, white beneath, and large white flowers with eight petals and a yellow centre, then fluffy seed heads; on limestone upland.

species.name: Drymochloa sylvatica
species.tip: Tall shade-loving fescue with broad flat leaves and a loose nodding panicle; found in ancient woods in the south and north, unlike tough Giant Fescue.

species.name: Dryopteris aemula
species.tip: Fronds triangular, finely divided, yellowish-green with curled-up pinna edges; smells of new hay when crushed. Western woods and shaded banks, mostly in Wales, Ireland and the west.

species.name: Dryopteris affinis
species.tip: Golden-brown scaly stalk and glossy leathery fronds with blunt, toothed tips of pinnules near the tip; darker spot at pinnule bases; woods and hedgebanks.

species.name: Dryopteris carthusiana
species.tip: Pale green, triangular, finely divided fronds held at an angle, with pale scales on stalk; damp woods and fens, rarer than Broad Buckler-fern.

species.name: Dryopteris cristata
species.tip: Narrow, upright, ladder-like fronds with pinnae held in a flat plane, unlike other buckler-ferns. Rare, in fens and wet woods of East Anglia and Ireland.

species.name: Dryopteris dilatata
species.tip: Large spreading arching fronds with darker central blotch on scales and dark-centred stalk scales; widespread in woods, the commonest buckler-fern.

species.name: Dryopteris expansa
species.tip: Triangular, pale yellowish-green fronds, thrice divided, with small pale-centred scales on the stalk. Damp upland woods and rocky slopes, mainly northern Britain.

species.name: Dryopteris filix-mas
species.tip: Shuttlecock of tall dull green fronds with rounded pinnule tips and a dark spot where pinnules join the midrib; common in woods and hedgerows.

species.name: Dryopteris oreades
species.tip: Golden-green fronds with a strong sweet smell when crushed, tightly tufted and tapering to the base. Mountain rocks and scree, common in the north and west.

species.name: Dryopteris submontana
species.tip: Stiff, greyish-green, leathery fronds with glandular undersides; lime-loving. Limestone pavement and rocks in northern England, north Wales and western Ireland.

species.name: Dysphania ambrosioides
species.tip: Aromatic annual or perennial, strongly scented when crushed, with narrow toothed leaves and tiny greenish flowers in leafy spikes; found on waste ground and pavements.

species.name: Echinochloa crus-galli
species.tip: Warm-season annual weed with a head made of several short, dense, one-sided racemes, often purplish; no ligule at all, which helps identify it.

species.name: Echinops bannaticus
species.tip: Spiny garden plant with ball-shaped blue heads and deeply cut leaves woolly beneath; rare escape, told from thistles by globe-shaped flower heads.

species.name: Echinops exaltatus
species.tip: Very tall spiny garden escape with ball-shaped whitish blue heads and deeply cut leaves white-felted beneath; uncommon on waste ground.

species.name: Echinops sphaerocephalus
species.tip: Tall spiny plant with big spherical grey-white to blue heads and deeply cut leaves, cobwebby underneath, with sticky glands; scattered garden escape.

species.name: Echium pininana
species.tip: Very tall bristly biennial forming a huge spire of pale blue flowers in its second summer. Naturalised mainly in Cornwall, Scilly and south-west coasts. Far taller than other viper's-buglosses.

species.name: Echium plantagineum
species.tip: Bristly plant with funnel flowers that are pink in bud, opening bright violet-blue, with five stamens sticking out. Mostly Cornwall, Scilly and Channel Islands; wider flowers than Viper's-bugloss.

species.name: Echium rosulatum
species.tip: Close to Purple Viper's-bugloss but with a looser, less leafy flower spike and smaller blue flowers. Very local, mainly the Lizard in Cornwall; needs expert confirmation.

species.name: Echium vulgare
species.tip: Bristly plant with spikes of funnel-shaped flowers, pink in bud turning bright blue, with protruding red stamens. Dry grassland, dunes and chalk.

species.name: Egeria densa
species.tip: Bright green waterweed with leaves in whorls of four to six and relatively large white three-petalled flowers above the surface. Introduced in ponds and canals.

species.name: Elaeagnus commutata
species.tip: Silvery, scaly shrub with oval leaves and small yellow fragrant flowers. A rare planted shrub that occasionally persists.

species.name: Elatine hexandra
species.tip: Tiny creeping annual with opposite oval leaves and minute pinkish or white flowers. Rare in the margins of ponds and lakes.

species.name: Elatine hydropiper
species.tip: Tiny annual of muddy margins with rounded leaves and minute flowers, the petals pinkish. Rare, in Britain mainly in northern England.

species.name: Eleocharis acicularis
species.tip: A tiny, creeping plant with hair-thin stems forming a green mat at the edges of ponds, with a small, pale spikelet at each stem tip and no leaf blades.

species.name: Eleocharis mamillata
species.tip: A northern spike-rush of lake and pond margins with a blunt single spikelet and a wide, prominent bump on top of the fruit; stems are stout and grooved, and a specialist may need to confirm.

species.name: Eleocharis multicaulis
species.tip: Slender spike-rush of wet heaths and bogs, one brown spikelet per stem; stems many, thin and round; the sheath mouth is oblique and reddish.

species.name: Eleocharis palustris
species.tip: Leafless round green stems, each with a single large oval brown spikelet; creeping in shallow water and wet ground; the stem is smooth and ridged when dry.

species.name: Eleocharis parvula
species.tip: A tiny, rare spike-rush of coastal muddy brackish margins in southern and eastern England, forming short, bright green turf with narrow stems and tiny single spikelets.

species.name: Eleocharis quinqueflora
species.tip: Short stiff stems with a single small dark brown spikelet of few flowers on damp base-rich ground; lowest scale clasps the spikelet's base completely.

species.name: Eleocharis uniglumis
species.tip: A spike-rush of damp grassland, dune slacks and brackish marsh with a single pointed spikelet, the lowest glume completely encircling the base; the spikelet is slimmer than Common Spike-rush.

species.name: Eleogiton fluitans
species.tip: Aquatic plant with thin, soft floating leaves in pools and ditches; tiny single spikelet at stem tips; stems trail and root; looks like a slender mat of green threads.

species.name: Elodea callitrichoides
species.tip: Narrow waterweed like Canadian Waterweed but with thinner, slightly twisted leaves. Specialist check needed; very rare, introduced in canals.

species.name: Elodea canadensis
species.tip: Submerged plant with whorls of three blunt, rather broad dark leaves that curve back; leaves widest near the middle and less pointed than in Nuttalls Waterweed.

species.name: Elodea nuttallii
species.tip: Submerged plant with whorls of three narrow, pointed, strongly curved leaves, paler and softer than Canadian Waterweed; common in ponds and canals, spreading in recent decades.

species.name: Elymus athericus
species.tip: Stiff, bluish-green couch of salt marsh edges with a flat spike of spikelets set edge-on in two rows; leaves rolled and ribbed on top.

species.name: Elymus caninus
species.tip: Tufted couch of woods and hedges with an arching spike and long awns on the spikelets; no creeping rhizomes unlike Common Couch.

species.name: Elymus junceiformis
species.tip: Blue-grey stiff couch of foredunes with a brittle spike, spikelets overlapping and unawned; leaves rolled and ribbed above, creeping by rhizomes.

species.name: Elymus repens
species.tip: Creeping weed forming patches with a flat two-rowed spike; narrow claw-like auricles at the leaf base and white rhizomes distinguish it.

species.name: Empetrum nigrum
species.tip: Low evergreen with needle-like leaves grooved beneath, tiny pinkish flowers in leaf axils and black berries; moorland and mountain heath, unlike heathers.

species.name: Epilobium alsinifolium
species.tip: Small mountain willowherb with a creeping base, pale pink flowers with notched petals, and small toothed leaves; grows by springs and streams in the northern uplands.

species.name: Epilobium anagallidifolium
species.tip: Tiny creeping willowherb with a nodding top and few, pale pink or reddish flowers; leaves almost smooth-edged; grows by mountain streams and in wet flushes.

species.name: Epilobium brachycarpum
species.tip: North American annual willowherb with flowers in a branched panicle, small pink petals and narrow toothed leaves; casual and increasing on waste ground in the south.

species.name: Epilobium brunnescens
species.tip: Tiny mat-forming willowherb with creeping rooting stems, rounded little leaves and solitary small flowers; common on paths, walls and rocky ground, mostly in the north and west.

species.name: Epilobium ciliatum
species.tip: Upright, often branching willowherb with narrow leaves, small pale pink flowers and glandular hairs on the upper stem; the seed pods are glandular too. Common weed of gardens and waste ground.

species.name: Epilobium hirsutum
species.tip: Tall, stout, softly hairy willowherb of ditches and streamsides with large rose-pink flowers and a four-lobed stigma; leaves clasp the stem and smell faintly fruity.

species.name: Epilobium komarovianum
species.tip: Low creeping willowherb, with small bronze-tinged oval leaves and tiny pale pink to white flowers; a New Zealand alien, so a specialist should confirm.

species.name: Epilobium lanceolatum
species.tip: Downy willowherb with leaves narrowing into stalks and pale pink petals; unlike Broad-leaved Willowherb, stigma is club-shaped; in southern England on waste ground.

species.name: Epilobium montanum
species.tip: Common willowherb of shady places and walls with short-stalked or unstalked, broad, opposite oval leaves, small pink flowers with a four-lobed stigma and a rounded, hairy stem.

species.name: Epilobium obscurum
species.tip: Slender willowherb of damp ground with a stem bearing raised lines, small pink flowers and short pods; leaves are narrow, stalkless and often reddish. Spreads by leafy runners in autumn.

species.name: Epilobium palustre
species.tip: Slender willowherb of bogs and fens with narrow, nearly untoothed leaves, small pale pink or whitish flowers and a rounded stem covered in short curved hairs.

species.name: Epilobium parviflorum
species.tip: Softly shaggy willowherb of wet places with stalkless, soft-hairy leaves and larger pink flowers than other small ones, with a four-lobed stigma; stem has spreading hairs.

species.name: Epilobium pedunculare
species.tip: New Zealand creeping willowherb with small round leaves and pale pink to white flowers; commonly escapes on paths, walls and rockeries.

species.name: Epilobium roseum
species.tip: Slender willowherb with distinct leaf stalks, tiny white flowers fading pink, and a club-shaped, unlobed stigma; grows in gardens, shade and waste places.

species.name: Epilobium tetragonum
species.tip: Upright willowherb with a stem bearing four raised lines, narrow stalkless leaves and small pink flowers with a four-lobed stigma; lacks glandular hairs. Common on open, disturbed ground.

species.name: Epipactis atrorubens
species.tip: Orchid with dark wine-red, vanilla-scented flowers and downy stems; grows on limestone in northern England, Wales and the Burren.

species.name: Epipactis dunensis
species.tip: Yellowish-green helleborine of dune slacks in northern England and north Wales, with mostly self-pollinated flowers; a specialist should confirm.

species.name: Epipactis helleborine
species.tip: Tall woodland orchid with oval, ribbed, spirally arranged leaves and a one-sided spike of nodding dull green and purple-pink flowers; often grows in shade, in hedgerows and urban spots.

species.name: Epipactis leptochila
species.tip: Slender helleborine of beechwoods with nodding yellowish-green flowers with a narrow lip, and leaves in two ranks; local in the south.

species.name: Epipactis palustris
species.tip: Marsh orchid with showy flowers whose lip is white and frilly, and brownish sepals; grows in fens and dune slacks.

species.name: Epipactis phyllanthes
species.tip: Helleborine with drooping, pale green flowers that hardly open and have a blunt lip; found in dunes and beechwoods; a specialist should confirm.

species.name: Epipactis purpurata
species.tip: Late-flowering helleborine with whitish-green flowers, leaves flushed violet below and stems in clumps; found in shady southern woodland.

species.name: Epipogium aphyllum
species.tip: Leafless, pale, nearly translucent orchid with a few pinkish-yellow flowers; extremely rare in deep shade of old beechwoods in the Chilterns.

species.name: Equisetum arvense
species.tip: Common weed with separate early pinkish fertile spring stems, then green sterile stems with simple whorled branches; sheaths have teeth, branches solid and ridged.

species.name: Equisetum fluviatile
species.tip: Horsetail of ponds and ditch edges with smooth, hollow, pale green stems with thin sheaths and branches few or none; fertile cones borne at tips of ordinary stems.

species.name: Equisetum hyemale
species.tip: Evergreen unbranched horsetail with stiff, rough, grey-green stems. Told from other horsetails by its black-banded sheath and very rough stem.

species.name: Equisetum palustre
species.tip: Horsetail of damp ground with grooved stems having wide black-edged sheath teeth with a white margin, and branches either absent or whorled; slender and spreading.

species.name: Equisetum pratense
species.tip: Slender horsetail with few whorled, simple branches and a rough texture. Very rare, found in a few Scottish areas.

species.name: Equisetum ramosissimum
species.tip: Slender, branching horsetail with grooved stems and small black-tipped teeth. Very rare, in damp places in Britain.

species.name: Equisetum sylvaticum
species.tip: Elegant horsetail of damp woodlands with feathery, repeatedly branched whorls that droop; sheaths on main stem are loose and reddish-brown, with fused teeth.

species.name: Equisetum telmateia
species.tip: Very large, robust horsetail of springs and wet banks; pale unbranched fertile stems in spring, later tall white-green stems with many dense, fine whorled branches.

species.name: Equisetum variegatum
species.tip: Slender evergreen horsetail with dark sheaths that have pale margins. Local in dunes and damp sand.

species.name: Eragrostis curvula
species.tip: Tufted South African grass with very fine curled leaves and a drooping lead-grey panicle; escapes from planting in towns and roadsides. Leaves are extremely thin and wiry.

species.name: Eragrostis pilosa
species.tip: Delicate annual with a very fine airy panicle of greyish spikelets and hairs at the throat; rare casual, mostly seen in towns and waste ground.

species.name: Eranthis hyemalis
species.tip: Garden escape in woods and parks; yellow cup flowers in mid-winter sitting on a ruff of deeply cut leaves.

species.name: Erepsia heteropetala
species.tip: South African succulent rarely met as a coastal garden escape; fleshy three-sided leaves and magenta daisy-like flowers make it look like other iceplants, so confirm with a specialist.

species.name: Erica ciliaris
species.tip: Heather with large pink bell flowers on one side of the spike and fringed leaves in threes. Local on southern heaths and in west Ireland.

species.name: Erica cinerea
species.tip: Bright reddish-purple bells in whorled clusters along the shoots; dry heaths and rocky slopes, flowering earlier than Cross-leaved Heath, which is paler and on wet ground.

species.name: Erica erigena
species.tip: Tall heath with pinkish-purple bells and protruding brown anthers that flower early in spring. Native in western Ireland, introduced elsewhere.

species.name: Erica lusitanica
species.tip: Tall evergreen heath with fine bright green leaves in whorls of three and white bells. Naturalised in Cornwall and Devon, flowering in winter.

species.name: Erica mackayana
species.tip: Heather with whorls of three leaves and pink-purple bells; hairy leaves distinguish it from cross-leaved heath. Native in western Ireland.

species.name: Erica terminalis
species.tip: Tall evergreen heath with narrow whorled leaves and many pink bells in clusters. Planted in gardens and occasionally naturalised.

species.name: Erica tetralix
species.tip: Pale pink bells in a terminal head and grey downy leaves in whorls of four forming a cross; wet heaths and bogs.

species.name: Erica vagans
species.tip: Dense heath with pink or white bells with dark anthers visible and dense leaves. Native on the Lizard in Cornwall only.

species.name: Erigeron acris
species.tip: Small daisy with thin lilac-purple rays and a yellow disc, hairy erect stem, narrow leaves. Dry grassland, walls and dunes on calcareous ground.

species.name: Erigeron annuus
species.tip: Slender daisy with many small white heads with very narrow rays, toothed hairy leaves; spreading on walls and verges, mainly England; taller than common daisy.

species.name: Erigeron bonariensis
species.tip: Tall weed of urban pavements and waste ground with small whitish heads in leafy clusters, rays barely longer than the bracts; stems grey-hairy.

species.name: Erigeron borealis
species.tip: Small mountain plant of Scottish high-level rock ledges, with few mauve to purple rayed heads with yellow centre; leaves basal and hairy, scarce.

species.name: Erigeron canadensis
species.tip: Tall, bristly, much-branched weed with masses of tiny whitish heads whose rays barely show. Waste ground, pavements and railway land, summer to autumn.

species.name: Erigeron floribundus
species.tip: Urban weed of walls and pavements with small whitish heads of tiny rays, narrow hairy toothed leaves; common in southern England, often mistaken for Canadian fleabane.

species.name: Erigeron glaucus
species.tip: Garden plant naturalised on coastal cliffs and walls with fleshy spoon-shaped leaves and big lilac to pink daisy heads with yellow centres.

species.name: Erigeron karvinskianus
species.tip: Wall-colonising daisy with white rays turning pink and yellow centres, often with three-lobed leaves. Flowers for months on walls, steps and rocks.

species.name: Erigeron philadelphicus
species.tip: Garden escape with pink or white daisy-like heads with numerous very slender rays, soft hairy stem and clasping leaves; walls and pavements.

species.name: Erigeron sumatrensis
species.tip: Tall hairy weed of urban waste ground, heads cream with tiny rays hidden in cluster; resembles Canadian fleabane but greyer and taller.

species.name: Erinus alpinus
species.tip: Small tufted plant on walls and rocks with spoon-shaped toothed leaves and short clusters of five-lobed purple-pink flowers. Established on old walls in a few places.

species.name: Eriocaulon aquaticum
species.tip: Aquatic plant with submerged narrow leaves and stalks bearing small greyish-white buttons. Very rare in Britain, in lochs of Skye, and in western Ireland.

species.name: Eriophorum angustifolium
species.tip: Several nodding white cottony heads per stem in acid bogs and wet moors; leaves keeled and triangular at tip; spreads by runners, not in tussocks.

species.name: Eriophorum gracile
species.tip: A rare cottongrass of wet bogs with usually one to three small drooping white cotton heads on thin stems and very narrow, triangular leaves; heads are less fluffy than in other species.

species.name: Eriophorum latifolium
species.tip: A cottongrass of calcareous fens with several nodding white heads and flat, broad leaves, rough edges and a stem that is three-sided above; the heads cluster, unlike Common Cottongrass.

species.name: Eriophorum vaginatum
species.tip: Single large white cottony head on each stem, forming dense tussocks on wet moorland and bogs; leaves thin and bristle-like; blooms early.

species.name: Erodium aethiopicum
species.tip: Low perennial rosette with feathery hairy leaves and pink flowers. Specialist check advised; sporadic as a garden escape or casual.

species.name: Erodium cicutarium
species.tip: Pink flowers with five petals and feathery pinnate leaves; fruit forms a long stork's bill; found on dry sandy and coastal soils, unlike the lobed leaves of Geranium.

species.name: Erodium manescavii
species.tip: Tufted perennial with pinnate leaves and bright magenta flowers having dark veins. Garden plant that rarely becomes naturalised.

species.name: Erodium maritimum
species.tip: Low plant with tiny pale pink or no petals and unlobed or slightly lobed leaves. Found on coastal turf in south-west England, Wales and Ireland.

species.name: Erodium moschatum
species.tip: Sticky, musk-scented plant with pinnate leaves having toothed leaflets and flowers with purple petals. Found on coastal banks and waste ground, mainly in the south and west.

species.name: Erophila glabrescens
species.tip: Tiny spring annual of dry bare ground with deeply notched white petals; one of a critical group of microspecies. Specialist needed to confirm.

species.name: Erophila majuscula
species.tip: Tiny annual whitlow-grass with deeply notched white petals; one of a critical microspecies group distinguished by fine detail. Specialist needed to confirm.

species.name: Erophila verna
species.tip: Tiny spring annual of walls and dry banks with a rosette of small leaves, leafless stems and white petals split nearly to the base.

species.name: Eruca vesicaria
species.tip: Salad plant with cream flowers veined purple and a peppery smell. Leaves have a large end lobe. Occasional escape on waste ground and verges.

species.name: Ervilia hirsuta
species.tip: Slender scrambling vetch with many pairs of narrow leaflets ending in tendrils and tiny pale lilac flowers; pods hairy with two seeds.

species.name: Ervilia sylvatica
species.tip: Scrambling vetch with many pairs of leaflets and drooping sprays of white flowers veined with purple. Local in woods, cliffs and rocky areas.

species.name: Ervum gracile
species.tip: Slender climbing vetch with small pale blue-lilac flowers in few-flowered stalked heads; leaflets narrow. Very local on waste ground and field margins. Check with a specialist.

species.name: Ervum tetraspermum
species.tip: Like Hairy Tare but flowers slightly larger, pale lilac, one or two together, and the pods hairless with about four seeds.

species.name: Eryngium amethystinum
species.tip: Spiny sea-holly relative with steel-blue stems and flower heads and stiff lobed leaves; a rare garden plant, only an occasional escape, needing specialist confirmation.

species.name: Eryngium campestre
species.tip: Spiny whitish-green thistle-like umbellifer with ribbed leaves and small rounded heads; very rare in a handful of southern sites, and a smaller plant than Sea-holly.

species.name: Eryngium giganteum
species.tip: Biennial garden plant with silvery-green spiny bracts around a steel-blue egg-shaped flower head, and heart-shaped basal leaves; seeds into gravel and waste ground.

species.name: Eryngium maritimum
species.tip: Steely blue-grey, spiny, leathery plant of sand and shingle, with round blue-violet flower heads wrapped in spiny bracts; a distinctive dune and beach plant.

species.name: Eryngium planum
species.tip: Branched garden plant with many small blue thistly heads and spiny-edged, flat leaves; has more heads than Sea-holly, which has a few larger ones. Occasional outcast.

species.name: Eryngium variifolium
species.tip: Grass-like leaved eryngo with spine-tipped narrow leaves and blue-white heads; an uncommon garden plant and a very rare escape, needing confirmation by a specialist.

species.name: Erysimum cheiranthoides
species.tip: Annual of arable fields and waste ground with narrow toothed leaves, small pale yellow flowers and thin four-sided pods pressed up the stem.

species.name: Erysimum cheiri
species.tip: Fragrant yellow to orange-brown flowers on old walls and cliffs; narrow dark green leaves and a woody base distinguish it from other yellow crucifers.

species.name: Erythranthe guttata
species.tip: Streamsides; large bright yellow two-lipped snapdragon-like flowers, often with small red spots in the throat; opposite toothed leaves.

species.name: Erythranthe moschata
species.tip: Sticky, softly hairy monkeyflower with pale yellow flowers and a musky smell, often now scentless. Wet places, widely naturalised.

species.name: Erythranthe peregrina
species.tip: Hybrid-derived monkeyflower with yellow flowers heavily blotched with red-brown, found by streams in parts of Scotland. Needs careful checking against other monkeyflowers.

species.name: Erythronium dens-canis
species.tip: Nodding pink flower with swept-back petals and blotched leaves in pairs, with no true stem. Naturalised locally in woods and grassy places.

species.name: Eschscholzia californica
species.tip: Garden escape of verges and waste ground with bright orange-yellow, silky four-petalled flowers and blue-green finely divided leaves.

species.name: Euonymus europaeus
species.tip: Shrub with green square-ish twigs, opposite finely toothed leaves and bright pink four-lobed fruits opening to orange seeds; hedges and scrub on chalk and limestone.

species.name: Euonymus japonicus
species.tip: Glossy evergreen shrub with thick, toothed, dark green leaves and small greenish flowers. Widely planted by the sea and sometimes self-sown in hedges.

species.name: Eupatorium cannabinum
species.tip: Tall plant with flat-topped clusters of tiny pale pink fluffy heads over hairy, palmately lobed opposite leaves. Wet places, fens and ditches, late summer.

species.name: Euphorbia amygdaloides
species.tip: Shady woodland spurge with evergreen, dark, hairy leaves in rosettes and reddish stems; yellow-green bracts form a branched head in spring, unlike the annual field spurges.

species.name: Euphorbia corallioides
species.tip: Tall hairy spurge with oval leaves and yellow-green flower heads with rounded, kidney-shaped glands. Casual or planted occasionally, escaped from gardens.

species.name: Euphorbia cyparissias
species.tip: Tufted spurge with many thin narrow leaves on short branches and yellow-green bracts turning reddish. Garden escape on dry banks and in graveyards.

species.name: Euphorbia dulcis
species.tip: Spurge with oval blunt leaves that turn purple, softly hairy; flower glands are purplish. Rare, naturalised in shady places, escaped from gardens.

species.name: Euphorbia esula
species.tip: Spurge with narrow leaves and yellow-green bracts, spreading by creeping roots. A group needing specialist confirmation; local casual on waste ground.

species.name: Euphorbia exigua
species.tip: Small slender annual of arable fields and bare ground with very narrow, grass-like leaves tipped with a tiny point; bracts are narrow and crescent-shaped glands have two horns.

species.name: Euphorbia helioscopia
species.tip: Common annual of cultivated land with rounded, finely toothed leaves broadest near the tip and a flat-topped umbel of five rays, like a tiny sun.

species.name: Euphorbia hyberna
species.tip: Hairy perennial spurge with oval leaves and warty fruits, yellow-green. Rare, in woods of south-west Ireland and a few places in south-west England.

species.name: Euphorbia lathyris
species.tip: Tall, blue-green biennial with crossed pairs of long narrow leaves up the stem; garden escape with fat green caper-like fruits.

species.name: Euphorbia oblongata
species.tip: Upright perennial spurge with narrow oval leaves finely toothed near the tip and yellowish-green flower heads. Garden escape, naturalised locally. Check against similar spurges with a specialist.

species.name: Euphorbia paralias
species.tip: Fleshy bluish-green spurge of sand dunes with crowded overlapping oval leaves in rows up the stem. Local on southern and western coasts.

species.name: Euphorbia peplus
species.tip: Small garden weed with smooth, stalked, blue-green oval leaves and a three-rayed umbel; glands bear long slender horns, unlike toothed Sun Spurge.

species.name: Euphorbia platyphyllos
species.tip: Softly hairy annual spurge with oval toothed leaves and three-lobed flower heads; warty fruits. Rare, in arable fields and bare ground in southern England.

species.name: Euphorbia portlandica
species.tip: Hairless blue-green spurge with oval leaves, often with red stems; sandy coast. Local on southern and western coasts of Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Euphorbia stricta
species.tip: Slender annual spurge with oval toothed leaves and small, warty-fruited flower heads. Very rare, in the Wye Valley and Gloucestershire woodland edges.

species.name: Euphorbia waldsteinii
species.tip: Spurge with narrow leaves and yellowish-green flower heads. Rare garden escape; hard to separate from Leafy Spurge, so a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Euphrasia arctica
species.tip: Small semi-parasitic eyebright of northern and western coasts and grassland with whitish to lilac flowers; best identified by habitat, glandular hairs and the leaf shape. Hard to separate from other eyebrights.

species.name: Euphrasia cambrica
species.tip: Small eyebright of short upland turf in Wales. Eyebrights are very difficult; a specialist is needed to confirm this species.

species.name: Euphrasia campbelliae
species.tip: Rare eyebright restricted to the Outer Hebrides. Specialist examination of hairs, leaves and corolla is needed to separate it from other eyebrights.

species.name: Euphrasia confusa
species.tip: Tufted eyebright of heath and acid grassland, with white or lilac flowers and toothed leaves; very similar to other eyebrights, which need careful examination to separate.

species.name: Euphrasia foulaensis
species.tip: Small, often branched eyebright of northern Scottish coasts and islands including Shetland. Eyebrights are a difficult group; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Euphrasia frigida
species.tip: Small eyebright of high Scottish mountain grassland and flushes, with slender stem and small flowers. Identification within the genus needs a specialist.

species.name: Euphrasia heslop-harrisonii
species.tip: Rare British eyebright found in few places in the north. A specialist is needed to confirm it among the many similar eyebright species.

species.name: Euphrasia marshallii
species.tip: Eyebright of northern Scottish coasts and islands, often short and rather stiff. Within this difficult group a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Euphrasia micrantha
species.tip: Small eyebright of heaths and dry grassland, with tiny pale lilac to whitish flowers, glandular hairs, and slender unbranched or sparsely branched stems.

species.name: Euphrasia nemorosa
species.tip: The commonest eyebright of grassland and heaths, with white or lilac flowers with a yellow spot and purple veins, and sharply toothed, dark-green leaves; no hairs on glands.

species.name: Euphrasia officinalis
species.tip: Small semi-parasitic annual with toothed opposite leaves and white flowers marked lilac and yellow. Many similar species exist; a specialist is needed to name the exact species.

species.name: Euphrasia ostenfeldii
species.tip: Small eyebright of northern coasts and islands, mainly in Scotland. As with other eyebrights, a specialist is needed to confirm the species.

species.name: Euphrasia pseudokerneri
species.tip: Eyebright of dry chalk and limestone grassland in southern and eastern England, usually branched. A specialist is needed to separate it from similar species.

species.name: Euphrasia rivularis
species.tip: Upland eyebright of wet places in Wales and northern England, often with a rather leafy stem. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Euphrasia rotundifolia
species.tip: Small eyebright with rounded leaves, found on north-western Scottish coasts and islands. A specialist is needed to tell it from other eyebrights.

species.name: Euphrasia salisburgensis
species.tip: Slender eyebright with narrow, almost hairless leaves and white flowers, on limestone pavement and dunes in western Ireland and north Wales. Check with a specialist.

species.name: Euphrasia scottica
species.tip: Eyebright of damp grassland and flushes in northern Britain and Ireland, often unbranched and rather leafy. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Euphrasia tetraquetra
species.tip: Eyebright of coastal and downland turf with a stiff, branched habit. The genus is difficult, so a specialist is needed to confirm the species.

species.name: Euphrasia vigursii
species.tip: Rare eyebright of heaths and cliff turf in Cornwall and south-west England, with relatively large flowers. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Euthamia graminifolia
species.tip: Tall North American goldenrod with narrow grass-like leaves bearing translucent dots, flat-topped clusters of tiny golden yellow heads; naturalised on damp waste ground.

species.name: Exaculum pusillum
species.tip: Tiny, slender annual with small pink-and-white flowers and thread-like stems. Found only on Guernsey and Jersey, on damp heathy ground.

species.name: Fagopyrum cymosum
species.tip: Robust perennial with arrow-shaped, triangular leaves and white flower clusters in branched heads. A rare garden escape; compare Buckwheat, which is annual and more slender.

species.name: Fagopyrum esculentum
species.tip: Annual crop with triangular heart-shaped leaves, red-tinged stems and clusters of white or pink flowers. Occasional casual on tips and field edges, grown for grain or game cover.

species.name: Fagus sylvatica
species.tip: Smooth grey bark, silky hairy edges to young glossy wavy-edged leaves and tiny catkins; tall woodland tree with copper autumn colour.

species.name: Falcaria vulgaris
species.tip: Blue-green, hairless umbellifer with long, narrow, saw-edged leaf segments in threes and many small white umbels; a rare, local plant of field edges and verges, mainly in the east.

species.name: Fallopia convolvulus
species.tip: Twining annual with small greenish flowers and heart-shaped leaves, lacking the large trumpet blooms of true bindweeds; arable fields and gardens, with dark, three-angled fruits.

species.name: Fallopia dumetorum
species.tip: Twining climber with heart-shaped leaves and tiny greenish-white flowers; fruits have three winged ridges. Native in hedgerows and woods, mostly south-east England; compare Black-bindweed, which has unwinged fruits.

species.name: Felicia bergeriana
species.tip: Tender blue daisy from South Africa with narrow bristly leaves and sky-blue yellow-centred heads; occasional garden escape.

species.name: Ferula communis
species.tip: Huge fennel-like plant with a thick hollow stem, glossy thread-like leaves and big yellow umbels; grown in gardens and sometimes naturalised in sunny places.

species.name: Festuca armoricana
species.tip: Rare fine-leaved fescue of Brittany type with a small panicle; a specialist should confirm it among the fine-leaved fescues, which are very difficult to separate.

species.name: Festuca filiformis
species.tip: Bristle-leaved fescue of dry acid grassland with fine hair-thin leaves, short awns and a narrow panicle; shoots tufted, distinct from Red Fescue.

species.name: Festuca gautieri
species.tip: Garden fescue forming dense cushions of bristly, rolled green leaves; occasionally escapes onto walls. Short panicle, otherwise like other fine fescues, so check carefully.

species.name: Festuca glauca
species.tip: Garden fescue with neat tufts of bright blue-grey bristle leaves and a short panicle; seen on walls and pavements. Colour distinguishes it from Sheep's-fescue.

species.name: Festuca heterophylla
species.tip: Tufted fescue with fine, bristly basal leaves and flat, broader stem leaves, giving two leaf types; mostly naturalised in woods and parks in the south.

species.name: Festuca huonii
species.tip: Small tufted fescue from Australasia, rarely grown in gardens; the very fine leaves look like other fine fescues, so a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Festuca lemanii
species.tip: One of the fine-leaved Sheep's-fescue group, with narrow tufted leaves and a dense little panicle; a specialist needs to examine the leaf anatomy to confirm it.

species.name: Festuca longifolia
species.tip: Blue-grey fine-leaved fescue forming tufts, close to Hard and Blue Fescues; a specialist is needed to confirm it, and it is rare outside gardens.

species.name: Festuca ovina
species.tip: Dense tussocks of bristle-fine bluish-green leaves on heaths and downs; small panicle with awned spikelets, leaves all rolled at the base.

species.name: Festuca rubra
species.tip: Creeping fescue of lawns and verges with reddish-tinged panicle; leaf sheaths of non-flowering shoots split, distinguishing it from Sheep's-fescue.

species.name: Festuca trachyphylla
species.tip: Stiff, bluish-green tufted fescue with rolled hard leaves that are rough to the touch; common on dry banks and verges. A specialist should confirm it among the fine-leaved fescues.

species.name: Festuca vivipara
species.tip: Upland tufted fescue whose spikelets turn into small leafy plantlets rather than flowers; tussocky on mountain grassland and rocks.

species.name: Ficaria verna
species.tip: Early spring; glossy heart-shaped leaves; 8 to 12 narrow, shiny yellow petals; often small bulbils where the leaves join the stem.

species.name: Filago germanica
species.tip: Small grey woolly annual of dry sandy ground, with clustered rounded heads on spiky pointed bracts; leaves narrow and erect, cudweed-like.

species.name: Filago lutescens
species.tip: Rare cudweed of sandy ground in eastern England, with woolly stems and heads in tight rounded clusters whose bract tips are reddish; specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Filago pyramidata
species.tip: Rare cudweed of chalky arable edges, with broad white-woolly leaves and pointed five-angled heads that overtop the leaves; southern England only.

species.name: Filipendula camtschatica
species.tip: Very tall hairy herb with large palmate lobed leaves and frothy heads of creamy-white to pinkish flowers; a rare garden escape of streamsides and damp ground.

species.name: Filipendula ulmaria
species.tip: Tall plant of damp places with frothy creamy flower heads, almond scent and divided leaves white-downy beneath; compare Dropwort of dry chalk.

species.name: Filipendula vulgaris
species.tip: Low plant of dry chalk and limestone grassland with fern-like, finely cut leaves and flat heads of creamy flowers, buds tinged pink; much smaller than Meadowsweet.

species.name: Foeniculum vulgare
species.tip: Tall aniseed-scented plant with feathery thread-like leaves and flat yellow umbels, lacking bracts; found on coasts, waste ground and roadsides, unlike any other yellow umbellifer.

species.name: Forsythia suspensa
species.tip: Shrub with arching branches, bright yellow bell flowers in early spring before leaves appear, and leaves that are often divided into three leaflets.

species.name: Fragaria ananassa
species.tip: Larger than Wild Strawberry in flower, fruit and leaves; white flowers often with more than five petals; escapes from gardens onto verges and waste ground.

species.name: Fragaria moschata
species.tip: Taller than wild strawberry, with large flowers and trifoliate leaves with spreading hairs on stalks; fruit pale red musky strawberries. Rare naturalised in woods and hedges.

species.name: Fragaria vesca
species.tip: Small creeping plant with three-leaflet leaves, white flowers and tiny red fruit with seeds on the surface; woods, banks. Barren Strawberry has dry fruit and notched petals.

species.name: Frangula alnus
species.tip: Thornless shrub with alternate smooth-edged leaves, straight veins and berries ripening red to black; wet woods and heaths, unlike thorny, toothed-leaved Purging Buckthorn.

species.name: Frankenia laevis
species.tip: Low, wiry mat-forming plant with tiny rolled grey-green leaves and small pink flowers. Rare, on drying saltmarsh edges in East Anglia and the south coast.

species.name: Fraxinus excelsior
species.tip: Tall tree with opposite pinnate leaves, grey furrowed bark and black buds in winter; flowers appear before the leaves, followed by bunches of winged keys.

species.name: Fritillaria meleagris
species.tip: Nodding bell with chequered purple or white petals on a slender stem with narrow grey-green leaves. Local in old damp meadows in southern and central England.

species.name: Fuchsia magellanica
species.tip: Garden escape shrub, widely used in hedges in the west, with dangling flowers with red tubes and sepals and purple petals; leaves are oval, in whorls or pairs.

species.name: Fumaria bastardii
species.tip: Scrambling plant with large pink flowers with dark tips, over 9 mm long, and broad leaf segments; mostly south-west England and Wales. Hard to separate from other fumitories.

species.name: Fumaria capreolata
species.tip: Strong climbing fumitory with creamy-white flowers with dark red tips, leaf-stalks that curl like tendrils; locally common in the south-west and Ireland.

species.name: Fumaria densiflora
species.tip: Compact fumitory with very small pale pink flowers packed in dense spikes and blue-grey, finely divided leaves; East Anglian arable fields.

species.name: Fumaria muralis
species.tip: Scrambling fumitory of arable and waste ground, with relatively large pink flowers with dark red tips, and stalks that are short compared with Common Fumitory.

species.name: Fumaria occidentalis
species.tip: Rare climbing fumitory with white or pale pink flowers, tipped dark red, with a long lower petal; confined to Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly.

species.name: Fumaria officinalis
species.tip: Weedy fumitory with grey-green finely cut leaves and spikes of small pink flowers tipped with dark red-purple; sepals are small and narrower than the corolla.

species.name: Fumaria parviflora
species.tip: Spiky fumitory with very narrow channelled leaf segments and small whitish-pink flowers tipped dark red; local arable weed, chiefly southern and eastern England.

species.name: Fumaria purpurea
species.tip: Sturdy climbing fumitory with large purplish-pink flowers, 10 to 12 mm, and toothed fruit sepals; found in hedges and cultivated land, mostly in the south and west.

species.name: Fumaria reuteri
species.tip: Climbing fumitory with pale pink flowers dark at tips, in dense clusters, and leaves with flat, broad segments; local in southern England.

species.name: Fumaria vaillantii
species.tip: Small slender fumitory with few tiny pale pink flowers in a loose spike, and very narrow blue-green leaf segments; arable land in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Furcraea parmentieri
species.tip: Giant agave-like rosette with stiff sword leaves and a huge branched flower spike of greenish-white blooms. Only a rare tender garden plant in the mildest places.

species.name: Gagea bohemica
species.tip: Small plant with yellow flowers having greenish backs and just two narrow leaves; one basal leaf only. Extremely rare, in Radnorshire and Pembrokeshire in Wales.

species.name: Gagea lutea
species.tip: Woodland bulb with a single broad flat basal leaf and a loose cluster of yellow stars, green-striped on the back; other Gagea species are rarer and narrower-leaved.

species.name: Gagea serotina
species.tip: Tiny white lily with purple-veined, bell-like petals and thread-like leaves, found only on a few high rock ledges in Snowdonia, North Wales.

species.name: Galanthus elwesii
species.tip: Garden snowdrop with wide, greyish-green leaves flat or folded, a larger white flower with a green mark at the base and tip of the inner petals.

species.name: Galanthus nivalis
species.tip: Early nodding white flower with three long outer petals and a green-marked inner ring; grey-green flat leaves; woods and churchyards in late winter.

species.name: Galanthus plicatus
species.tip: Snowdrop with broad leaves that are folded back at the edges, hence pleated, with large white flowers; garden escape, found on woodland edges and churchyards.

species.name: Galanthus woronowii
species.tip: Snowdrop with bright green narrow leaves and a single green mark on each inner petal near the base only; garden escape of woodland and verges.

species.name: Galatella linosyris
species.tip: Rare limestone cliff plant with narrow stalkless leaves and clusters of yellow heads, usually lacking rays; sea cliffs in south-west England and Wales.

species.name: Galega officinalis
species.tip: Tall hairless pea with pinnate leaves and upright spikes of lilac-blue or white flowers. Garden escape on roadsides and rough ground.

species.name: Galeopsis angustifolia
species.tip: Annual hemp-nettle with narrow, almost entire leaves and bright pinkish-red flowers in whorls. Rare on arable fields and bare ground in southern England.

species.name: Galeopsis bifida
species.tip: Bristly annual hemp-nettle with small flowers whose lower lip has a pale blotch and two small teeth, and with oval toothed leaves. Common in arable fields and waste ground.

species.name: Galeopsis speciosa
species.tip: Stout annual hemp-nettle with big pale yellow flowers with a violet lower lip and a stem swollen below each node. Arable fields, mainly in Scotland and northern England.

species.name: Galeopsis tetrahit
species.tip: Bristly stem that swells just below each pair of leaves.

species.name: Galinsoga parviflora
species.tip: Small hairy annual of gardens and waste ground with tiny white three-rayed heads around yellow discs, oval toothed leaves; Shaggy-soldier is hairier.

species.name: Galinsoga quadriradiata
species.tip: Weed of gardens and arable land with tiny daisies of five short white rays and a yellow centre, opposite leaves, hairy stems. Distinguished from Gallant-soldier by hairier stems.

species.name: Galium album
species.tip: Tall bedstraw of hedges and verges with whorls of narrow leaves, a square smooth stem and frothy clusters of white flowers; flowers larger than those of Lady's Bedstraw.

species.name: Galium aparine
species.tip: Sticky scrambler of hedges and gardens with whorls of narrow leaves, a rough stem and leaves covered in hooked hairs that cling to clothes; flowers tiny greenish-white.

species.name: Galium boreale
species.tip: Stiff upright stems with whorls of four three-veined leaves, and bright white flower clusters. Rocky northern Britain and Ireland, damp or rocky meadows.

species.name: Galium constrictum
species.tip: Thin, weak, sprawling stems with whorls of narrow, blunt leaves and small white or pink flowers. Marshes in the south-west, Midlands and Ireland.

species.name: Galium murale
species.tip: Tiny annual, small whorled leaves, clustered tiny yellowish flowers; prickly fruits. Rare on walls and sandy ground, a few Channel Islands and south coast places.

species.name: Galium odoratum
species.tip: Low woodland plant of shady spots, with whorls of narrow-oval leaves and clusters of small white flowers, and a hay-like smell when dried.

species.name: Galium palustre
species.tip: Straggly bedstraw of wet meadows and ditches with whorls of blunt narrow leaves, black when dry, and loose clusters of white flowers; stem is square and smooth.

species.name: Galium parisiense
species.tip: Slender annual, with whorls of narrow, backward-prickly leaves and tiny greenish flowers. Rare on old walls and shingle in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Galium pumilum
species.tip: Slender, with narrow leaves in whorls of six to eight and white flowers in loose, open sprays. Dry chalk grassland in southern England.

species.name: Galium saxatile
species.tip: Low, mat-forming bedstraw of acid grass and heaths, with small bristle-tipped leaves in whorls, backward-pointing, and dense clusters of white flowers.

species.name: Galium spurium
species.tip: Cleavers-like, but with smooth, small green fruits and greenish flowers. Rare arable weed, mostly southern England; the fruits are not hooked.

species.name: Galium sterneri
species.tip: Mat-forming relative of Heath Bedstraw, with leaves in sixes that bear forward-pointing prickles on edges. Limestone grassland in northern England, Wales and Scotland; specialist may confirm.

species.name: Galium tricornutum
species.tip: Climbing annual with whorled leaves and tiny white flowers, but large, smooth, curved fruit stalks, unlike Cleavers. Rare arable weed, mostly in southern England.

species.name: Galium uliginosum
species.tip: Slender bedstraw of calcareous fens with leaves in whorls with prickles that point forwards and leaf tips with a bristle; stems are rough, with a loose white flower cluster.

species.name: Galium verum
species.tip: Bedstraw of dry grassland and dunes with frothy masses of tiny golden-yellow, honey-scented flowers and narrow whorled leaves with black edges that curl under.

species.name: Gamochaeta purpurea
species.tip: Low woolly annual of bare ground and paths, narrow grey-green leaves, small brownish heads clustered into a spike; scarce but spreading.

species.name: Gastridium ventricosum
species.tip: Slender annual with a shining, narrow, spike-like panicle of glossy spikelets bearing a bent awn; rare, on arable field edges and tracks in the south of England.

species.name: Gaudinia fragilis
species.tip: Slender grass with an unbranched spike, spikelets in two rows with a bent awn from the back, and hairy sheaths; local on damp meadows in the south and Channel Islands.

species.name: Gaultheria mucronata
species.tip: Prickly, evergreen shrub with small white flowers and plum, pink or white berries. Often planted and occasionally naturalised.

species.name: Gaultheria procumbens
species.tip: Low creeping evergreen with glossy oval leaves smelling of wintergreen when crushed; nodding white bells and bright red berries. Garden escape, naturalised in a few acid woods.

species.name: Gaultheria shallon
species.tip: Dense evergreen thicket shrub with leathery oval leaves and sticky-hairy stems; pinkish-white urn flowers in one-sided spikes, dark purple berries. Widely planted and naturalised in woods.

species.name: Gazania rigens
species.tip: Garden plant with big orange or yellow daisy heads and dark lobed leaves white-felted beneath; casual escape, especially on southern coasts.

species.name: Genista aetnensis
species.tip: Tall nearly leafless broom with arching green stems and many yellow flowers in summer. Rare, planted shrub, occasionally casual.

species.name: Genista anglica
species.tip: Low spiny shrub with small narrow hairless leaves and yellow pea flowers; spines distinguish from other greenweeds. Local on heaths and moors.

species.name: Genista hispanica
species.tip: Dense, spiny small shrub with narrow leaves and clusters of yellow flowers on short stems. Garden shrub, very rarely escaping.

species.name: Genista monspessulana
species.tip: Tall evergreen broom shrub with trifoliate leaves and sweet-scented yellow flowers. Garden plant, rare casual in the south-west.

species.name: Genista pilosa
species.tip: Low spineless shrub with small hairy narrow oval leaves and yellow flowers in the axils. Very rare, on southern and western sea cliffs and heaths.

species.name: Genista tinctoria
species.tip: Spineless low shrub with narrow, oval leaves and yellow pea flowers in spikes; pods hairless. Local in old grassland and rough pastures.

species.name: Gentiana acaulis
species.tip: Tufted alpine with large deep blue trumpet flowers on short stems and green-spotted throats. Garden plant; not native.

species.name: Gentiana asclepiadea
species.tip: Arching leafy stems bearing blue trumpets in pairs in the upper leaf axils; leaves willow-like. Garden plant, seldom escaping.

species.name: Gentiana nivalis
species.tip: Tiny annual with small bright blue flowers on short stems. Extremely rare, restricted to Scottish mountain turf in Perthshire and Argyll.

species.name: Gentiana pneumonanthe
species.tip: Slender plant with deep blue trumpets striped green outside, on wet heaths. Late flowering and scarce, mainly in the south and north-west.

species.name: Gentiana verna
species.tip: Tiny tufted plant with intense bright blue star flowers, at ground level. Very rare, in Upper Teesdale and Burren, Ireland.

species.name: Gentianella amarella
species.tip: Purple flowers with five petals and a fringe of hairs in the throat, with a tube typically five-lobed; chalk grassland and dunes, flowering late; Field Gentian is four-lobed.

species.name: Gentianella campestris
species.tip: Biennial with four-lobed purple-blue flowers; outer calyx lobes are broad and overlap the inner pair. Found on acid grassland in the north and west.

species.name: Gentianella germanica
species.tip: Short biennial with five-lobed lilac-blue flowers in clusters. Rare, on chalk grassland in southern England, mainly the Chilterns.

species.name: Gentianopsis ciliata
species.tip: Slender plant with single blue flowers with fringed petal edges. Grown in gardens; not native in Britain or Ireland.

species.name: Geranium columbinum
species.tip: Deep pink flowers on very long stalks; leaves are cut almost to the base into narrow lobes; fruits smooth. Found on dry calcareous grass and rocky slopes.

species.name: Geranium dalmaticum
species.tip: Low, mat-forming perennial with rounded, deeply cut glossy leaves and pale pink flowers. Occasional garden escape.

species.name: Geranium dissectum
species.tip: Small pink flowers with notched petals in pairs on short stalks; deeply cut leaves; sepals have a short point; fruits are hairy but beakless. Common on arable land.

species.name: Geranium endressii
species.tip: Garden escape with fairly large pink flowers veined darker, with a distinct white eye, and glossy deeply cut leaves; roadside and waste ground, mostly in the south-west.

species.name: Geranium herrerae
species.tip: Garden crane's-bill with deeply cut leaves and pink flowers. Specialist check needed; rare casual.

species.name: Geranium himalayense
species.tip: Clump-forming garden plant with big violet-blue flowers with reddish veins, and deeply lobed leaves. Occasional escape.

species.name: Geranium ibericum
species.tip: Garden perennial with large violet-blue flowers on branched stems and deeply cut hairy leaves. Occasional escape on verges.

species.name: Geranium lucidum
species.tip: Glossy, rounded, shallowly lobed leaves often tinged red, and small pink flowers with a wrinkled, keeled calyx; grows on walls, rocks and shady banks, especially on limestone.

species.name: Geranium macrorrhizum
species.tip: Garden escape with strongly aromatic, sticky hairy leaves, rounded shallow lobes and magenta-pink flowers with long protruding stamens; naturalised on banks and walls.

species.name: Geranium maderense
species.tip: Tall, fleshy-stemmed garden geranium with big divided leaves and magenta flowers. Tender; naturalised only in mild south-west areas.

species.name: Geranium molle
species.tip: Soft, rounded, shallowly lobed grey-green leaves and pink flowers with deeply notched petals; fruits are smooth and wrinkled; common on lawns, verges and dry grassland.

species.name: Geranium nodosum
species.tip: Woodland garden geranium with glossy three-lobed leaves and lilac flowers having darker veins. Occasionally naturalised.

species.name: Geranium phaeum
species.tip: Clump-forming perennial with nodding, almost black-purple, reflexed-petalled flowers. Naturalised on shady roadsides and hedge banks.

species.name: Geranium platypetalum
species.tip: Garden geranium with large violet-blue, purple-veined flowers and rounded, lobed hairy leaves. Rare escape.

species.name: Geranium pratense
species.tip: Large violet-blue flowers with dark veins in lush meadows and verges; deeply cut leaves; the largest-flowered wild blue crane's-bill, flowers more open than Wood Crane's-bill.

species.name: Geranium psilostemon
species.tip: Tall garden crane's-bill with big magenta flowers with a black central eye. Occasionally escapes.

species.name: Geranium purpureum
species.tip: Small, strong-smelling annual like Herb-Robert with a reddish stem, ridged nutlets and small pink flowers. Found on shingle and walls in south-west England and Ireland.

species.name: Geranium pusillum
species.tip: Tiny pale lilac to pinkish flowers with notched petals, and only five fertile stamens; leaves rounded with shallow lobes; soft hairy on disturbed bare ground.

species.name: Geranium pyrenaicum
species.tip: Mauve-purple flowers in pairs with deeply notched petals, larger than Dove's-foot, and softer leaves; stems have long soft hairs; grows on grassy verges and hedge banks.

species.name: Geranium reuteri
species.tip: Herb-Robert-like plant from Atlantic islands with pink flowers; specialist check needed. Naturalised in Cornwall and southern coasts.

species.name: Geranium robertianum
species.tip: Strongly smelling, often red-tinged plant with pinnately divided ferny leaves and small pink flowers with white stripes; shady walls, woods and shingle.

species.name: Geranium rotundifolium
species.tip: Softly hairy plant with round, shallowly lobed leaves and small pink flowers with unnotched petals; sepals have a short point; fruit smooth. Southern hedgebanks and walls.

species.name: Geranium sanguineum
species.tip: Large, bright magenta flowers with notched petals and deeply cut small leaves turning red in autumn; sprawling, on limestone grassland, sand dunes and coastal cliffs.

species.name: Geranium sylvaticum
species.tip: Violet-blue flowers with a whitish centre, more bowl-shaped than Meadow Crane's-bill; tall plant of northern upland meadows, woods and verges with deeply cut leaves.

species.name: Geranium versicolor
species.tip: Garden geranium with whitish flowers lined with fine violet veins. Naturalised on banks and verges in places.

species.name: Geranium yeoi
species.tip: Garden-origin crane's-bill with pink flowers and lobed leaves. Specialist check needed; sporadic escape.

species.name: Geum macrophyllum
species.tip: Hairy herb with a huge, rounded end lobe on its lower leaves and yellow five-petalled flowers; fruit heads are burrs with hooked spines. Rare naturalised in northern Britain.

species.name: Geum rivale
species.tip: Nodding bell-like flowers dull orange-pink with purple-brown sepals; damp woods, meadows, streamsides. Hybridises with Wood Avens, giving intermediate flowers.

species.name: Geum urbanum
species.tip: Upright yellow five-petalled flowers and hooked fruit burrs; lower leaves pinnate with big terminal lobe; shady hedgerows and woods. Flowers face up, unlike Water Avens.

species.name: Gladiolus communis
species.tip: Tall plant with sword-shaped leaves and spikes of bright magenta flowers. Garden escape; naturalised locally in the south-west, especially Cornwall and Scilly.

species.name: Gladiolus illyricus
species.tip: Slim spike of rich purple-pink flowers among bracken and heath. Very rare native, found only in the New Forest and nearby parts of Hampshire and Dorset.

species.name: Glaucium flavum
species.tip: Shingle plant with large yellow poppy flowers, blue-grey wavy leaves and long curved horn-like seed pods. Coastal shingle, mostly in southern and eastern Britain.

species.name: Glebionis segetum
species.tip: Bright yellow large daisy with greyish, toothed to lobed hairless leaves clasping the stem. Arable fields and waste ground, summer.

species.name: Glechoma hederacea
species.tip: Kidney-shaped, round-toothed leaves on long creeping stems; smells pungent when crushed.

species.name: Glyceria canadensis
species.tip: North American manna-grass with a broad, spreading, nodding panicle of oval spikelets that look like a rattlesnake tail; rare naturalised plant of wet ground.

species.name: Glyceria declinata
species.tip: Low, creeping, often muddy-margin grass with a slender raceme and spikelets on short stalks; leaves are bluish-green and the ligule is long.

species.name: Glyceria fluitans
species.tip: Wet-ground grass floating in ponds and ditches with a long, narrow, one-sided raceme of nearly stalkless spikelets; ligule long and pointed.

species.name: Glyceria maxima
species.tip: Very tall water-edge grass making dense stands, with a big pyramidal panicle of small spikelets and broad leaves; shorter ligule than Floating Sweet-grass.

species.name: Glyceria notata
species.tip: Wet-ground sweet-grass with an open panicle of lined spikelets, branches spreading; leaves medium broad and shorter than Reed Sweet-grass.

species.name: Gnaphalium uliginosum
species.tip: Low grey woolly plant with clusters of dull brownish-yellow heads at stem tops, surrounded by leaves. Damp bare ground in tracks, fields and gardens.

species.name: Gonocarpus micranthus
species.tip: Tiny creeping plant with small toothed leaves and minute greenish flowers. Naturalised from Australasia in western Scotland and Ireland. Specialist check advised.

species.name: Goodyera repens
species.tip: Small orchid with a rosette of net-veined, oval leaves and a one-sided spike of white flowers with downy hairs; grows in pine woods.

species.name: Grindelia stricta
species.tip: Sticky North American coastal plant with large yellow daisies, sticky white gum on bracts, and toothed clasping leaves; casual on saltmarsh edges.

species.name: Groenlandia densa
species.tip: Submerged stems with opposite, clasping, pointed leaves in pairs, looking unlike other pondweeds. Clear, calcareous ponds, ditches and streams, mostly south and east.

species.name: Gunnera tinctoria
species.tip: Huge, rhubarb-like plant with prickly stalks and giant lobed leaves. Dense, cone-like reddish flower spikes appear. Invasive on streamsides in western Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Gymnadenia borealis
species.tip: Smaller than other fragrant-orchids with short pink spikes, flowers with a short spur; grows in acid grassland and heaths in the north and west.

species.name: Gymnadenia conopsea
species.tip: Orchid with a long slender spike of pink scented flowers with a very long thin spur and narrow leaves; chalk grassland.

species.name: Gymnadenia densiflora
species.tip: Stouter, later flowering fragrant-orchid with a dense spike of pink flowers with a short spur, broader leaves; wet meadows and fens.

species.name: Gymnocarpium dryopteris
species.tip: Delicate creeping fern of shady rocky woods and screes with a pale, triangular frond divided into three roughly equal branches; fronds are held flat.

species.name: Gymnocarpium robertianum
species.tip: Triangular, matt, grey-green fronds with sticky glandular hairs that smell faintly of resin, growing on limestone screes. Distinct from oak fern by hairs and dull colour.

species.name: Gypsophila paniculata
species.tip: Tall, much-branched plant with a cloud of tiny white flowers and narrow, grey-green leaves. Garden plant, occasionally found on waste ground and sandy banks.

species.name: Hammarbya paludosa
species.tip: Tiny yellow-green orchid growing in sphagnum, with minute flowers and small leaves with bulbils at the tips; rare in wet bogs.

species.name: Hedera algeriensis
species.tip: Ivy with large, shallowly lobed, bright green leaves that are scarcely toothed, carrying star-shaped scale hairs. Occasional garden escape; larger and paler than common ivy. Specialist check advised.

species.name: Hedera colchica
species.tip: Ivy with very large, glossy, unlobed heart-shaped leaves, often over 15 cm, and a faint celery smell when crushed. Common in parks and gardens, sometimes escaping.

species.name: Hedera helix
species.tip: Evergreen climber with lobed leaves on creeping stems and unlobed on flowering stems; round green-yellow umbels in autumn feed insects, followed by black berries.

species.name: Helianthemum apenninum
species.tip: Low shrubby plant with white flowers and leaves white-downy beneath. Very rare, on limestone in the Avon Gorge, Brean Down and a few Yorkshire sites.

species.name: Helianthemum nummularium
species.tip: Low spreading evergreen with bright yellow, crumpled-petal flowers and opposite narrow oval leaves, white beneath; sunny chalk grassland and rocks.

species.name: Helianthemum oelandicum
species.tip: Small mat-forming rock-rose with yellow flowers and greyish downy leaves, lacking stipules. Very rare, on limestone in Durness, Teesdale and the Brecon area.

species.name: Helianthus tuberosus
species.tip: Tall sunflower relative with many yellow daisy heads in autumn, rough stems and broad toothed leaves; found on waste ground and river banks.

species.name: Helichrysum bellidioides
species.tip: Creeping mat-forming plant with small white-woolly rounded leaves and papery whitish button heads; rare garden escape, mostly in the south and west.

species.name: Helichrysum italicum
species.tip: Silver-leaved aromatic shrubby plant smelling of curry, with narrow leaves and flat clusters of small golden yellow button heads; garden escape on walls.

species.name: Helichrysum petiolare
species.tip: Sprawling garden plant with felted grey-white rounded leaves and small creamy button heads in clusters; rare casual on waste ground.

species.name: Helictochloa pratensis
species.tip: Oat-grass of chalk grassland with stiff, blue-green leaves and few large spikelets with a bent awn; leaves are folded and hairless.

species.name: Helleborus argutifolius
species.tip: Garden escape with leathery evergreen leaves of three spiny-toothed leaflets and pale green cup flowers in winter.

species.name: Helleborus foetidus
species.tip: Evergreen; dark leaves cut into narrow fingers; nodding pale green bells rimmed with purple in late winter.

species.name: Helleborus orientalis
species.tip: Garden escape; nodding cup flowers in late winter and spring, cream, pink or purple; leathery leaves.

species.name: Helleborus viridis
