species.tip: Dies down in winter; flat, open green flowers in early spring; leaves cut into toothed fingers; woods on lime.

species.name: Helminthotheca echioides
species.tip: Coarse, bristly plant with warty-based bristles on leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads, bracts heart-shaped and leafy. Verges, field edges and waste ground.

species.name: Helosciadium inundatum
species.tip: Small plant of pond edges and shallow water with thread-like submerged leaves, pinnate upper leaves and tiny umbels of two or three rays.

species.name: Helosciadium nodiflorum
species.tip: Sprawling in shallow water and ditches; pinnate leaves with toothed leaflets like watercress; small white umbels on short stalks opposite the leaves.

species.name: Helosciadium repens
species.tip: Low, creeping, hairless celery relative rooting at nodes, with small white umbels almost stalkless opposite leaves; very rare, in wet grassland in a few counties.

species.name: Hemerocallis fulva
species.tip: Clump of long arching strap leaves with tall stems of large tawny-orange trumpet flowers, each lasting one day. Common garden escape on roadsides and waste ground.

species.name: Hemerocallis lilioasphodelus
species.tip: Clumps of strap leaves with scented clear yellow lily-like trumpet flowers on tall stems. Rare garden escape; the common orange day-lily has tawny flowers.

species.name: Hepatica nobilis
species.tip: Early spring woodland plant with violet-blue, sometimes pink or white, star-like flowers and distinctive leathery three-lobed leaves; flowers appear before the new leaves. Rare garden escape.

species.name: Heracleum mantegazzianum
species.tip: Huge plant to over 3 m with purple-blotched, thick bristly stems and giant umbels and leaves; sap can cause severe blistering, so do not touch. Far larger than Hogweed.

species.name: Heracleum sphondylium
species.tip: Common coarse umbellifer of verges and rough grass with hairy ridged stems and broad lobed leaves; much smaller than Giant Hogweed and often pinkish-white with unequal outer petals.

species.name: Herminium monorchis
species.tip: Small orchid with tiny honey-scented yellow-green flowers and two leaves at the base; found in short chalk grassland in southern England.

species.name: Herniaria ciliolata
species.tip: Prostrate plant with tiny oval leaves, green flowers in clusters, and leaves with short fringed hairs. Very rare, on coastal gravel in the Lizard, Cornwall.

species.name: Herniaria glabra
species.tip: Mat-forming plant with tiny green flower clusters along the stem and shiny, hairless, small leaves. Rare, found on sandy and gravelly ground, and paths.

species.name: Hesperis matronalis
species.tip: Tall garden escape with sweetly scented purple, lilac or white flowers in spring; unlike phlox it has four petals and long thin pods.

species.name: Hieracium alpinum
species.tip: Short mountain hawkweed of Scottish hills, with a single large yellow head, leaves mostly in a basal rosette, shaggy bristly stem; specialist needed to confirm.

species.name: Hieracium amplexicaule
species.tip: Hawkweed with glandular sticky hairs and stem leaves clasping the stem, yellow heads; grows on rocks and walls; specialist needed to confirm microspecies.

species.name: Hieracium anglicum
species.tip: Hawkweed microspecies with yellow dandelion-like heads and toothed leaves rosette-forming; widespread on rocks and walls in northern Britain; specialist needed to confirm.

species.name: Hieracium hethlandiae
species.tip: Hawkweed microspecies endemic to Shetland, found on cliffs and rocky ledges, with yellow dandelion-like heads; specialist needed to confirm identification.

species.name: Hieracium holosericeum
species.tip: Hawkweed microspecies of mountain cliffs with silky white hairs on leaves and yellow heads; specialist needed to confirm identification from others.

species.name: Hieracium lanatum
species.tip: Hawkweed microspecies with grey woolly leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads; a specialist is needed to confirm it among similar hawkweeds.

species.name: Hieracium lanceolatum
species.tip: Hawkweed microspecies with narrow lance-shaped leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads; a specialist is needed to confirm identification.

species.name: Hieracium latobrigorum
species.tip: One of many similar hawkweeds with leafy stems, toothed leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads; only a specialist can confirm the species. Mainly upland Britain.

species.name: Hieracium leyi
species.tip: A critical hawkweed with yellow dandelion-like heads and toothed leaves on a branched stem; needs a specialist to confirm. Very local, chiefly in Wales and the Welsh borders.

species.name: Hieracium lingulatum
species.tip: A critical hawkweed with yellow heads and tongue-shaped leaves; separating it from other hawkweeds needs a specialist. Mainly rocky upland sites.

species.name: Hieracium prenanthoides
species.tip: Tall hawkweed with many stem leaves that clasp the stem, upper leaves heart-based, pale green; heads yellow with dark hairy bracts. Rocky ground and walls, mainly upland.

species.name: Hieracium proximum
species.tip: A critical hawkweed with yellow dandelion-like heads and toothed leaves; specialist needed to confirm. Rare and local, mostly northern Britain.

species.name: Hieracium sabaudum
species.tip: Leafy hawkweed with many narrow-ish toothed stem leaves and clusters of yellow heads in late summer. Woods, hedgebanks and heathy places; hawkweeds are hard to identify precisely.

species.name: Hieracium speluncarum
species.tip: A critical hawkweed of rocky crags with yellow heads and toothed leaves; specialist needed to confirm. Very local, mainly Scotland and northern England.

species.name: Hieracium subcrocatum
species.tip: A critical hawkweed with orange-yellow dandelion-like heads and leafy stems; specialist needed to confirm. Rare, mainly Scotland.

species.name: Hieracium trichocaulon
species.tip: A critical hawkweed with a hairy stem, toothed leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Hieracium umbellatum
species.tip: Leafy hawkweed with many narrow, nearly stalkless leaves up the stem and a flat-topped umbel of yellow heads. Heaths, dry woodland edges and railway banks.

species.name: Hieracium vagum
species.tip: A critical hawkweed with yellow dandelion-like heads, leafy stems and toothed leaves; a specialist is needed to confirm it. Local in upland Britain.

species.name: Hieracium villosum
species.tip: Densely shaggy with long white hairs on stem and leaves, which clasp the stem; large yellow heads. Rock ledges on limestone and mountain crags in northern Britain.

species.name: Hierochloe odorata
species.tip: Sweet-scented rhizomatous grass with a loose bronze panicle of shining spikelets, flowering early; very rare in northern Scotland and Ireland on damp stream banks.

species.name: Himantoglossum hircinum
species.tip: Tall robust orchid with grey-green flowers with an extremely long twisted lip, and a goat-like smell; local in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Hippocrepis comosa
species.tip: Low spreading pea with pinnate leaves and heads of yellow flowers; horseshoe-shaped pods. Local on chalk and limestone grassland.

species.name: Hippocrepis emerus
species.tip: Shrub with pinnate leaves, small leaflets and pairs of pale yellow flowers on short stalks; pods are thin and jointed. Planted in gardens, rarely naturalised.

species.name: Hippophae rhamnoides
species.tip: Thorny coastal shrub with narrow silvery leaves and dense bunches of orange berries in autumn; dunes and sea cliffs, sometimes spreading inland.

species.name: Hippuris vulgaris
species.tip: Aquatic plant with erect stems bearing whorls of narrow leaves like tiny pines; flowers are minute and green in leaf axils. Not related to horsetail; grows in shallow still or slow water.

species.name: Hirschfeldia incana
species.tip: Grey-green, bristly plant of roadsides and waste ground with small pale yellow flowers, pods tight against the stem and a lobed lower leaf.

species.name: Holcus lanatus
species.tip: Softly downy, grey-green grass with velvety leaves and sheaths; pinkish-white panicle with spikelets bearing a short hooked awn; ligule short.

species.name: Holcus mollis
species.tip: Similar to Yorkshire-fog but leaves hairless with hairy nodes and creeping rhizomes; spikelet awns stick out clearly beyond the glumes.

species.name: Homogyne alpina
species.tip: Small mountain plant with round toothed glossy leaves and a leafless stem topped by a pinkish-purple tuft of tubular florets. Rare, Scottish mountains only.

species.name: Honckenya peploides
species.tip: Fleshy, yellowish-green creeping plant on shingle and sand, with pairs of thick oval leaves and small greenish-white flowers. Strandline species.

species.name: Hordelymus europaeus
species.tip: Woodland grass with a nodding barley-like spike, spikelets in threes, awned; leaves are broad and hairy at the sheath. Local on shady calcareous ground in the south.

species.name: Hordeum distichon
species.tip: Cultivated cereal with a stiff nodding head of long-awned spikelets, only the central one of each three fertile; leaves broad.

species.name: Hordeum jubatum
species.tip: Barley with soft, silky, nodding spike of long, spreading awns, often tinged purple; a casual on roadsides, widely seen on salted verges.

species.name: Hordeum marinum
species.tip: Short barley of saltmarshes and sea walls, with a narrow spike where the central spikelet is stalkless and the others outward-awned; Sea Barley has short stiff leaves.

species.name: Hordeum murinum
species.tip: Annual of walls and waysides with a bristly, yellowish-green spike that breaks up; central spikelet of each three is stalkless, laterals stalked.

species.name: Hordeum secalinum
species.tip: Perennial barley of old damp meadows with a narrower, shorter-awned spike than Wall Barley, blue-green leaves and a bristly feel.

species.name: Hordeum vulgare
species.tip: Cultivated cereal with a large spike of long awns, either two- or six-rowed; relict on field margins and tips, with broad leaves and clasping auricles.

species.name: Hornungia petraea
species.tip: Tiny, delicate annual of limestone rocks and bare soil with minute white flowers and neat, finely divided leaves. Local, found mostly on southern limestone.

species.name: Hottonia palustris
species.tip: Floating or submerged feathery leaves, with whorls of pale lilac flowers above water on leafless stalks. Clean ditches and ponds, mostly lowland England and Ireland.

species.name: Houttuynia cordata
species.tip: Spreading garden escape with heart-shaped, bluish-green leaves that smell of orange peel when crushed, and a small cone of tiny flowers cupped by four white bracts.

species.name: Humulus lupulus
species.tip: Climbing twining plant of hedges with rough lobed leaves and green papery cones on female plants; grows clockwise, flowering summer.

species.name: Huperzia selago
species.tip: Erect, forked tufts of crowded stiff, pointed leaves with yellowish bulbils at tips; no cones; upland heath, rock ledges and mountain grassland.

species.name: Hyacinthoides hispanica
species.tip: Garden escape with broad leaves and upright, stout stem; wide open bells all round the spike, blue-purple, pink or white, with blue pollen, unlike native Bluebell.

species.name: Hyacinthoides italica
species.tip: Spring bulb with a conical spike of starry pale blue flowers and narrow strap leaves, upright rather than nodding. Naturalised rarely on grassy ground; smaller than bluebell.

species.name: Hyacinthoides non-scripta
species.tip: Native woodland carpet with a nodding, one-sided flower spike of narrow, deep violet-blue bells whose tips curl back and have cream pollen; sweetly scented.

species.name: Hydrilla verticillata
species.tip: Submerged, whorled waterweed with leaves in fours to eight with sharp spiny-toothed edges. Native only in Esthwaite Water, Cumbria; also introduced elsewhere.

species.name: Hydrocharis morsus-ranae
species.tip: Floating plant with small round heart-shaped leaves and three-petalled white flowers with yellow centres. Found in still lowland ditches and ponds in England and Wales.

species.name: Hydrocotyle moschata
species.tip: Small creeping New Zealand pennywort with rounded, shallowly scalloped leaves covered in hairs, forming mats on damp ground. Rare introduction, mainly in western Scotland and Ireland.

species.name: Hydrocotyle novae-zeelandiae
species.tip: Mat-forming creeper with small round, scalloped, nearly hairless leaves on slender stalks. Introduced, naturalised on damp lawns and banks, mainly in western Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Hydrocotyle ranunculoides
species.tip: Invasive aquatic with bright glossy, rounded, shallowly lobed leaves floating or standing above water, forming dense rafts. Tiny whitish flowers hide among the leaves. Spreading in southern England.

species.name: Hydrocotyle vulgaris
species.tip: Creeping plant of bogs and wet ground with round, shield-like scalloped leaves on long stalks; flowers tiny and hidden beneath. Not related to Navelwort.

species.name: Hylotelephium telephium
species.tip: Fleshy grey-green oval toothed leaves on upright stems, topped by dense flat heads of reddish-purple starry flowers; woodland edges and hedgebanks.

species.name: Hymenophyllum tunbrigense
species.tip: Tiny translucent, moss-like fern with fronds one cell thick and wedge-shaped, toothed lobes. Found on damp shady rocks, trees and rock walls in the west, and Tunbridge Wells.

species.name: Hymenophyllum wilsonii
species.tip: Tiny translucent, filmy fern with fronds one cell thick, forming mats. Distinguished from Tunbridge Filmy-fern by narrower, entire-edged lobes. Found on damp shady rocks and bark in the west.

species.name: Hyoscyamus niger
species.tip: Sticky, foul-smelling hairy annual with lobed leaves and cream funnel-shaped flowers netted with purple veins, then urn-shaped fruits. Sandy coasts and disturbed ground; poisonous.

species.name: Hypericum androsaemum
species.tip: Shrubby plant with large paired oval leaves, yellow flowers in small clusters and berry-like fruit that turns from red to black; woods and hedgerows.

species.name: Hypericum calycinum
species.tip: Evergreen garden shrub with big solitary yellow flowers full of stamens; spreads by suckers on banks and waste ground.

species.name: Hypericum canadense
species.tip: Slender plant with narrow stalkless leaves and tiny pale yellow flowers with five petals. Rare native of western Ireland on damp sandy or peaty ground.

species.name: Hypericum elodes
species.tip: Densely grey-hairy plant of boggy ground with rounded woolly leaves and pale yellow flowers. The soft felty look separates it from other St John's-worts.

species.name: Hypericum forrestii
species.tip: Garden shrub with leafy arching stems and large golden flowers with many stamens. Occasionally escapes; confirm species against other cultivated shrubby St John's-worts.

species.name: Hypericum hirsutum
species.tip: Softly hairy stem and leaves without translucent dots on leaf edges; woods and hedges, with pale yellow flowers and black-dotted sepals.

species.name: Hypericum humifusum
species.tip: Low sprawling wiry plant with small pale yellow flowers and small leaves with black dots; acid heaths and tracks, shorter than other St John's-worts.

species.name: Hypericum linariifolium
species.tip: Narrow, almost linear leaves with rolled edges and small yellow flowers. Very rare native of rocky heath in Devon and Cornwall, scarce elsewhere.

species.name: Hypericum maculatum
species.tip: Stem with four raised lines and few or no translucent dots on leaves; sepals blunt and not pointed; grassland, scrub and woods.

species.name: Hypericum montanum
species.tip: Pale lemon flowers and stalkless leaves with black dots on the margins only. Hairy upper stem. Local on limestone and calcareous scrub in England and Wales.

species.name: Hypericum nummularium
species.tip: Low rock-garden plant with small rounded greyish leaves and few yellow flowers. Rarely seen outside gardens; check against other trailing garden St John's-worts.

species.name: Hypericum olympicum
species.tip: Low, greyish rock-garden shrublet with narrow blue-green leaves and large lemon-yellow flowers. Cultivated and only an occasional garden escape.

species.name: Hypericum perforatum
species.tip: Stem with two raised lines and leaves full of see-through dots when held to the light; common on grassland, verges and scrub.

species.name: Hypericum pseudohenryi
species.tip: Garden shrub with large, bright golden flowers and many stamens, close to other cultivated shrubby kinds. Rare outside gardens; identification needs checking.

species.name: Hypericum pulchrum
species.tip: Slender plant with round stem and red-tinged buds, flowers with red streaks beneath; leaves clasping with transparent dots; heaths and acid grass.

species.name: Hypericum tetrapterum
species.tip: Stem with four narrow wings on the angles and translucent dots on the leaves; wet meadows, ditches and fens.

species.name: Hypericum undulatum
species.tip: Leaves with wavy margins, stems with narrow wings, and small pale yellow flowers marked red. Rare plant of damp acid ground in Cornwall, Devon and Wales.

species.name: Hypericum xylosteifolium
species.tip: Evergreen-ish shrub with oval, rather soft leaves and large bright yellow flowers followed by red fruit. Occasionally persists near gardens and in hedges.

species.name: Hypochaeris glabra
species.tip: Small hairless cat's-ear with shiny, lobed leaves and small yellow heads that barely open. Rare, on sandy or gravelly ground, mostly in south and east England.

species.name: Hypochaeris maculata
species.tip: Large yellow heads on a stem with a few scales, rough leaves usually blotched with purple spots; unlike common cat's-ear. Very rare on sea cliffs and limestone in Devon and Wales.

species.name: Hypochaeris radicata
species.tip: Dandelion-like but with branched, nearly leafless stems bearing small scale-like bracts and a flat rosette of hairy, lobed leaves. Grassland and lawns, summer.

species.name: Hypolepis ambigua
species.tip: Creeping fern with delicate, finely divided, hairy fronds along a long rhizome. A rare, localised garden escape or introduction.

species.name: Hypopitys monotropa
species.tip: Leafless, waxy pale yellowish plant with scale leaves and a nodding head of bells, parasitic on fungi in shady beech and pine woods and dunes. No green colour.

species.name: Hyssopus officinalis
species.tip: Aromatic evergreen shrubby plant with narrow leaves and dense one-sided spikes of deep blue flowers, grown in gardens and occasionally escaping onto old walls and dry banks.

species.name: Iberis amara
species.tip: Flat-topped heads of white or lilac-tinged flowers, with two petals larger than the others. Rare, found on chalk in the Chilterns and a few other southern sites.

species.name: Ilex aquifolium
species.tip: Evergreen tree or shrub with glossy spiny leaves, though upper leaves are sometimes smooth; small white flowers and red berries on female trees.

species.name: Illecebrum verticillatum
species.tip: Prostrate plant with whitish papery stems like a string of beads and tiny white flowers in clusters. Very rare, on damp sandy ground in southern England.

species.name: Impatiens capensis
species.tip: Tall, succulent plant with oval toothed leaves and hanging orange trumpet flowers spotted with brown, having a curved spur. Naturalised along rivers and canals in southern England.

species.name: Impatiens glandulifera
species.tip: Very tall annual with pink-purple hooded flowers, whorled leaves with red stems, and exploding seed pods; common on riverbanks, strongly scented.

species.name: Impatiens noli-tangere
species.tip: Succulent plant with swollen stem joints, oval toothed leaves and yellow trumpet flowers with a hooked spur. Native only in a few streamside woods in north-west England and Wales.

species.name: Impatiens parviflora
species.tip: Slender balsam with pointed toothed leaves and small pale yellow flowers with a short straight spur. Common weed of shady waste ground and woodland edges.

species.name: Imperatoria ostruthium
species.tip: Stout plant with three-lobed leaves with broad, toothed segments and large flat umbels of pinkish-white flowers; naturalised in damp ground and old cottage gardens in northern Britain.

species.name: Inula conyzae
species.tip: Tall, sticky-hairy, aromatic plant with rather dull yellowish-brown button heads with short rays, and broad woolly leaves. Dry chalk and limestone scrub and banks.

species.name: Inula helenium
species.tip: Very tall plant with huge, rough, softly downy leaves and big yellow shaggy-rayed heads; leaves white-felted beneath. Old medicinal plant, naturalised on roadsides and hedgerows.

species.name: Inula hookeri
species.tip: Garden plant with solitary large yellow heads with very narrow, spreading rays, and sticky-hairy stems; occasional garden escape on rough ground.

species.name: Inula orientalis
species.tip: Garden perennial with large solitary yellow heads on woolly stems, rays narrow and ragged; rare escape on tips and waste ground.

species.name: Inula salicina
species.tip: Stiff plant with hairless, shiny, stalkless leaves clasping the stem by heart-shaped bases, and yellow heads. Lake shores in Ireland and a few sites in Britain.

species.name: Iris foetidissima
species.tip: Evergreen iris of woods and scrub, with dull purplish-yellow flowers and a smell of roast beef from crushed leaves; seed pods split to show bright orange-red seeds.

species.name: Iris germanica
species.tip: Large blue-purple flowers with a fuzzy yellow beard on each lower petal, and stout fans of sword leaves. Garden plant surviving on tips and verges.

species.name: Iris laevigata
species.tip: Blue-purple flowers with flattened, beardless petals and broad pale-green leaves. Garden pond plant that sometimes persists beside water.

species.name: Iris latifolia
species.tip: Large violet-blue flowers with a yellow patch on each lower petal and broad grassy leaves. Cultivated garden plant; occasional escape.

species.name: Iris orientalis
species.tip: White flowers marked with a yellow blotch on the lower petals, plus tall stems and narrow grey-green leaves. Rare garden relic.

species.name: Iris pseudacorus
species.tip: Tall wetland iris with sword-like leaves and bright yellow flowers; found along ponds, ditches and marshes, and flowers larger than any other yellow wetland plants.

species.name: Iris sibirica
species.tip: Slender stems carry several blue-violet beardless flowers above very narrow grassy leaves. Garden plant occasionally persisting in damp grass near gardens.

species.name: Iris spuria
species.tip: Tall iris of grassland with narrow leaves and lilac-blue flowers with a small yellow-veined blotch. Rare garden escape or relic.

species.name: Iris tuberosa
species.tip: Odd green and black-purple flowers with hooded form, on short stems with square-sectioned leaves. Naturalised in a few spots in southern England.

species.name: Iris versicolor
species.tip: Violet-purple flowers veined darker with a yellow centre, rather like Yellow Iris in leaf shape. Damp-ground garden escape, uncommon.

species.name: Isatis tinctoria
species.tip: Tall blue-green plant with big branching sprays of small yellow flowers and hanging dark pods like flattened black spoons. Grown formerly for dye, naturalised on cliffs and banks.

species.name: Isoetes echinospora
species.tip: Tuft of stiff, quill-like leaves under water, no flowers; spiny spores need microscope checks. Rare in soft-water lakes and pools in Wales, Scotland and Ireland.

species.name: Isoetes histrix
species.tip: Tiny tuft of short, bristle-like leaves on damp ground, no flowers, which disappears in summer. Very rare, known from Cornwall and the Channel Islands.

species.name: Isoetes lacustris
species.tip: Rosette of stiff, dark-green quill leaves on the bed of clear mountain lakes, no flowers. Local in upland Wales, Scotland, Ireland and the Lake District.

species.name: Isolepis cernua
species.tip: A tiny, tufted rush-like plant of damp seepage and dune slacks with a single small, pale brown, nodding spikelet and hair-like leaves, narrow and grass-like; fine and pale.

species.name: Isolepis setacea
species.tip: Tiny tufted plant with thread-like stems, a few small brown spikelets clustered at the side, and one longer bract; damp bare ground and paths.

species.name: Ixia campanulata
species.tip: Slender wiry stems carry a spike of reddish bell-shaped flowers over thin sword leaves. Rare garden plant, uncertain outside cultivation.

species.name: Jacobaea aquatica
species.tip: Ragwort of wet places with hairless, little-divided leaves and a broad top; yellow rays spread rather than hang down. Ditches, wet meadows and fens.

species.name: Jacobaea erucifolia
species.tip: Ragwort with narrow-lobed leaves white and cottony beneath, and flat-topped yellow heads. Grassy places on chalk and roadsides, mainly south-east England.

species.name: Jacobaea maritima
species.tip: Silvery-white woolly plant with deeply lobed leaves and yellow daisy-like heads; looks unlike common ragworts. Planted, naturalised on south and west coasts.

species.name: Jacobaea paludosa
species.tip: Tall ragwort with narrow, toothed, stalkless leaves woolly beneath and many yellow heads. Very rare, fens of East Anglia, reintroduced at Wicken Fen.

species.name: Jacobaea vulgaris
species.tip: Branched ragwort with ragged, deeply cut leaves and flat-topped clusters of yellow daisies. Very common on grassland and waste ground; poisonous to livestock.

species.name: Jasione montana
species.tip: Looks like a scabious but with a rounded blue pom-pom head of fused-based petals and no bracts like a daisy; dry acid grass and cliffs.

species.name: Jasminum beesianum
species.tip: Scrambling shrub with pinkish-red flowers fading to paler, scented, and oval leaves; occasional garden shrub, rarely persisting.

species.name: Jasminum nudiflorum
species.tip: Green-stemmed scrambler with bright yellow flowers appearing in winter on bare stems, and leaves of three leaflets; common garden plant, occasionally naturalised.

species.name: Jasminum officinale
species.tip: Vigorous climber with white, sweetly scented flowers and pinnate leaves of five to nine leaflets; a common garden plant, rarely escaping.

species.name: Juglans nigra
species.tip: Large tree with long leaves of many toothed leaflets, deeply furrowed dark bark and round green fruits. Planted in parks; sometimes self-sown.

species.name: Juglans regia
species.tip: Large tree with aromatic pinnate leaves with 5 to 9 leaflets and long green catkins; planted and self-sown near fruiting trees, with big green-husked nuts.

species.name: Juncus acutiflorus
species.tip: Tall tufted rush of wet pastures with dark, pointed flower heads and hollow cross-partitioned leaves; branches of the inflorescence spread out; tepals are pointed.

species.name: Juncus acutus
species.tip: Very stout, sharply spine-tipped grey-green rush forming tussocks. Local on coastal dunes and damp slacks in Wales, south and east England and Ireland.

species.name: Juncus alpinoarticulatus
species.tip: Slender creeping rush with dark brown flower clusters at stem ends, flowering heads rather loose. Rare plant of wet upland flushes in northern Britain; a specialist should confirm.

species.name: Juncus articulatus
species.tip: Rush of wet ground with flattened or knotty stems and leaves with visible cross-partitions; flowers dark in clusters whose tepals are pointed; fruits glossy and blunt, shorter than similar rushes.

species.name: Juncus balticus
species.tip: Rhizomatous rush with stems spaced out along the rhizome and a lateral brown flower cluster. Coastal dune slacks in Scotland, northern England, Wales and Ireland.

species.name: Juncus biglumis
species.tip: Short rush with only two dark flowers in a terminal head and a leaf-like bract below. Rare on wet mountain flushes in the Scottish Highlands.

species.name: Juncus bufonius
species.tip: Small spreading annual of wet bare paths and pond edges with slender branched stems and flowers singly along the branches, green tepals with a white edge.

species.name: Juncus bulbosus
species.tip: Weak, slender, often floating rush of acid bogs and pools whose base swells into bulb-like tufts; flowers are tiny, green and clustered in small heads.

species.name: Juncus capitatus
species.tip: Tiny tufted annual rush with a few small reddish-brown flower heads. Very rare, on damp bare ground, mainly Cornwall, Devon and Channel Islands.

species.name: Juncus castaneus
species.tip: Rush with large chestnut-brown flower heads at stem tops, with stems and leaves flat. Rare in wet mountain flushes in the central Scottish Highlands.

species.name: Juncus compressus
species.tip: Flattened wiry stems, unlike thread-like ones of the commoner rushes, and round-fruited loose brown heads. Scarce on damp grass in south and east England.

species.name: Juncus conglomeratus
species.tip: Green, soft tufted rush with finely ridged stems and an inflorescence appearing from the side, held tight in compact flower clusters; pith is interrupted and stem ridged when dry.

species.name: Juncus dudleyi
species.tip: Slender rush resembling Tuberculate relatives, with clear ear-like auricles on the leaf sheath. Introduced from North America and very local; a specialist should confirm.

species.name: Juncus effusus
species.tip: Common tufted rush of damp pastures with smooth, glossy, unribbed green stems when fresh and continuous white pith; flower cluster arises low on stem, often loose.

species.name: Juncus filiformis
species.tip: Very slender rush with thread-like stems, and flower clusters appearing on the side of the stem. Rare in upland Britain, by lakes and streams in Scotland.

species.name: Juncus foliosus
species.tip: Perennial rush with flattened leaves and star-like clusters of pointed fruits. Easily confused with Jointed Rush; a specialist is needed to confirm. Mainly in western areas.

species.name: Juncus gerardii
species.tip: Fine, flat leaves with bristly dark flower heads in saltmarshes; two-ranked leaves and brownish-black tepals; grows in salt-influenced grassland near the coast.

species.name: Juncus inflexus
species.tip: Blue-green, strongly ridged stiff stems with interrupted pith, and flower clusters emerging well below the stem tip; found in wet, heavy clay or calcareous soils.

species.name: Juncus maritimus
species.tip: Tall, stiff grey-green rush with sharp spine-tipped stems, and a loose branched flower cluster below the tip. Common in salt marshes and coastal flats.

species.name: Juncus planifolius
species.tip: Rush with flat, grass-like leaves and small round heads of green-brown flowers. Introduced from Australasia; rare, mostly in damp turf and lawns.

species.name: Juncus pygmaeus
species.tip: Tiny tufted annual rush with minute yellow-brown flowers and awl-shaped leaves. Very rare, on damp bare ground on the Lizard in Cornwall.

species.name: Juncus ranarius
species.tip: Small, branched, spreading annual, with tiny flower clusters at branch tips. Can be mistaken for Toad Rush; a close look at fruits is needed. Introduced.

species.name: Juncus squarrosus
species.tip: Tufted rush with a rosette of stiff, grooved, curved leaves and dark flower spikes; typical of acid moorland, bog and heath, quite unlike other rushes.

species.name: Juncus subnodulosus
species.tip: Tall rush with rough, ridged stems, and blunt flowers in loose clusters. Similar to Sharp-flowered Rush; found in fens and wet meadows, mainly lowland England and Ireland.

species.name: Juncus tenuis
species.tip: Wiry, slender rush of paths and tracks with long leafy bracts overtopping the loose cluster of pale green-brown flowers; naturalised in North American origin.

species.name: Juncus trifidus
species.tip: Dense wiry tufts with stiff stems that bear three leaf-like bracts under a small flower cluster. Upland rush of Scottish mountain tops and rocky ledges.

species.name: Juncus triglumis
species.tip: Small rush with three pale to brown flowers in a terminal cluster, with pointed bracts. Local in wet mountain flushes in the Scottish Highlands and northern Ireland.

species.name: Juncus xiphioides
species.tip: Flat, sword-like leaves arranged like an iris, with long creeping stems and branched flower clusters. Introduced garden plant, rarely spreads in wet ground.

species.name: Juniperus communis
species.tip: Prickly conifer shrub with needles in threes, each with a white stripe above, and berry-like cones turning blue-black; chalk downs, moors and uplands.

species.name: Kalmia angustifolia
species.tip: Small evergreen shrub with narrow oval leaves in whorls or pairs and small crimson-pink saucer flowers set below the shoot tips. Rare garden plant, hardly naturalised.

species.name: Kalmia latifolia
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with glossy laurel-like leaves; pink buds open to pale pink cup flowers with ten pouches holding the anthers. Planted in gardens, rarely persisting in the wild.

species.name: Kalmia polifolia
species.tip: Low evergreen with narrow leaves rolled at the edges and whitish beneath, topped by clusters of rose-pink saucers. Garden plant, occasionally naturalised on peat.

species.name: Kalmia procumbens
species.tip: Mat-forming creeping evergreen of Scottish mountain tops, with tiny rolled narrow leaves and tiny pink bells. Looks like a dwarf heather but leaves are opposite.

species.name: Kerria japonica
species.tip: Arching green-stemmed shrub with pointed double-toothed leaves and bright golden-yellow flowers, often double in the common form; naturalised on hedges and banks.

species.name: Kickxia elatine
species.tip: Trailing annual of arable fields with arrow-shaped leaves with two spreading basal lobes; flowers have a purple upper lip and yellow lower lip. Stalks hairless. Compare Round-leaved Fluellen.

species.name: Kickxia spuria
species.tip: Trailing annual of arable fields with rounded to oval leaves lacking basal lobes; flower stalks are hairy and the flowers have a deep purple upper lip and yellow lower lip.

species.name: Knautia arvensis
species.tip: Rounded heads of lilac-blue flowers, outer florets larger, on tall stems; lobed leaves; tall and hairy, unlike Small Scabious; found on dry grassland and verges.

species.name: Kniphofia uvaria
species.tip: Tough tufted plant with keeled grassy leaves rough on the edges and a dense torch-like spike of orange-red tubular flowers. Garden escape on coastal cliffs and dunes.

species.name: Koeleria macrantha
species.tip: Dense, shiny, pale spike-like panicle on dry calcareous grassland; leaves bluish with soft hairs at the base and no awns.

species.name: Koeleria vallesiana
species.tip: Tufted grass with a dense shining cylindrical panicle and tough rolled leaves with fibrous old sheaths; extremely rare, on limestone in the Avon Gorge, Somerset.

species.name: Koelreuteria paniculata
species.tip: Planted small tree with large pinnate leaves of coarsely lobed leaflets, big airy yellow flower sprays in summer, then papery lantern-like three-sided fruits.

species.name: Koenigia alpina
species.tip: Tall garden knotweed with narrow pointed leaves and big airy sprays of tiny white flowers. Occasional garden escape on waste ground; less coarse than Japanese Knotweed.

species.name: Koenigia campanulata
species.tip: Clump-forming knotweed with white-felted undersides to leaves and nodding pink or white bell-like flowers. Widespread garden escape on damp banks and roadsides, especially in the west.

species.name: Koenigia islandica
species.tip: Tiny, weak, mat-forming annual with small oval leaves and minute greenish flowers. Very rare, found only on a few mountain sites in Skye and Mull.

species.name: Koenigia mollis
species.tip: Tall garden knotweed with broad softly hairy oval leaves and large branched sprays of tiny white flowers. Rare escape; best checked with a specialist.

species.name: Koenigia polystachya
species.tip: Dense patch-forming plant with long narrow pointed leaves and rounded clusters of pink-white flowers. Aggressive garden escape on damp roadsides and streamsides, widely naturalised.

species.name: Koenigia weyrichii
species.tip: Tall garden knotweed with long oval leaves white-felted beneath and large sprays of tiny white flowers. Very rare escape; specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Laburnum anagyroides
species.tip: Small garden tree with trifoliate leaves and long hanging chains of yellow pea flowers; all parts are poisonous; often self-sown.

species.name: Lactuca saligna
species.tip: Slender lettuce with very narrow, often lobed leaves held upright against the stem, and small pale yellow heads. Rare, dry grassland and sea walls, south-east England.

species.name: Lactuca sativa
species.tip: Cultivated lettuce, bolting to a tall stem with small pale yellow heads; leaves oval, clasping the stem and not prickly. Occasional escape on tips and waste ground.

species.name: Lactuca serriola
species.tip: Tall, greyish lettuce with leaves twisted to face north-south, prickles along the midrib beneath, and small pale yellow heads. Waste ground and walls.

species.name: Lactuca tatarica
species.tip: Tall hairless lettuce with deeply cut leaves and pale blue-lilac heads. Rare casual of waste ground and shingle, chiefly coastal.

species.name: Lactuca virosa
species.tip: Tall robust lettuce with big undivided, broad leaves held horizontally and small pale yellow heads in a large pyramid. Waste ground, chalk and coasts; purplish stem.

species.name: Lagarosiphon major
species.tip: Submerged plant with leaves spirally arranged, crowded and strongly curled backwards, giving a bottlebrush look; stiff stems, unlike the whorled leaves of Elodea. Garden pond escape.

species.name: Lagurus ovatus
species.tip: Annual with a soft woolly ovoid head and long bent awns, easily recognised; Mediterranean plant naturalised on dunes in the Channel Islands, casual elsewhere.

species.name: Lamium galeobdolon
species.tip: Yellow flowers with reddish streaks on the lower lip; an ancient-woodland indicator.

species.name: Lamium album
species.tip: Looks like a stinging nettle but has white flowers and does not sting.

species.name: Lamium amplexicaule
species.tip: Upper leaves have no stalk and clasp the stem in pairs beneath the flowers.

species.name: Lamium confertum
species.tip: Small annual dead-nettle with pink flowers whose corolla tube is longer than the calyx, and with blunt, rounded, shallowly toothed leaves. Arable land mainly in northern Scotland.

species.name: Lamium hybridum
species.tip: Annual dead-nettle with leaves deeply and sharply toothed or cut, and purplish-pink flowers. Told from Red Dead-nettle by its cut leaf bases and sharper teeth. Common on arable land.

species.name: Lamium maculatum
species.tip: Garden dead-nettle with a white stripe down the middle of each leaf and large pinkish-purple flowers. Established on hedgebanks and roadsides near gardens.

species.name: Lamium purpureum
species.tip: Upper leaves crowded and tinged purple; an annual of gardens and bare ground.

species.name: Lampranthus aureus
species.tip: Sprawling shrubby succulent with narrow fleshy leaves and bright orange-yellow daisy-like flowers; a rare escape on warm south-western coasts, easily mistaken for related iceplants.

species.name: Lampranthus falciformis
species.tip: Low succulent with curved, sickle-shaped fleshy leaves and pink-purple daisy-like flowers; rare garden relic on southern coasts and not easy to separate from relatives.

species.name: Lampranthus roseus
species.tip: Small shrubby succulent with narrow fleshy leaves and rose-pink daisy-like flowers; occasional on southern coasts as an escape, with many similar relatives needing an expert.

species.name: Laphangium luteoalbum
species.tip: Grey woolly cudweed with small clusters of yellowish-brown heads at the stem tips and leaves wrapping around the stem. Damp sandy ground, local in southern England.

species.name: Lapsana communis
species.tip: Slender, branched plant with many small pale yellow heads that open only in the morning, and fruits with no hairy parachute. Hedgebanks, walls and waste places.

species.name: Larix decidua
species.tip: Deciduous conifer with soft needles in tufts, bright green in spring; cones small with straight scales and twigs yellowish, unlike Japanese Larch.

species.name: Larix kaempferi
species.tip: Deciduous conifer with blue-green needles, reddish twigs and cones with scales curved back like a rose; widely planted, unlike European Larch.

species.name: Lathraea clandestina
species.tip: Leafless parasite with violet flowers in one-sided spikes and pale scaly stems; flowers are mauve-purple, unlike the pale pinkish Toothwort. Naturalised by streams under willow or alder.

species.name: Lathraea squamaria
species.tip: Pale pinkish-white parasitic plant with no green colour, drooping one-sided spike of flowers and scaly stems, growing on hazel and elm roots in woods.

species.name: Lathyrus aphaca
species.tip: Hairless, grey-green climbing plant with no leaflets, but with pairs of arrow-shaped stipules and a tendril; solitary yellow flowers. Rare, in southern England on waste ground.

species.name: Lathyrus grandiflorus
species.tip: Climbing perennial pea with large purple and pink flowers, usually two per stalk, and winged stems absent. Garden escape on waste ground.

species.name: Lathyrus heterophyllus
species.tip: Climbing pea with broad winged stem and pink flowers in few-flowered clusters, leaves of two or three pairs of leaflets. Rare garden escape.

species.name: Lathyrus hirsutus
species.tip: Slender annual pea with hairy pods and small blue and pink flowers in pairs. Rare, in southern England in disturbed ground.

species.name: Lathyrus japonicus
species.tip: Fleshy, spreading pea of shingle beaches with grey-green pinnate leaves and purple-and-blue flowers. Local on the coasts of Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Lathyrus latifolius
species.tip: Climber with winged stems, two broad leaflets, tendrils and large bright pink flower clusters; garden escape on rough ground.

species.name: Lathyrus linifolius
species.tip: Slender plant of woods and heaths with no tendrils, pinnate leaves, and flowers turning from crimson to blue-green; stem is winged.

species.name: Lathyrus niger
species.tip: Upright pea with blue-green leaflets turning black when dried and purple flowers fading blue. Rare, in woods of Scotland and the north.

species.name: Lathyrus nissolia
species.tip: Looks like a grass until it flowers: leaves are narrow and unbranched, with small crimson flowers on long stalks, in rough grassland.

species.name: Lathyrus oleraceus
species.tip: Familiar crop pea with large leaf-like stipules, tendrils and white or purple flowers. Relic of cultivation on tips and rough ground.

species.name: Lathyrus palustris
species.tip: Winged-stemmed climbing pea of fens with narrow leaflets and bluish-purple flower clusters. Rare, in fens in East Anglia and a few other sites.

species.name: Lathyrus pratensis
species.tip: Yellow pea flowers in short spikes in grassland and verges; paired narrow pointed leaflets with a simple tendril and a pair of arrow-shaped stipules.

species.name: Lathyrus sylvestris
species.tip: Large winged-stemmed climbing pea with narrow leaflets and pink flowers; branched tendrils. Local in hedges and scrub.

species.name: Lathyrus tuberosus
species.tip: Slender unwinged pea with pairs of leaflets and bright magenta-pink flowers; underground tubers. Rare casual in cornfields and waste ground.

species.name: Lathyrus vernus
species.tip: Upright pea with no tendrils, pairs of pointed leaflets and nodding flowers opening purple and fading blue-green. Garden plant, rarely escaping.

species.name: Laurus nobilis
species.tip: Evergreen shrub or tree with glossy, aromatic, pointed oval leaves and small yellow-green flower clusters. Often planted; self-sown seedlings found near gardens.

species.name: Lavandula angustifolia
species.tip: Familiar grey-green shrub with narrow leaves and spikes of fragrant violet-blue flowers. A garden plant that is only occasionally found on walls or dry banks.

species.name: Leersia oryzoides
species.tip: Rhizomatous grass of ditches and pond edges with a wide airy panicle and flat leaves with razor-sharp edges that cut skin; local in southern England.

species.name: Legousia hybrida
species.tip: Low arable annual with small violet star-shaped flowers whose petals are shorter than the sepals, and wavy-edged clasping leaves. Local on chalky cornfield margins in southern England.

species.name: Legousia speculum-veneris
species.tip: Annual with bright violet-purple flat flowers, petals longer than the sepals, in loose branched clusters; larger-flowered than Venuss-looking-glass. Rare casual of arable land and gardens.

species.name: Lemna gibba
species.tip: Floating duckweed whose rounded fronds are swollen and spongy-looking underneath; fronds are bigger and more rounded than Common Duckweed. Flowers are seldom seen.

species.name: Lemna minor
species.tip: The common duckweed of still ponds, with small flat oval single-rooted fronds, three-veined and floating; flowers are rare and very tiny.

species.name: Lemna minuta
species.tip: Tiny non-native duckweed with very small, narrow-oval fronds having one vein, and spreads rapidly on ponds; smaller than Common Duckweed. Flowers are very rare.

species.name: Lemna trisulca
species.tip: Duckweed submerged under the water surface, with translucent, flat, lance-shaped fronds joined in branching crosses, and only reaches surface during flowering.

species.name: Lemna turionifera
species.tip: Tiny floating duckweed with plants often reddish below, oval and without a ridge or tooth; flowers are almost never seen; specialist confirmation needed.

species.name: Leontodon hispidus
species.tip: Rosette plant with bristly leaves with forked hairs and single yellow dandelion-like heads on unbranched, leafy-scale stalks. Grassland, mostly on chalk and lime.

species.name: Leontodon saxatilis
species.tip: Small, slender plant with hairless or sparsely hairy leaves, drooping buds and small yellow heads that are red-striped beneath. Short grass, lawns and coastal turf.

species.name: Leonurus cardiaca
species.tip: Tall plant with deeply palmately lobed leaves and spiny-calyxed pink flowers in dense whorls up the stem. A scarce relic of cultivation on waste ground and hedgerows.

species.name: Lepidium campestre
species.tip: Hairy plant of dry grassland and field edges with arrow-shaped stem leaves clasping the stem, small cream flowers and rough heart-shaped pods.

species.name: Lepidium coronopus
species.tip: Flat mat on trampled ground and paths with deeply cut leaves and flower clusters opposite the leaves; pods wrinkled, flattened and not notched.

species.name: Lepidium didymum
species.tip: Strong-smelling annual weed with finely divided leaves, tiny flowers and notched twin-lobed pods; upright and finer than Swine-cress.

species.name: Lepidium draba
species.tip: Patch-forming perennial of roadsides with grey downy foliage, arrow-shaped clasping stem leaves and dense domed clusters of white flowers.

species.name: Lepidium heterophyllum
species.tip: Greyish perennial pepperwort of waste ground and walls with violet anthers on white flowers and oval, clasping upper leaves.

species.name: Lepidium latifolium
species.tip: Tall, hairless perennial with broad leaves and dense heads of tiny white flowers. Mostly found on coastal salt marshes and sea walls, with a few inland.

species.name: Lepidium ruderale
species.tip: Foul-smelling annual with tiny greenish flowers lacking petals. The lower leaves are lobed and the upper leaves entire. Found on waste ground and by roads.

species.name: Lepidium sativum
species.tip: Grown as a salad; fine, divided bright green leaves and tiny white flowers. Casual escape on waste ground, with small round flat pods.

species.name: Leucanthemella serotina
species.tip: Tall late-flowering plant with white daisy-like heads and narrow toothed leaves; looks like a big oxeye daisy but flowers in autumn. Garden escape on waste ground and roadsides.

species.name: Leucanthemum vulgare
species.tip: Large white daisy with yellow centre on tall stems, and rounded toothed spoon-shaped basal leaves. Common in meadows and verges, summer.

species.name: Leucojum aestivum
species.tip: Taller than Snowdrop with several white bells, each petal tipped green, on one stem; wet meadows and riverbanks in spring, mainly Thames valley and Ireland.

species.name: Leucojum vernum
species.tip: Snowdrop-like bulb with bell-shaped white flowers with equal petals, each tipped green; larger than Snowdrop and flowering a little later; scattered garden escape and rare natives.

species.name: Leucothoe fontanesiana
species.tip: Arching evergreen shrub with long pointed oval leaves and dangling spikes of small white urn flowers from the leaf axils. Garden shrub, occasionally naturalised.

species.name: Levisticum officinale
species.tip: Tall, glossy celery-scented plant with greenish-yellow umbels and shiny, toothed leaflets; an old herb persisting near gardens and on waste ground.

species.name: Leycesteria formosa
species.tip: Shrub with hollow green bamboo-like stems and hanging spikes of white flowers among purple-red bracts, followed by dark berries; garden escape on waste ground.

species.name: Leymus arenarius
species.tip: Stout blue-grey coastal grass forming broad clumps, with a thick spike of paired spikelets in two rows; widely spreading rhizomes make it a dune builder.

species.name: Libertia formosa
species.tip: Clump of tough, narrow evergreen leaves with sprays of three-petalled white flowers on stiff stems. Garden plant occasionally found on mild-area waste ground.

species.name: Ligusticum scoticum
species.tip: Seashore plant with shiny dark-green, thrice-divided, celery-scented leaves and small white umbels; grows on rocky shores and sea cliffs in Scotland, northern England and Ireland.

species.name: Ligustrum vulgare
species.tip: Semi-evergreen shrub with opposite, narrow dark glossy smooth-edged leaves and heavy-scented creamy flower spikes, followed by shiny black berries; on chalk and limestone scrub.

species.name: Lilium martagon
species.tip: Tall lily with nodding, pinkish-purple spotted flowers whose petals curl right back, and leaves in whorls up the stem; naturalised in a few woods.

species.name: Lilium pyrenaicum
species.tip: Garden escape with greenish-yellow, dark-spotted turk's-cap flowers that smell unpleasant, on a leafy stem with many alternate narrow leaves; naturalised locally in the west.

species.name: Limbarda crithmoides
species.tip: Fleshy, hairless coastal plant with narrow, succulent leaves and golden-yellow daisy heads; unlike rock samphire its heads are not umbels. Salt marshes and sea cliffs.

species.name: Limnanthes douglasii
species.tip: Garden annual with yellow petals tipped white, and shiny divided leaves with toothed lobes, often escaping on damp disturbed ground.

species.name: Limonium auriculae-ursifolium
species.tip: Mediterranean sea-lavender with a rosette of broad oval leaves and branched lilac flower sprays. A rare escape; sea-lavenders need a specialist to confirm.

species.name: Limonium bellidifolium
species.tip: Small, dense sea-lavender with leaves that wither before flowering and small pale lilac flowers in compact spikes. Very rare, on sandy and shingly saltmarsh edges in East Anglia.

species.name: Limonium binervosum
species.tip: Compact sea-lavender of rocky coasts with spoon-shaped leaves with one or three veins and lilac flowers in short spikes. Aggregate of many microspecies; a specialist is needed to name it.

species.name: Limonium britannicum
species.tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of southern coastal cliffs with leathery spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in short spikes. A specialist is needed to name it with certainty.

species.name: Limonium dodartiforme
species.tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of sea cliffs with spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in spreading spikes. A specialist is needed to confirm which microspecies it is.

species.name: Limonium humile
species.tip: Sea-lavender of the upper saltmarsh with narrow spoon-shaped, one-veined leaves and loose, sparse spikes of lilac flowers. Compare Common Sea-lavender, which has broader leaves and denser heads.

species.name: Limonium hyblaeum
species.tip: Mediterranean sea-lavender with broad oval leaves and branched sprays of lilac flowers. Very rare introduction; sea-lavenders need a specialist to confirm identification.

species.name: Limonium loganicum
species.tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of Cornish coastal rocks, with small spoon-shaped leaves and short lilac flower spikes. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Limonium normannicum
species.tip: Low sea-lavender of the Channel Islands, with spoon-shaped leaves and short lilac flower spikes on sea cliffs. A rock sea-lavender microspecies needing a specialist to name it.

species.name: Limonium paradoxum
species.tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies restricted to coastal rocks near Oban in western Scotland, with spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers on short spikes. Confirm with a specialist.

species.name: Limonium parvum
species.tip: Very small rock sea-lavender microspecies with tiny spoon-shaped leaves and short lilac spikes on sea cliffs. Separation from other rock sea-lavenders needs a specialist.

species.name: Limonium platyphyllum
species.tip: Robust garden sea-lavender with large oval leaves and big airy branched sprays of lilac flowers. A rare escape well away from the coast, unlike native sea-lavenders.

species.name: Limonium procerum
species.tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of western coasts with larger spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in longer spikes. A specialist is needed to confirm identification.

species.name: Limonium recurvum
species.tip: Rock sea-lavender found only on limestone cliffs and quarries on Portland, Dorset, with spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in curved spikes. A specialist can confirm it.

species.name: Limonium transwallianum
species.tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of western coasts, with spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in short spikes. Very similar to other microspecies, so a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Limonium vulgare
species.tip: Saltmarsh perennial with broad leaves with one main vein and dense, branched sprays of lilac flowers. Common on muddy estuary marshes; Lax-flowered Sea-lavender has narrower leaves and sparse spikes.

species.name: Limosella aquatica
species.tip: Tiny annual of drying mud with rosettes of long-stalked spoon-shaped leaves and minute whitish flowers on short stalks. Found on pond and reservoir margins, mostly in England and Wales.

species.name: Limosella australis
species.tip: Tiny mud plant like Mudwort but with narrow, awl-like leaves and no spoon-shaped blade. Very rare, known from estuary mud in Wales.

species.name: Linaria arenaria
species.tip: Small sticky-hairy annual with tiny pale yellow flowers and a short spur, on coastal dunes. Introduced, naturalised in a few places such as south-west England.

species.name: Linaria dalmatica
species.tip: Tall blue-grey toadflax with broad, clasping, pointed leaves and big lemon-yellow snapdragon flowers with orange throat. Larger and broader-leaved than Common Toadflax; garden escape.

species.name: Linaria pelisseriana
species.tip: Slender, upright toadflax with narrow leaves and violet flowers with a white throat. Native in Jersey; elsewhere in Britain only a rare casual or garden escape.

species.name: Linaria purpurea
species.tip: Garden escape on walls and waste ground; tall, grey-green and slender with spikes of small violet-purple spurred flowers. Plants with pink forms occur; Common Toadflax is yellow.

species.name: Linaria repens
species.tip: Greyish toadflax with whorled narrow leaves and white or pale lilac flowers streaked with violet veins. Spreads by suckers on banks and waste ground; mainly southern and eastern England.

species.name: Linaria supina
species.tip: Low, spreading toadflax with grey-green narrow leaves and yellow flowers with an orange palate. A rare casual or garden escape on waste ground, not a native.

species.name: Linaria vulgaris
species.tip: Spikes of yellow snapdragon-like flowers with an orange patch and long spur; narrow grey-green leaves crowded up the stem. Grassy banks, verges and hedgerows.

species.name: Linnaea borealis
species.tip: Evergreen creeping subshrub with paired nodding pink bells on slender forked stalks and small rounded leaves. Rare plant of Scottish pine woods and mossy ground.

species.name: Linum bienne
species.tip: Slender flax with pale blue flowers, often streaked veins, and narrow single-veined leaves; differs from cultivated flax by being a wiry perennial of grassland near the coast.

species.name: Linum catharticum
species.tip: Slender annual with tiny white four-to-five-petalled flowers and opposite narrow leaves; chalk and limestone grassland, dunes, short turf, unlike cultivated blue Flax.

species.name: Linum perenne
species.tip: Taller, more tufted flax with sky-blue flowers and many narrow leaves; a garden escape, and a scarce native subspecies grows on chalk in East Anglia.

species.name: Linum radiola
species.tip: Tiny branched annual of damp acid sandy tracks with paired oval leaves and many minute white four-petalled flowers.

species.name: Linum usitatissimum
species.tip: Tall slender annual with bright blue flowers, narrow alternate leaves and rounded seed capsules; relic of cultivation on waste ground and field edges.

species.name: Lipandra polysperma
species.tip: Low sprawling annual with reddish stems and small, untoothed oval leaves; dense clusters of green flowers; not mealy; local on disturbed damp ground and field edges.

species.name: Liparis loeselii
species.tip: Small yellow-green orchid with two glossy ribbed leaves and a few flowers with a narrow lip; rare, in dune slacks and fens.

species.name: Lithospermum officinale
species.tip: Upright rough plant of scrub and chalk edges with small dull cream flowers and remarkably hard, shiny white nutlets like tiny porcelain beads.

species.name: Littorella uniflora
species.tip: Small tufted plant of lake shores with narrow, pointed, quill-like leaves in a low mat; flowers inconspicuous on short stalks. Resembles a tiny plantain but grows on gravelly or muddy margins.

species.name: Lobelia dortmanna
species.tip: Submerged rosettes of stiff, hollow, quill-like leaves in clear acid lakes; a bare flower stem rising above water bearing a few pale lilac nodding flowers. Upland Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Lobelia erinus
species.tip: Small blue bedding plant with two-lipped flowers with a white eye, straggling stems and toothed leaves; occasional escape on pavements and walls.

species.name: Lobelia urens
species.tip: Slender upright plant of damp acid grassland with small blue-violet two-lipped flowers in a spike and toothed oblong leaves. Very local in southern England, especially Devon and Sussex.

species.name: Lobularia maritima
species.tip: Low, tufted garden escape with grey narrow leaves and masses of small honey-scented white flowers on walls and paving, flowering for months.

species.name: Logfia gallica
species.tip: Tiny grey woolly annual which forks repeatedly, with clusters of small heads set in the forks and pointed leaves. Rare on sandy fields in south and east England.

species.name: Logfia minima
species.tip: Tiny, upright grey woolly annual with small clustered heads at stem tips and tiny narrow leaves. Dry sandy heaths and grassland, scattered.

species.name: Lolium multiflorum
species.tip: Rye-grass with awns on the spikelets and rolled young leaves, broader and glossier than Perennial Rye-grass; short-lived, sown in leys.

species.name: Lolium perenne
species.tip: Common sown grass with a flat two-rowed spike, spikelets facing the stem edge-on and awnless; young leaves folded, shiny underneath.

species.name: Lolium temulentum
species.tip: Annual rye-grass with a long spike and spikelets bearing a long awn, much longer glumes than Perennial Rye-grass; very rare as a relict weed of cereals.

species.name: Lonicera caprifolium
species.tip: Climber whose upper pairs of leaves are fused around the stem, forming a disc; creamy-yellow fragrant flowers in clusters. Rare woodland and hedge escape, flowering earlier than common honeysuckle.

species.name: Lonicera henryi
species.tip: Evergreen climber with narrow dark glossy leaves and clusters of small dull purplish-red and yellowish flowers followed by black berries. Rare garden escape.

species.name: Lonicera japonica
species.tip: Twining semi-evergreen climber with paired, fragrant white flowers ageing yellow, and black berries; rare escape, differing from native Honeysuckle in having hairy shoots.

species.name: Lonicera periclymenum
species.tip: Native twining climber of hedges and woods with pairs of tubular, creamy yellow flowers flushed pink, strongly scented at night; red berries in clusters in autumn.

species.name: Lonicera xylosteum
species.tip: Upright shrub with paired, hairy oval leaves and pairs of cream-yellow flowers held on short stalks, followed by joined red berries. Rare native of woods and scrub on chalk.

species.name: Lotus angustissimus
species.tip: Small, slender annual with tiny trifoliate leaves and one or two yellow flowers; pods very slender. Rare, in the south on dry open ground.

species.name: Lotus corniculatus
species.tip: Yellow flowers often with orange buds in heads of 2-6; five leaflets, solid stem and pods spreading like a bird's foot.

species.name: Lotus maritimus
species.tip: Low, spreading pea with leaves of three leaflets plus stipules, and large pale yellow flowers singly; winged pods. Rare, introduced on grassland.

species.name: Lotus pedunculatus
species.tip: Taller than Common Bird's-foot-trefoil with hollow stems, wetter habitats and heads of 5-12 flowers, blue-green leaflets and flowers reddish in bud.

species.name: Lotus subbiflorus
species.tip: Small hairy annual trefoil with one to two yellow flowers per head and narrow stipules; local on coast grassland in the south and west.

species.name: Lotus tenuis
species.tip: Slender trefoil with narrow leaflets, and long thin stalks bearing small yellow flower heads. Local in damp grassland, mostly in the south and east.

species.name: Ludwigia grandiflora
species.tip: Invasive aquatic plant with large bright yellow five-petalled flowers and oblong hairy leaves in stands; wide choking in ponds and ditches; mainly in the south.

species.name: Ludwigia palustris
species.tip: Creeping plant of wet muddy places with opposite oval leaves and tiny green petalless flowers in leaf axils; rare, mainly in the New Forest.

species.name: Luma apiculata
species.tip: Evergreen with peeling orange-cinnamon bark, small oval aromatic leaves and white cup-shaped flowers with many stamens; garden shrub in mild western areas.

species.name: Lunaria annua
species.tip: Garden escape with heart-shaped toothed leaves, purple or white flowers and, later, round papery silvery seed discs.

species.name: Lupinus arboreus
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with silvery leaves of palmate leaflets and spikes of pale yellow, sometimes bluish, scented flowers. Naturalised on sand and shingle in the south and west.

species.name: Lupinus nootkatensis
species.tip: Perennial lupin with hairy palmate leaves and spikes of blue-purple flowers. Introduced and naturalised on river shingle in Scotland and northern England.

species.name: Lupinus polyphyllus
species.tip: Tall lupin with palmate leaves of many leaflets and dense spikes of colourful flowers. Naturalised on roadsides, riverbanks and waste ground.

species.name: Luronium natans
species.tip: Aquatic with narrow ribbon submerged leaves and small oval floating leaves, white flowers with a yellow spot; mainly Wales and north-west England in lakes and canals.

species.name: Luzula arcuata
species.tip: Small tufted wood-rush, with arching nodding dark clusters on thin stems. Only on high Scottish mountain tops, in bare stony ground and snowbeds.

species.name: Luzula campestris
species.tip: Short, early-flowering grass-like plant with hairy leaves and spread-out clusters of dark brown flowers with yellow anthers; lawns and meadows; flowers earlier than other wood-rushes.

species.name: Luzula forsteri
species.tip: Slender wood-rush with a few hairs on leaf edges and sparse branched clusters of small brown flowers. Local in woods in south and east England.

species.name: Luzula luzuloides
species.tip: Larger tufts with hairy leaves and loose clusters of pale whitish flowers. Introduced, naturalised in woods and on acidic ground in a few places.

species.name: Luzula multiflora
species.tip: Clump-forming and hairy-leaved, with flowers in several dense brown heads on stalks of unequal length; acid grassland and heaths, flowering later than Field Wood-rush.

species.name: Luzula pallescens
species.tip: Hairy-edged grassy leaves and compact heads of small shiny brown flowers. Introduced from Europe, spreading in lawns and woodland edges, especially in the south and east.

species.name: Luzula pilosa
species.tip: Woodland species with broad, hairy grass-like leaves and flowers solitary on drooping stalks, then fruits that bend down; the flowers are chestnut brown.

species.name: Luzula spicata
species.tip: Short wood-rush with a nodding spike-like head of dark brown flowers, and leaves with few hairs. Mountain rush of Scottish uplands and Lake District fells.

species.name: Luzula sylvatica
species.tip: Large tussock-forming wood-rush with glossy, broad, shiny leaves edged with long hairs; dense brown flower heads in spring; grows in damp, shady woods and on mountain ledges.

species.name: Lycium barbarum
species.tip: Lax, spiny-tipped shrub of hedges and waste ground with narrow grey-green leaves, small purple funnel-shaped flowers and orange-red berries.

species.name: Lycium chinense
species.tip: Spiny or thorny shrub with arching stems, narrow leaves and small purple funnel flowers, then orange-red berries. Hard to separate from Duke of Argyll Teaplant, so a specialist helps.

species.name: Lycopodiella inundata
species.tip: Small creeping clubmoss with spreading leaves and cones raised on thin upright stalks; grows on bare wet peaty heathland, mostly in the south and west.

species.name: Lycopodium annotinum
species.tip: Creeping clubmoss with upright branches clothed in spiky leaves and stalkless cones; leaves sit in distinct bands of yearly growth; upland heaths in the north.

species.name: Lycopodium clavatum
species.tip: Creeping clubmoss with leaves bearing a white hair tip and spore cones on slim stalks in pairs; heaths and moors, unlike erect Fir Clubmoss.

species.name: Lycopodium lagopus
species.tip: Clubmoss with creeping stem, with each upright shoot topped by a single cone ending in a white hair; not truly British, so a specialist should confirm.

species.name: Lycopsis arvensis
species.tip: Bristly annual of sandy arable land with small bright blue flowers whose throat is closed by white scales. Leaves are wavy-edged and very rough to the touch.

species.name: Lycopus europaeus
species.tip: Deeply toothed to lobed leaves; tiny purple-dotted white flowers in tight whorls.

species.name: Lysichiton americanus
species.tip: Large garden escape of wet woods and stream banks with huge, cabbage-like leaves, and a bright yellow hooded spathe appearing in spring; has a skunk-like smell.

species.name: Lysichiton camtschatcensis
species.tip: Huge, glossy, paddle-shaped leaves and a white spathe around a thick greenish spike; invasive-looking pond-edge plant, introduced to some wet habitats, and foul smelling.

species.name: Lysimachia arvensis
species.tip: Low sprawling annual of bare and cultivated ground; small orange-red five-petalled flowers that close in dull weather; opposite unstalked oval leaves dotted beneath.

species.name: Lysimachia ciliata
species.tip: Yellow flowers nodding on long stalks, with opposite leaves with fringed stalks. Garden escape in damp places, scattered through England and Ireland.

species.name: Lysimachia europaea
species.tip: Northern woods and moors; a single whorl of shiny leaves at the top of a slender stem with one or two starry white flowers of about seven petals.

species.name: Lysimachia foemina
species.tip: Low, annual, with small, blue flowers on thin stalks and opposite oval leaves. Very rare weed of arable land in southern England; scarlet Pimpernel is redder.

species.name: Lysimachia maritima
species.tip: Low fleshy plant of saltmarshes and coastal rocks; small pink flowers with no petals, sitting in the leaf joints; opposite oval leaves.

species.name: Lysimachia minima
species.tip: Minute annual of damp bare sandy or peaty ground, often under 5 cm; tiny pinkish flowers hidden in the leaf joints.

species.name: Lysimachia nemorum
species.tip: Creeping woodland plant with solitary star-like yellow flowers on slender stalks and pointed oval paired leaves; shady woods and streamsides.

species.name: Lysimachia nummularia
species.tip: Trailing mat with rounded paired leaves and large cup-shaped yellow flowers singly in leaf axils; damp grass and riverbanks.

species.name: Lysimachia punctata
species.tip: Garden escape with whorled hairy leaves and whorls of yellow flowers with fringed edges and orange spots; stands upright on verges and waste ground.

species.name: Lysimachia tenella
species.tip: Creeping mats in wet acid ground with tiny round paired leaves and delicate pale pink bell-shaped flowers on long thin stalks.

species.name: Lysimachia terrestris
species.tip: Spreading, stoloniferous marsh plant with spikes of yellow flowers. Alien, naturalised by lakes and ponds, but absent from many counties; rare outside the Sphagnum.

species.name: Lysimachia thyrsiflora
species.tip: Dense, stalked, rounded clusters of small yellow flowers rising from the leaf bases midway up the stem. Rare, in fens and lake margins in northern Britain.

species.name: Lysimachia vulgaris
species.tip: Tall plant of waterside with paired or whorled lance-shaped leaves and big branched panicle of yellow flowers; riverbanks and fens.

species.name: Lythrum hyssopifolia
species.tip: Slender, branched annual with tiny pink flowers sitting singly in leaf axils and narrow leaves; very rare on seasonally flooded ground in the south and east.

species.name: Lythrum portula
species.tip: Small creeping annual of wet muddy places with opposite spoon-shaped leaves and tiny stalkless flowers in leaf axils; flowers are easily overlooked.

species.name: Lythrum salicaria
species.tip: Tall plant of wet places with leafy spikes of vivid magenta flowers and opposite or whorled narrow leaves, in summer; unlike willowherbs, has six petals.

species.name: Mahonia aquifolium
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with glossy holly-like pinnate leaves and dense upright yellow flower clusters in early spring; later blue-black berries. Planted and naturalised, no spines on stem.

species.name: Maianthemum bifolium
species.tip: Low woodland plant with only two glossy heart-shaped stem leaves and a small spike of tiny white four-petalled flowers. Very rare, in a few northern English woods.

species.name: Maianthemum kamtschaticum
species.tip: Spreading woodland plant like May lily but with several broad oval, pointed leaves up the stem and a spike of small white flowers. Rare garden escape.

species.name: Malcolmia maritima
species.tip: Low annual garden flower with pink, red, lilac or white fragrant flowers and long thin pods. Established on coastal sand and shingle in places.

species.name: Malus domestica
species.tip: Cultivated apple escaping from gardens: leaves downy beneath, white flowers flushed pink, large sweet fruit. Wild Crab Apple has hairless leaves and small sour fruit.

species.name: Malus sylvestris
species.tip: Native tree of woods and hedges with blossom white flushed pink; leaves hairless when mature, small sour yellow-green fruit; twigs sometimes spiny. Cultivated Apple has downy leaves.

species.name: Malva alcea
species.tip: Mallow with large pink flowers with notched petals, and upper leaves cut into narrow deep lobes; star-shaped hairs on stems.

species.name: Malva arborea
species.tip: Tall, woody-based biennial with soft lobed leaves and purple-centred pink flowers; grows on coastal cliffs, rocks and waste ground, mainly western coasts.

species.name: Malva moschata
species.tip: Roadside and grassland mallow with large, pale pink flowers with notched petals; the upper leaves are deeply cut into narrow segments, unlike Common Mallow.

species.name: Malva multiflora
species.tip: Resembles Tree-mallow but flowers are paler lilac-pink and clustered on shorter stalks; casual or naturalised near the coast in the south-west.

species.name: Malva neglecta
species.tip: Low, spreading weed of waste ground with small, pale lilac-white flowers and rounded, shallowly lobed leaves; fruiting stalks bend down and the petals are barely longer than the sepals.

species.name: Malva setigera
species.tip: Rare casual with pale pink flowers and lobed hairy leaves, easily mistaken for other mallows; a specialist should confirm identification.

species.name: Malva sylvestris
species.tip: Tall, bushy plant of verges and waste ground, with pink-purple flowers veined darker and five-lobed leaves; petals are much longer than the sepals and are notched.

species.name: Marrubium vulgare
species.tip: Woolly white-grey plant with wrinkled rounded leaves and dense whorls of small white flowers with spiny-hooked calyx teeth. Dry grassland near the coast and chalk.

species.name: Matricaria chamomilla
species.tip: Finely divided feathery leaves smelling sweetly of apples, and small white-rayed daisies with a cone-shaped hollow yellow centre. Arable land and waste ground.

species.name: Matricaria discoidea
species.tip: Greenish-yellow rayless button heads, feathery leaves that smell of pineapple when crushed. Trampled ground, gateways and paths.

species.name: Matteuccia struthiopteris
species.tip: Tall shuttlecock of large pale green fronds, with separate dark brown fertile fronds in the centre. Garden escape, naturalised beside streams in a few places.

species.name: Matthiola incana
species.tip: Grey, densely downy shrubby plant with sweetly scented pink to purple flowers and leaves not lobed. Grows on sea cliffs, notably Isle of Wight, Dorset and Sussex.

species.name: Matthiola sinuata
species.tip: Biennial grey plant of sandy coasts with lilac-purple flowers and wavy-lobed woolly leaves; stickily hairy pods. Very rare, found in south-west Britain and Wales.

species.name: Medicago arabica
species.tip: Clover-like leaves with a dark central blotch and small yellow flowers in clusters of 1-5; coiled spiny pods; lawns and dry ground.

species.name: Medicago arborea
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with grey-green trefoil leaves and clusters of yellow pea flowers followed by coiled pods. Rare, planted and escaped in the south, usually coastal.

species.name: Medicago littoralis
species.tip: Small, hairy annual medick with clover-like leaves and a few small yellow flowers. Rare, in a few sandy sites in the south.

species.name: Medicago lupulina
species.tip: Low yellow clover-like plant with small round flower heads and kidney-shaped black pods, leaflets with a tiny point on the tip.

species.name: Medicago minima
species.tip: Small downy annual medick with spiny burs coiled in several turns; leaves clover-like. Local on sandy soils, such as Breckland and coasts.

species.name: Medicago polymorpha
species.tip: Spreading, almost hairless annual with trefoil leaves and clusters of small yellow flowers; flat spiny coiled pods. Local on grassland and waste ground.

species.name: Medicago sativa
species.tip: Purple flower clusters in tall oblong spikes with clover-like leaves on field edges; pods coiled like small springs.

species.name: Medicago truncatula
species.tip: Rare annual medick with trifoliate leaves, small yellow flowers and barrel-shaped coiled pods. Casual on waste ground and tips.

species.name: Melampyrum arvense
species.tip: Annual with showy pink-purple bracts and yellow-and-purple flowers, narrow leaves on a hairy stem. A very rare arable weed mainly in southern England.

species.name: Melampyrum cristatum
species.tip: Dense four-sided spike of overlapping purple-pink crested bracts with yellow flowers peeping out; narrow opposite leaves. Rare in woodland rides in eastern England.

species.name: Melampyrum pratense
species.tip: Semi-parasitic annual of woods and heaths with opposite narrow leaves and pale yellow, closed tubular flowers in pairs, all facing one side of the stem.

species.name: Melampyrum sylvaticum
species.tip: Slender annual of woods with small yellow flowers hanging in pairs, with the lower lip bent down; leaves narrow and untoothed. Mainly northern Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Melanoselinum decipiens
species.tip: Large, tropical-looking parsley with stout stems and big coarse leaves, dark leaf stalks and big white umbels; very rare garden outcast, needing specialist confirmation.

species.name: Melica nutans
species.tip: Woodland grass with a one-sided raceme of purple-brown nodding spikelets, leaves rough, and bases swollen; scarce in limestone woods and often in the north and west.

species.name: Melica uniflora
species.tip: Woodland grass with delicate loose raceme of few brownish-purple spikelets; no awns, sheaths slightly hairy and ligule short with a lobe.

species.name: Melilotus albus
species.tip: Tall plant with long spikes of small white flowers and trifoliate toothed leaves; smells of new hay; waste ground and roadsides.

species.name: Melilotus altissimus
species.tip: Yellow-flowered melilot with hairy, downy pods and wings and keel of equal length; keel equals standard, pods black when ripe.

species.name: Melilotus indicus
species.tip: Annual melilot with trifoliate toothed leaves and tiny pale yellow flowers in slender spikes. Casual, on waste ground, tips and roadsides.

species.name: Melilotus officinalis
species.tip: Yellow melilot with hairless, transversely ribbed pods that are brown when ripe; wings longer than keel; roadsides and waste ground.

species.name: Melissa officinalis
species.tip: Lemon-scented perennial with oval toothed leaves and small whitish flowers in leafy whorls. Established garden escape on hedgebanks and waste ground.

species.name: Melittis melissophyllum
species.tip: Distinctive woodland labiate with large flowers, white with a pink or purple blotch on the lip, in pairs in the leaf axils. Rare in south-west England and Wales.

species.name: Mentha aquatica
species.tip: Rounded lilac flower head at the stem tip; strong mint smell.

species.name: Mentha arvensis
species.tip: Flowers only in whorls up the stem; the stem ends in leaves, not flowers.

species.name: Mentha pulegium
species.tip: Low, creeping, strong-smelling mint with tiny rounded whorls of lilac flowers along the stem. Found on seasonally flooded grassy ground and pond edges, mostly in southern England.

species.name: Mentha requienii
