species.tip: Tiny, mat-forming mint with leaves just a few millimetres across and pale lilac flowers in the axils. Strong peppermint smell. Naturalised on damp paths and shaded ground.

species.name: Mentha spicata
species.tip: Garden mint with smooth, pointed, almost stalkless leaves and slender spikes of pale pink-lilac flowers. Common naturalised on damp waste ground and roadsides.

species.name: Mentha suaveolens
species.tip: Hairy, grey-green mint with rounded, wrinkled leaves, and spikes of white or pale pink flowers. Frequent in damp places and gardens, especially in the south-west.

species.name: Menyanthes trifoliata
species.tip: Wetland plant with three-leaflet leaves and spikes of white to pink fringed star-like flowers; shallow water, bogs and fens in spring.

species.name: Mercurialis annua
species.tip: Weed of gardens and arable land with bright green, shiny toothed leaves; male and female flowers on separate plants, tiny and green, in leaf axils. Stem is branched and brittle.

species.name: Mercurialis perennis
species.tip: Carpeting woodland perennial of ancient woods, unbranched hairy stems with toothed dark green leaves; tiny green flowers in early spring, poisonous and unscented.

species.name: Mertensia maritima
species.tip: Fleshy blue-grey creeping plant of northern shingle beaches, with bell flowers opening pink then turning blue. Leaves taste faintly of oysters. Mainly Scotland, northern England and Ireland.

species.name: Mespilus germanica
species.tip: Small crooked tree with large oval leaves and single big white flowers, then brown apple-like fruits with a wide open top; local in hedges and old woods in southern England.

species.name: Meum athamanticum
species.tip: Upland plant with aromatic, very finely feathered leaves in tufts and white or purple-tinged umbels; grows in meadows and mountain pastures in northern England and Scotland.

species.name: Mibora minima
species.tip: Tiny annual with a minute purplish flat spike, flowering very early on bare sandy ground; rare, from Cornwall, Anglesey, Gower and the Channel Islands.

species.name: Micranthes nivalis
species.tip: Tiny mountain plant with a flat rosette of rounded, blunt-toothed leaves and a compact head of small whitish-purple flowers on a hairy stem. Rare in the Scottish and Lake District hills.

species.name: Micranthes stellaris
species.tip: Upland streamsides and wet rocks; rosettes of toothed leaves and starry white flowers with two yellow spots on each petal and red anthers.

species.name: Microthlaspi perfoliatum
species.tip: Small annual with tiny white flowers and pale green stem leaves clasping the stem. Rare on arable land and walls, especially in the Cotswolds.

species.name: Milium effusum
species.tip: Tall, graceful woodland grass with a large open panicle of drooping branches, small unawned spikelets, broad flat soft leaves and a long ligule.

species.name: Milium vernale
species.tip: Small annual of dry sandy ground and open sites with a loose, small panicle; very rare, found in Channel Islands, with flowering in early spring.

species.name: Minuartia recurva
species.tip: Tufted perennial with white flowers on short stalks, and narrow, curved, spiky leaves. Rare plant of serpentine and rocky ground; may be misidentified.

species.name: Misopates orontium
species.tip: Upright annual of arable fields with narrow leaves and pink snapdragon flowers, lacking a spur but with a swollen base. Local, mainly in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Mitella ovalis
species.tip: Low woodland garden plant with heart-shaped toothed basal leaves and slender spikes of tiny fringed greenish-white flowers. A rare garden escape; specialist check advised.

species.name: Moehringia trinervia
species.tip: Woodland plant with oval leaves showing three clear veins and small white flowers with petals shorter than sepals. Weak straggling stems in shady, damp woods.

species.name: Moenchia erecta
species.tip: Small grey-green annual with white flowers held upright, with petals shorter than the sepals, on short erect stems. Local on dry open grass and heaths in southern England.

species.name: Molinia caerulea
species.tip: Large tussocks on wet heath with a narrow purplish panicle; ligule is a fringe of hairs and the stem has only one node near the base.

species.name: Moneses uniflora
species.tip: Tiny evergreen with a ring of rounded leaves and a single large nodding white flower with a long green style. Rare, in a few Scottish pine woods.

species.name: Montia fontana
species.tip: Tiny, pale green, bright, spreading plant of wet springs, flushes and seepages with minute white flowers and opposite spoon-shaped leaves; much smaller than the purslanes.

species.name: Montia parvifolia
species.tip: Low succulent annual with tiny oval leaves and minute white to pink flowers; a rare naturalised alien so a specialist should confirm.

species.name: Morus nigra
species.tip: Spreading tree with rough heart-shaped toothed leaves and dark purple edible fruits like blackberries; planted in gardens, rarely escaping.

species.name: Muehlenbeckia complexa
species.tip: Wiry, tangled evergreen climber with tiny round leaves and small greenish flowers followed by white fleshy fruits. Naturalised on walls and hedges in the south-west and Scilly.

species.name: Muscari armeniacum
species.tip: Garden escape on verges and waste ground with narrow, floppy leaves and a dense spike of small, rounded blue urn-shaped flowers with a white rim.

species.name: Muscari botryoides
species.tip: Small bulb with upright narrow leaves and a short dense spike of globular blue flowers with white teeth. Naturalised on grassy ground.

species.name: Muscari comosum
species.tip: Distinct spike with dull brownish fertile flowers below and a bright violet-blue tuft of sterile flowers on top. Rare introduction on arable ground in the south-east.

species.name: Muscari neglectum
species.tip: Dense spike of small dark blue urn flowers with pale teeth; leaves narrow and floppy. Native in sandy Breckland grassland of East Anglia, widely naturalised elsewhere.

species.name: Mycelis muralis
species.tip: Slender, hairless plant with a loose spray of tiny heads of only five yellow florets and leaves with a large terminal lobe. Shady walls and woodland.

species.name: Myosotis alpestris
species.tip: Rare mountain forget-me-not with large, deep sky-blue flowers in a dense, short head. Found on a few high rocky ledges in Scotland and Teesdale.

species.name: Myosotis arvensis
species.tip: Hairy forget-me-not with small blue flowers and a calyx covered in hooked hairs, with style shorter than calyx. Arable land and open ground.

species.name: Myosotis discolor
species.tip: Tiny flowers that change from cream or yellow to blue as they age, within a coiled spike; calyx with hooked hairs. Dry sandy grassland and fields.

species.name: Myosotis laxa
species.tip: Forget-me-not of wet places with tiny pale blue flowers, with open calyx without hooked hairs, and fruit stalks longer than calyx. Compare Water Forget-me-not.

species.name: Myosotis ramosissima
species.tip: Tiny early-flowering annual with sky-blue flowers on short stalks, and calyx with hooked hairs. Dry open ground, flowering from early spring.

species.name: Myosotis scorpioides
species.tip: Stems rooting in wet places, flowers sky-blue with yellow eye, calyx with short teeth. Stream sides, ditches and marshes; larger flowers than other wet-place forget-me-nots.

species.name: Myosotis secunda
species.tip: Perennial of wet, acidic, upland places, creeping with rooting stems and bright blue flowers; calyx with open lobes in fruit. Streams and flushes.

species.name: Myosotis sicula
species.tip: Tiny annual forget-me-not with minute pale blue flowers on short stems in dry sandy turf. Confined to Jersey, in the Channel Islands.

species.name: Myosotis stolonifera
species.tip: Creeping forget-me-not of upland springs and stream sides, with pale blue flowers and sprawling leafy runners. Mostly northern England and Scotland; flowers smaller and paler than Water Forget-me-not.

species.name: Myosotis sylvatica
species.tip: Larger flowers in woods than other forget-me-nots, bright blue with a yellow centre, on hairy stems; calyx with hooked hairs. Woodland and garden escapes.

species.name: Myosurus minimus
species.tip: Tiny plant with grass-like leaves; the fruiting head stretches into a long, thin, mouse-tail spike.

species.name: Myrica gale
species.tip: Fragrant low shrub of wet heaths and bogs with aromatic grey-green leaves and reddish catkins before the leaves appear; crush leaf to smell resin.

species.name: Myrica pensylvanica
species.tip: Shrub with aromatic, waxy-fruited, narrow oval leaves with a few teeth near the tip and white fruits; planted, rarely naturalised in bogs.

species.name: Myriophyllum alterniflorum
species.tip: Submerged plant with feathery whorled leaves, flower spike tip often drooping and flowers alternately arranged; in acid, peaty waters, unlike coarser Spiked Water-milfoil.

species.name: Myriophyllum aquaticum
species.tip: Aquatic, with emergent feathery blue-green whorled leaves held above water. Female flowers are rare. Invasive in ponds and ditches across lowland Britain.

species.name: Myriophyllum spicatum
species.tip: Submerged plant with feathery leaves in whorls of four and more than 13 pairs of thread-like segments; erect red-tinged flower spikes in hard, base-rich water.

species.name: Myriophyllum verticillatum
species.tip: Submerged plant with whorled feathery leaves and flowers in whorls on a spike above the water. Bracts are longer than the flowers. Found in rich still water, mainly southern England.

species.name: Myrrhis odorata
species.tip: Aniseed-scented, softly hairy plant of northern grassy verges with fern-like leaves often marked with white blotches; fruits are large, long and glossy brown.

species.name: Najas flexilis
species.tip: Slender submerged annual with narrow, finely toothed leaves in small tufts. Rare, in lochs in Scotland and in Ireland.

species.name: Najas marina
species.tip: Brittle submerged plant with broad, spiny-toothed leaves. Very rare, in Norfolk Broads and nearby waters.

species.name: Narcissus bicolor
species.tip: Garden daffodil with a white spreading perianth and a yellow trumpet; naturalised only locally, and there are many daffodil hybrids; specialist advised to confirm.

species.name: Narcissus bulbocodium
species.tip: Tiny daffodil with a wide flaring trumpet and very narrow petals, almost rush-like leaves; naturalised in a few grassy places, unlike the larger wild daffodil.

species.name: Narcissus cyclamineus
species.tip: Small daffodil whose petals sweep sharply backwards from a narrow trumpet, giving a windswept look; a garden escape in damp grass, mainly in western Britain.

species.name: Narcissus hispanicus
species.tip: Robust, large daffodil with a deep golden trumpet that has a frilled, rolled rim and petals of similar colour; a garden escape in grassy places.

species.name: Narcissus minor
species.tip: Smaller than wild daffodil, with a trumpet that is all yellow and petals that are the same shade; a garden escape of grassy banks.

species.name: Narcissus moschatus
species.tip: Nodding daffodil with white or very pale cream, drooping flowers and twisted petals; a rare garden escape in western grassland, easily told by its colour.

species.name: Narcissus nobilis
species.tip: Big, upright wild-type daffodil with a deep yellow trumpet and paler or equal petals; a naturalised garden plant needing comparison with other trumpet daffodils.

species.name: Narcissus obvallaris
species.tip: Sturdy daffodil with an all-golden flower, short stout stem and blue-green leaves; famed around Tenby in Pembrokeshire and found in scattered naturalised sites elsewhere.

species.name: Narcissus poeticus
species.tip: Flat white petals around a small yellow cup edged red, fragrant, one flower per stem; late-flowering, in grassland or as an escape.

species.name: Narcissus pseudonarcissus
species.tip: Smaller than garden daffodils with pale yellow twisted petals and a deeper yellow trumpet; grassy woods and meadows in early spring.

species.name: Narcissus radiiflorus
species.tip: Poet-type narcissus with pure white spreading petals and a tiny yellow cup edged in red; usually one flower per stem; naturalised in meadows.

species.name: Narcissus triandrus
species.tip: Delicate narcissus with two to three nodding, creamy white flowers per stem and backswept petals around a bell-shaped cup; rare escape, often in western grassland.

species.name: Nardus stricta
species.tip: Wiry, bristly-leaved tussock of acid upland grass with a slim one-sided spike of purplish spikelets; leaves stiff and harsh, bleached in winter.

species.name: Narthecium ossifragum
species.tip: Tufts of flat iris-like leaves and spikes of star-shaped yellow flowers with orange anthers on wet moors and bogs; orange fruit follows.

species.name: Nassella tenuissima
species.tip: Fine hair-leaved tufted garden grass with a silky, feathery pale panicle that soon becomes airy; an escape from gardens now self-sown on paths and walls.

species.name: Nasturtium microphyllum
species.tip: Water-cress growing in streams with leaves turning bronze-purple in autumn; fruit narrow and in a single row of seeds per segment.

species.name: Nasturtium officinale
species.tip: Edible aquatic plant of streams and ditches with glossy dark pinnate leaves that stay green; fruit seeds in two rows.

species.name: Neotinea maculata
species.tip: Short spike of many small whitish to greenish flowers with pinkish markings on lip; very local on Burren limestone and Isle of Man.

species.name: Neotinea ustulata
species.tip: Small orchid with a dense head with dark red-brown buds that look scorched and open to white spotted lips; short chalk grassland.

species.name: Neottia cordata
species.tip: Tiny orchid of moorland among heather and moss, with one pair of small heart-shaped leaves and a few minute reddish-green flowers; much smaller than Common Twayblade.

species.name: Neottia nidus-avis
species.tip: Leafless, honey-brown plant with a nest-like root tangle and brown flowers; grows in deep shade of beech and hazel woods.

species.name: Neottia ovata
species.tip: Orchid of woods, meadows and dunes with just two large oval opposite leaves at mid-stem and a long spike of yellow-green flowers with a forked lip.

species.name: Nepeta cataria
species.tip: Grey, downy, minty plant with heart-shaped toothed leaves and whorled spikes of white flowers spotted with purple. Rare on dry hedgebanks and chalk in England.

species.name: Nigella damascena
species.tip: Garden escape; blue flowers in a ruff of thread-like bracts; swollen, balloon-like seed pods.

species.name: Noccaea caerulescens
species.tip: Small tufted plant with a rosette and small white flowers with violet anthers. Native on lead-rich soil, such as old mine spoil in the Pennines and Wales.

species.name: Nothofagus alpina
species.tip: Chilean southern beech with narrow-oval, deeply veined leaves with sharp double teeth, much larger than Roble Beech; planted in parks, woods and forestry.

species.name: Nothofagus obliqua
species.tip: Fast-growing Chilean tree with small, wavy-edged oval leaves with uneven bases and tiny flowers; unlike true beech the leaf is toothed; planted in parks and forestry.

species.name: Nothoscordum borbonicum
species.tip: Garlic-like bulbous plant with an umbel of white flowers striped greenish or pink beneath, with no oniony smell; established in a few warm coastal spots in the south-west.

species.name: Nuphar advena
species.tip: American relative of Yellow Water-lily with similar floating heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers; very rarely planted so a specialist should confirm.

species.name: Nuphar lutea
species.tip: Floating oval leaves with notch at base and rounded yellow ball-like flowers held at the surface, smelling of alcohol; ponds, canals and slow rivers.

species.name: Nuphar pumila
species.tip: Smaller than Yellow Water-lily, with flowers only up to 3 cm across and leaves under 10 cm with a pointed lobe; local in northern lakes.

species.name: Nymphaea alba
species.tip: Large white flowers with many petals and yellow centre floating on round, deeply notched leaves; lakes and ponds, bigger and whiter than any other native water plant.

species.name: Nymphoides peltata
species.tip: Floating plant with small water-lily-like heart-shaped leaves and yellow five-petalled fringed flowers held above water; ponds and slow rivers, not a true water-lily.

species.name: Odontites jaubertianus
species.tip: Rare red-bartsia type with pink flowers in a one-sided spike and narrow toothed leaves. Probably a casual in Britain; identification uncertain, so check with a specialist.

species.name: Odontites vernus
species.tip: Branched annual of grassy and disturbed ground with narrow toothed leaves and spikes of small pink-red flowers, with a one-sided flowering spike; stems often reddish.

species.name: Oemleria cerasiformis
species.tip: Early-leafing suckering shrub with oval leaves smelling of cucumber and drooping clusters of small white flowers in spring; fruits are plum-like. Rare escape.

species.name: Oenanthe aquatica
species.tip: Water plant with finely cut submerged leaves and small, stalked white umbels opposite the leaves; found in still water, and differs from other water-dropworts by its hollow, hairless stem.

species.name: Oenanthe crocata
species.tip: Very poisonous plant of ditches and wet places with celery-like glossy leaves, thick hollow stems and rounded umbels; sap turns yellowish-orange when cut.

species.name: Oenanthe fistulosa
species.tip: Water-dropwort with hollow, tubular stems and leaf stalks, creeping runners, and dense, spherical umbels with few rays; common in ponds, ditches and reedbeds.

species.name: Oenanthe fluviatilis
species.tip: Tall plant of rivers and streams with hollow stem, large round-lobed leaflets and large umbels opposite the leaves; much taller than Fine-leaved Water-dropwort. Mostly southern England.

species.name: Oenanthe lachenalii
species.tip: Stout plant of damp grassland and saltmarsh, with parsley-like leaves and spherical umbels of white flowers; the stem is solid, unlike hollow-stemmed relatives, and the fruit is clearly angled.

species.name: Oenanthe pimpinelloides
species.tip: Water-dropwort with root tubers and finely divided leaves; stem is solid and spreading; has only one dense, domed umbel; local, in damp grassland in the south and west.

species.name: Oenanthe silaifolia
species.tip: Tall water-dropwort of damp meadows with narrow, long, pointed leaflets and a hollow, ridged stem; local, in the Midlands and southern England.

species.name: Oenothera biennis
species.tip: Tall biennial of sands and waste ground with pale yellow flowers opening at dusk; flowers are smaller than Large-flowered Evening-primrose and sepals are green without red stripes.

species.name: Oenothera glazioviana
species.tip: Tall, robust evening-primrose of dunes and waste ground with big bright yellow flowers, red-based hairs on the stem and red-striped buds, flowers larger than Common Evening-primrose.

species.name: Oenothera stricta
species.tip: Yellow evening-primrose with narrow leaves and flowers fading orange-red, with a sweet scent; rare, casual in dunes and waste ground.

species.name: Olearia macrodonta
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with holly-like leaves, wavy and spiny-toothed, white felted beneath, and clusters of white daisies. Planted in gardens, rarely persisting near the south-west coast.

species.name: Oloptum miliaceum
species.tip: Mediterranean grass with a large open panicle of tiny glossy spikelets bearing a short awn; casual near ports and on waste ground in the south.

species.name: Omalotheca norvegica
species.tip: Upright mountain cudweed with several brown-bracted heads in a spike along the stem, leaves green above and woolly beneath. Rare, Scottish mountains.

species.name: Omalotheca supina
species.tip: Tiny tufted mountain cudweed with one to few brown-bracted heads close to the ground and grey woolly leaves. Mountain tops in Scotland, northern England and Wales.

species.name: Omalotheca sylvatica
species.tip: Upright, grey-woolly plant with narrow leaves and a spike of small brown-tipped heads in leaf axils. Open heathy ground and tracks.

species.name: Omphalodes verna
species.tip: Low spring garden escape that spreads in shady places, with sky-blue flowers having a white eye and heart-shaped leaves. Not the same as the similar Common Forget-me-not.

species.name: Onobrychis viciifolia
species.tip: Dense spikes of pink veined flowers on chalk grassland and verges; leaves pinnate with many narrow leaflets, no tendrils.

species.name: Onoclea sensibilis
species.tip: Broad, deeply wavy-lobed, pale green sterile fronds in a spreading patch, with separate beaded brown fertile fronds. Rare garden escape in damp places.

species.name: Ononis reclinata
species.tip: Small sticky-hairy restharrow with trifoliate leaves, pink flowers shorter than the calyx and no thorns. Very rare, on a few southern coasts.

species.name: Ononis repens
species.tip: Low, spreading, hairy, sticky plant with pink pea flowers and small toothed trifoliate leaves; unlike Spiny Restharrow it has no spines.

species.name: Ononis spinosa
species.tip: Spiny low shrub with pink pea flowers and trifoliate toothed leaves, forming tangled mats. Local on rough grassland, mostly on lime-rich soils.

species.name: Onopordum acanthium
species.tip: Huge, silvery-woolly thistle with broad spiny wings on the stem and large purple heads. Waste ground, field edges and roadsides, mainly eastern England.

species.name: Ophioglossum azoricum
species.tip: Tiny fern with a single oval leaf blade and a short spore spike; very rare, found in short turf near the coast, mainly in Scilly.

species.name: Ophioglossum lusitanicum
species.tip: Very small winter-green fern with a narrow undivided blade and a minute spike; found only in Scilly and the Channel Islands.

species.name: Ophioglossum vulgatum
species.tip: Small fern with one oval, undivided green blade and a spore spike rising from its base like a snake tongue; damp meadows and old grassland.

species.name: Ophrys apifera
species.tip: Orchid of calcareous grass and quarries with flowers resembling a bumblebee, pink petals and a brown velvety lip with yellow markings; stems bear a few narrow leaves.

species.name: Ophrys fuciflora
species.tip: Orchid with large pink sepals and a rounded velvety brown lip marked pale; flowers later than Early Spider-orchid; confined to Kent.

species.name: Ophrys insectifera
species.tip: Slender orchid with flowers resembling flies, a dark purple velvety lip with a blue patch and thin green sepals; woods on chalk.

species.name: Ophrys sphegodes
species.tip: Orchid with a rounded velvety dark brown lip marked with an H-shape, yellow-green sepals; flowers earlier than Late Spider-orchid; chalk grassland in the south.

species.name: Orchis anthropophora
species.tip: Spike of small yellow-green flowers whose lips look like dangling little men with arms and legs; grows on chalk and limestone in the south.

species.name: Orchis mascula
species.tip: Spring orchid of woods and meadows with leaves usually blotched purple-black, a loose spike of magenta flowers and a long spur; smells unpleasantly of tomcat in older flowers.

species.name: Orchis militaris
species.tip: Orchid with a pale pink to white spike with lilac hoods, each lip like a small figure; confined to a few sites in the Chilterns and Suffolk.

species.name: Orchis purpurea
species.tip: Stout orchid with large dark brown hoods and a pale pink lip dotted purple, shaped like a lady in a skirt; local in Kent woods.

species.name: Orchis simia
species.tip: Orchid with pinkish-white hooded flowers and a narrow-limbed pink lip with dark tips and a dense spike; very rare in Kent and Oxfordshire.

species.name: Oreopteris limbosperma
species.tip: Tufted fern of hill slopes and acid woods with fronds tapering at both ends and smelling of lemon when crushed; the lowest pinnae are tiny. Has yellow glands beneath.

species.name: Origanum vulgare
species.tip: Loose, branched clusters with purple bracts; smells of oregano.

species.name: Ornithogalum arabicum
species.tip: Large white starry flowers with a conspicuous glossy black centre in a flat-topped cluster, with strap leaves. Only a tender garden or casual plant here.

species.name: Ornithogalum nutans
species.tip: Nodding white flowers in a one-sided raceme, with a broad green stripe on the outside of each petal; leaves narrow with a pale midstripe. Naturalised in grass, churchyards and orchards.

species.name: Ornithogalum pyrenaicum
species.tip: Tall spike of many greenish-white flowers, the lower ones opening first, and narrow leaves that wither before flowering. Local in woods and hedges around Bath and the south-west.

species.name: Ornithogalum umbellatum
species.tip: Bulb with narrow, grass-like leaves with a white midstripe, and starry white flowers striped green on the back; opens only in sun; garden escape in grass.

species.name: Ornithopus compressus
species.tip: Hairy, low annual with pinnate leaves and small pale yellow flowers in clusters of few; pods curved. Rare, in the Channel Islands or casual elsewhere.

species.name: Ornithopus perpusillus
species.tip: Small, hairy annual of sandy heaths with tiny pinkish-white flowers in clusters and feathery pinnate leaves; pods curved like bird claws.

species.name: Ornithopus pinnatus
species.tip: Slender, feathery annual with pinnate leaves and small orange-yellow flowers veined with red, in small heads. Rare, in the Isles of Scilly, Channel Islands and some sandy heaths.

species.name: Ornithopus sativus
species.tip: Sprawling annual with pinnate leaves and small pale pink flowers in tiny heads; the curved, beaded pods resemble a bird's foot. Cultivated, occasionally casual on sandy ground.

species.name: Orobanche alba
species.tip: Parasitic purplish-red plant without green leaves, flowers with a red-purple tint, growing on wild thyme. Coastal and upland grassland in Wales, Scotland and Ireland.

species.name: Orobanche caryophyllacea
species.tip: Stout yellowish-brown broomrape with purple tinges and a sweet carnation scent, on bedstraws; very rare, now mainly Kent coastal grassland.

species.name: Orobanche crenata
species.tip: Large broomrape with creamy-white flowers veined with violet, parasitic on beans and other legumes. A rare casual of crops, mainly in southern England.

species.name: Orobanche elatior
species.tip: Tall yellowish broomrape with dull yellow flowers often tinged brown, on knapweed roots in calcareous grassland, mostly southern and eastern England.

species.name: Orobanche hederae
species.tip: Slender broomrape with creamy flowers tinged purple, growing at the base of ivy; stigma yellow. Commonest near the coast and in gardens.

species.name: Orobanche minor
species.tip: Leafless, yellowish-brown parasitic plant with scales rather than leaves, usually on clovers and other legumes; flowers have a purple-tinged tube and curved lip.

species.name: Orobanche picridis
species.tip: Yellowish broomrape with purple-tinged, sweet-scented flowers on bristly oxtongue; found on coastal cliffs and clay slopes in south-east England.

species.name: Orobanche rapum-genistae
species.tip: Tall, stout, dull yellow-brown broomrape with reddish veins growing on broom and gorse. Locally frequent, mainly in the south and west.

species.name: Orobanche reticulata
species.tip: Broomrape with yellowish flowers tinged purple, parasitic on thistles, with a dark purple stigma. Rare, in limestone and calcareous grassland in northern England and the south.

species.name: Orontium aquaticum
species.tip: Floating, water-repellent oval blue-green leaves and a thick white stalk tipped with a golden spike of tiny yellow flowers; an introduced plant in ponds and bog pools.

species.name: Orthilia secunda
species.tip: Wintergreen with one-sided spike of nodding greenish-white bells and a long straight style; leaves are pointed and often in a lopsided rosette. Local in damp woods and dunes.

species.name: Oscularia deltoides
species.tip: Shrubby succulent with small, flat triangular blue-green leaves that are finely toothed near the tip and pink flowers; naturalised on Channel Islands and Scilly coasts.

species.name: Osmunda regalis
species.tip: Tall fern with twice-pinnate fronds, rounded leaflets, and brown spore clusters at the frond tip; wet woods and bogs, large and distinctive.

species.name: Osteospermum jucundum
species.tip: Mat-forming garden daisy with pink-purple rays, dark centre and toothed leaves; the garden escape is found in warm sheltered spots near the south-west coast.

species.name: Oxalis acetosella
species.tip: Delicate woodland plant with clover-like, heart-shaped drooping leaflets and nodding white flowers with purple veins on slender stalks; leaves fold at night.

species.name: Oxalis articulata
species.tip: Garden escape with clover-like leaves on hairy stalks from a rhizome and heads of bright pink flowers with darker veins; found on verges and waste ground.

species.name: Oxalis corniculata
species.tip: Creeping weed of paths and gardens with clover-like green or purple leaves and small yellow flowers; stipules are present and the stems root at nodes.

species.name: Oxalis debilis
species.tip: Garden weed with clover-like leaves on long stalks, bright pink flowers with a darker throat; bulbil-bearing roots; common in the south and west.

species.name: Oxalis decaphylla
species.tip: Garden escape with many leaflets, up to about ten per leaf, and pale pink flowers; leaves are not clover-like in structure. Very rare casual.

species.name: Oxalis dillenii
species.tip: Small hairy yellow-sorrel with clover-like leaves and no runners, flowers in groups of two to three; rare alien in southern England.

species.name: Oxalis exilis
species.tip: Very small, creeping New Zealand plant of lawns and paths with tiny clover-like leaves and single small yellow flowers; leaves have no purple tinge.

species.name: Oxalis incarnata
species.tip: Leafy-stemmed pink-sorrel with pale pink to lilac flowers and small bulbils; naturalised in warm sheltered places in the south and west.

species.name: Oxalis latifolia
species.tip: Pink-flowered clover-like sorrel with bulb-like roots, forming dense patches in beds and paths, mainly in the south and west.

species.name: Oxalis megalorrhiza
species.tip: Garden escape with tuberous roots, fleshy stems and yellow flowers; rare and naturalised in warm gardens, such as in south-west England.

species.name: Oxalis pes-caprae
species.tip: Clump of clover-like leaves with bright yellow, larger flowers with a flushed throat in winter and spring; weed of bulb fields in Scilly and Cornwall.

species.name: Oxalis rosea
species.tip: Slender pink-flowered sorrel with clover-like leaves, usually in gardens; a rare escape. Check carefully against other pink-sorrels.

species.name: Oxalis stricta
species.tip: Yellow-flowered sorrel with an upright stem, clover-like leaves and no bulbils or runners; a common garden weed in many parts of Britain.

species.name: Oxalis tetraphylla
species.tip: Pink-sorrel with four leaflets per leaf, each with a dark purple band; flowers pink with a yellow throat. Common in gardens, mainly in warm areas.

species.name: Oxalis valdiviensis
species.tip: Rare garden escape with clover-like leaves and yellow flowers, sometimes veined orange; identification uncertain so check with a specialist.

species.name: Oxybasis chenopodioides
species.tip: Rare mealy-leaved annual of brackish saltmarsh edges in the south and east, with small triangular leaves with two basal teeth and dense clustered flowers.

species.name: Oxybasis glauca
species.tip: Low spreading goosefoot with oak-like lobed leaves that are green above and clearly mealy white below; found on disturbed damp ground and farmyards.

species.name: Oxybasis rubra
species.tip: Fleshy, often red-tinged goosefoot of manure heaps, pond margins and saltmarsh edges with diamond-shaped toothed leaves and dense green flower spikes.

species.name: Oxybasis urbica
species.tip: Rare goosefoot with diamond-shaped, coarsely toothed leaves and long erect spikes; the plant is slightly mealy; scattered in southern and eastern England on waste ground.

species.name: Oxyria digyna
species.tip: Mountain plant with fleshy, kidney-shaped leaves, a sour taste and tiny greenish-red flowers turning to flat winged fruits. Common on damp rocks in Scottish and Welsh uplands.

species.name: Oxytropis campestris
species.tip: Silky tufted plant with pinnate leaves and pale creamy-yellow, often purple-tinged flowers in short heads. Rare, on Scottish mountain rock ledges, notably Clova and Glen Shee.

species.name: Oxytropis halleri
species.tip: Tufted silky plant with pinnate leaves and bluish-purple pea flowers in rounded heads. Shorter-stalked than Yellow Oxytropis; grows on dry coastal Scottish grassland and rocks.

species.name: Pachyphragma macrophyllum
species.tip: Spring woodland garden plant with big heart-shaped leaves and clusters of white flowers with an unpleasant garlic smell. Naturalised in a few damp shady places.

species.name: Paeonia mascula
species.tip: Large crimson bowl-shaped flowers and deeply lobed leaves on stout stems; very rare and found only on Steep Holm in the Bristol Channel.

species.name: Pancratium maritimum
species.tip: Large, fragrant white trumpet flowers with a toothed cup, sprouting from dune sand with blue-grey strap leaves; rare, on southern dunes, mainly Channel Islands and the Scillies.

species.name: Papaver atlanticum
species.tip: Garden poppy with orange or yellow, saucer-shaped flowers and bristly hairy stems; leaves lobed. A rare casual, so identification may need checking.

species.name: Papaver cambricum
species.tip: Poppy with bright yellow flowers, bright green lobed leaves and yellow sap. Native in south-west England and Wales, widely planted and escaped elsewhere.

species.name: Papaver dubium
species.tip: Poppy with paler scarlet flowers, hairs pressed against the stem, and a long narrow smooth seed capsule; the capsule is more than twice as long as it is wide.

species.name: Papaver lecoqii
species.tip: Poppy with scarlet flowers like Long-headed Poppy but with yellow latex that darkens when exposed; lobed leaves. A scarce arable weed in southern England.

species.name: Papaver rhoeas
species.tip: Familiar field poppy with bright scarlet petals, often with a dark blotch, spreading hairs on stems and a rounded, smooth seed capsule.

species.name: Papaver setiferum
species.tip: Opium Poppy relative with lilac flowers, glaucous leaves and a few stiff bristles on the stem. Garden escape or casual, not common.

species.name: Papaver somniferum
species.tip: Tall blue-grey poppy of waste ground and gardens, hairless, with large white, pink or mauve flowers often dark at the base and big globe-like seed capsules.

species.name: Parapholis incurva
species.tip: Tiny annual with a curved, stiff, narrow spike that is partly hidden in the sheath; lower than Hard-grass and restricted to coastal mud and shingle in the south.

species.name: Parapholis strigosa
species.tip: Annual of saltmarsh edges with a stiff, nearly straight spike that breaks up in pieces; longer and straighter than Curved Hard-grass, on southern and eastern coasts.

species.name: Parentucellia viscosa
species.tip: Sticky hairy annual with pale yellow flowers in a leafy spike and opposite narrow toothed leaves; damp grassland, mainly in the south and west.

species.name: Parietaria judaica
species.tip: Bushy perennial of walls and rocks with reddish, softly hairy stems and alternate, untoothed oval leaves; tiny clustered green flowers in leaf axils, no stings.

species.name: Parietaria officinalis
species.tip: Sprawling hairy perennial with alternate pointed oval leaves and tiny green flowers in leaf-axil clusters; leaves lack stinging hairs. Walls, hedge banks and rocky ground in south England.

species.name: Paris quadrifolia
species.tip: Woodland plant with a single whorl of four oval leaves and one green star-like flower with a dark purple central berry-like ovary.

species.name: Parnassia palustris
species.tip: White five-petalled flower with green veins, fan of false stamens, on a stem with single clasping leaf; wet, peaty and calcareous flushes, late summer. Not a grass.

species.name: Parthenocissus quinquefolia
species.tip: Climbing vine with leaves of five leaflets and tendrils with sticky pads, turning scarlet in autumn; garden escape on walls and hedges.

species.name: Parthenocissus tricuspidata
species.tip: Self-clinging wall climber with three-lobed or compound leaves that colour brilliantly red in autumn; inconspicuous greenish flowers and blue berries. Differs from Virginia-creeper in having sucker discs.

species.name: Paspalum distichum
species.tip: Creeping sprawler with paired, thin spikes joined at the tip in a V-shape and short ligules; rare naturalised on wet ground and pond margins in the south.

species.name: Pastinaca sativa
species.tip: Only common umbellifer with yellow flowers and simple once-pinnate leaves with broad lobed leaflets; furrowed hairy stems, smelling of parsnip, on calcareous grassland.

species.name: Paulownia tomentosa
species.tip: Small tree with huge heart-shaped hairy leaves and upright clusters of pale violet foxglove-like flowers opening before the leaves. Planted, sometimes self-sown in cities.

species.name: Pedicularis palustris
species.tip: Hairless plant of wet meadows and fens with finely cut, fern-like leaves and clustered pink-red flowers with a toothed hood; stem often branched.

species.name: Pedicularis sylvatica
species.tip: Low plant of damp heaths and moors with finely cut leaves and pink flowers on short stems; calyx is inflated and stems are sprawling, unlike taller Marsh Lousewort.

species.name: Pelargonium inodorum
species.tip: Sprawling, rare pelargonium relative with lobed leaves and whitish or pinkish flowers. Garden or casual, southern and coastal.

species.name: Pelargonium tomentosum
species.tip: Soft, velvety, strongly mint-scented garden pelargonium with big heart-shaped lobed leaves and small white flowers. Tender and rarely seen outside gardens.

species.name: Peltaria alliacea
species.tip: Very rare garden-escape perennial with blue-grey clasping leaves and heads of white flowers. Smells of garlic when crushed. Needs a specialist to confirm.

species.name: Pentaglottis sempervirens
species.tip: Large bristly perennial with bright blue flowers with white centres and big dark green oval leaves. Hedgebanks and roadsides, naturalised from gardens.

species.name: Pericallis hybrida
species.tip: Pot plant with heart-shaped toothed leaves and clusters of showy daisies in many colours; occasional on tips and waste ground, rarely persisting.

species.name: Persicaria amphibia
species.tip: Pink flower spikes are broad and blunt; either floating glossy leaves in ponds and ditches or a hairy land form on damp soil.

species.name: Persicaria hydropiper
species.tip: Slender spikes of small greenish-pink flowers, drooping at the tips and speckled with glands; leaves have a hot peppery taste and wet places are favoured.

species.name: Persicaria lapathifolia
species.tip: Thick, dense, blunt spikes of pale pink to greenish-white flowers, usually nodding; stalks bear glands beneath; leaves often have a dark blotch. Arable fields and damp places.

species.name: Persicaria maculosa
species.tip: Spikes of pink flowers held upright, with stalks lacking glands, and leaves often with a dark blotch; reddish stem joints; common annual in arable land and waste ground.

species.name: Persicaria minor
species.tip: Slender low annual of damp ground with narrow leaves and thin spikes of tiny pink flowers. Stipule sheaths have long bristles; unlike Water-pepper, leaves are not peppery.

species.name: Persicaria mitis
species.tip: Annual of damp places with narrow leaves and slender, often nodding pink spikes; the leaves are not hot to taste. Stipule sheaths have long bristles. Local in southern England.

species.name: Persicaria nepalensis
species.tip: Low spreading annual with winged leaf stalks, triangular-oval leaves and round heads of tiny white or pink flowers. Garden escape of damp waste ground.

species.name: Petasites albus
species.tip: Spreading plant with round, heart-shaped, toothed leaves, white felted beneath, appearing after small whitish heads. Naturalised near streams and in woods, mainly Scotland and northern England.

species.name: Petasites hybridus
species.tip: Early spikes of pale pink flower heads appear before giant, rhubarb-like round leaves. Wet verges and riverbanks.

species.name: Petasites japonicus
species.tip: Huge, rounded leaves up to a metre across on stout stalks, with pale greenish-yellow heads in early spring; much larger than butterbur. Naturalised by streams and in wet woods.

species.name: Petasites pyrenaicus
species.tip: Winter-flowering plant with vanilla-scented pale lilac-white heads and rounded kidney-shaped leaves forming dense patches. Common on roadsides and banks.

species.name: Petrorhagia dubia
species.tip: Slender hairy annual with small pink flowers in tight heads, and narrow leaves. Rare introduction on waste ground and sandy ground, in southern England.

species.name: Petrorhagia nanteuilii
species.tip: Slender annual with small pink flowers, one at a time, with notched petals and papery bracts. Very rare, on the south coast of England and the Isle of Wight.

species.name: Petrorhagia prolifera
species.tip: Slender annual with small pink flowers in a head wrapped with brown papery bracts, and narrow leaves. Rare on sandy and gravelly ground.

species.name: Petrorhagia saxifraga
species.tip: Wiry, tufted perennial with small flowers in loose clusters, pale pink or white with notched petals. Rare garden escape, on walls and dry banks.

species.name: Petrosedum forsterianum
species.tip: Yellow stonecrop with flat, bluish-green leaves and flower buds that droop, unlike the reflexed stonecrop. Found on rocks and walls in the west.

species.name: Petrosedum rupestre
species.tip: Yellow stonecrop with leaves bent backwards and flowerheads nodding in bud. Grows on walls, rocks and roofs, and often spills from gardens.

species.name: Petrosedum sediforme
species.tip: Grey-green stonecrop with pale yellowish-white flowers and thick, flat leaves arranged spirally. Naturalised on walls and rocks in a few places in southern England.

species.name: Petroselinum crispum
species.tip: Bright green, shiny, curly or flat leaved herb with tiny yellow-green umbels; found as a casual on tips, walls and waste ground.

species.name: Peucedanum officinale
species.tip: Tall, sulphur-yellow umbellifer with long, thread-like leaf segments forming big drooping masses; very rare, on coastal marshes and grassland in Kent and Essex.

species.name: Phacelia tanacetifolia
species.tip: Tall annual with feathery deeply cut leaves and dense coiled spikes of lilac-blue flowers with protruding stamens, loved by bees. Sown as green manure and field margins.

species.name: Phalaris aquatica
species.tip: Tufted canary-grass with a dense oblong head and swollen stem base; uncommon casual on waste ground, with shorter heads than Reed Canary-grass.

species.name: Phalaris arundinacea
species.tip: Tall riverside grass making stands, with a lobed greenish-purple panicle becoming buff; flat, broad, rough-edged leaves and long ligule.

species.name: Phalaris canariensis
species.tip: Birdseed casual with a short, egg-shaped, dense head of pale striped spikelets with winged keels; stem leaves broad and unawned.

species.name: Phalaris minor
species.tip: Annual with a dense egg-shaped head of white and green striped spikelets that do not shatter whole; casual weed of arable and waste ground in the south.

species.name: Phalaris paradoxa
species.tip: Annual canary-grass with a dense head of spikelets in clusters, sterile ones with short awns; a casual on waste ground and docks in the south.

species.name: Phedimus hybridus
species.tip: Garden stonecrop with toothed, flat, fleshy leaves and yellow flowers in flat heads. An occasional escape on walls and waste ground.

species.name: Phedimus kamtschaticus
species.tip: Robust garden stonecrop with toothed alternate leaves and flat heads of yellow flowers. Escapes onto walls and banks.

species.name: Phedimus spurius
species.tip: Mat-forming stonecrop with flat toothed leaves in opposite pairs and pink or purplish flowers. Often escapes from gardens onto walls.

species.name: Phedimus stellatus
species.tip: Annual stonecrop with flat, lobed or toothed leaves and starry pinkish flowers in leafy spikes. A rare garden casual.

species.name: Phegopteris connectilis
species.tip: Fern of damp, shady rocky banks with a triangular, pale green hairy frond with the lowest pair of leaflets bent down and pointing forwards; fronds are held flat.

species.name: Phelipanche purpurea
species.tip: Slender broomrape with violet-blue flowers and bluish stem, parasitic on yarrow. Very rare in England and the Channel Islands.

species.name: Phleum alpinum
species.tip: Mountain cat's-tail with a short, fat, dark purplish head and awned spikelets; the head is stubbier than Timothy. Found on high damp rocky ground in Scotland.

species.name: Phleum arenarium
species.tip: Small annual of dune sand with a short ovoid head and distinctive hair-fringed keel; coastal, mainly in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Phleum bertolonii
species.tip: Short cylindrical head with short awns and a wedge-shaped, shorter spikelet than Timothy; smaller grass of dry grassland, tapered cylinder.

species.name: Phleum phleoides
species.tip: Slim tufted cat's-tail with a long thin spike and truncate glumes with short awns; very rare in the Breckland of East Anglia, on dry sandy soil.

species.name: Phleum pratense
species.tip: Long, narrow, evenly cylindrical head, soft and pale green; spikelets with short awns, and the stem base is swollen into a bulb.

species.name: Phlomis russeliana
species.tip: Large garden perennial with big heart-shaped, felty leaves and tiered whorls of hooded yellow flowers. Occasionally escapes onto roadsides and waste ground.

species.name: Phormium cookianum
species.tip: Tall fountain of stiff, arching sword-like leaves with a flower spike of dull yellowish-green tubular flowers and twisted pods. Less stiff than New Zealand flax; planted in mild places.

species.name: Phormium tenax
species.tip: Large clump of tall stiff sword leaves, sometimes with coloured stripes, and tall spikes of dull red tubular flowers. Planted widely in coastal gardens, seldom established.

species.name: Phragmites australis
species.tip: Very tall, reedy grass of fens and margins forming vast stands with purplish silky plumes; ligule is a fringe of hairs and leaves are broad.

species.name: Phygelius capensis
species.tip: Garden shrub with opposite oval leaves and tall spikes of drooping tubular red-orange flowers with yellow throats. Occasional escape on waste ground.

species.name: Phyllodoce caerulea
species.tip: Dwarf heath-like evergreen with narrow needle-like leaves and nodding purple-pink urn flowers on sticky stalks. Extremely rare, in the Scottish Highlands (Cairngorms area).

species.name: Phymatosorus diversifolius
species.tip: Leathery, glossy, undivided to deeply lobed fronds arising from a creeping rhizome. Naturalised mainly in mild western spots such as Ireland; confirm locally.

species.name: Physospermum cornubiense
species.tip: Large plant with lobed, three-parted leaves and white umbels; the fruits are bladder-like, and notched; very rare, in woods and hedges in Devon and Cornwall.

species.name: Phyteuma orbiculare
species.tip: Chalk-grassland plant with tight globe-shaped heads of deep blue-violet flowers with curved, claw-like buds and narrow toothed stem leaves. Local on the South Downs and Wiltshire chalk.

species.name: Phyteuma scheuchzeri
species.tip: Mountain rampion with rounded heads of violet-blue flowers on leafy stems; lower leaves heart-shaped on long stalks. Rare garden escape, not native in Britain or Ireland.

species.name: Phyteuma spicatum
species.tip: Woodland plant with dense oblong spikes of cream-white flowers tipped green and heart-shaped stalked basal leaves. Rare native of woods and hedgebanks, restricted to East Sussex.

species.name: Phytolacca polyandra
species.tip: Tall herb with oval leaves and upright spikes of small white or pale pink flowers turning into purple-black berries. Rare naturalised garden plant.

species.name: Picea abies
species.tip: Typical Christmas-tree spruce with hanging long cones and four-sided needles that are not sharp; planted widely in forests.

species.name: Picea sitchensis
species.tip: Spruce with sharp, spiky flattened needles, blue-white beneath, and short cones with papery scales; widely planted in wet upland forests.

species.name: Picris hieracioides
species.tip: Tall, bristly plant with unlobed narrow leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads with dark bristly bracts, on branching stems. Dry grassland and banks, mostly on chalk.

species.name: Pilosella aurantiaca
species.tip: Orange-red dandelion-like heads, several to a stem, with black-hairy bracts and hairy rosette leaves. Garden escape on grassy banks, walls and verges.

species.name: Pilosella caespitosa
species.tip: Mouse-ear-hawkweed relative with pale yellow heads in tight clusters and bristly stem; lacks the orange-red of fox-and-cubs. Garden escape on banks and walls.

species.name: Pilosella flagellaris
species.tip: Mouse-ear hawkweed with leafy runners rooting at the tips and a solitary yellow head; leaves bristly and star-haired. A specialist may be needed to confirm it.

species.name: Pilosella officinarum
species.tip: Low mat-forming plant with silvery-white, felted leaf undersides and pale lemon, single heads, red-striped beneath. Dry banks, walls and short turf.

species.name: Pilosella peleteriana
species.tip: Mat-forming plant covered in long shaggy white hairs, with solitary pale yellow heads on short stems. Local on sandy ground and dunes, mostly coastal.

species.name: Pilosella praealta
species.tip: Tall hawkweed relative with compact clusters of small yellow heads and narrow bristly leaves; usually without runners. Rare, naturalised on banks and waste ground.

species.name: Pilularia globulifera
species.tip: Aquatic fern of muddy pond edges with thin, grass-like, curled leaves and tiny round spore cases at the base; local in shallow water.

species.name: Pimpinella major
species.tip: Taller than Burnet-saxifrage with a hollow, angled stem and undivided, deeply toothed leaflets on upper leaves; flowers white or pinkish, in hedgerows and damp grass.

species.name: Pimpinella peregrina
species.tip: Slender, hairy-stemmed annual or biennial with simple basal leaves and divided stem leaves and tiny white umbels; a rare casual, specialist confirmation needed.

species.name: Pimpinella saxifraga
species.tip: Slender, wiry plant of dry grassland with round-toothed lower leaflets and finely cut upper leaves; stem is solid, finely ridged and not angled, with no bracts.

species.name: Pinguicula grandiflora
species.tip: Sticky yellow-green leaf rosette with big violet flowers on a long stalk. Local in damp rocks and bogs in south-west Ireland.

species.name: Pinguicula lusitanica
species.tip: Pale lilac small flowers with yellow throat above flat, sticky greenish rosette. Local in wet heath and bog in western Scotland, Wales, south-west England and Ireland.

species.name: Pinguicula vulgaris
species.tip: Sticky yellow-green rosette of rolled-edge leaves trapping insects, with single violet flower on a leafless stalk; wet moors, bogs and flushes.

species.name: Pinus contorta
species.tip: Pine with paired twisted dark green needles and small prickly cones that stay on the tree; planted on poor wet peaty ground.

species.name: Pinus nigra
species.tip: Tall pine with long, grey-green, twisted needles in pairs and a straight trunk; planted on sandy soils and coasts, unlike Scots Pine.

species.name: Pinus sylvestris
species.tip: Pine with short blue-green paired needles, orange-red upper bark and flat-topped crown with age; native pinewoods and widely planted.

species.name: Pittosporum crassifolium
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with leathery oval leaves white-felted below and dark red small flowers in clusters; planted, often near the coast in the south and west.

species.name: Pittosporum tenuifolium
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with wavy-edged pale green oval leaves on dark twigs and tiny dark purple, honey-scented flowers; planted, naturalising in mild coastal areas.

species.name: Plagiobothrys scouleri
species.tip: Very rare small annual with tiny white flowers on coiled spikes and narrow leaves. A casual introduction, mostly in damp disturbed ground; needs checking by a specialist.

species.name: Plantago arenaria
species.tip: Annual plantain with leafy branching stems and narrow opposite leaves; tiny brownish flower heads. Introduced casual of waste ground, sometimes with bird seed; unlike other plantains it has no rosette.

species.name: Plantago coronopus
species.tip: Flat rosette of narrow leaves cut into toothed lobes like antlers, with curved stalks and slender spikes. Coastal turf, sandy and gravelly places; also inland on dry gravel.

species.name: Plantago lanceolata
species.tip: Narrow ribbed leaves in a rosette, and a short dark brown head with a ring of white stamens on a long furrowed stalk. Very common in grassland and lawns.

species.name: Plantago major
species.tip: Broad oval leaves with five to nine strong veins and a long rat-tail spike of tiny greenish flowers. Common on paths, gateways and trampled ground.

species.name: Plantago maritima
species.tip: Rosette of narrow, fleshy, slightly toothed or smooth leaves on salt marshes, sea cliffs and mountain rocks; stiff narrow spikes. Distinguished from Ribwort by its fleshy leaves and coastal habitat.

species.name: Plantago media
species.tip: Broad downy oval leaves pressed flat in a rosette; fragrant lilac-pink stamens in a short head on a long stalk. Calcareous grassland and lawns.

species.name: Platanthera bifolia
species.tip: Two broad oval leaves at the base and greenish-white scented flowers whose two pollen masses are parallel, unlike the Greater Butterfly-orchid where they diverge.

species.name: Platanthera chlorantha
species.tip: Orchid of woods and meadows with two large oval leaves near base and greenish-white flowers with parallel pollen sacks; flowers are larger than Lesser Butterfly-orchid and scented at night.

species.name: Pleioblastus chino
species.tip: Spreading garden bamboo with slender stems and narrow leaves; naturalised in a few places, rarely flowers in Britain. A specialist may be needed to confirm among dwarf bamboos.

species.name: Pleioblastus pygmaeus
species.tip: Low, dense, spreading bamboo only about knee-high, used as ground cover; flowers essentially never seen in Britain. Told from taller bamboos by size.

species.name: Pleioblastus simonii
species.tip: Tall clump-forming garden bamboo with solid green canes and long narrow leaves; escapes from plantings occasionally. Rarely flowers here.

species.name: Poa alpina
species.tip: Small tufted meadow-grass of high mountain ledges with short, broad, blunt leaves and compact purplish panicles often with bulbils; only in Scottish and northern uplands.

species.name: Poa angustifolia
species.tip: Meadow-grass with narrow, stiff, rolled blue-green leaves and creeping rhizomes; panicle open and slightly smaller than Smooth Meadow-grass.

species.name: Poa annua
species.tip: Small, pale-green, tufted grass flowering all year; crinkled leaf blades with a boat-shaped tip and a spreading panicle; very common on paths.

species.name: Poa bulbosa
species.tip: Small meadow-grass with a swollen bulb-like stem base and spikelets that sprout into tiny leafy bulbils; found on dry coastal grass and sandy ground in the south and east.

species.name: Poa chaixii
species.tip: Large meadow-grass with flattened stems and broad leaves in dense tufts, and a big open panicle; naturalised in woods and verges, especially in Scotland.

species.name: Poa compressa
species.tip: Distinctive for its flat, wiry stems and blue-green leaves; narrow dense panicle, creeping rhizomes, grows on walls and dry ground.

species.name: Poa flexuosa
species.tip: Delicate mountain meadow-grass with wavy, fine stems and a small panicle; very local on high Scottish summits. A specialist may be needed to confirm it.

species.name: Poa glauca
species.tip: Blue-grey meadow-grass of mountain cliffs and ledges with a stiff, open panicle; limited to a few base-rich uplands in Scotland, Wales and England.

species.name: Poa humilis
species.tip: Meadow-grass similar to Smooth Meadow-grass, with blue-green leaves and slender creeping rhizomes; panicle more open with spreading branches.

species.name: Poa infirma
species.tip: Little annual meadow-grass that flowers in winter and early spring, with a small compact panicle; confined to warm coasts of the south-west and Channel Islands.

species.name: Poa nemoralis
species.tip: Slender woodland meadow-grass with wiry, thin stems and a thin open panicle; leaves narrow and tufted with a very short ligule.

species.name: Poa palustris
species.tip: Tall, loose meadow-grass of wet ground with a nodding yellowish-brown panicle and slightly rhizomatous base; naturalised from North America and rare.

species.name: Poa pratensis
species.tip: Common meadow-grass spreading by rhizomes with smooth sheaths and a short ligule; leaf tips boat-shaped, with twin lines along the leaf blade.

species.name: Poa trivialis
species.tip: Meadow-grass of damp shaded ground with a long pointed ligule and rough sheaths; stoloniferous and light green, with panicle open.

species.name: Polemonium caeruleum
species.tip: Tall plant with ladder-like pinnate leaves and nodding to upright violet-blue bowl-shaped flowers with orange anthers. Rare native of limestone dales in northern England; also a garden escape.

species.name: Polycarpon tetraphyllum
species.tip: Small annual with whorls of four small oval leaves and tiny white flowers in clusters. Rare in dry open places, mostly on the south coast and in the Channel Islands.

species.name: Polygala amarella
species.tip: Small milkwort with the lower leaves larger and broader, forming a rosette, which taste bitter. Rare, on chalk and limestone grassland in Kent and the north.

species.name: Polygala calcarea
species.tip: Low milkwort with a basal rosette of larger leaves and bright blue flowers, rarely white. Lives on chalk and limestone grassland in southern England; Common Milkwort lacks the rosette.

species.name: Polygala serpyllifolia
species.tip: Small, wiry plant with lower leaves opposite, small blue, pink or white flowers; acid heaths and grassland, unlike Common Milkwort, leaves all alternate.

species.name: Polygala vulgaris
species.tip: Low plant with all leaves alternate, narrow, and spikes of small blue, pink or white flowers; chalk and neutral grassland, versus Heath Milkwort.

species.name: Polygonatum multiflorum
species.tip: Arching, rounded stem with oval leaves in two ranks and clusters of two to five hanging green-tipped white bells from each leaf joint. Woods; common in gardens.

species.name: Polygonatum odoratum
species.tip: Stem sharply angled, with bells usually one or two together, white with green tips and scented. A rare plant of limestone woods and rocky slopes.

species.name: Polygonatum verticillatum
species.tip: Narrow leaves in whorls of four to eight around the stem, with small greenish-white bells hanging in the axils. Very rare, in a few Scottish and northern English woods.

species.name: Polygonum aviculare
species.tip: Mat-forming, wiry, much-branched annual with tiny flowers in leaf axils, tiny pink-edged green petals, and grey-green small leaves; trampled paths, arable fields and waste ground.

species.name: Polygonum boreale
species.tip: Sprawling knotgrass of the north with oval to narrow leaves and pinkish-white flowers in leaf axils. Scarcely separable from Knotgrass without fruit, so specialist advice is useful.

species.name: Polygonum cognatum
species.tip: Mat-forming knotgrass with small thick, grey-green leaves and clustered pink-green flowers. Rare casual from the east; confirm with a specialist.

species.name: Polygonum depressum
species.tip: Low mat-forming knotgrass with small oval leaves and tiny pinkish-green flowers in the leaf axils. Close to Equal-leaved Knotgrass, so a specialist is needed.

species.name: Polygonum maritimum
species.tip: Rare coastal knotgrass with thick leathery grey-green leaves with rolled margins and silvery stipules; flowers small and white or pink. Found on sand and shingle beaches on southern coasts.

species.name: Polygonum oxyspermum
species.tip: Coastal knotgrass of strandlines with fleshy leaves and small greenish-white or pink flowers. Ripe fruits protrude beyond the perianth. Scarce on sand and shingle, mostly on northern and western coasts.

species.name: Polygonum rurivagum
species.tip: Slender, wiry knotgrass with very narrow leaves and pinkish flowers in the leaf axils. Scarce plant of arable fields, mostly in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Polypodium cambricum
species.tip: Large, pale green fronds with long, tapering, finely toothed pinnae, unlike the blunter common polypody. Wet western rocks, walls and banks; fronds appear in winter.

species.name: Polypodium interjectum
species.tip: Evergreen fern on walls, trees and rocks with fronds longest in the middle; sori oval and fronds with finely toothed tips, unlike the other polypody.

species.name: Polypodium vulgare
species.tip: Evergreen rock and tree fern with once-cut fronds having parallel sides and blunt tips; round orange sori; differs from Intermediate Polypody by rounded outline.

species.name: Polypogon monspeliensis
species.tip: Annual with a dense, soft, bristly cylindrical head of long-awned spikelets, resembling a foxtail; rare casual of wet places and coasts in the south.

species.name: Polypogon viridis
species.tip: Introduced grass of damp places with a dense, green, lobed cylindrical panicle that has no awns; stems often creeping and ligule long.

species.name: Polystichum aculeatum
species.tip: Stiff, glossy dark green fronds with spiny, bristle-tipped pinnules that overlap and are once divided; woods and shaded banks.

species.name: Polystichum lonchitis
species.tip: Stiff, dark, glossy, spiny-toothed pinnae, narrow frond once divided. Rare, on mountain rock ledges and base-rich crags in Scotland and northern England.

species.name: Polystichum munitum
species.tip: Large evergreen sword-shaped fronds, undivided pinnae with a small ear at base and fine teeth. Planted and self-sown in damp woods, mostly in the west.

species.name: Polystichum setiferum
species.tip: Soft, drooping, twice-cut fronds with bristle-tipped pinnules, thinner than Hard Shield-fern; shaded lanes and woods in the west.

species.name: Pontederia cordata
species.tip: Upright spikes of blue-violet flowers with a yellow spot, above glossy heart-shaped leaves in shallow water. Garden pond plant, rarely naturalised in the south.

species.name: Populus alba
species.tip: Large suckering tree with leaves that are lobed and maple-like and snowy-white felted beneath; bark is pale with diamond-shaped marks. Catkins appear early spring.

species.name: Populus nigra
species.tip: Rare native tree of floodplains with big burry trunk, drooping branches and triangular, finely toothed hairless leaves; female trees are scarce. Hybrid poplars are far more frequent.

species.name: Populus tremula
species.tip: Poplar with rounded leaves on long flat stalks, so they tremble in even a slight breeze; forms suckering thickets on heaths, woodland edges and in the north.

species.name: Populus trichocarpa
species.tip: Tall poplar with sticky, strongly balsam-scented buds and large, heart-based leaves that are white beneath. Widely planted; occasionally self-sown by rivers.

species.name: Portulaca oleracea
species.tip: Fleshy, reddish, sprawling stems with paddle-shaped leaves and tiny yellow flowers opening only in sun. Garden weed and bare ground, mainly southern England.

species.name: Potamogeton acutifolius
species.tip: All-submerged, flattened, bristle-tipped narrow leaves with many veins and a pointed tip. Scarce, in clean lowland ponds and ditches of England and Ireland.

species.name: Potamogeton alpinus
species.tip: Reddish-tinged floating and translucent submerged leaves, both stalkless-ish and narrow oval. Peaty or acid waters, mainly in northern and western Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Potamogeton berchtoldii
species.tip: Slender submerged pondweed with narrow, translucent, three-veined leaves tapering to a point and flowers held in small short spikes; leaves are broader than in Lesser Pondweed.

species.name: Potamogeton coloratus
species.tip: Thin, translucent, net-veined leaves, submerged and floating, in base-rich fen pools and ditches. Local in England, Wales and Ireland; leaves are almost see-through.

species.name: Potamogeton compressus
species.tip: Flattened stems with long, ribbon-like leaves ending in a tiny point; all submerged. Rare, in lowland lakes and canals of eastern England and Ireland.

species.name: Potamogeton crispus
species.tip: Submerged pondweed with distinctive wavy, finely toothed, crinkled translucent leaves like seaweed; stems flattened and reddish-brown, in ponds, canals and ditches.

species.name: Potamogeton epihydrus
species.tip: Ribbon-like submerged leaves with floating oval ones, resembling Bog Pondweed plants in structure. Very rare, in Outer Hebrides lochs only; specialist should confirm.

species.name: Potamogeton friesii
species.tip: Narrow, stalkless, many-veined leaves with a notched or blunt tip and flattened stems. Local in lowland, nutrient-rich waters across England and Ireland.

species.name: Potamogeton gramineus
species.tip: Both submerged narrow stalkless leaves and floating oval ones, with a thickened stalk under the flower spike. Upland lakes and rivers, mostly north and west.

species.name: Potamogeton lucens
species.tip: Large, translucent, wavy, glossy submerged leaves with a short stalk and a point. Clear, deeper water of lakes, canals and rivers, mostly lowland.

species.name: Potamogeton natans
species.tip: Common pondweed with floating, leathery, oval leaves on long stalks with a distinct joint near the blade; also narrow submerged leaves; flower spike held above water.

species.name: Potamogeton nodosus
species.tip: Long-stalked, leathery floating and large submerged leaves with a rounded base. Slow rivers of southern and central England and Ireland; found along the Loddon.

species.name: Potamogeton obtusifolius
species.tip: Narrow, blunt, translucent, stalkless leaves with three main veins, all submerged. Still fertile ponds and canals, widespread but local throughout lowland Britain.

species.name: Potamogeton perfoliatus
species.tip: Submerged pondweed whose broad, oval, translucent leaves clasp the stem at the base, with no stalks and no floating leaves; in clear, base-rich water.

species.name: Potamogeton polygonifolius
species.tip: Pondweed of acid pools, bog ditches and streams, with oval floating leaves on long stalks that lack the joint seen in Broad-leaved Pondweed; also lance-shaped submerged leaves.

species.name: Potamogeton praelongus
species.tip: Large, clasping submerged leaves with a hooded tip, plus a very long flower stalk. Deep, clear lakes and rivers, mostly north and west.

species.name: Potamogeton pusillus
species.tip: Slender, fine submerged pondweed with narrow, linear, three-veined leaves with a blunt or short-pointed tip and no floating leaves; spikes of few widely spaced flowers.

species.name: Potamogeton rutilus
species.tip: Fine, narrow, pointed submerged leaves with a thin stem, similar to Hairlike Pondweed. Very rare, in Scottish islands lochs and a few in western Ireland; specialist needed.

species.name: Potamogeton trichoides
species.tip: Hair-thin, dark, pointed leaves with three veins, like thin threads in dull ponds. Scarce, in lowland ditches and ponds of southern and eastern England.

species.name: Potentilla anglica
species.tip: Creeping yellow cinquefoil with stalked leaves of three or five leaflets, flowers with four or five petals, rooting at nodes later; heaths, woods. Compare Tormentil and Creeping Cinquefoil.

species.name: Potentilla anserina
species.tip: Creeping plant with silvery feathery leaves and solitary yellow flowers on long stalks, rooting stolons; trampled grassland, tracks, damp ground.

species.name: Potentilla argentea
species.tip: Cinquefoil with five-fingered leaves that are white-felted beneath with rolled edges, and small yellow flowers; found on dry sandy and gravelly ground, mainly in eastern England.

species.name: Potentilla crantzii
species.tip: Tufted mountain cinquefoil with five-fingered leaves, basal leaflets toothed at the tips only, and golden flowers often with an orange spot; Scottish, Welsh and northern upland rocks.

species.name: Potentilla erecta
species.tip: Slender yellow flower with four petals, unlike other cinquefoils; leaves stalkless with three or five leaflets; heaths, moors, acid grassland.

species.name: Potentilla indica
species.tip: Creeping strawberry-like plant with trifoliate leaves, yellow flowers and bright red strawberry-like fruits that are dry and tasteless, with leafy bracts beneath; garden escape.

species.name: Potentilla montana
species.tip: Mat-forming cinquefoil with trifoliate or fingered leaves, silky beneath, and white flowers; a rare garden escape, in contrast to the native white-flowered barren strawberry.

species.name: Potentilla norvegica
species.tip: Upright, hairy annual or short-lived cinquefoil with three-parted leaves and small yellow flowers with petals shorter than the sepals; casual of waste ground and disturbed soil.

species.name: Potentilla recta
species.tip: Tall hairy cinquefoil with five to seven narrow toothed leaflets and large pale lemon-yellow flowers in flat clusters; naturalised on roadsides, banks and waste ground.

species.name: Potentilla reptans
species.tip: Long creeping rooting stems; leaves with five stalked leaflets, yellow flowers with five petals; hedgebanks, roadsides, grassland. Compare Trailing Tormentil with fewer leaflets.

species.name: Potentilla rupestris
species.tip: Rare upright plant with pinnate leaves and white flowers about 2 cm across; known only from a few rocky outcrops in Wales, Herefordshire and Sutherland.

species.name: Potentilla sterilis
species.tip: Looks like Wild Strawberry but petals are white with gaps between, the end leaflet tooth shorter, and no fleshy fruit; very early flowers on dry banks and woodland edges.

species.name: Potentilla verna
species.tip: Low, mat-forming, golden-yellow cinquefoil of dry limestone grassland, with five-fingered leaves and flowers in spring; in Britain mostly Upper Teesdale. Close to creeping cinquefoil but with upright stems.

species.name: Poterium sanguisorba
species.tip: Chalk grassland plant with rounded green-purple flower heads, red stigmas at top and stamens below; leaves of many toothed leaflets, cucumber-scented. Compare Great Burnet, taller with dark red heads.

species.name: Pratia angulata
species.tip: Mat-forming creeper with tiny rounded toothed leaves rooting along stems and small white flowers, flushed purple, on slender stalks. Rare garden escape of lawns and damp paths.

species.name: Pratia pedunculata
species.tip: Dense mat of tiny oval leaves rooting along creeping stems, with small pale blue flowers on very short stalks. Garden escape found on paths and damp grass.

species.name: Primula denticulata
species.tip: Dense, ball-shaped heads of lilac flowers on a stout stalk, above rosettes of toothed leaves. Garden plant that occasionally escapes onto damp banks.

species.name: Primula elatior
species.tip: Pale yellow flowers, one-sided cluster on a single stalk, with hairy leaves. Rare, in ancient East Anglian woods; the False Oxlip is a hybrid.

species.name: Primula farinosa
species.tip: Rosettes with mealy undersides to leaves, and pink flowers with yellow centre in heads. Rare, in limestone grasslands of northern England and Scotland.

species.name: Primula florindae
species.tip: Tall, with fragrant yellow bells in a drooping umbel, above large heart-based leaves. Garden escape by streams and wet banks, mostly Scotland and the north.

species.name: Primula japonica
species.tip: Tiered whorls of white, pink or crimson flowers on tall stalks, above large rosettes of leaves. Garden escape in damp streamsides, scattered.

species.name: Primula juliae
species.tip: Low, mat-forming primrose with purple-magenta flowers and rounded wrinkled leaves. Garden plant, occasionally found as an escape; confirm by hybrid parentage.

species.name: Primula prolifera
species.tip: Tiered whorls of golden-yellow flowers on mealy stalks, above large toothed rosettes. Garden escape on wet banks and streams, scattered.

species.name: Primula pulverulenta
species.tip: Tiers of crimson flowers on stalks dusted with white meal, above leafy rosettes. Garden escape on damp stream banks, scattered in Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Primula scotica
species.tip: Tiny, dark, purple flowers with a yellow eye on a short stalk, above a mealy rosette. Rare, in coastal turf of north Scotland and Orkney.

species.name: Primula veris
species.tip: Nodding one-sided cluster of small deep yellow, scented flowers with tubular calyx on a tall stem from a rosette of wrinkled leaves; grassland, April.

species.name: Primula vulgaris
species.tip: Pale yellow solitary flowers on separate hairy stalks from a rosette of crinkled leaves; woods, banks and hedges in early spring.

species.name: Prunella grandiflora
species.tip: Selfheal with larger violet flowers and mostly unstalked upper leaves, held in a neat terminal head. Scarce on chalk and limestone grassland, often as an escape.

species.name: Prunella laciniata
species.tip: Selfheal with creamy-white flowers and variably lobed or cut leaves, forming a terminal head. Rare on dry chalk grassland in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Prunella vulgaris
species.tip: Dense, squarish flower head with purple-tinged bracts and a pair of leaves just below it. Common in lawns.

species.name: Prunus avium
species.tip: Tall tree with white flowers in clusters, glossy red-brown peeling bark with horizontal lines, drooping leaves; fruit red to black. Flowers April, with the new leaves.

species.name: Prunus cerasifera
species.tip: Early white flowers, often before leaves, from February; twigs green and hairless, often thornless; bears round red or yellow plums. Hedges and bushes. Blackthorn flowers later and is thorny.

species.name: Prunus cerasus
species.tip: Smaller than wild cherry, often suckering, with glossy leaves and white flowers in short-stalked clusters; the sour red fruits are borne on long stalks. Often found in hedges.

species.name: Prunus domestica
species.tip: Includes Bullace and Damson; larger oval leaves, downy twigs, flowers white in pairs; fruit bigger than Blackthorn sloes. Hedgerow tree from gardens; sometimes slightly spiny.

species.name: Prunus incisa
species.tip: Small tree or shrub with deeply double-toothed, sharply pointed leaves and early pink-white blossom; planted in parks and gardens and not often naturalised.

species.name: Prunus laurocerasus
species.tip: Large evergreen shrub with big glossy leathery leaves, almond smell when crushed, and upright spikes of small white flowers; black cherry-like fruit. Compare Portugal Laurel with red leaf stalks.

species.name: Prunus lusitanica
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with dark glossy leaves on red stalks, long spikes of fragrant white flowers appearing in summer, later than Cherry Laurel; fruit dark purple.

species.name: Prunus mahaleb
species.tip: Small tree with round, glossy, finely toothed leaves and short upright spikes of fragrant white flowers; fruit black and bitter. Rare in hedges and scrub, mostly in the south.

species.name: Prunus padus
species.tip: Drooping spikes of white almond-scented flowers; leaves oval, finely toothed; black bitter fruit; damp woods, northern England and Scotland. Compare Wild Cherry with clusters not spikes.

species.name: Prunus pensylvanica
species.tip: Tree with narrow glossy red-brown leaves, flowers in small stalked umbels of white blossom, and small red cherries; rarely planted in Britain.

species.name: Prunus serotina
species.tip: Tree with long glossy leaves and long hanging spikes of small white flowers, then black fruits; naturalised in sandy woods and heaths, with red-brown hairs under the midrib.

species.name: Prunus spinosa
species.tip: Spiny black-barked thicket shrub with white flowers on bare twigs in early spring; fruit are blue-black sloes. Hawthorn flowers later and has lobed leaves.

species.name: Pseudofumaria alba
species.tip: Wall plant with finely cut greyish leaves and creamy-white tubular flowers with a yellow lip tip; walls and rocks, widely naturalised across Britain.

species.name: Pseudofumaria lutea
species.tip: Tufted garden escape on old walls and rocks with soft, fern-like blue-green leaves and many tubular yellow flowers; long flowering season.

species.name: Pseudognaphalium undulatum
species.tip: Grey woolly cudweed with wavy-edged leaves clasping the stem and clusters of whitish heads. Casual from gardens or ports, occasional in the south.

species.name: Pseudorchis albida
species.tip: Small, dense spike of tiny greenish-white vanilla-scented flowers with a short blunt lip; basal leaves oval-oblong and the upper ones small. Mostly northern and western upland grassland.

species.name: Pseudosasa japonica
species.tip: Common tall garden bamboo with stout canes and large glossy leaves, often naturalised; flowers extremely seldom in Britain.

species.name: Pseudoturritis turrita
species.tip: Tall greyish biennial with creamy flowers and clasping leaves, similar to Tower Mustard but with leaves having hairs. Rare casual; needs checking by a specialist.

species.name: Pteridium aquilinum
species.tip: Very tall coarse fern forming dense stands from creeping rhizomes with large triangular fronds, dying brown in autumn; heaths, hillsides and woods.

species.name: Pteris cretica
species.tip: Pinnate fronds with narrow, ribbon-like, finely toothed pinnae, often paler centre. Garden or greenhouse escape on walls and drains in mild urban places.

species.name: Pterocarya fraxinifolia
species.tip: Big tree with long ridged leaf-stalks bearing many leaflets, and hanging chains of winged green fruits. Planted in parks, often spreading by suckers.

species.name: Puccinellia distans
species.tip: Grass of saltmarsh and salted road verges with branches bent downwards once flowering has finished; small spikelets and no awns.

species.name: Puccinellia fasciculata
species.tip: Small tufted annual of bare saltmarsh edges and sea walls with a stiff, short, one-sided panicle; branches stay erect in fruit, unlike the spreading Common Saltmarsh-grass. Mainly southern and eastern coasts.

species.name: Puccinellia maritima
