species.tip: Creeping grass of salt marshes with bluish-green flat or folded leaves and a stiff panicle with spreading branches; no awns.

species.name: Puccinellia rupestris
species.tip: Rigid saltmarsh grass with a stiff, spreading panicle on wiry, one-sided branches; grows on drier coastal sites, unlike Common Saltmarsh-grass with its flexible branches.

species.name: Pulicaria dysenterica
species.tip: Hairy plant with wavy-edged, clasping leaves and flat-topped clusters of golden, rather narrow-rayed daisies. Damp meadows, ditches and wet roadsides.

species.name: Pulicaria vulgaris
species.tip: Small, branching, grey-hairy annual with little yellow daisies with short rays and wavy-edged leaves. Wet sandy hollows, very local, mainly the New Forest.

species.name: Pulmonaria longifolia
species.tip: Lungwort with long, narrow, evenly pale-spotted leaves tapering to a point, and flowers pink turning blue. Rare, in Hampshire, the Isle of Wight and Dorset woods.

species.name: Pulmonaria obscura
species.tip: Lungwort with plain dark green leaves lacking pale spots, and flowers that turn from pink to blue. Native to a few woods in Suffolk and Essex.

species.name: Pulmonaria officinalis
species.tip: Spotted oval leaves and flowers that change from pink to blue-violet. Garden escape in woods and hedges, flowering early in spring.

species.name: Pulmonaria rubra
species.tip: Early spring garden escape with unspotted soft leaves and salmon or brick-red flowers that never turn blue, unlike other lungworts.

species.name: Pulsatilla vulgaris
species.tip: Silky-hairy plant of chalk and limestone grassland with large purple bell flowers in spring, then feathery seed heads.

species.name: Pyracantha coccinea
species.tip: Thorny evergreen with clusters of small white flowers and bright orange or red berries in autumn; walls, hedges and waste ground. Cotoneasters lack thorns.

species.name: Pyrola media
species.tip: Wintergreen with a straight style projecting beyond the whitish-pink bells, longer than Common Wintergreen. Rare in northern Britain and Ireland, in damp woods and moors.

species.name: Pyrola minor
species.tip: Wintergreen with small globular whitish-pink bells whose style is short and does not project. Local in damp woods, dunes and mountain ledges.

species.name: Pyrola rotundifolia
species.tip: Wintergreen with rounded glossy leaves and white open flowers with a long down-curved style. Local in fens, dune slacks and damp rocky places.

species.name: Pyrus communis
species.tip: Tree with glossy oval leaves, white flowers with purple anthers, branches sometimes spiny; gritty pear fruit. Apple has hairier leaves and pink-tinged flowers.

species.name: Pyrus cordata
species.tip: Very rare small thorny pear with small oval leaves, white flowers and tiny brown pears; known wild from hedges around Plymouth, Devon, and in Cornwall.

species.name: Quercus cerris
species.tip: Oak with bristly acorn cups and narrow pointed lobed leaves, rough on the surface; planted tree in parks, spreading in the south.

species.name: Quercus ilex
species.tip: Evergreen oak with dark leathery leaves white-felted beneath, often spiny when young; widely planted and naturalised near coasts.

species.name: Quercus petraea
species.tip: Oak with long-stalked leaves and stalkless acorns; leaf base wedge-shaped with star-hairs on veins beneath; mainly western upland woods.

species.name: Quercus robur
species.tip: Oak with stalked acorns on long stems and almost stalkless leaves with small ear-like lobes at base; common in lowland woods and hedges.

species.name: Quercus rubra
species.tip: Planted oak with large leaves having pointed bristle-tipped lobes, turning red in autumn; acorn cups flat and shallow.

species.name: Ranunculus aconitifolius
species.tip: Tall branched plant with palmately divided leaves like monkshood and white buttercup-like flowers; double form is Bachelor's-buttons. Garden escape in damp grassland, mainly northern Britain.

species.name: Ranunculus acris
species.tip: Tall and hairy with no runners; leaves deeply cut like a hand; flower stalks round and smooth, not furrowed.

species.name: Ranunculus aquatilis
species.tip: White flowers on the water; both floating lobed leaves and submerged thread-like leaves; ponds and ditches. Water-crowfoots are a tricky group: check with a specialist.

species.name: Ranunculus arvensis
species.tip: Rare cornfield weed with pale yellow flowers and large seeds covered in sharp spines.

species.name: Ranunculus auricomus
species.tip: Woodland buttercup whose petals are often missing or misshapen; rounded basal leaves, narrow finger-like stem leaves.

species.name: Ranunculus baudotii
species.tip: Water-crowfoot of brackish coastal ditches and pools; floating and thread-like leaves.

species.name: Ranunculus bulbosus
species.tip: Sepals folded right back down the flower stalk; stem base swollen like a small bulb; dry grassland.

species.name: Ranunculus circinatus
species.tip: Stiff, flat, circular fans of short thread-like leaves that keep their shape when lifted out of water.

species.name: Ranunculus flammula
species.tip: Narrow, spear-shaped leaves and small yellow buttercup flowers; wet ground and pond edges.

species.name: Ranunculus fluitans
species.tip: Very long, dark green, tassel-like submerged leaves in fast rivers; no floating leaves.

species.name: Ranunculus hederaceus
species.tip: Small creeping plant of shallow water and mud with only ivy-shaped leaves (no thread-like ones) and tiny white flowers.

species.name: Ranunculus lingua
species.tip: Tall water-edge plant with long narrow leaves and large (3 to 5 cm) yellow flowers.

species.name: Ranunculus marginatus
species.tip: Small annual buttercup with pale yellow flowers, reflexed sepals and flattened achenes with a distinct rim; lower leaves are kidney-shaped. Rare casual of waste and arable ground. Specialist should confirm.

species.name: Ranunculus muricatus
species.tip: Annual buttercup with shiny, rounded, lobed leaves and spiny fruits in a spreading head; petals pale and small. Local, in damp arable ground and ditch edges, mostly in the south.

species.name: Ranunculus omiophyllus
species.tip: Like Ivy-leaved Crowfoot but leaves more deeply lobed and flowers larger; western, on acid mud and in streams.

species.name: Ranunculus ophioglossifolius
species.tip: Very rare; oval to heart-shaped lower leaves and small pale yellow flowers in muddy pools.

species.name: Ranunculus paludosus
species.tip: Hairy perennial with tuberous, swollen root fibres, lobed basal leaves and narrow upper leaves, plus bright yellow flowers; found in Channel Islands, not mainland Britain. Specialist should confirm.

species.name: Ranunculus parviflorus
species.tip: Sprawling hairy annual with tiny yellow flowers and rounded, lobed leaves; seeds covered in hooked bumps.

species.name: Ranunculus peltatus
species.tip: Floating rounded leaves plus thread-like submerged ones; large white flowers; ponds and slow water.

species.name: Ranunculus penicillatus
species.tip: Long trailing submerged threads in flowing rivers, sometimes with floating leaves; large white flowers.

species.name: Ranunculus repens
species.tip: Long runners that root at the joints; leaves with three leaflets, the middle one on its own stalk; flower stalks furrowed.

species.name: Ranunculus reptans
species.tip: Very rare; slender arching runners that root at each joint, with narrow leaves; stony lake shores.

species.name: Ranunculus sardous
species.tip: Like Bulbous Buttercup (sepals bent back) but paler yellow, hairier and with no swollen stem base; damp ground, often near the coast.

species.name: Ranunculus sceleratus
species.tip: Hairless, shiny, often hollow stem; tiny pale yellow flowers with a large green fruiting head in the middle; muddy pond edges.

species.name: Ranunculus trichophyllus
species.tip: Only short, submerged thread-like leaves that collapse out of water; small white flowers; ponds and ditches.

species.name: Ranunculus tripartitus
species.tip: Rare, south-west; tiny white flowers; deeply three-lobed floating leaves, sometimes thread-like ones too; seasonal pools.

species.name: Raphanus raphanistrum
species.tip: Yellow, white or lilac flowers with dark veins and long beaded pods constricted between seeds; bristly arable weed with lobed leaves.

species.name: Raphanus sativus
species.tip: Familiar salad plant with white or lilac veined flowers and beaded pods. Casual on waste ground; wild forms are bristly, with lobed leaves.

species.name: Rapistrum perenne
species.tip: Tall, bristly yellow-flowered perennial with pods that narrow in joints. Rare casual of waste ground and verges, mainly eastern and southern England.

species.name: Rapistrum rugosum
species.tip: Hairy annual with pale yellow veined flowers and knobbly pods. Lower leaves are lobed. Casual on waste ground, mainly in the south.

species.name: Reseda alba
species.tip: Tall, with dense spikes of small white flowers and pinnately cut wavy leaves. Casual on waste ground and roadsides, mostly in southern England.

species.name: Reseda lutea
species.tip: Biennial or perennial with deeply cut leaves and dense spikes of small pale yellow flowers; chalk and disturbed ground, unlike the undivided leaves of Weld.

species.name: Reseda luteola
species.tip: Tall biennial with a basal rosette and narrow undivided wavy-edged leaves; long slender spikes of small yellowish-green flowers on waste ground.

species.name: Reseda phyteuma
species.tip: Short, spiky pale yellow-green flowers on a spike, and divided linear leaves. Rare casual on arable land and waste ground, mostly south.

species.name: Reynoutria japonica
species.tip: Dense thickets of zigzag, bamboo-like red-speckled stems with broad leaves cut straight across at the base; sprays of creamy flowers in autumn.

species.name: Reynoutria sachalinensis
species.tip: Huge knotweed with large leaves, heart-shaped at the base and hairy beneath, and drooping cream flower sprays. Larger than Japanese Knotweed; invasive on roadsides and riverbanks.

species.name: Rhamnus alaternus
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with glossy, toothed oval leaves and small greenish flowers, unlike the thorny buckthorns. Planted, occasionally self-sown in the south.

species.name: Rhamnus cathartica
species.tip: Often thorn-tipped shrub with finely toothed oval leaves in curved veins, opposite buds and black berries; on chalk and limestone scrub, unlike thornless Alder Buckthorn.

species.name: Rhaponticum repens
species.tip: Creeping knapweed with narrow grey-green leaves, the lower ones lobed, and pinkish-purple thistle-like heads without spines. Rare casual on waste ground.

species.name: Rhinanthus angustifolius
species.tip: Taller than Yellow-rattle, with yellow flowers whose upper-lip teeth are longer and often violet; leaves narrow and toothed. Rare in northern Scotland and eastern England.

species.name: Rhinanthus minor
species.tip: Semi-parasitic annual of meadows, with bright yellow flowers in a leafy spike, inflated seed pods that rattle when ripe, and narrow, coarsely toothed opposite leaves.

species.name: Rhodiola rosea
species.tip: Sea cliffs and mountain ledges; fleshy grey-blue leaves densely clothing thick stems topped by heads of yellowish flowers; roots smell of roses.

species.name: Rhododendron groenlandicum
species.tip: Low evergreen with narrow leaves rolled at the edges and rusty woolly beneath, topped by white flower clusters. Rare garden escape on peaty ground.

species.name: Rhododendron luteum
species.tip: Deciduous shrub with sticky hairy leaves and strongly scented bright yellow funnel flowers in clusters before or with the leaves. Planted, naturalised in some woods.

species.name: Rhododendron ponticum
species.tip: Large evergreen shrub with big glossy leaves and mauve-purple trumpet flowers in domed clusters; invasive in woods and heaths, dense and shading everything below.

species.name: Rhus copallina
species.tip: Small shrubby sumach with pinnate leaves whose stalk is winged between the leaflets, turning red in autumn; rarely grown and very rarely self-sown. Needs specialist confirmation.

species.name: Rhus coriaria
species.tip: Shrub with pinnate, coarsely toothed leaves, hairy shoots and dense greenish flower spikes, reddish fruit; a rare escape or relic near gardens.

species.name: Rhus typhina
species.tip: Suckering small tree with velvety stems and long pinnate leaves turning red in autumn; dense red conical fruit heads; planted in gardens and escaping.

species.name: Rhynchospora alba
species.tip: A tufted bog plant with clusters of white or cream spikelets at stem ends and grass-like leaves; the fruits are beaked, and the white heads set it apart from Brown Beak-sedge.

species.name: Rhynchospora fusca
species.tip: A very local creeping plant of damp heath hollows in the New Forest and Surrey, with rich brown spikelets in small clusters on slim stems; browner and rarer than White Beak-sedge.

species.name: Ribes alpinum
species.tip: Small, upright shrub with three-lobed leaves and small greenish flowers in separate male and female spikes. Found in limestone woods in northern England and Wales.

species.name: Ribes nigrum
species.tip: Shrub with strongly aromatic, yellow-gland-dotted, lobed leaves and hanging spikes of dull greenish bells; black berries; escapes in damp woods and hedges.

species.name: Ribes rubrum
species.tip: Shrub with unscented lobed leaves and drooping spikes of tiny green flowers; shiny red berries in strings; found in wet woods and hedges, with no spines.

species.name: Ribes sanguineum
species.tip: Garden shrub often seen in hedges and waste ground, with hanging clusters of bright pink-red flowers appearing before the leaves; strongly scented leaves.

species.name: Ribes spicatum
species.tip: Rare northern currant with lobed leaves and hairy undersides; greenish flowers in hairy racemes. Found in limestone woods in northern England and Orkney.

species.name: Ribes uva-crispa
species.tip: Spiny shrub of hedges and woods with small lobed leaves and green-pink flowers hanging singly or in twos; fruits are hairy or smooth green berries.

species.name: Robinia pseudoacacia
species.tip: Tree with deeply furrowed bark, pinnate leaves and hanging scented white pea flowers in spring; twigs bear short paired thorns.

species.name: Rodgersia podophylla
species.tip: Large garden perennial with big hand-shaped leaves of five coarsely toothed leaflets, bronze when young, and tall plumes of small creamy flowers. Occasional escape near water.

species.name: Roemeria argemone
species.tip: Poppy with small pale scarlet flowers with a dark spot, bristly stems, and long narrow pods with a few bristles; fruits are club-shaped. Arable land, mostly in the south.

species.name: Roemeria hispida
species.tip: Poppy with small dark red flowers and bristly globose pods, with stems rough from stiff hairs. Rare arable weed on chalk in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Romulea columnae
species.tip: Tiny crocus-like plant with lilac, white-throated flowers opening only in sun. Very rare coastal turf in Cornwall, Devon and the Channel Islands.

species.name: Rorippa amphibia
species.tip: Tall stout waterside plant with narrow, toothed or lobed leaves and many small yellow flowers; pods are short and oval. Common by rivers and ponds in England.

species.name: Rorippa austriaca
species.tip: Rhizomatous yellow-cress with undivided toothed, clasping stem leaves and small yellow flowers. Rare introduction, on river banks and waste ground in places.

species.name: Rorippa islandica
species.tip: Small, mainly upland yellow-cress of wet stony places with pinnately lobed leaves and short pods. Very rare, in the Scottish Highlands; needs careful checking.

species.name: Rorippa palustris
species.tip: Small pale yellow flowers on a branched plant of muddy edges with deeply lobed leaves; short plump pods are longer than their stalks.

species.name: Rorippa sylvestris
species.tip: Creeping roots and finely divided leaves on bare damp ground and roadsides; slender pods longer than stalk, flowers bright yellow.

species.name: Rosa agrestis
species.tip: Sweet-briar rose with leaves bearing a smell of apples (less strong), white or pale pink flowers, hairless sepals and stalks; mostly southern limestone hedges. Roses of this group need a specialist.

species.name: Rosa arvensis
species.tip: Trailing white-flowered rose with green purple-tinged stems, hooked prickles; styles joined into a column; woods and hedges, mainly southern England. Flowers later than Dog-rose.

species.name: Rosa caesia
species.tip: Dog-rose group with hairy leaves and leaflets that are double-toothed, bluish-green; usually sepals persistent on hip; northern and western hedges. Needs careful checking against Dog-rose.

species.name: Rosa canina
species.tip: Commonest wild rose, arching stems with hooked prickles, pale pink or white flowers, hairless leaflets; sepals soon reflexed and drop. Compare Sweet-briar scented and Field-rose with joined styles.

species.name: Rosa corymbifera
species.tip: Dog-rose group member with downy leaves, hairy beneath, and hooked prickles; widespread in hedgerows. Told from true dog-rose by the hairy leaves, and distinct from sweet-briars by lack of apple scent.

species.name: Rosa gallica
species.tip: Low suckering rose with rough, stiff leaves, deep pink to crimson large fragrant flowers and many stiff prickles and bristles; rare escape of grassy banks and hedges.

species.name: Rosa glauca
species.tip: Rose with distinctive purple-grey, hairless leaves and stems, rich pink flowers with white centres, and few straight prickles; widely planted and often naturalised on verges.

species.name: Rosa luciae
species.tip: Trailing, ground-hugging rose with glossy small leaves and clusters of fragrant white flowers in late summer; often used on banks and sometimes escaped. Small hooked prickles.

species.name: Rosa micrantha
species.tip: Sweet-briar with smaller pink flowers, scented apple-like glands on leaves underneath, and hairless sepals; mainly in southern English scrub and hedges. A specialist is needed to confirm this group.

species.name: Rosa mollis
species.tip: Rose with soft, bluish-grey downy leaves, bristly stalks, deep pink flowers and nearly straight prickles; found in northern and western hills of Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Rosa multiflora
species.tip: Vigorous arching rose bearing large panicles of small white fragrant flowers and fringed leaf stipules; fruit tiny red hips. Naturalised from gardens, scrambling over hedges and scrub.

species.name: Rosa rubiginosa
species.tip: Rose with apple-scented sticky glands under leaflets, strong hooked and straight prickles, bright pink flowers; calcareous scrub and grassland. Smell crushed leaves.

species.name: Rosa rugosa
species.tip: Dense bushy garden rose with wrinkled leaves, very bristly stems, large magenta or white flowers and big tomato-like hips; common on dunes and verges.

species.name: Rosa setigera
species.tip: Climbing rose with three-leaflet leaves, long arching stems, rose-pink flowers in clusters that fade to white, flowering late in summer; rare escape in hedges.

species.name: Rosa sherardii
species.tip: Dog-rose relative with soft hairy leaves, glandular, bluish; pink flowers; hip bristly, sepals persistent; northern and western hedges and rocky places. Needs careful checking.

species.name: Rosa spinosissima
species.tip: Low suckering rose of dunes and heaths with dense straight prickles, small ferny leaves and creamy white flowers; hips round and black-purple.

species.name: Rosa squarrosa
species.tip: Dog-rose relative with leaning, spreading sepals and bristly-free stems; needs a rose specialist to separate from other dog-rose group members by leaf toothing and hairs.

species.name: Rosa stylosa
species.tip: Climbing white field-rose with styles joined into a short column, unlike the loose styles of dog-roses; mostly southern England, Wales and Ireland.

species.name: Rosa tomentella
species.tip: Dog-rose group member with rounded, hairy, glandular-toothed leaflets and stout hooked prickles; a specialist is needed to confirm it among similar hairy-leaved roses.

species.name: Rosa tomentosa
species.tip: Densely downy leaflets with gland-tipped double teeth and a sticky resin smell; pink flowers and bristly hips separate it from the glabrous dog-rose.

species.name: Rosa villosa
species.tip: Large bristly hips and softly hairy, gland-scented leaves with few prickles; deep pink flowers. Mainly northern Britain and Wales, often by streams and hedges.

species.name: Rosa virginiana
species.tip: Garden escape with glossy, hairless leaflets, bright pink flowers and near-straight paired prickles; leaves turn red in autumn. Hips are small and round.

species.name: Rosa vosagiaca
species.tip: Greyish-purple tinged leaflets with simple teeth, hairless, and pink flowers; a specialist is needed to separate it from the red-leaved rose and other forms. Rare, mostly northern Britain.

species.name: Rosmarinus officinalis
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with narrow, leathery, aromatic leaves and small pale blue flowers in the upper axils. Cultivated and occasionally persisting on old walls and dry banks.

species.name: Rubia peregrina
species.tip: Evergreen scrambler with glossy, leathery leaves in whorls with prickly edges and keel, with tiny greenish-yellow flowers. Hedges and cliffs in southern and western coastal areas.

species.name: Rubia tinctorum
species.tip: Scrambling, prickly stems with whorls of leaves, and greenish-yellow flowers, like Wild Madder but less glossy. Occasional relic of cultivation, rare in the south.

species.name: Rubus caesius
species.tip: Trailing slender bramble with bluish waxy bloom on stems and few big drupelets; leaves of three leaflets; flowers white; calcareous grassland and damp sites. Fewer prickles than Bramble.

species.name: Rubus chamaemorus
species.tip: Low upland herb with single white flowers and lobed, crinkled leaves, no prickles; fruit ripens from red to amber. Northern moors and bogs.

species.name: Rubus cockburnianus
species.tip: Arching stems coated in chalky white bloom, small purplish flowers and black fruit; a garden shrub sometimes naturalised near habitation.

species.name: Rubus fissus
species.tip: Bramble microspecies of the southern and eastern heaths and woods; a batologist is needed to confirm it from other brambles by stem, leaf and prickle details.

species.name: Rubus fruticosus
species.tip: Hundreds of microspecies needing a specialist; arching prickly stems, white or pink flowers, black fruit in summer and autumn. Raspberry has white-felted leaves; Dewberry has bloom.

species.name: Rubus idaeus
species.tip: Upright stems with weak prickles, leaves white-felted beneath, small white flowers with narrow petals; red fruit that parts from the core; heaths, woods and clearings.

species.name: Rubus nessensis
species.tip: Low arching bramble with weak slender prickles and hairy, rather few leaflets; a bramble specialist must confirm it. Scattered in Scotland and northern England on acid soils.

species.name: Rubus odoratus
species.tip: Unarmed garden shrub with large maple-like lobed leaves, bristly glandular stems and showy magenta-pink flowers; sometimes naturalised in hedges.

species.name: Rubus parviflorus
species.tip: Unarmed shrub with large soft maple-like leaves and white flowers; fruit is a flat red thimble. Naturalised in a few places from gardens.

species.name: Rubus phoenicolasius
species.tip: Stems and flower buds covered with dense red glandular bristles; leaves white-felted beneath with three leaflets; orange-red raspberry-like fruit in a hairy calyx.

species.name: Rubus saxatilis
species.tip: Low unarmed herb of rocky northern slopes with three-leaflet leaves, small white narrow-petalled flowers and few red berries; no strong prickles. Spreads by runners.

species.name: Rubus scissus
species.tip: Bramble microspecies with deeply toothed leaflets; local, mainly in southern England, and needing a specialist to confirm among the many similar brambles.

species.name: Rubus spectabilis
species.tip: Naturalised garden shrub with three-leaflet leaves, magenta flowers in spring, weak prickles and orange to red raspberry-like fruit; found in a few scattered woods.

species.name: Rubus tricolor
species.tip: Evergreen ground cover with undivided, heart-shaped leaves dark above and white beneath, and bristly red stems; a garden escape on banks.

species.name: Rudbeckia laciniata
species.tip: Tall plant with deeply lobed leaves and drooping yellow rays around a greenish-yellow conical centre. Garden escape on riverbanks and waste ground.

species.name: Rumex acetosa
species.tip: Sour-tasting dock with arrow-shaped leaves clasping the stem, and red-flushed flower spikes on separate male and female plants; common in meadows and grassland.

species.name: Rumex acetosella
species.tip: Small, slender sorrel with narrow spear-shaped leaves having outward-pointing basal lobes; reddish flower spikes, abundant on acid, sandy and heathy soils.

species.name: Rumex alpinus
species.tip: Large dock with big rounded, heart-based leaves with wavy edges and dense green flower spikes. Naturalised near old farms and villages, mostly in northern England and Scotland.

species.name: Rumex aquaticus
species.tip: Tall water dock with big triangular heart-based leaves and dense whorled flower spikes. Very rare, around Loch Lomond in Scotland. Compare Water Dock, which is more widespread.

species.name: Rumex confertus
species.tip: Tall dock with hairy veins under heart-based leaves and dense, narrow flower spikes. Naturalised on waste ground and roadsides, mainly in eastern England.

species.name: Rumex conglomeratus
species.tip: Branches are zigzag, spreading widely with flowers in distinct whorled clusters, each leafy; all three fruit valves bear a swollen wart; damp places.

species.name: Rumex crispus
species.tip: Narrow leaves with strongly crinkled, wavy margins; dense branched spikes, fruit valves with at most one wart; common on waste ground, shingle and arable land.

species.name: Rumex cristatus
species.tip: Large dock with big wavy heart-based leaves and dense spikes with big fruiting valves. Naturalised on waste ground, mainly in south-east England.

species.name: Rumex cuneifolius
species.tip: Dock with wedge-shaped, spoon-like leaf bases and red-tinged fruit spikes. Introduced; established in a few places in southern England and sandy ground.

species.name: Rumex hydrolapathum
species.tip: Very tall dock of watersides with huge, long, lance-shaped leaves, and fruit valves all bearing warts; dense erect spikes, flowering later than most docks.

species.name: Rumex longifolius
species.tip: Large dock of northern streamsides and verges with broad leaves whose base is blunt or heart-shaped, and warts missing on the fruit valves; mostly upland and northern.

species.name: Rumex maritimus
species.tip: Annual dock of muddy pond margins, with narrow leaves and whorls of golden-yellow fruits with spiny valves. Local in lowland England; slimmer than Marsh Dock.

species.name: Rumex obtusifolius
species.tip: Familiar weed with broad, heart-based leaves and fruit valves with toothed margins and a single wart; spikes less crowded than Curled Dock; also fields and gardens.

species.name: Rumex palustris
species.tip: Annual or biennial dock with narrow leaves and golden-brown whorled fruits with bristle-like teeth. Rare, on muddy pond and ditch margins, mainly south-east England.

species.name: Rumex patientia
species.tip: Tall, robust dock with broad, long-stalked leaves rounded or slightly wedge-shaped at the base. Fruits heart-shaped, one with a swollen grain. Naturalised on waste ground, mainly in the south.

species.name: Rumex pulcher
species.tip: Dock with leaves narrowed in the middle like a fiddle, and widely spreading branches with fruits that have spiny teeth. Common on dry grassy ground in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Rumex rupestris
species.tip: Rare dock of coastal shingle and rocks, with blue-green, pointed, shortly toothed leaves and wavy margins. Declined, now confined to south-west England, Wales and Ireland.

species.name: Rumex salicifolius
species.tip: Dock with narrow willow-like leaves and slender flowering spikes. Rare introduction from North America; identity best confirmed with a specialist.

species.name: Rumex sanguineus
species.tip: Slender dock with erect, spreading branches, narrow leaves and fruit with a single wart; leaf veins may be red in var. sanguineus; shady woods and hedgerows.

species.name: Rumex scutatus
species.tip: Greyish, waxy, arrow-shaped leaves with spreading basal lobes, unlike the greener common sorrels. Escape on walls, railways and rubble, mainly in England.

species.name: Ruppia maritima
species.tip: Submerged, thread-like leaves and tiny flower pair on spike with long stalks; in brackish pools. Coastal brackish lagoons and ditches, scattered around the coast.

species.name: Ruppia spiralis
species.tip: Submerged thread-like leaves; fruit stalks coiled spirally after flowering, unlike Beaked Tasselweed. Brackish lagoons and ditches, scattered, mostly east and south coasts.

species.name: Ruschia caroli
species.tip: Rare South African succulent seen only as a garden throw-out, with small fleshy leaves and pink or white daisy-like flowers; hard to place without a specialist.

species.name: Ruscus aculeatus
species.tip: Evergreen, stiff, prickly shrub of woods and hedges; leaf-like flattened stems end in sharp spines, with tiny pale flowers in the middle and red berries.

species.name: Ruscus hypoglossum
species.tip: Evergreen with flattened leaf-like green stems lacking a spine tip, bearing tiny greenish flowers on the surface. Rare garden escape in woods; prickly butchers-broom has sharp points.

species.name: Ruta graveolens
species.tip: Blue-green, strongly smelling, much-divided leaves and clusters of yellow-green flowers with four petals. Old garden herb, sometimes persisting on walls and waste ground.

species.name: Sabulina rubella
species.tip: Small tufted mountain plant with white flowers on short stalks, and narrow, pointed leaves with sticky glandular hairs. Very rare, on base-rich rocks in Scotland.

species.name: Sabulina stricta
species.tip: Dwarf tufted plant with white flowers with petals shorter than sepals, and thread-like leaves. Rare, restricted to Upper Teesdale, on sugar limestone.

species.name: Sabulina tenuifolia
species.tip: Slender annual with white flowers in loose branched clusters, petals shorter than the sepals, and thread-like leaves. Rare, on dry calcareous ground in southern England.

species.name: Sabulina verna
species.tip: Low tufts of short narrow leaves on limestone, lead-mine spoil and mountain ledges, covered in starry white five-petalled flowers.

species.name: Sagina apetala
species.tip: Tiny annual with narrow leaves and four-parted flowers; petals are minute or absent and the sepals are pressed close to the capsule. Bare gravelly and sandy ground.

species.name: Sagina maritima
species.tip: Fleshy small pearlwort of coastal turf and salt-affected paths; capsule-pressed sepals, petals very small or absent, and fleshy blunt leaves. Annual of the coast.

species.name: Sagina nivalis
species.tip: Tiny tufted pearlwort of mountain rocks with flowers on short stalks, with petals longer than sepals, with very short stems. Very rare, in the Scottish Highlands.

species.name: Sagina nodosa
species.tip: Perennial pearlwort with little leaf clusters along the stem like knots, and white flowers larger than most pearlworts. Damp sandy ground and dune slacks.

species.name: Sagina procumbens
species.tip: Common mat-forming pearlwort in paths and lawns, with four-petalled flowers with minute petals and a central rosette; sepals spread out in fruit.

species.name: Sagina saginoides
species.tip: Small pearlwort with flowers on stalks, with five petals, and narrow leaves in tufts. Local on mountain rocks and wet ground in Scotland.

species.name: Sagina subulata
species.tip: Mat-forming pearlwort with small white flowers on glandular-hairy stalks, with five petals, and bristle-like leaves. Local on dry sandy heaths and coastal rocks.

species.name: Sagittaria graminea
species.tip: North American pond plant rarely naturalised; very narrow strap-like leaves and white three-petalled flowers lacking arrow-shaped leaves, so unlike native Arrowhead.

species.name: Sagittaria latifolia
species.tip: Introduced arrowhead with broad arrow-shaped leaves and white flowers in whorls; larger than native Arrowhead, with bracts and sepals that look different, in canals and ponds.

species.name: Sagittaria rigida
species.tip: Introduced aquatic arrowhead with narrow strap-like submerged leaves and sometimes a few broader floating ones, white flowers held low; confirmation by a specialist is advised.

species.name: Sagittaria sagittifolia
species.tip: Aquatic plant with distinctive arrow-shaped aerial leaves, ribbon-like submerged leaves and whorls of three-petalled white flowers with purple centres. Slow rivers and canals.

species.name: Salicornia disarticulata
species.tip: Fleshy leafless annual of muddy saltmarsh with jointed, green stems and tiny flowers; glasswort species look alike, so a specialist is needed to confirm.

species.name: Salicornia europaea
species.tip: Upright jointed fleshy annual of saltmarsh mud, green and turning red in autumn, with tiny flowers sunk in the spike; glasswort species need a specialist to separate.

species.name: Salicornia obscura
species.tip: Annual glasswort of upper saltmarsh with greyish, bluish, jointed stems and tiny sunken flowers; a specialist is needed to separate it from other glassworts.

species.name: Salicornia procumbens
species.tip: Low spreading annual glasswort with shiny, bright green jointed stems and tiny sunken flowers; found on muddy saltmarsh in south-east England; specialist needed to confirm.

species.name: Salix alba
species.tip: Large riverside willow with narrow, silky silvery-hairy leaves on both sides; catkins appear with the leaves, and branches are upright and yellow-green.

species.name: Salix arbuscula
species.tip: Low shrub with shiny, small oval leaves that are hairy beneath at first. Rare, on damp mountain rocks in the Scottish Highlands; hybridises.

species.name: Salix aurita
species.tip: Small shrubby willow of damp heath and woods with wrinkled, grey-hairy oval leaves with a twisted tip and ear-like leafy stipules at the base of the leaf stalk.

species.name: Salix caprea
species.tip: Large shrub or small tree with broad oval, wavy leaves, grey-felted beneath, and large fat silky catkins (pussy willow) before the leaves in early spring.

species.name: Salix cinerea
species.tip: Common bushy willow of wet ground with oval leaves grey-hairy beneath and short hairy twigs; rusty-haired in one subspecies, with ridges under the bark when stripped.

species.name: Salix eriocephala
species.tip: Hairy twigs and heart-based oval leaves; a rare introduced American willow. Specialist needed to confirm; naturalised only locally.

species.name: Salix herbacea
species.tip: Tiny creeping plant with rounded, shiny leaves, only a few centimetres high. Mountain tops and rocks in Scotland, Wales, northern England and Ireland.

species.name: Salix lanata
species.tip: Low, rounded shrub with silvery woolly leaves and thick, yellowish catkins. Rare, on high Scottish rocky ledges; the leaves are broad and rounded.

species.name: Salix lapponum
species.tip: Shrub with narrow, grey, woolly-white leaves beneath and large silvery catkins. Rare, on upland Scottish and northern English crags.

species.name: Salix myrsinifolia
species.tip: Dark green leaves that blacken when dried, hairless or slightly hairy, and finely toothed. Scottish and northern English streamsides; hybrids common, so specialist may confirm.

species.name: Salix myrsinites
species.tip: Low, spreading, with small, glossy, finely toothed leaves and purple twigs. Rare, on mountain rocks in the Scottish Highlands, on base-rich rocks.

species.name: Salix pentandra
species.tip: Shrubby willow of northern damp ground with glossy dark green, bay-like, leathery leaves that are aromatic when crushed; catkins appear late, after the leaves.

species.name: Salix phylicifolia
species.tip: Shrub with shiny dark leaves, silvery beneath, and smooth twigs. Streamsides and rocks in northern England and Scotland; hybridises.

species.name: Salix purpurea
species.tip: Slender shrub of wet places with narrow bluish-green leaves that are often paired or opposite and bitter; catkins are narrow, with purple anthers.

species.name: Salix repens
species.tip: Low straggly shrub of heaths, bogs and dunes with small oval grey-silky leaves underneath; catkins small and upright, stems often sprawling or creeping underground.

species.name: Salix reticulata
species.tip: Creeping mat plant with rounded, net-veined, leathery leaves. Rare, on damp, base-rich mountain ledges in the Scottish Highlands.

species.name: Salix triandra
species.tip: Tall shrub with narrow, glossy, finely toothed leaves and a flaking bark. Osier beds and riverbanks, mostly in southern England.

species.name: Salix viminalis
species.tip: Tall shrub often grown in osier beds, with very long narrow leaves white silky-felted beneath and long straight unbranched shoots.

species.name: Salpichroa origanifolia
species.tip: Scrambling, trailing plant with small oval leaves and creamy-white bell-shaped flowers, then egg-shaped pale berries. Naturalised on walls and hedgebanks in southern England.

species.name: Salsola kali
species.tip: Sprawling grey-green annual of sandy shores with fleshy, spine-tipped narrow leaves and flowers tucked in leaf axils; spiny to touch, unlike Sea-blite.

species.name: Salvia glutinosa
species.tip: Tall sage with sticky hairs and large pale yellow hooded flowers marked brownish, and arrow-shaped leaves. Rare naturalised plant in woods and hedges.

species.name: Salvia pratensis
species.tip: Showy sage with whorled spikes of bright violet-blue flowers and wrinkled, mostly basal leaves. Local on dry chalk and limestone grassland, mainly in the south and Cotswolds.

species.name: Salvia verbenaca
species.tip: Sage-like plant with wrinkled, lobed leaves and small lilac-blue flowers in whorls on a slender spike. Dry grassland, roadsides and banks, mostly in the south and near coasts.

species.name: Salvia verticillata
species.tip: Hairy clary with heart-shaped basal leaves and dense whorls of small lilac-purple flowers, with a foetid scent. Naturalised in rough grassland and waste ground.

species.name: Sambucus canadensis
species.tip: Shrub with pinnate leaves and large flat heads of white flowers, similar to Elder but with more leaflets and larger flower heads. Rare garden escape.

species.name: Sambucus ebulus
species.tip: Herb-like patch-forming elder with pinnate leaves with leaf-like stipules, white pink-tinged flowers with purple anthers and black berries. Foul smell when crushed; scattered across England and Wales.

species.name: Sambucus nigra
species.tip: Shrub or small tree with flat heads of creamy-white scented flowers and compound leaves; hedgerows and waste ground, black berries in autumn.

species.name: Sambucus racemosa
species.tip: Shrub with pinnate leaves and compact egg-shaped heads of cream-green flowers in spring, followed by bright red berries. Naturalised across the north and in woodland.

species.name: Samolus valerandi
species.tip: Small white flowers in a loose spike with a ring of tiny scales within; spoon-shaped leaves; damp coastal places and flushes, unlike the primulas.

species.name: Sanguisorba canadensis
species.tip: Tall perennial with long white bottle-brush spikes and pinnate leaves; no petals. Garden plant, rarely escaping to damp ground, flowering late summer.

species.name: Sanguisorba officinalis
species.tip: Tall plant of damp meadows with oval dark crimson heads and divided leaves with toothed leaflets; flowers lack petals. Salad Burnet is shorter, dry and green-purple.

species.name: Sanicula europaea
species.tip: Not a typical umbellifer: shiny, palmately lobed dark leaves and small rounded heads of tiny whitish or pinkish flowers in beech and oak woodland on lime-rich soil.

species.name: Saponaria ocymoides
species.tip: Trailing perennial with masses of small pink flowers and small oval hairy leaves. Garden plant, occasionally escaped onto rocks, walls and banks.

species.name: Saponaria officinalis
species.tip: Tall perennial with clustered pale pink five-petalled flowers and oval leaves with three to five veins. Hedgebanks, roadsides and waste ground, often a garden escape.

species.name: Sarcocornia perennis
species.tip: Woody-based perennial glasswort with creeping stems and jointed fleshy shoots that stay green and leafless; found on upper saltmarsh in the south and east, unlike annual glassworts.

species.name: Sarracenia flava
species.tip: Tall green-yellow trumpet-shaped insect-trapping leaves with a lid, and a nodding yellow flower on a long stem. Naturalised in a few bogs.

species.name: Sarracenia purpurea
species.tip: Low rosette of red-veined pitchers that hold rainwater, open-mouthed with no upright lid, and a single nodding maroon flower. Naturalised in bogs in Ireland and Britain.

species.name: Sasa palmata
species.tip: Garden bamboo with big broad hand-like leaves at the stem tips, spreading by rhizomes; the largest-leaved bamboo you may meet. Flowering unknown here.

species.name: Sasa veitchii
species.tip: Low garden bamboo with big broad leaves that bleach at the margins in winter, forming dense patches; escapes occasionally. Flowers practically never seen.

species.name: Sasaella ramosa
species.tip: Hybrid bamboo with many fine branches and slightly hairy leaves, forming spreading thickets; occasional escape. Flowering is very rare in Britain.

species.name: Satureja montana
species.tip: Small, woody, aromatic plant with narrow pointed leaves and pale pink-white flowers in whorls. Grown in gardens and occasionally found on dry walls and chalk banks.

species.name: Saussurea alpina
species.tip: Mountain thistle relative without spines, leaves narrow and toothed, white woolly beneath, with dense clusters of purple heads. Rare, mountain ledges in Scotland, northern England, Wales.

species.name: Saxifraga aizoides
species.tip: Mat-forming plant of wet mountain flushes with fleshy narrow pointed leaves and starry yellow to orange flowers, often spotted. Distinct from yellow stonecrops by its leaf shape and five petals.

species.name: Saxifraga cernua
species.tip: Tiny arctic-alpine with lobed kidney-shaped leaves, a single white flower on a hairy stem and red bulbils in the leaf axils. Very rare, on a few Scottish summits.

species.name: Saxifraga cespitosa
species.tip: Dense cushions of hairy, three-lobed leaves with a few creamy-white flowers on short glandular stems. Mountain rocks in Wales and Scotland; compare Mossy Saxifrage with its long runners.

species.name: Saxifraga cuneifolia
species.tip: Neat rosettes of rounded, long-stalked, toothed leaves and airy sprays of tiny white flowers with yellow and red spots. Garden plant that sometimes escapes onto walls.

species.name: Saxifraga cymbalaria
species.tip: Small, leafy, branched annual or biennial with kidney-shaped lobed leaves and small yellow flowers on slender stems. Naturalised in a few places, mostly on walls and rocks.

species.name: Saxifraga granulata
species.tip: Grassland plant with kidney-shaped, blunt-lobed hairy leaves, small bulbils at the base, and loose heads of large white flowers veined green; flowers held on tall stems.

species.name: Saxifraga hirculus
species.tip: Rare bog plant with narrow leaves and large yellow flowers marked with orange dots; stem has rusty hairs. Few northern English and Scottish sites; looks like no other wetland saxifrage.

species.name: Saxifraga hirsuta
species.tip: Hairy rosette plant with round-kidney leaves on long hairy stalks and loose sprays of white flowers with small yellow and pink spots. Damp shady rocks in southwest Ireland, naturalised elsewhere.

species.name: Saxifraga hypnoides
species.tip: Cushion-forming plant with trailing leafy runners, narrow three-lobed leaves and loose clusters of white flowers on slender stems. Common on limestone and mountain rocks in the north.

species.name: Saxifraga oppositifolia
species.tip: Mat of tiny opposite scale-like leaves, with big purple-pink stemless flowers early in spring. Mountain rocks, Wales, northern England, Scotland and Ireland.

species.name: Saxifraga rivularis
species.tip: Very small arctic-alpine of wet snow patches with lobed, long-stalked leaves and one to three small white flowers. Rare and confined to high Scottish mountains.

species.name: Saxifraga rosacea
species.tip: Tufted plant with glossy three- to five-lobed leaves and white flowers with widely spaced petals. Mountain rocks and stream gravel in Ireland, plus a few Welsh and Scottish sites.

species.name: Saxifraga rotundifolia
species.tip: Hairy plant with rounded, coarsely toothed basal leaves and a many-flowered spray of white flowers spotted with red and yellow. Garden escape on banks and walls.

species.name: Saxifraga spathularis
species.tip: Tough rosette plant of western Irish mountains with leathery spoon-shaped, toothed leaves and white yellow-spotted flowers. Differs from London Pride by its longer, narrower leaf blades.

species.name: Saxifraga stolonifera
species.tip: House-plant escape with rounded hairy marbled leaves, long red runners with plantlets, and white flowers with one long lower petal. Naturalised on a few walls.

species.name: Saxifraga tridactylites
species.tip: Tiny, sticky-hairy annual of walls and bare ground with three-lobed leaves often turning red and small white flowers with notched petals.

species.name: Saxifraga umbrosa
species.tip: Garden plant with rosettes of leathery oval toothed leaves and airy sprays of small pink-spotted white flowers. A parent of London Pride; occasionally escapes. Specialist confirmation helps.

species.name: Scabiosa atropurpurea
species.tip: Annual garden plant with domed heads of dark crimson to purple flowers on tall stems, with lobed leaves. Rare casual on waste ground and tips.

species.name: Scabiosa columbaria
species.tip: Slender plant of dry chalk and limestone grassland with blue-lilac flower heads, and finely cut leaves on stems; shorter and less hairy than Field Scabious.

species.name: Scandix pecten-veneris
species.tip: Annual of arable fields, with finely cut leaves, small white umbels, and long beaked fruits like needles; once frequent but now very rare.

species.name: Schedonorus arundinaceus
species.tip: Coarse, tall tufted grass with broad rough leaves, auricles with hairs on the edge, and a large panicle; spikelets awnless or shortly awned.

species.name: Schedonorus giganteus
species.tip: Woodland grass with a large nodding panicle of long-awned spikelets and broad shiny leaves with small auricles; shade-loving.

species.name: Schedonorus pratensis
species.tip: Meadow grass with a narrow panicle with shiny, unawned spikelets, hairless auricles and glossy leaves, shorter than Tall Fescue and finer.

species.name: Scheuchzeria palustris
species.tip: Rare bog plant with narrow channelled grass-like leaves each ending in a tiny pore and a loose spike of few greenish flowers. Peaty pools in Scotland, Ireland and mid Wales.

species.name: Schizostylis coccinea
species.tip: Spikes of bright crimson-pink star-shaped flowers in autumn over narrow sword leaves. Garden plant occasionally escaping into damp, sheltered ground.

species.name: Schoenoplectus lacustris
species.tip: Tall leafless round green stems with a drooping cluster of brown spikelets near the tip, in lakes and rivers; stem is dark green, not glaucous like Grey Club-rush.

species.name: Schoenoplectus pungens
species.tip: A rare tall brackish-water club-rush of south-west coasts with sharply three-angled, pointed stems and clustered brown spikelets, with a short sharp bract continuing the stem; rare in Britain.

species.name: Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani
species.tip: Very similar to Common Club-rush but stems greyish-blue and glaucous, spikelets paler with rough hairy scales; brackish and freshwater edges.

species.name: Schoenoplectus triqueter
species.tip: A very rare, tall club-rush of tidal river mud in the Thames, Tamar and few estuaries, with sharply three-sided green stems and a small cluster of brown spikelets close below the tip.

species.name: Schoenus ferrugineus
species.tip: A very rare, tufted, dark-headed plant of lime-rich wet flushes in Scotland, with stiff wiry stems and a small cluster of dark chestnut brown spikelets above a long bract.

species.name: Schoenus nigricans
species.tip: Stiff dark tufts of narrow rush-like leaves in fens and wet heath; shiny blackish-brown, small spikelet head at stem tip with a long leafy bract.

species.name: Scilla autumnalis
species.tip: Small bulb flowering in late summer with a short head of starry lilac-blue flowers before the very narrow leaves appear. Local on dry coastal turf in southern England.

species.name: Scilla bifolia
species.tip: Early spring bulb with two narrow leaves and a loose spike of one to few starry, bright blue flowers. Rare garden escape on grass and in parks.

species.name: Scilla bithynica
species.tip: Spring bulb with broad, shiny leaves and a loose spike of up to twelve small pale blue starry flowers. Occasional escape in parks and churchyards.

species.name: Scilla forbesii
species.tip: Early spring bulb with bright blue starry flowers having a white centre, upward facing, several on one stem, with narrow leaves. Naturalised in grass near gardens.

species.name: Scilla liliohyacinthus
species.tip: Robust bulb with broad strap leaves and a tall spike of many pale blue bells with darker veins. Rare garden escape in woodland, mostly southern England.

species.name: Scilla luciliae
species.tip: Early spring bulb with large, bright blue starry flowers with white centres, one to three per stem, held upward. Naturalised on lawns and verges; larger flowers than Forbes form.

species.name: Scilla messeniaca
species.tip: Spring bulb with a loose spike of small pale blue bells and narrow leaves. A rare garden escape, hard to separate from other squills without specialist help.

species.name: Scilla peruviana
species.tip: Large domed head of many violet-blue starry flowers on stout stem above broad leaves fringed with fine hairs. Rare garden escape on south-western coasts and banks.

species.name: Scilla sardensis
species.tip: Early spring bulb with small nodding-to-erect rich blue flowers lacking a distinct white centre, borne in a loose cluster above narrow leaves. Rare garden relic.

species.name: Scilla siberica
species.tip: Intense deep blue nodding bell flowers, one to three per stem, with broad glossy leaves. Widely naturalised in grass, churchyards and parkland in early spring.

species.name: Scilla verna
species.tip: Low tuft with narrow curled leaves and a short head of bright blue starry flowers. Local on short coastal turf of west and north Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Scirpoides holoschoenus
species.tip: A tall, tufted plant with rounded heads of reddish-brown spikelets on rigid stems, found in a tiny number of southern coastal sites; one of few sedges with globular heads.

species.name: Scirpus sylvaticus
species.tip: Tall plant of damp woods with broad leaves, a large branched head of many tiny clustered green spikelets, and a triangular stem; resembles a rush but is a sedge relative.

species.name: Scleranthus annuus
species.tip: Small spreading annual with tiny green flowers in clusters and narrow, spiny, bristle-like leaves. Local on dry, sandy, arable and waste ground.

species.name: Scleranthus perennis
species.tip: Tiny greenish flowers in tight clusters on a tufted, wiry perennial with needle-like paired leaves. Very rare, on dry rocky ground in Radnorshire and Worcestershire.

species.name: Scorzonera humilis
species.tip: Plant with narrow grass-like leaves and solitary pale yellow dandelion-like heads on a tall stem. Very rare, on damp grassland in Dorset.

species.name: Scorzoneroides autumnalis
species.tip: Slender, branched plant with scaly stems that swell below the heads and hairless, narrow, lobed leaves. Grassland and lawns, late summer into autumn.

species.name: Scrophularia auriculata
species.tip: Tall, stout wetland figwort with winged square stems, rounded blunt-toothed leaves and small brown-purple flowers with a green sepal rim; flower scale lacks purple, unlike Common Figwort.

species.name: Scrophularia nodosa
species.tip: Woodland and hedgerow figwort with square, unwinged stems, pointed toothed leaves and small, red-brown globular flowers with a green lip; root has knobbly tubers.

species.name: Scrophularia peregrina
species.tip: Hairless, branched annual figwort with heart-shaped toothed leaves and dark purple small flowers. Rare casual from southern Europe, seen in the south of England.

species.name: Scrophularia scopolii
species.tip: Softly hairy figwort with oval toothed leaves and dull brownish-green small flowers in spreading clusters. Very rare casual; identification needs a specialist.

species.name: Scrophularia scorodonia
species.tip: Tall softly hairy figwort with wrinkled, heart-shaped leaves and dull purple-red flowers in broad clusters. Very rare in Cornwall, Devon and the Channel Islands.

species.name: Scrophularia umbrosa
species.tip: Tall winged-stemmed figwort of damp ground with hairless oval leaves and olive-green flowers with a yellowish flap on the upper lip. Rare introduction, scattered in the north.

species.name: Scrophularia vernalis
species.tip: Softly hairy plant with heart-shaped leaves and unmistakable small greenish-yellow flowers in tight clusters. Naturalised in shady spots, mainly in southern England.

species.name: Scutellaria altissima
species.tip: Tall skullcap with long one-sided spikes of blue-violet flowers and oval toothed leaves. Naturalised in hedges and rough ground, notably in Somerset and the south-west.

species.name: Scutellaria galericulata
species.tip: Flowers in pairs in the leaf axils, all facing one way; calyx has a small hump.

species.name: Scutellaria minor
species.tip: Small creeping skullcap with pale pink flowers in the leaf axils and narrow, nearly stalkless leaves. Wet heaths and boggy ground, mainly in the west.

species.name: Secale cereale
species.tip: Tall cereal with a long dense spike and long awns, hairs just beneath the spike; occasional relic on field edges and tips, taller than wheat or barley.

species.name: Securigera varia
species.tip: Sprawling hairless pea with pinnate leaves and rounded heads of pink and white flowers. Pods break into joints. Escape from cultivation on roadsides and waste ground.

species.name: Sedum acre
species.tip: Mat-forming succulent of dunes, walls and dry grassland with tiny, fleshy, scale-like overlapping leaves tasting peppery, and star-like yellow flowers.

species.name: Sedum album
species.tip: Mat-forming succulent with small, cylindrical, bright green leaves often tinged red, and flat clusters of tiny white star flowers; walls and rocks.

species.name: Sedum anglicum
species.tip: Low succulent of rocks, dunes and coastal cliffs with small, egg-shaped, grey-green leaves often reddish, with white-pink star flowers, pink-backed.

species.name: Sedum dasyphyllum
species.tip: Tiny blue-green stonecrop with plump opposite leaves and small white flowers flushed with pink. Naturalised on old walls.

species.name: Sedum hispanicum
species.tip: Greyish tufted stonecrop with narrow leaves and white flowers, often pink-streaked, held in loose branched heads. Occasional on walls and rocks.

species.name: Sedum kimnachii
species.tip: Rare garden stonecrop with narrow succulent leaves and yellow flowers. A specialist may be needed to confirm it among other yellow stonecrops.

species.name: Sedum lydium
species.tip: Tiny, mat-forming stonecrop with crowded narrow green leaves tinged red and small white or pink flowers. Naturalised on walls and rocks.

species.name: Sedum praealtum
species.tip: Robust stonecrop with bright green shiny leaves in dense rosettes and clusters of yellow flowers. Naturalised on walls and banks.

species.name: Sedum sexangulare
species.tip: Dense mats of tiny, six-ranked cylindrical leaves and yellow flowers; unlike biting stonecrop, it tastes bland. Naturalised on walls and rocks.

species.name: Sedum spathulifolium
species.tip: Rosettes of flat, spoon-shaped, grey-blue leaves with yellow flowers. Naturalised on walls, rocks and banks, especially in the north and west.

species.name: Sedum villosum
species.tip: Small biennial with sticky, hairy, alternate leaves and pink flowers. Local in damp, rocky mountain places in northern England and Scotland.

species.name: Selaginella kraussiana
species.tip: Mossy creeping plant with tiny pale green scale-like leaves in flat, two-ranked branches. Escapes from gardens and greenhouses, widespread in mild areas.

species.name: Selaginella selaginoides
species.tip: Small moss-like creeping plant with soft, spreading bristly-toothed leaves and an upright cone; damp flushes in upland grassland and dune slacks.

species.name: Selinum carvifolia
species.tip: Rare plant with hollow, ridged stems and finely cut leaves like carrot; white umbels have smaller bracts than Milk-parsley; fens and wet grassland in a few places.

species.name: Senecio cambrensis
species.tip: Fertile hybrid ragwort with small yellow heads, short rays and lobed leaves; looks like a mix of groundsel and Oxford ragwort. Local on waste ground in Wales and England.

species.name: Senecio doria
species.tip: Tall garden ragwort with big oval toothed leaves and loose clusters of yellow daisy-like heads. Rare escape in gardens.

species.name: Senecio doronicum
species.tip: Low plant with large solitary orange-yellow heads on woolly stems and oval, softly woolly leaves. Garden escape on rocky or waste ground.

species.name: Senecio glastifolius
species.tip: Shrubby South African plant with spiny-edged, holly-like leaves and lilac daisies with yellow centres. Casual or planted, mainly near the coast.

species.name: Senecio grandiflorus
species.tip: Tall garden species with purplish daisy-like heads; rarely escapes into waste ground. Not well known in the wild.

species.name: Senecio inaequidens
species.tip: Branched ragwort with narrow, unlobed linear leaves and many small yellow daisies; invader of railways, roadsides and docks, flowering until winter.

species.name: Senecio minimus
species.tip: Tall, upright annual with toothed or lobed leaves and untidy greenish-white heads without rays. Casual on cleared woodland and burnt ground.

species.name: Senecio ovatus
species.tip: Tall woodland ragwort with oval, toothed, short-stalked leaves and open clusters of yellow heads; leaves less lobed than common ragwort. Rare naturalised plant.

species.name: Senecio sarracenicus
species.tip: Tall riverside ragwort with undivided, broad, finely toothed leaves and many yellow heads. Uncommon, river banks and damp woods in northern Britain.

species.name: Senecio smithii
species.tip: Large white-rayed ragwort with big yellow centre, broad leaves and woolly stalks. Naturalised on wet ground in Scotland, Ireland and western Britain.

species.name: Senecio squalidus
species.tip: Low, hairless ragwort with shiny deeply cut leaves and yellow daisies with black-tipped bracts. Walls, railways and pavements; flowers almost year-round.

species.name: Senecio sylvaticus
species.tip: Sticky-hairy groundsel with short, rolled-back rays and sticky leaves, taller and narrower than Sticky Groundsel; heaths and sandy ground.

species.name: Senecio viscosus
species.tip: Strongly sticky and smelly groundsel with rolled-back short rays, and yellow heads in leafy clusters. Disturbed ground, railway tracks and gardens.

species.name: Senecio vulgaris
species.tip: Small weed with lobed leaves and clusters of narrow yellow heads without rays, black-tipped bracts and fluffy seeds. Flowers almost all year in gardens.

species.name: Serapias lingua
species.tip: Large dark purplish-red flowers with a long tongue-like lip hanging down from a hood; narrow leaves. Very rare in Britain, mainly the Channel Islands and the south-west.

species.name: Serapias parviflora
species.tip: Similar to Tongue Orchid but with smaller, paler orange-brown flowers and a narrower lip; a very rare Mediterranean orchid in the Channel Islands and Cornwall.

species.name: Serratula tinctoria
species.tip: Thistle lookalike without spines, with purple heads in loose clusters and finely saw-toothed, often deeply lobed leaves. Damp grassland, woodland rides and heaths.

species.name: Seseli libanotis
species.tip: Chalk and limestone plant with grey-green, feathery leaves, grooved stems and white, slightly pinkish umbels with many bracts; rare, in the Cambridge region and Sussex.

species.name: Sesleria caerulea
species.tip: Tufted grass of limestone with a blue-purple dense ovoid head, flowering very early in spring; abundant in northern England and Scotland on calcareous turf.

species.name: Setaria viridis
species.tip: Annual with a bristly cylindrical head, each spikelet backed by green bristles with forward-pointing barbs; casual on arable land and waste, mostly in the south.

species.name: Sherardia arvensis
species.tip: Small sprawling annual of arable ground and dry banks with whorls of narrow leaves and tiny pink to lilac flower heads, each surrounded by leafy bracts.

species.name: Sibbaldia procumbens
species.tip: Tiny mountain plant with greyish three-toothed trefoil leaves and clustered, very small yellowish flowers; Scottish high mountains, snow patches and ledges.

species.name: Sibthorpia europaea
species.tip: Creeping evergreen with hairy kidney-shaped scalloped leaves and minute pink-and-white flowers. Grows in shady damp banks and lanes in south-west England, Wales and Ireland.

species.name: Sigesbeckia serrata
species.tip: Annual with sticky glandular hairs, oval toothed leaves and small yellow daisies backed by sticky green bracts. Rare casual on waste ground.

species.name: Silaum silaus
species.tip: Slender plant of old meadows on heavy soil with greenish-yellow flowers and finely cut, shiny leaves; stem ridged and slightly flushed purple, unlike pale-flowered umbellifers.

species.name: Silene acaulis
species.tip: Forms a dense, bright green cushion on mountain rocks, studded with stemless pink flowers. Compare cushion saxifrages, which lack the notched pink petals.

species.name: Silene alpestris
species.tip: Garden escape with white fringed petals and sticky stems beneath the flowers. Told from bladder campion by its fringed petal tips and small, narrow leaves.

species.name: Silene baccifera
species.tip: Straggling plant with small greenish-white flowers followed by shiny black berries instead of dry capsules. A rare casual, mostly of waste ground.

species.name: Silene catholica
species.tip: Rare casual of waste ground with small pinkish flowers on a stickily hairy, branched stem. A specialist may be needed to separate it from other annual catchflies.

species.name: Silene chalcedonica
species.tip: Garden plant with dense flat heads of bright scarlet flowers, each with four deeply notched petals. Occasionally escapes onto banks and verges.

species.name: Silene conica
species.tip: Small annual of coastal sands with an inflated, ribbed, hairy calyx and tiny pink flowers. Rare, found mainly on dunes and sandy ground in eastern and southern Britain.

species.name: Silene coronaria
species.tip: Garden escape with felted silvery-white stems and leaves and bright magenta flowers. The dense white wool makes it unmistakable among campions.

species.name: Silene dioica
species.tip: Pink-red flowers with five notched petals, hairy stems and leaves, on woodland edges and hedgerows. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants; compare White Campion.

species.name: Silene flos-cuculi
species.tip: Pink flowers with each petal cut into four narrow lobes giving a tattered look. Wet meadows and fens, with narrow leaves and sparsely hairy stems.

species.name: Silene gallica
species.tip: Sticky, hairy annual with small white or pink flowers held in one-sided spikes. Lacks the inflated calyx of bladder campion and the sand catchfly.

species.name: Silene italica
species.tip: Sticky biennial with creamy flowers whose petals roll inwards by day and open at dusk. Local on dry, sandy and rocky ground in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Silene latifolia
species.tip: White flowers with five notched petals and sticky hairy stems and leaves, opening in the evening. Arable edges and hedgebanks; compare with Bladder Campion with its inflated calyx.

species.name: Silene multifida
species.tip: Rare casual with narrow, divided lower leaves and small whitish flowers in loose clusters. Easily overlooked among other white catchflies, so confirm with a specialist.

species.name: Silene noctiflora
species.tip: Sticky annual of arable fields whose white or pinkish flowers open in the evening. Has three styles and a hairy calyx, unlike white campion.

species.name: Silene nutans
species.tip: Nodding flowers with white petals curled inwards by day and opening at dusk; stems are sticky above. Local on dry grassland, cliffs and shingle.

species.name: Silene otites
species.tip: Tall slender plant with whorls of tiny yellowish-green flowers on a long spike. Rare, confined mostly to sandy Breckland heaths in East Anglia.

species.name: Silene schafta
species.tip: Low garden plant forming mats with bright magenta flowers late in the year. A rare escape with notched petals and narrow leaves.

species.name: Silene suecica
species.tip: Small tufted plant with sticky bands on the stem and bright pink flowers with notched petals. Very rare, on mountain rocks in Cumbria and Angus.

species.name: Silene uniflora
species.tip: Mat-forming plant with inflated white-veined calyx, white notched petals and fleshy grey-green leaves. Coastal cliffs and shingle, also mountain rocks.

species.name: Silene viscaria
species.tip: Tall plant with a sticky band beneath each node and spikes of magenta flowers. Local on dry rocky outcrops in Wales and Scotland, and sandy places.

species.name: Silene vulgaris
species.tip: Hairless blue-green plant with an inflated veined calyx like a bladder, and white deeply notched petals. Grassy places and roadsides.

species.name: Silybum marianum
species.tip: Thistle with large glossy leaves marbled with white veins, spiny edges, and big purple spiny heads with curved spiny bracts. Roadsides and waste ground.

species.name: Simethis mattiazzii
species.tip: Tufted plant with grassy leaves and loose starry white flowers tinged purple outside, with yellow stamens. Extremely rare in Ireland, on Kerry heathy slopes, and in the south of England.

species.name: Sinacalia tangutica
species.tip: Tall leafy perennial with large lobed, hairless leaves and spires of small yellow ragwort-like heads. Occasional garden escape.

species.name: Sinapis alba
species.tip: Bristly plant with yellow flowers, and beaked pods with stiff spreading hairs; leaves lobed like an oak and the long beak is a sword shape.

species.name: Sinapis arvensis
species.tip: Common arable weed with bright yellow flowers, rough bristly stems and leaves, and smooth pods with a short beak ending the pod.

species.name: Sison amomum
species.tip: Slender, strong-smelling plant with a petrol-like odour and few-rayed small umbels of long unequal stalks; found on roadsides and hedgerows in southern England.

species.name: Sison segetum
species.tip: Slender hairless annual with narrow leaflets and tiny white umbels; a rare casual of arable or waste ground, specialist confirmation needed.

species.name: Sisymbrium altissimum
species.tip: Tall annual with pale yellow flowers and very long thin pods, held erect. The upper leaves are narrow and thread-like. Casual of waste ground.

species.name: Sisymbrium loeselii
species.tip: Annual with small yellow flowers, pods short and pressed to the stem, and arrow-shaped terminal lobe. Occasional casual on waste ground.

species.name: Sisymbrium officinale
species.tip: Stiff, wiry plant with widely spreading branches and tiny pale yellow flowers; pods pressed close to the stem. Common on verges and wasteland.

species.name: Sisymbrium orientale
species.tip: Pale yellow flowers on a tall hairy annual of roadsides and waste land; very long thin pods held away from the stem, lobed leaves.

species.name: Sisymbrium strictissimum
species.tip: Tall perennial with pale yellow flowers, toothed oval undivided leaves and long thin pods. A rare naturalised plant on waste ground and verges.

species.name: Sisymbrium volgense
species.tip: Rare creeping-rooted perennial with pale yellow flowers and deeply lobed leaves, found in waste places. Specialist needed to confirm.

species.name: Sisyrinchium bermudiana
species.tip: Flat, winged stems with narrow leaves and violet-blue flowers with a yellow eye. Rare native in western Ireland near lakes and damp pasture.

species.name: Sisyrinchium californicum
species.tip: Narrow irislike leaves and yellow six-petalled flowers on flat stems. Garden plant, naturalised locally in damp grassland in western Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Sisyrinchium montanum
species.tip: Flattened winged stems and narrow grey-green leaves, with violet-blue flowers with a yellow eye. Naturalised in damp grass and roadsides, especially northern Britain.

species.name: Sium latifolium
species.tip: Tall, stout, hollow-stemmed plant of ditches and ponds, with once-pinnate toothed leaves, big white umbels and leafy bracts below; fairly local, in lowland England.

species.name: Smyrnium olusatrum
species.tip: Early-flowering coastal and roadside plant with glossy, bright green three-parted leaves and yellow-green flowers; black fruits and celery smell separate it from other umbellifers.

species.name: Smyrnium perfoliatum
species.tip: Yellow-green flowering plant with rounded, toothed upper leaves that clasp the stem completely, unlike Alexanders; a naturalised plant of verges and old gardens.

species.name: Solanum chenopodioides
species.tip: Branched, nearly hairless annual with small white flowers having reflexed petals and green berries that stay green, wrapped by an enlarged calyx. Rare casual in the south.

species.name: Solanum dulcamara
species.tip: Scrambling woody climber of hedges and wetlands with purple flowers with bent-back petals around a yellow cone, and oval red berries; leaves often eared at base.

species.name: Solanum laciniatum
species.tip: Large shrubby nightshade with deeply cut leaves and violet flowers bigger than those of Black Nightshade, then orange egg-shaped berries. Rare escape in mild southern places.

species.name: Solanum nigrum
species.tip: Weed of cultivated land with small white flowers with yellow centres, drooping in clusters, and green then black berries; leaves are wavy-toothed oval, unlike Bittersweet.

species.name: Solanum nitidibaccatum
species.tip: Hairy low annual with small white flowers and berries that remain green; difficult to separate from relatives. Rare casual on waste ground, requires specialist confirmation.

species.name: Solanum sarrachoides
species.tip: Sticky-hairy annual with small white flowers and green berries almost enclosed by a long, enlarged calyx. Rare casual on waste ground; a specialist should confirm it.

species.name: Solanum triflorum
species.tip: Low, spreading, hairy annual with deeply lobed leaves and small white flowers in clusters of two or three. Rare casual from North America on waste ground.

species.name: Solanum tuberosum
species.tip: Crop plant sometimes found on tips and field edges, with pinnate leaves of uneven leaflets and clusters of white or pale purple star-like flowers with yellow centres.

species.name: Soleirolia soleirolii
species.tip: Mat-forming evergreen of damp walls and paths with tiny, rounded, bright green leaves on creeping hairy stems and almost invisible flowers in the leaf axils.

species.name: Solidago canadensis
species.tip: Tall garden escape with spiky one-sided plumes of tiny yellow heads, hairy stem upper half and three-veined leaves. Waste ground and railway banks in late summer.

species.name: Solidago gigantea
species.tip: Tall goldenrod with smooth, hairless stem, and wide-spreading plumes of small yellow heads. Naturalised on waste ground and riversides.

species.name: Solidago rugosa
species.tip: Tall goldenrod with hairy stems and wrinkled, oval, sharply toothed leaves; plume of small yellow heads. Naturalised on waste ground.

species.name: Solidago sempervirens
species.tip: Fleshy-leaved goldenrod of the coast with smooth, untoothed leaves and plumes of yellow heads. Rare garden escape on sea walls and sand.

species.name: Solidago virgaurea
species.tip: Native goldenrod with short, upright spikes of golden daisies, leaves broader at base. Woods, heaths, cliffs, hedgebanks and rocky ground.

species.name: Sonchus arvensis
species.tip: Tall creeping plant with large golden-yellow dandelion-like heads and glandular yellow-hairy stalks, soft-spined leaves. Arable fields, ditches and coastal marshes.

species.name: Sonchus asper
species.tip: Glossy leaves with sharp spiny teeth and rounded clasping lobes at the base, and small pale yellow heads. Waste ground and gardens.

species.name: Sonchus oleraceus
species.tip: Soft sow-thistle with soft-toothed leaves whose basal lobes are pointed, and pale yellow heads. Weed of gardens and waste ground.

species.name: Sonchus palustris
species.tip: Very tall sow-thistle with narrow, deeply cut leaves and blue-green stems with dark glandular hairs; pale yellow heads. Very rare, fens and marshes in East Anglia and Kent.

species.name: Sorbaria sorbifolia
species.tip: Unarmed suckering shrub with long pinnate leaves and big plumes of small white flowers; garden escape on banks and waste ground.

species.name: Sorbaria tomentosa
species.tip: Similar to False Spiraea but pinnate leaves woolly beneath and large plumes of white flowers; rare garden relict. Do not confuse with meadowsweet.

species.name: Sorbus admonitor
species.tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain; leaves oval, white-felted beneath. A specialist is needed to confirm it among the whitebeam group.

species.name: Sorbus anglica
species.tip: Whitebeam with shallowly lobed leaves, grey-felted beneath, and red fruit; local in SW England, Wales and Ireland, on limestone. A specialist confirms the species.

species.name: Sorbus aria
species.tip: Tree with oval toothed leaves strongly white-felted beneath; white flowers, red fruits. Rowan has pinnate leaves; Sorbus has specialist microspecies groups. Chalk and limestone woodland.

species.name: Sorbus arranensis
species.tip: Endemic to Arran: deeply lobed to pinnate leaves with grey felt beneath, red fruit; confirmed only by specialists against the Arran Whitebeam.

species.name: Sorbus arvonicola
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of north-west Wales; oval grey-felted leaves, a specialist is needed to confirm identification.

species.name: Sorbus aucuparia
species.tip: Tree with pinnate leaves of toothed leaflets, flat clusters of creamy flowers and orange-red berries; heaths, woods and hills. Sorbus has specialist microspecies groups, mainly whitebeams.

species.name: Sorbus bristoliensis
species.tip: Whitebeam confined to the Avon Gorge with broad oval leaves, grey-white beneath, and orange-red fruit with pale spots; specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Sorbus cambrensis
species.tip: Rare Welsh whitebeam microspecies on cliffs, with oval leaves white-felted beneath; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus cheddarensis
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam restricted to Cheddar Gorge, Somerset; oval leaves white-felted beneath. Only a specialist can confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus croceocarpa
species.tip: Obscure whitebeam-group taxon with orange fruit; leaves lobed or oval and felted beneath. A specialist is essential to identify it.

species.name: Sorbus cuneifolia
species.tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies with wedge-shaped leaves, white beneath; localised in western Britain and requires specialist confirmation.

species.name: Sorbus devoniensis
species.tip: Large tree whitebeam of Devon and Somerset with broad oval leaves and big, sparsely dotted, yellowish-red fruit; specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Sorbus domestica
species.tip: Pinnate-leaved tree like rowan but with sticky buds, bark scaly and fruit large and pear- or apple-shaped; very rare native on Glamorgan cliffs, sometimes planted.

species.name: Sorbus eminens
species.tip: Whitebeam with rounded oval leaves, white beneath, and red fruit; local on limestone in Wye Valley, Avon Gorge, Wales and Ireland. Specialist advised.

species.name: Sorbus eminentiformis
species.tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies resembling Round-leaved Whitebeam; a specialist must confirm it. Occurs very locally in western Britain.

species.name: Sorbus eminentoides
species.tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies near Round-leaved Whitebeam; occurs very locally in western Britain and a specialist is needed.

species.name: Sorbus evansii
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval felted leaves; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus glabriuscula
species.tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies, leaves oval with only thin felt beneath; localised, and confirmation needs a specialist.

species.name: Sorbus greenii
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval leaves grey-felted beneath; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus herefordensis
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of the Welsh borders and Wye Valley; oval felted leaves, needs specialist confirmation.

species.name: Sorbus hibernica
species.tip: Irish endemic hybrid-origin whitebeam with leaves pinnately lobed at the base and grey beneath; red fruit. Specialist confirmation is advised.

species.name: Sorbus intermedia
species.tip: Planted tree with lobed leaves grey-felted beneath, shallowly cut, between Whitebeam and Rowan; flowers white, fruit orange-red; street and park tree that self-sows.

species.name: Sorbus lancastriensis
species.tip: Whitebeam of limestone in Lancashire, Cumbria and north Wales, with lobed leaves grey-felted beneath and red fruit; a specialist should confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus latifolia
species.tip: Large whitebeam with broad, shallowly lobed leaves, grey beneath, and brownish-red fruit; local in Devon and Somerset. Specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Sorbus leighensis
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies restricted to the Avon Gorge area; oval leaves felted beneath. A specialist is needed.

species.name: Sorbus leptophylla
species.tip: Rare whitebeam with thin oval leaves, whitish beneath, found on limestone cliffs in the Wye Valley; specialist confirmation needed.

species.name: Sorbus leyana
species.tip: Extremely rare small whitebeam of cliffs in the Brecon Beacons, with deeply lobed leaves grey-felted beneath; only a specialist can confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus margaretae
species.tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies of the Mendip area; oval leaves white-felted beneath and a specialist is needed to confirm it.
