species.name: Sorbus minima
species.tip: Small shrubby whitebeam of Brecon limestone cliffs and Cumbria, with oval leaves grey beneath and red fruit; very rare, specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Sorbus parviloba
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain; leaves oval to shallowly lobed, felted beneath. A specialist is needed.

species.name: Sorbus porrigentiformis
species.tip: Whitebeam of limestone in SW England, Wales and Ireland with oval, grey-green leaves, lightly felted beneath; red fruit. A specialist should confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus pseudofennica
species.tip: Endemic to Arran: leaves lobed at the tip but pinnate at the base, grey beneath, with red fruit. Specialists separate it from Arran Service-tree.

species.name: Sorbus pseudomeinichii
species.tip: Rare whitebeam-group microspecies with lobed leaves felted beneath; localised in western Britain and needs specialist confirmation.

species.name: Sorbus richii
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval felted leaves; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus rupicola
species.tip: Native whitebeam of limestone cliffs in western Britain and Ireland, with leaves narrowing to the base, grey beneath, and scarlet fruit; specialists confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus rupicoloides
species.tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies similar to Rock Whitebeam, with oval leaves felted beneath; only a specialist can confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus saxicola
species.tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies of rocky limestone sites in the west; oval leaves white beneath. A specialist is needed for identification.

species.name: Sorbus scannelliana
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies with oval leaves felted beneath; localised in the west, and requires specialist confirmation.

species.name: Sorbus spectans
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval felted leaves; identification must be confirmed by a specialist.

species.name: Sorbus stenophylla
species.tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies of south Wales, with narrower oval leaves grey beneath; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus stirtoniana
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval leaves felted beneath; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Sorbus subcuneata
species.tip: Whitebeam of the Somerset and Devon coast and gorges, with oval, white-felted leaves and red fruit; specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Sorbus torminalis
species.tip: Woodland tree with maple-like lobed leaves, hairless, turning red in autumn; clusters of white flowers; small brown speckled fruit. Ancient woods, mainly southern England.

species.name: Sorbus vexans
species.tip: Whitebeam of Somerset and Devon with oval leaves grey-felted beneath and deep red fruit; specialist confirmation advised.

species.name: Sorbus whiteana
species.tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies in the Wye Valley and Avon Gorge area; oval leaves felted beneath. A specialist is needed.

species.name: Sorbus wilmottiana
species.tip: Rare whitebeam of the Avon Gorge with oval leaves white-felted beneath and orange-red fruit; confirmation needs a specialist.

species.name: Sparganium angustifolium
species.tip: Aquatic bur-reed of acid lakes with long floating ribbon-like leaves and a few unbranched, stalkless female heads; fruit beaked; zig-zag stem rising slightly above the water.

species.name: Sparganium emersum
species.tip: Bur-reed of slow rivers and ditches with keeled, triangular leaves in the lower part, unbranched flower stem, and a mix of male and female heads along it.

species.name: Sparganium erectum
species.tip: Tall marginal plant of ponds and ditches with stiff sword-like leaves and a branched flower spike carrying spiky round green heads, later burr-like.

species.name: Sparganium natans
species.tip: Slender aquatic with floating or submerged narrow leaves and small round white-green flower heads, usually only one male head at top. Lakes and pools, mostly in the north and west.

species.name: Spartina alterniflora
species.tip: American cord-grass of saltmarsh mud with thick stems, many spikes and long smooth leaves; rare, in a few southern estuaries where it forms patches.

species.name: Spartina anglica
species.tip: Dense stout grass of muddy estuaries with several erect spikes pressed together; the commonest cord-grass, with stems up to a metre or more and a fringe of hairs.

species.name: Spartina maritima
species.tip: Native cord-grass of upper saltmarsh with one to three short spikes and fine inrolled leaves; very rare in Dorset, Hampshire and Essex, thinner than Common Cord-grass.

species.name: Spartina patens
species.tip: Fine, wiry mat-former of salt marsh with curly inrolled leaves and spreading spikes; rare introduction from North America on a few southern sites.

species.name: Spartina pectinata
species.tip: Tall stout cord-grass with long, arching leaves that cut the hands; planted on estuaries and banks, with many spikes in rows along the stem.

species.name: Spartium junceum
species.tip: Tall, rush-like shrub with almost leafless green stems and large fragrant yellow pea flowers. Differs from Broom by round stems, no ridges, and larger flowers. Naturalised locally.

species.name: Spergula arvensis
species.tip: Annual with thread-like whorled leaves and tiny white five-petalled flowers on sticky stalks. Light arable soils and disturbed sandy ground.

species.name: Spergula morisonii
species.tip: Tiny slender annual with thread-like leaves and little white flowers. Very rare, on sandy arable and heathy ground, mainly in East Anglia. Needs careful checking against pearlworts.

species.name: Spergularia bocconei
species.tip: Small pink-flowered annual of coastal sand and grass, with short fleshy leaves and a brown papery stipule. Rare, mostly on south-west coasts.

species.name: Spergularia marina
species.tip: Fleshy annual of salt marshes with narrow leaves and small pink flowers with whitish centres; petals shorter than sepals. Seeds without wing.

species.name: Spergularia media
species.tip: Perennial sea-spurrey with fleshy leaves and larger, pale pink flowers with white centres; petals longer than the sepals. Salt marshes and estuaries.

species.name: Spergularia rubra
species.tip: Small, spreading annual or biennial with thread-like leaves and pink flowers, silvery stipules and sticky hairy capsules. Sandy heaths and tracks, away from salt.

species.name: Spergularia rupicola
species.tip: Clump-forming, sticky perennial of sea cliffs with fleshy leaves and pink flowers with white centres. Told from other sea-spurreys by its woody base and stickiness.

species.name: Spinacia oleracea
species.tip: Familiar vegetable with large, soft, triangular or oval stalked leaves and tiny green flowers in clusters; an occasional escape on tips and verges.

species.name: Spiraea alba
species.tip: American shrub with narrow oval leaves, hairless, and slender white flower spikes; rare garden escape, unlike pink steeple-bush flowers.

species.name: Spiraea chamaedryfolia
species.tip: Garden shrub with elm-like oval double-toothed leaves and rounded clusters of white flowers; rare escape in hedges and waste ground.

species.name: Spiraea douglasii
species.tip: Common suckering escape with spires of deep pink flowers and oval leaves, white-woolly beneath; forms thickets in damp ground, unlike Bridewort.

species.name: Spiraea salicifolia
species.tip: Suckering shrub with narrow willow-like leaves and dense spikes of pale pink flowers; naturalised in damp places, unlike hairy steeple-bush.

species.name: Spiraea tomentosa
species.tip: American relative of steeple-bush with dense pink spires and rounded leaves woolly-white beneath; rare garden relict.

species.name: Spiranthes romanzoffiana
species.tip: Spike of creamy-white flowers in three spiral rows, with the lip frilled and constricted; leaves are all on the stem, unlike Autumn Lady's-tresses. Western Ireland, Scotland and Devon.

species.name: Spiranthes spiralis
species.tip: Slender spiral of small white flowers in one row; the leaf rosette sits beside the flowering stem, not below it. Short turf, flowering late summer.

species.name: Spirodela polyrhiza
species.tip: Floating plant with flat round fronds up to 1 cm, each having several roots hanging beneath, and purplish below; much larger than other duckweeds with fewer roots.

species.name: Sporobolus indicus
species.tip: Tufted tropical grass with a long narrow spike-like panicle of tiny spikelets; an uncommon casual near ports and on roadsides, often with leaf rust.

species.name: Stachys alpina
species.tip: Stinking, hairy woundwort with dull pink-purple flowers in spaced whorls and heart-shaped leaves. Very rare, in a few old limestone woods in Wales and western England.

species.name: Stachys arvensis
species.tip: Small, sprawling, hairy annual with tiny pale pink flowers in few-flowered whorls and blunt, heart-shaped leaves. Weed of acid arable fields, often near the coast.

species.name: Stachys germanica
species.tip: Tall woundwort densely covered in white woolly hairs, with pink-purple flowers in compact whorls. Very rare, now confined to Oxfordshire on field edges and chalky ground.

species.name: Stachys palustris
species.tip: Paler pinkish-purple flowers than Hedge Woundwort; narrow leaves with little or no stalk.

species.name: Stachys recta
species.tip: Woundwort with pale yellow flowers in whorls and narrow, toothed, stalkless upper leaves. Naturalised on dry walls, banks and waste ground.

species.name: Stachys sylvatica
species.tip: Dark wine-red flowers with white markings; stinks when crushed.

species.name: Stellaria alsine
species.tip: Slender stitchwort of wet places with oval leaves and tiny white flowers with petals shorter than the sepals, deeply cut. Streams, springs and flushes.

species.name: Stellaria aquatica
species.tip: Like a large straggling chickweed of wet ground and riverbanks, with heart-based leaves and white flowers whose petals are split almost to the base, five styles.

species.name: Stellaria graminea
species.tip: Slender, grass-like stitchwort with narrow, smooth leaves and loose, branched clusters of small white flowers (petals cleft almost to the base). Grassy banks, heaths and roadsides.

species.name: Stellaria holostea
species.tip: Large white star-like flowers with petals cleft halfway, on brittle square stems with rough narrow leaves. Hedgebanks and woodland edges in spring.

species.name: Stellaria media
species.tip: Sprawling plant with a single line of hairs on the stem and tiny white flowers with deeply cleft petals. Ubiquitous weed in gardens and arable land.

species.name: Stellaria neglecta
species.tip: Chickweed of damp shady places, larger and more robust than Common Chickweed, with ten stamens and larger petals; mostly in woods and by streams.

species.name: Stellaria nemorum
species.tip: Broad, stalked, heart-based leaves and loose clusters of white flowers with deeply cleft petals. Grows in damp shady woods, mostly in northern and western Britain.

species.name: Stellaria pallida
species.tip: Tiny pale chickweed of sandy ground with minute or absent petals and few stamens. Flowers early, in sandy, coastal or disturbed places.

species.name: Stellaria palustris
species.tip: Waxy, bluish-green plant with narrow leaves and white flowers whose petals are cut almost to the base. Rare, in base-rich fens and marshes.

species.name: Sternbergia lutea
species.tip: Crocus-like yellow goblets appearing in autumn alongside glossy green strap leaves; a garden escape in dry, sunny banks, flowering well after any spring bulb.

species.name: Stratiotes aloides
species.tip: Floating rosette of stiff, spiky, pineapple-like leaves; white flowers rise above the water. Native in the Norfolk Broads and Yorkshire, otherwise introduced.

species.name: Strobilanthes pentastemonoides
species.tip: Rare garden plant with toothed, pointed oval leaves and nodding tubular purple-blue flowers in late season; unlikely in the wild and seldom flowering outdoors in Britain.

species.name: Stuckenia filiformis
species.tip: Like Fennel Pondweed but smaller with fine thread-like leaves in clear northern lakes, often in sand; flower spike long and widely interrupted.

species.name: Stuckenia pectinata
species.tip: Submerged pondweed with very narrow thread-like leaves fanning out from long sheaths, and short interrupted flower spikes; ponds, canals and brackish water.

species.name: Suaeda maritima
species.tip: Fleshy annual of saltmarsh and shingle with thick, narrow, blunt leaves, often tinged red, with small green flowers in the leaf axils.

species.name: Suaeda vera
species.tip: Woody evergreen shrub of shingle and sea walls in the south and east, with fleshy, blue-green narrow leaves that are pointed and small green flowers.

species.name: Subularia aquatica
species.tip: Tiny submerged aquatic with a rosette of awl-shaped leaves and small white flowers held above the water. Found in clear, acidic lakes in uplands.

species.name: Succisa pratensis
species.tip: Rounded dark blue-purple heads on a plant with undivided oval, untoothed leaves in damp grassland, bog and heath; blooms later than the other scabious species.

species.name: Symphoricarpos albus
species.tip: Suckering shrub with oval opposite leaves and small pinkish bell flowers followed by large white spongy berries; escape from gardens, hedges and waste ground.

species.name: Symphoricarpos orbiculatus
species.tip: Small suckering shrub with tiny pink-white flowers in leaf axils and clusters of purplish-pink berries on arching twigs. Naturalised rarely in hedges and shrubberies.

species.name: Symphyotrichum laeve
species.tip: Michaelmas-daisy with bluish-grey, hairless stems and thick leaves clasping the stem, with lilac-blue rays. Garden escape on waste ground.

species.name: Symphyotrichum lanceolatum
species.tip: Garden Michaelmas-daisy with narrow lance-shaped leaves, small white to pale lilac rayed heads and many on panicles; spreads on waste ground.

species.name: Symphyotrichum novae-angliae
species.tip: Tall, hairy, sticky plant with leaves clasping the stem and deep violet-purple rays; heads larger than other Michaelmas-daisies. Garden escape on waste ground.

species.name: Symphyotrichum novi-belgii
species.tip: Common garden escape with blue-violet daisies with yellow centres on leafy stems, found on riverbanks and waste ground in autumn.

species.name: Symphyotrichum pilosum
species.tip: Bushy plant with hairy stems, narrow leaves and many small white or pale-lilac daisies. Waste ground and railway land, uncommon.

species.name: Symphyotrichum puniceum
species.tip: Tall with rough, hairy stems, and leaves with a clasping base; large lilac-purple daisies. Garden escape on roadsides and waste ground.

species.name: Symphyotrichum squamatum
species.tip: Branched annual with small, pale lilac-white daisies with short rays and narrow, hairless leaves. Casual on waste ground, mostly southern England.

species.name: Symphytum asperum
species.tip: Tall comfrey whose stems and leaves are covered in sharp prickles. Flowers open pink and turn blue-violet. Naturalised in hedgerows and waste ground.

species.name: Symphytum bulbosum
species.tip: Low comfrey spreading by small tubers, bearing pale creamy-yellow flowers in spring. Leaves are not running down the stem. Uncommon naturalised garden escape.

species.name: Symphytum caucasicum
species.tip: Low comfrey with grey-downy leaves and flowers that open pink and turn sky blue. An infrequent garden escape in rough grass and verges.

species.name: Symphytum grandiflorum
species.tip: Low spreading comfrey with pale yellow-cream tubular flowers and hairy stems. Garden escape forming dense carpets under shade in woods and shady verges.

species.name: Symphytum officinale
species.tip: Tall hairy perennial with decurrent leaf bases forming wings on the stem and drooping bell-shaped clusters of cream, pink or purple flowers. Riverbanks, ditches and damp ground.

species.name: Symphytum orientale
species.tip: Grey-green softly hairy comfrey with white flowers, and stalked upper leaves unlike Common Comfrey. Naturalised garden escape on roadsides and waste ground, flowering early.

species.name: Symphytum tuberosum
species.tip: Slender comfrey with creamy-yellow flowers and unwinged stems, with a knobbly rhizome. Woodland and shady streamsides.

species.name: Syringa vulgaris
species.tip: Large garden shrub or small tree with opposite heart-shaped leaves and dense, sweetly scented lilac or white flower clusters in spring; naturalised on hedges and old sites.

species.name: Tamus communis
species.tip: Twining climber of hedges with glossy heart-shaped leaves and tiny green flowers; red berries in autumn. Climbs anticlockwise with no tendrils, unlike White Bryony.

species.name: Tanacetum balsamita
species.tip: Aromatic plant with oval, toothed grey-green leaves smelling of mint and clusters of button-like yellow heads, rays often absent. Old herb persisting on banks.

species.name: Tanacetum macrophyllum
species.tip: Tall tansy with large, finely divided leaves and flat clusters of small white-rayed daisies. Occasional garden escape.

species.name: Tanacetum parthenium
species.tip: Strongly bitter-scented plant with yellowish-green, divided leaves and clusters of small white daisies with flat yellow centres. Walls, gardens and waste ground.

species.name: Tanacetum vulgare
species.tip: Dense flat clusters of yellow button heads without rays, over dark green, finely divided leaves with strong aromatic smell. Verges and riverbanks.

species.name: Taraxacum croceiflorum
species.tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Distinguished only by detailed leaf, bract and pollen features; yellow-orange heads.

species.name: Taraxacum duplidentifrons
species.tip: A dandelion microspecies in the large group of common weedy dandelions; specialist needed to confirm. Distinguished by fine leaf and bract details.

species.name: Taraxacum euryphyllum
species.tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Leaf shape and bract details separate it from other dandelions.

species.name: Taraxacum faeroense
species.tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Mainly northern, Atlantic localities; leaf shape and bracts are the key.

species.name: Taraxacum hamatum
species.tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Identified by leaf lobes and bract features, not visible to a beginner.

species.name: Taraxacum lacistophyllum
species.tip: A small dandelion microspecies of dry grassland, with small heads and narrow, deeply cut leaves; specialist needed to confirm it.

species.name: Taraxacum obliquum
species.tip: A small dandelion microspecies of dry sandy or calcareous ground, with narrow, deeply cut leaves; specialist needed to confirm it.

species.name: Taraxacum palustre
species.tip: A dandelion group of wet meadows and fens, with narrow, nearly untoothed leaves and small pale heads; specialist needed to confirm. Local.

species.name: Taraxacum platyglossum
species.tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Wide ray florets and leaf details separate it from other dandelions.

species.name: Taxus baccata
species.tip: Evergreen conifer with flat dark green needles, red cup-like fleshy arils around the seed, and reddish flaking bark; woods, churchyards and chalk slopes.

species.name: Teesdalia nudicaulis
species.tip: Small annual of sandy, acid soils, with a rosette of lobed leaves and tiny white flowers whose outer petals are larger. Local on heaths and dunes.

species.name: Tellima grandiflora
species.tip: Garden escape in woods and verges with rounded, hairy, scalloped leaves like a Heuchera and spikes of green bells whose fringed petals turn pink.

species.name: Tephroseris integrifolia
species.tip: Low, woolly plant with a rosette of oval leaves and yellow daisy-like heads in a flat cluster. Dry chalk grassland, southern and eastern England.

species.name: Teucrium botrys
species.tip: Small annual with deeply cut, oak-like leaves, and pink flowers in whorls that have no upper lip. Scarce on bare chalk and limestone in southern England.

species.name: Teucrium chamaedrys
species.tip: Low evergreen with shiny small toothed leaves and pink-purple flowers lacking an upper lip, in whorls forming one-sided spikes. Rare escape on walls, banks and rough ground.

species.name: Teucrium scordium
species.tip: Hairy plant smelling of garlic when crushed, with pink flowers lacking an upper lip in axillary pairs. Rare in damp dune slacks and fen edges in England and Ireland.

species.name: Teucrium scorodonia
species.tip: Pale greenish-yellow flowers with no upper lip; wrinkled, sage-like leaves; acid soils.

species.name: Thalictrum alpinum
species.tip: Small mountain plant with a few drooping purplish flowers on a slender stalk; leaves with small rounded leaflets.

species.name: Thalictrum flavum
species.tip: Tall plant of fens and riversides with dense clusters of fluffy pale yellow stamens; leaves with many leaflets.

species.name: Thalictrum minus
species.tip: Finely divided leaves like maidenhair fern; loose sprays of small drooping greenish-yellow flowers that are mostly stamens. Dunes and limestone.

species.name: Thalictrum speciosissimum
species.tip: Very tall meadow-rue with large airy plumes of fluffy pale yellow flowers and finely divided leaves; much taller than native meadow-rues. Rare garden escape on damp verges and rough ground.

species.name: Thelypteris palustris
species.tip: Slender creeping fern with thin, pale green, twice-divided fronds with untoothed lobes, growing in fen and wet carr. Local, mainly in lowland East Anglia and Ireland.

species.name: Thermopsis montana
species.tip: Upright perennial with clover-like three-part leaves and a tall spike of bright yellow pea flowers. Garden escape, occasionally naturalised.

species.name: Thesium humifusum
species.tip: Small creeping semi-parasite of chalk turf with narrow one-veined leaves and tiny greenish-white five-lobed flowers; much smaller than flax. Local in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Thlaspi alliaceum
species.tip: Smells of garlic when crushed. Bushy annual with small white flowers and leaves clasping the stem. Rare, casual on waste ground and field edges.

species.name: Thlaspi arvense
species.tip: Hairless annual of fields with arrow-shaped clasping leaves and round flat winged pods that look like discs, notched at the tip.

species.name: Thuja occidentalis
species.tip: Evergreen conifer with flat sprays of scale-like leaves and small upright cones. Often planted in gardens and sometimes self-sown.

species.name: Thuja plicata
species.tip: Large conifer with flat sprays of scale-like glossy leaves smelling of pineapple when crushed and small upright cones; widely planted in forestry and parks.

species.name: Thymus drucei
species.tip: Low mats of tiny leaves; stems hairy on two opposite sides only.

species.name: Thymus pulegioides
species.tip: Thyme with erect flowering stems that are square and hairy only on the angles, and small oval leaves. Grassy chalk banks and dry slopes.

species.name: Thymus serpyllum
species.tip: Mat-forming thyme with stems hairy all round and leaves with hairy margins at the base. Found only on sandy Breckland heath and grassland in East Anglia.

species.name: Thymus vulgaris
species.tip: Small bushy shrub with narrow, strongly aromatic leaves curled under at the edges, and pale pink or white flowers. Garden herb, occasionally escaping to dry banks and walls.

species.name: Thysselinum palustre
species.tip: Tall, slender plant of fens with finely cut leaves, a hollow-ridged stem, white umbels and milky sap when cut; rare, in East Anglia, and scattered elsewhere.

species.name: Tilia cordata
species.tip: Lime tree with small heart-shaped leaves, dark green above and blue-green beneath with rusty hair tufts in vein junctions; fragrant flowers hang under a bract. Ancient woods.

species.name: Tilia platyphyllos
species.tip: Lime tree with larger, softly hairy leaves, hairy twigs and flowers in small clusters beneath a pale bract; fruits ribbed and downy, unlike Small-leaved Lime.

species.name: Tofieldia pusilla
species.tip: Tiny tufted plant of wet upland flushes with grass-like, flat leaves and a short compact head of small whitish-green flowers. Northern England and Scotland only.

species.name: Tolmiea menziesii
species.tip: Garden escape with softly hairy heart-shaped lobed leaves that grow plantlets at the leaf base, and slender spikes of small greenish-brown flowers. Shady damp banks and walls.

species.name: Tordylium maximum
species.tip: Hairy umbellifer with large outer petals on the white to pinkish flowers and wide, coarsely toothed leaflets; very rare, with a few sites near the Thames estuary.

species.name: Torilis arvensis
species.tip: Stiff, hairy, annual with long-stalked umbels, small white to pink flowers and spiny, hooked fruit; rare arable weed in southern and eastern England.

species.name: Torilis japonica
species.tip: Hairy, rough hedge-bank plant with small, white to pinkish umbels on long stalks and spiny fruits; flowers later than Cow Parsley, July onward, and has long stalks.

species.name: Torilis nodosa
species.tip: Low, spreading, often sprawling annual with tiny stalkless clusters of flowers opposite the leaves, and spiny knobbly fruit clusters; open dry grassland and field edges.

species.name: Trachelium caeruleum
species.tip: Tall plant with large dense flat-topped heads of tiny violet tubular flowers and toothed oval leaves. Naturalised on old walls and cliffs, mainly in southern and western Britain.

species.name: Trachystemon orientalis
species.tip: Early spring plant with violet-blue flowers whose petals curl right back, with stamens protruding. Huge heart-shaped hairy leaves appear after flowering. Shady garden escape.

species.name: Tragopogon porrifolius
species.tip: Tall plant with grass-like leaves and large purple dandelion-like heads, closing by midday, with bracts longer than the florets. Stalks swell below the head. Roadsides and grassland.

species.name: Tragopogon pratensis
species.tip: Grass-like grey-green leaves and large yellow heads that close by midday, with bracts longer than the rays, and big fluffy clocks. Meadows and verges.

species.name: Trichomanes speciosum
species.tip: Delicate translucent fern with leathery, dark green, divided fronds creeping from a hairy rhizome. Very rare in damp, shaded ravine rocks in Ireland and western Britain.

species.name: Trichophorum cespitosum
species.tip: A densely tufted bog plant with wiry round stems, each carrying one small, pale brown spikelet and with leaves reduced to sheaths; very common on upland blanket bog and wet heath.

species.name: Trichophorum germanicum
species.tip: Dense tufts in moorland and bog, wiry round stems each with a small single brown spikelet; leaves reduced to sheaths with only tiny blades.

species.name: Trifolium arvense
species.tip: Soft grey-pink furry cylindrical heads with fluffy sepals; low annual on sandy ground and dunes, with narrow trifoliate leaves.

species.name: Trifolium aureum
species.tip: Yellow clover with golden globular heads that turn brown with age. Larger than Hop Trefoil, with leaflets all attached together. Rare, mainly on northern and western grassland.

species.name: Trifolium bocconei
species.tip: Small hairy annual clover with pink flowers in stalkless clustered pairs at stem branches. Very rare, on dry coastal turf in Cornwall, especially the Lizard.

species.name: Trifolium campestre
species.tip: Yellow clover with globular heads of 20-40 flowers turning brown like hops; central leaflet has a longer stalk than the side leaflets.

species.name: Trifolium dubium
species.tip: Smallest yellow clover, with heads of only 3-15 flowers; central leaflet is only slightly stalked. Common in lawns and grassland.

species.name: Trifolium fragiferum
species.tip: Low creeping clover; pink heads become inflated and pinkish like small strawberries or balloons when fruiting. Grows on damp grassland, often near the coast.

species.name: Trifolium glomeratum
species.tip: Low, hairless annual clover with tight, stalkless balls of small pink flowers at each stem joint. Spiky star-shaped fruiting calyces. Found on sandy ground in south and east England.

species.name: Trifolium hybridum
species.tip: Pink and white flower heads fading brown, with stalked heads and leaflets lacking a white mark; stems are not creeping; roadsides and fields.

species.name: Trifolium incarnatum
species.tip: Upright hairy clover with long cylindrical heads of vivid crimson flowers. Wild Cornish plants have paler cream-pink flowers. Frequent as a field crop or casual.

species.name: Trifolium medium
species.tip: Zigzag stems, reddish-purple flowers in heads and leaflets with narrow pale markings, often in grassland and woodland margins.

species.name: Trifolium micranthum
species.tip: Very small, slender yellow clover with heads of 2-6 tiny flowers and an unstalked-looking central leaflet; short grassland, often on sandy soil.

species.name: Trifolium occidentale
species.tip: Low clover with small white heads and leaflets often bearing a pale V mark. Rooting stems and early flowering distinguish it from White Clover. Found coastally in south-west England, Wales and Ireland.

species.name: Trifolium ochroleucon
species.tip: Upright, hairy clover with big, blunt, creamy-yellow heads. Very rare, on clay grassland and verges in East Anglia and the southern Midlands.

species.name: Trifolium ornithopodioides
species.tip: Tiny prostrate plant with few-flowered white or pinkish heads and trefoil leaves. Pods spread like a bird's foot. Found on damp heathy ground in the south and west.

species.name: Trifolium pratense
species.tip: Pink-purple rounded heads in meadows, leaflets with a pale crescent mark and hairy stipules, stems upright.

species.name: Trifolium repens
species.tip: Creeping stems that root at the nodes, round white flower heads and leaflets with a pale V mark; abundant in lawns and pastures.

species.name: Trifolium scabrum
species.tip: Low, stiff, hairy annual with small white or pinkish heads tucked into leaf axils. Fruiting calyces are rigid and curved. Grows on dry bare banks and coastal turf.

species.name: Trifolium squamosum
species.tip: Low annual clover with small pink heads at stem tips, lying on a pair of leaves. Calyces become spiky and star-like in fruit. Found on coastal grassland in the south.

species.name: Trifolium stellatum
species.tip: Hairy annual with pinkish-white heads, whose red-tinged spreading calyx teeth form a starry fruiting head. Naturalised since 1900s on shingle at Shoreham, Sussex.

species.name: Trifolium striatum
species.tip: Small pink clover on dry grassland with stalkless heads in the leaf axils and hairy, furrowed striped leaves, and short oval heads.

species.name: Trifolium strictum
species.tip: Small, slender, hairless clover with small pink heads on long stalks and narrow leaflets. Very rare, restricted to the Lizard peninsula, Cornwall, in short grassland.

species.name: Trifolium subterraneum
species.tip: Hairy, prostrate annual with few creamy-white flowers. After flowering, the head buries itself in the soil. Found on dry sandy turf, mainly in southern England.

species.name: Trifolium suffocatum
species.tip: Tiny prostrate annual forming tight, stalkless clusters of white flowers pressed to the ground. Rare, on bare sandy or gravelly coastal ground in the south and east.

species.name: Triglochin maritima
species.tip: Grass-like plant of saltmarsh with fleshy narrow leaves and tall spikes of small green flowers, fruit with six parts; coastal, versus Marsh Arrowgrass inland.

species.name: Triglochin palustris
species.tip: Grass-like plant of freshwater marshes and fens with slender flower spike and fruit splitting into three parts at the base; inland, unlike Sea Arrowgrass.

species.name: Trigonella foenum-graecum
species.tip: Upright, hairy annual with clover-like leaves and pale cream-yellow flowers singly or in pairs. Spice-scented; long beaked pods. Casual from birdseed or cultivation.

species.name: Trinia glauca
species.tip: Small, blue-green, hairless, dioecious plant with very finely cut leaves and tiny white umbels; very rare, on limestone in Devon, nowadays near Torquay and Plymouth.

species.name: Tripleurospermum inodorum
species.tip: Unscented, feathery leaves and white-rayed daisies with a domed yellow solid centre; common weed of arable land and waste ground.

species.name: Tripleurospermum maritimum
species.tip: Fleshy, spreading plant of shingle and sea cliffs with thick, finely divided leaves and large white daisies. Coastal; stems often sprawling.

species.name: Tripolium pannonicum
species.tip: Fleshy-leaved plant of saltmarshes with lilac-rayed yellow-centred daisies, occasionally rayless. Grows in muddy estuaries and creeks.

species.name: Trisetum flavescens
species.tip: Shining golden-yellow panicle on hay meadows; spikelets have a fine bent awn and sheaths and leaves are softly hairy; ligule short.

species.name: Tristagma uniflorum
species.tip: Low tuft of grey-green, onion-scented, grass-like leaves with solitary six-pointed pale blue stars; a common garden outcast on verges and tips.

species.name: Triteleia laxa
species.tip: Wiry stem topped by a loose umbel of violet-blue funnel flowers, with grassy leaves. Rare Californian bulb occasionally escaping from gardens.

species.name: Triticum aestivum
species.tip: Cultivated cereal with a stiff, thick, two-rowed ear; either awnless or awned varieties, with broader leaves and short ligule.

species.name: Triticum spelta
species.tip: Ancient wheat with a lax, brittle ear of awnless to short-awned spikelets in two rows; occasional relic of cultivation on arable edges and tips.

species.name: Trocdaris verticillata
species.tip: Slender plant with leaf segments cut into whorled, thread-like lobes giving a bottlebrush look, and white umbels; local in damp pastures in western Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Trollius europaeus
species.tip: Large globe-shaped yellow flowers of incurved petals; damp upland meadows and streamsides in the north.

species.name: Tropaeolum speciosum
species.tip: Climbing garden plant with leaves of six long lobes and vivid scarlet flowers, followed by blue berries. Scrambles through hedges and shrubs, mainly in the north and Scotland.

species.name: Tsuga heterophylla
species.tip: Conifer with drooping leading shoot, short flat needles of unequal lengths with white lines beneath, and tiny cones; shady forestry plantations.

species.name: Tuberaria guttata
species.tip: Yellow annual whose petals each bear a dark red spot at the base. Very rare, found on coastal rocks in Wales, Channel Islands and western Ireland.

species.name: Tuberaria lignosa
species.tip: Rosette-forming perennial with yellow flowers on a leafless stem, lacking the dark petal spots of spotted rock-rose. Very rare casual.

species.name: Tulipa saxatilis
species.tip: Small tulip with pale pink to lilac flowers and a yellow centre, with glossy shiny leaves; a rare escape, usually near gardens in Britain.

species.name: Tulipa sylvestris
species.tip: Slender tulip with a nodding bud that opens to a yellow star, outer petals greenish; naturalised in old orchards, parks and gardens.

species.name: Turritis glabra
species.tip: Tall greyish biennial with a basal rosette and upright spike; stem leaves clasp the stem with arrow-shaped bases and pale cream flowers give way to long, upright, flattened pods.

species.name: Tussilago farfara
species.tip: Yellow dandelion-like flowers on scaly stems appear in early spring before the large, hoof-shaped leaves, which are white-felted beneath. Disturbed clay soils.

species.name: Typha angustifolia
species.tip: Tall marginal plant with narrow, grey-green leaves and slender brown cigar-shaped catkin, with a clear gap between the upper male and lower female parts.

species.name: Typha latifolia
species.tip: Tall marginal plant of ponds with broad blue-green leaves and thick, dark brown sausage-shaped female flower spike touching the male part above it.

species.name: Typha minima
species.tip: Small bulrush with thin grass-like leaves and a short rounded brown female spike, separated from the male spike above. Rare naturalised plant of a few riversides.

species.name: Ugni molinae
species.tip: Small evergreen shrub with glossy oval leaves, pink-tinged white nodding bell flowers and later red aromatic berries; grown in mild gardens.

species.name: Ulex europaeus
species.tip: Dense spiny evergreen shrub with coconut-scented bright yellow flowers; spines are strong and furrowed; flowers on and off all year.

species.name: Ulex gallii
species.tip: Smaller, more compact gorse of western heaths and cliffs; flowers late summer to autumn, with short bracteoles and spines weaker than Gorse.

species.name: Ulex minor
species.tip: Low, spiny shrub of heaths, with small deep yellow flowers in late summer. Smaller than Gorse, with weaker spines and tiny bracteoles. Flowers when Western Gorse is also present.

species.name: Ulmus glabra
species.tip: Large tree with very large rough leaves with a short stalk, often lopsided and with overlapping base lobes, and no suckers; winged fruits with central seed.

species.name: Ulmus laevis
species.tip: Tree with asymmetric toothed leaves and flowers and fruits dangling on long stalks, with fringed winged fruit. Rare planted tree, differing from English Elm by those long stalks.

species.name: Ulmus minor
species.tip: Suckering elm with smaller smooth to slightly rough leaves, asymmetric at base, often forming hedgerows; highly variable and difficult to separate from relatives.

species.name: Umbilicus rupestris
species.tip: Succulent of walls, rocks and hedgebanks with round, dimpled, scalloped leaves like little saucers and a spike of drooping greenish-white tubular flowers.

species.name: Urtica dioica
species.tip: Familiar stinging perennial with opposite, heart-based toothed leaves and drooping green catkin-like flower clusters; the stinging hairs are on both stem and leaves.

species.name: Urtica membranacea
species.tip: Nettle relative with oval toothed leaves and tiny green flowers, lacking the strong stings of Common Nettle. Rare casual of Mediterranean origin; needs specialist confirmation.

species.name: Urtica urens
species.tip: Smaller, bushy annual nettle of cultivated ground with paired, deeply toothed oval leaves and short stalked flower clusters; stings strongly; shorter than Common Nettle.

species.name: Utricularia australis
species.tip: Floating aquatic with finely cut leaves bearing small bladders and yellow flowers on a stem above water. Similar to Greater Bladderwort; specialist check needed.

species.name: Utricularia bremii
species.tip: Floating aquatic with finely divided leaves and small yellow flowers; a close relative of other bladderworts. Extremely rare and needs specialist confirmation.

species.name: Utricularia intermedia
species.tip: Aquatic with two kinds of shoots: green ones with bristly forked leaves, and pale ones carrying bladders buried in peat. Pale yellow flowers; in bog pools.

species.name: Utricularia minor
species.tip: Small aquatic with fine bladder-bearing leaves and pale yellow flowers with a flattish lip. Rarely flowers; found in peaty pools and ditches.

species.name: Utricularia ochroleuca
species.tip: Aquatic with pale buried bladder shoots and pale yellow flowers, rarely produced. Very local in peaty pools in north-west Scotland and western Ireland.

species.name: Utricularia stygia
species.tip: Aquatic bladderwort with fine leaves and pale yellow flowers, rarely seen in bloom. Very local in Scotland and western Ireland; a specialist is needed to confirm.

species.name: Utricularia vulgaris
species.tip: Floating aquatic with feathery leaves bearing dark bladders and a spike of bright yellow flowers held above the water. Local in clean ditches and ponds.

species.name: Vaccinium corymbosum
species.tip: Tall deciduous shrub with oval leaves and small white urn flowers; large blue berries. Garden plant, rarely escaping, bigger than native Bilberry.

species.name: Vaccinium macrocarpon
species.tip: Creeping evergreen with oval leaves and pink flowers with back-curved petals; fruit large red berries. Garden plant naturalised on bogs, bigger than native Cranberry.

species.name: Vaccinium microcarpum
species.tip: Wiry creeping evergreen of peat bogs with tiny narrow leaves, whitish beneath, and pink flowers with swept-back petals. A specialist may be needed to separate from related cranberries.

species.name: Vaccinium myrtillus
species.tip: Small green angular twigs, bright green deciduous toothed leaves and solitary globular pinkish-green flowers; acid woods and moors with blue-black berries.

species.name: Vaccinium oxycoccos
species.tip: Wiry creeping stems with tiny oval leaves white underneath and pink flowers with swept-back petals; wet bogs and sphagnum lawns.

species.name: Vaccinium uliginosum
species.tip: Low deciduous shrub of moors with blue-grey oval leaves and round stems; small pink-white urns and bluish berries. Local in northern uplands.

species.name: Vaccinium vitis-idaea
species.tip: Evergreen leathery leaves dotted beneath with black glands and a nodding cluster of white-pink bells; upland moors and pinewoods, red berries.

species.name: Valeriana dioica
species.tip: Small, dioecious plant of wet meadows and fens with undivided basal leaves and pinnate stem leaves; clusters of tiny pale pink flowers, spreading by runners.

species.name: Valeriana officinalis
species.tip: Tall plant with pinnate leaves of many toothed leaflets and dense clusters of pale pink flowers; stout, hairy and grooved stem, and a distinctive smell; damp places.

species.name: Valeriana phu
species.tip: Tall perennial with creamy-white flower heads; lower leaves are plain, upper ones divided into leaflets. Often grown for gold foliage; rare garden outcast.

species.name: Valeriana pyrenaica
species.tip: Tall plant of shady damp places with heart-shaped, toothed leaves and rounded clusters of small pale pink flowers. Naturalised in woods and stream banks, mainly in western Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Valerianella carinata
species.tip: Small annual of arable fields and bare ground with tiny pale flowers in forked clusters; fruit is keeled, with a groove, which distinguishes it from Common Cornsalad.

species.name: Valerianella dentata
species.tip: Small forked annual cornfield weed with tiny pale lilac flowers and fruits that are narrow with an obvious tooth. Rare, mainly on calcareous arable land in southern England.

species.name: Valerianella eriocarpa
species.tip: Annual cornsalad with tiny pale lilac or white flowers and fruits covered with hairs, with a prominent calyx tooth. Rare arable weed on chalky soil in southern England.

species.name: Valerianella locusta
species.tip: Low forking annual with tiny pale blue flowers in clusters and spoon-shaped leaves; fruit flattened with a corky swelling on one side; dry banks, walls and arable.

species.name: Valerianella rimosa
species.tip: Cornfield annual with tiny pale pink flowers and fruits inflated, broadly egg-shaped and hollow. Rare arable weed on chalky soil, southern England.

species.name: Vallisneria spiralis
species.tip: Submerged plant with long, ribbon-like leaves. Female flowers float on a spiral stalk. Naturalised in warm-water areas such as canals and warm outflows.

species.name: Verbascum chaixii
species.tip: Branched, hairy mullein with nettle-like leaves, and yellow flowers with purple-haired stamens in slim spikes. Rare escape or introduction mostly in southern England.

species.name: Verbascum lychnitis
species.tip: Tall branched mullein with loosely felted grey leaves and flowers in pale yellow or white, with stamens bearing whitish hairs. Native on chalky, disturbed ground, mostly in the south and east.

species.name: Verbascum nigrum
species.tip: Slender mullein with a long unbranched spike of yellow flowers with violet hairy stamens; leaves green and not felted, lower ones heart-shaped at base.

species.name: Verbascum pulverulentum
species.tip: Branched mullein covered in dense white felt that rubs off, with yellow flowers in single clusters, unlike the unbranched Great Mullein. Eastern England and some southern sites.

species.name: Verbascum speciosum
species.tip: Tall candelabra mullein, with branched whitish woolly spikes and clusters of yellow flowers; leaves are broad and covered with star-shaped hairs. Garden plant that seldom escapes.

species.name: Verbascum thapsus
species.tip: Tall, grey-felted biennial with a stout spike and thick white woolly leaves forming a large rosette; pale yellow flat flowers of dry soils.

species.name: Verbascum virgatum
species.tip: Sticky-glandular mullein with slender usually unbranched spikes, yellow flowers in small clusters of one to five, and cut-toothed upper leaves. Rare in southwest England.

species.name: Verbena bonariensis
species.tip: Tall, wiry, branched plant with square stems, narrow rough toothed leaves and flat clusters of small purple flowers; garden escape, now on waste ground and verges.

species.name: Verbena officinalis
species.tip: Wiry plant with deeply lobed lower leaves and thin spikes of tiny pale lilac flowers; dry grassland, roadsides and waste ground.

species.name: Veronica agrestis
species.tip: Small sprawling annual of arable fields with pale blue flowers, the lowest petal white; individual flower stalks are shorter than the leaf, and the sepals are unequal. Comparable to Grey Field-speedwell.

species.name: Veronica alpina
species.tip: Mountain speedwell with a short terminal cluster of small dark blue flowers and oval leaves on mostly unbranched stems. Rare, on high Scottish mountains.

species.name: Veronica anagallis-aquatica
species.tip: Stout hairless water-edge speedwell with stalkless, clasping, pointed leaves and many pale blue-violet flower spikes. Compare Pink Water-speedwell with narrower leaves and pink flowers; Brooklime has stalked leaves.

species.name: Veronica arvensis
species.tip: Small, hairy annual with tiny blue flowers in leafy spikes; upper leaves are small and bract-like. Found on walls, paths and cultivated land; flowers are smaller than those of Germander Speedwell.

species.name: Veronica beccabunga
species.tip: Fleshy, shiny rounded leaves with short stalks and loose spikes of bright blue flowers from the leaf axils. Streams, ditches and wet muddy ground.

species.name: Veronica catenata
species.tip: Water-edge speedwell with narrower, pointed stalkless leaves than Brooklime and pale pink veined flowers in spikes. Compare Blue Water-speedwell, which has bluer flowers and broader leaves.

species.name: Veronica chamaedrys
species.tip: Bright blue flowers with a white eye, with two distinctive hairy lines on the stem. Common on grassy verges, hedgebanks and woodland edges, the commonest speedwell of banks.

species.name: Veronica crista-galli
species.tip: Mat-forming speedwell from south-east Europe with spikes of blue flowers and toothed leaves; not native. Rare garden relic, uncertain identity so check with a specialist.

species.name: Veronica filiformis
species.tip: Creeping, mat-forming plant with pale blue single flowers on long thin stalks, forming dense lawn patches; leaves small and kidney-shaped. Non-native, spreads in lawns and grassland.

species.name: Veronica fruticans
species.tip: Small tufted mountain speedwell with a few deep blue flowers with a red eye in short clusters, leaves oval and slightly leathery. Rare, on Scottish mountain rocks.

species.name: Veronica hederifolia
species.tip: Small annual with pale lilac-blue flowers and ivy-like leaves with a few large pointed lobes. Flowers early in the year in hedgebanks, gardens and arable fields.

species.name: Veronica longifolia
species.tip: Tall speedwell with long narrow toothed leaves and dense spikes of lilac-blue flowers. A garden plant, escaped on riverbanks and waste ground; much taller than native spiked species.

species.name: Veronica montana
species.tip: Woodland speedwell with oval, stalked, toothed leaves and pale lilac flowers on long thin stalks; the stem is hairy all round. Ancient woods and damp shady banks.

species.name: Veronica officinalis
species.tip: Mat-forming hairy plant with rounded leaves and dense spikes of pale lilac flowers. Heaths, dry grassland and woodland edges, on acid soil.

species.name: Veronica persica
species.tip: Large bright blue flowers, the lowest petal paler, on long stalks; leaves are hairy and strongly toothed. Very common weed of gardens and arable fields, flowering most of the year.

species.name: Veronica polita
species.tip: Annual weed with bright blue flowers that have a short corolla; leaves are greyish and hairy. Smaller than Common Field-speedwell, with sepals that are broad and overlapping.

species.name: Veronica praecox
species.tip: Small spring annual with glandular hairs, toothed oval leaves and single deep blue flowers in the leaf axils. Very rare, found on sandy arable ground in Breckland.

species.name: Veronica salicifolia
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with narrow smooth leaves and dense spikes of white or lilac-tinged flowers. Planted and naturalised near coasts in the south-west and Ireland; not like any herbaceous speedwell.

species.name: Veronica scutellata
species.tip: Slender creeping plant of marshy ground with narrow, lance-shaped leaves and few-flowered spikes of pale lilac-white flowers; seed capsules are notched. Bog margins and wet places.

species.name: Veronica serpyllifolia
species.tip: Creeping, rooting stems and small rounded smooth leaves; white or very pale blue flowers with darker veins in terminal spikes. Lawns, paths and heaths.

species.name: Veronica spicata
species.tip: Upright speedwell with long dense spikes of blue flowers and toothed oval leaves. Rare native of dry limestone and chalk turf in East Anglia and Wales; also garden forms.

species.name: Veronica triphyllos
species.tip: Small annual with deep blue flowers and leaves cut into finger-like lobes, on sandy arable land. Rare, mainly in East Anglia (Breckland).

species.name: Veronica verna
species.tip: Tiny, upright, glandular-hairy annual with lobed leaves and small blue flowers in leafy spikes. Very rare, on dry sandy ground in Breckland and a few other sites.

species.name: Viburnum lantana
species.tip: Shrub with leaves wrinkled and covered by greyish star-shaped down, flat white flower heads; chalk scrub and hedges, black berries.

species.name: Viburnum opulus
species.tip: Shrub with maple-like lobed leaves, flat flower heads with large sterile white flowers around the rim and red berries; damp woods and fens.

species.name: Viburnum tinus
species.tip: Evergreen shrub with oval dark glossy leaves and flat heads of pink buds opening white from winter into spring, then dark blue berries. Common in gardens, sometimes escapes.

species.name: Vicia bithynica
species.tip: Climbing vetch with pinnate leaves, two to three pairs of leaflets, and one to three purple and yellow flowers. Rare, on coastal slopes in south-west England and Wales.

species.name: Vicia cracca
species.tip: Climbing, one-sided spikes of many blue-violet flowers and pinnate leaves with branched tendrils; hedgerows and grassland.

species.name: Vicia faba
species.tip: Upright, square stem with no tendrils, large white flowers with black blotches and thick pods; a crop escape.

species.name: Vicia lathyroides
species.tip: Tiny, short, softly hairy annual with solitary small purple flowers. Pods black and hairy. Found on sandy ground, dunes and heaths.

species.name: Vicia lens
species.tip: Slender annual vetch with few small pale bluish-white flowers and short flat pods. Casual crop escape on tips and waste ground.

species.name: Vicia lutea
species.tip: Sprawling, hairless or hairy vetch with large pale yellow flowers, singly or in pairs, and large hairy pods. Rare, on coastal shingle and cliffs.

species.name: Vicia orobus
species.tip: Upright vetch with no tendrils and many leaflet pairs; flowers cream-white with purple veins. Found on western rocky woods and hill pastures.

species.name: Vicia pannonica
species.tip: Annual vetch with dull yellowish or brownish-purple flowers, one to three together, and hairy pods. Rare casual or escape from cultivation.

species.name: Vicia sativa
species.tip: Pink-purple flowers singly or in pairs at the leaf bases, with a black spot on the stipule; leaflets vary from narrow to oval.

species.name: Vicia sepium
species.tip: Branched tendrils and two to six dull purple flowers in short-stalked clusters; leaflets oval; hedges, woodland edges and rough grassland.

species.name: Vicia tenuifolia
species.tip: Tall, climbing vetch with long spikes of violet-blue flowers on lengthy stalks, and narrow leaflets. Found on grassy banks, mostly in England.

species.name: Vicia villosa
species.tip: Tall climbing vetch with dense one-sided spikes of violet and whitish flowers, hairy stems and wide spreading calyx. Often sown, and persisting on field edges.

species.name: Vinca difformis
species.tip: Evergreen trailing plant with pale blue flowers having wide, overlapping petals, and shiny, hairless oval leaves; a garden escape in hedgerows in south-west Britain.

species.name: Vinca major
species.tip: Large trailing evergreen with big blue flowers and heart-shaped, hairy-edged leaves; bigger than Lesser Periwinkle with sepals fringed, in hedges and banks.

species.name: Vinca minor
species.tip: Trailing evergreen with smaller glossy narrow oval leaves and blue flowers, calyx hairless; woodland and hedge banks, smaller than Greater Periwinkle.

species.name: Viola arvensis
species.tip: Small cream-yellow flowers shorter than the sepals, with a little purple at times; arable fields and disturbed ground, unlike larger Wild Pansy.

species.name: Viola canina
species.tip: Blue flowers with pale spur, narrow oval leaves and no basal rosette; heaths and dry grassland, slender and often less leafy than other dog-violets.

species.name: Viola cornuta
species.tip: Garden perennial with long-spurred, violet-blue flowers on a creeping rootstock, with a spur longer than the petals. Occasionally naturalised on banks and walls.

species.name: Viola hirta
species.tip: Scentless violet with distinctly hairy stalks and leaves, narrow leaf base lobes and pale violet flowers; calcareous grassland and scrub.

species.name: Viola kitaibeliana
species.tip: Tiny annual with narrow pale cream flowers often tinged with violet, shorter than the leafy sepals. Rare on dunes in Scilly and the Channel Islands.

species.name: Viola lactea
species.tip: Violet with pale bluish-white flowers with a curved greenish spur, and narrow, triangular leaves. Rare on heaths, mostly in the south-west of England and Ireland.

species.name: Viola lutea
species.tip: Upland grassland pansy with yellow, violet or bicoloured flowers larger than Wild Pansy, with leaves held on slender stems from creeping stolons. Hills of northern England, Wales and Scotland.

species.name: Viola odorata
species.tip: Fragrant violet with runners, deep violet or white flowers and rounded heart-shaped leaves; hedgebanks and woodland edges, early spring.

species.name: Viola palustris
species.tip: Pale lilac flowers with darker veins, kidney-shaped hairless leaves and creeping stems; wet bogs and marshes.

species.name: Viola reichenbachiana
species.tip: Violet with dark, narrow, straight spur and narrow petals that do not overlap; no leaf rosette in flower; woods and hedgebanks.

species.name: Viola riviniana
species.tip: Common violet with pale, thick, notched spur and overlapping bluer petals; rosette of heart-shaped leaves; woods, hedges and grassland.

species.name: Viola rupestris
species.tip: Small, downy violet with rounded heart-shaped leaves and blue-violet flowers with a short spur, close to Common Dog-violet. Only on limestone turf in upper Teesdale.

species.name: Viola stagnina
species.tip: Pale blue-white violet with a violet-tinged spur and long narrow heart-based leaves, hairless. Wet fens and lake shores in East Anglia and Ireland; very rare.

species.name: Viola tricolor
species.tip: Large flowers of purple, yellow or mixed colour, petals longer than sepals; deeply lobed leafy stipules; grassland and dunes.

species.name: Viscum album
species.tip: Evergreen parasitic shrub forming round balls on tree branches, with paired yellow-green oval leaves and white berries; on apple, lime and poplar.

species.name: Vitis vinifera
species.tip: Tendril-bearing climber with large lobed leaves and dense clusters of small green flowers, then grapes. Escapes locally, mostly in the south of England.

species.name: Vulpia bromoides
species.tip: Small annual with a short, stiff, curved spike-like raceme, spikelets with a long awn; upper sheath not enclosing the panicle base.

species.name: Vulpia ciliata
species.tip: Annual fescue with very long awns and a stiff curved panicle held in one side; rare on sandy ground near the coast in southern England.

species.name: Vulpia fasciculata
species.tip: Annual fescue with a dense, one-sided spike-like panicle and long awns, with the upper sheath enclosing the base; local on sand dunes around the coasts.

species.name: Vulpia myuros
species.tip: Annual of dry waste ground with a long, thin, curved head whose lower part is often hidden in the upper leaf sheath; spikelets long-awned.

species.name: Vulpia unilateralis
species.tip: Tiny annual fescue with an unbranched, one-sided stiff spike, resembling Mat-grass; very rare on chalk and coastal turf in southern England.

species.name: Wahlenbergia hederacea
species.tip: Delicate creeping plant of damp acid ground with ivy-shaped, pointed-lobed leaves and single pale blue bells on hair-thin stalks. Native of western and southern Britain and Ireland.

species.name: Watsonia borbonica
species.tip: Tall spikes of tubular pinkish-orange flowers over stiff, sword-shaped leaves. Garden plant of mild areas, rarely escaping.

species.name: Wolffia arrhiza
species.tip: Microscopic floating green fronds like grains of meal, and no roots at all; a rare, introduced plant of ponds and canals, mostly in the south-east.

species.name: Woodsia alpina
species.tip: Very small tufted fern of mountain rock crevices with narrow, hairy, divided fronds that curl at the edges. Extremely rare, in a few Scottish and Welsh upland sites.

species.name: Woodsia ilvensis
species.tip: Small tufted fern with narrow, once-divided fronds with oblong, rusty-hairy leaflets, growing in cliff crevices. Extremely rare in a few Scottish and Welsh upland sites.

species.name: Woodwardia radicans
species.tip: Large evergreen fern with leathery, arching, twice-divided fronds producing small buds near the tips. Garden plant, naturalised on a few wooded banks in the south-west.

species.name: Yushania anceps
species.tip: Tall clump-forming bamboo with thin canes arching out into a fountain shape; planted in gardens, but flowering is not recorded in the wild.

species.name: Zannichellia obtusifolia
species.tip: Slender submerged plant with thread-like opposite leaves and tiny stalkless flowers, resembling Horned Pondweed. Brackish, rarely recorded; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

species.name: Zannichellia palustris
species.tip: Thread-like submerged plant with opposite, very narrow grass-like leaves and tiny flowers in the leaf axils; the curved, beaked fruits in clusters distinguish it.

species.name: Zantedeschia aethiopica
species.tip: Large garden lily with glossy arrow-shaped leaves and a white funnel-like spathe around a yellow spike; naturalised in ditches and damp ground in the south-west.

species.name: Zizania latifolia
species.tip: Tall aquatic grass with large drooping panicle, male spikelets awnless and female ones awned; a rare plant of pond edges and rivers, mostly in cultivation.

species.name: Zostera marina
species.tip: Marine plant with long ribbon-like leaves with three to seven veins, rooted in sand or mud below low tide, and spikes hidden in the sheath. Larger than Dwarf Eelgrass.

species.name: Zostera noltei
species.tip: Small marine plant of muddy shores with narrow thread-like leaves with a notched tip and one vein, and rooted in intertidal mud. Much slimmer than Eelgrass.

species.name: Taraxacum officinale agg.
species.tip: The familiar dandelion: a single yellow head on a hollow leafless stalk above a rosette of toothed leaves, milky sap, then a round seed clock. Hundreds of microspecies, which need a specialist.
